News.title: Afghan migrants raped & assaulted autistic girl, 14, in horror toilet attack on busy commuter train, court hears
News.content:
Next

TWO Afghan migrants raped and sexually assaulted an autistic 14-year-old girl on a packed train, with one allegedly abusing her in the toilet, a court heard.

Baryalai Rahimi, 25, and Mirebadurahman Sadat, 29, are said to have targeted the runaway teen after following her onto a London-bound train at a rural station in Kent.

The pair are accused of taking turns to abuse the girl as dozens of unsuspecting passengers travelled on the Southeastern service to London Bridge on February 5.

Jurors at Inner London Crown Court heard the men told the teenager: “We share everything, girls, drinks, everything”.





Footage played to the court shows the girl sitting on Rahimi’s lap as he appears to touch her chest.

A ticket inspector then walks through the carriage, before Rahimi allegedly continues to hug and kiss the youngster.

He is then seen leading her towards the toilet, brushing past passengers who had just boarded the busy mid-afternoon service.

Prosecutors allege Rahimi raped the girl twice inside the cubicle.

The teen later told officers: “I was scared of him, he was in control of me.”

CCTV footage shows the pair leaving the toilets separately minutes later before sitting just two rows behind an unsuspecting commuter.

Further intimate touching then appears to take place.

Prosecutor Richard Witcombe told jurors Rahimi and Sadat “each appear to have an object in their hand” as they seemingly communicate over the phone.



Sadat is seen sitting in a two-seater as Rahimi gets up and walks towards the toilet.

The prosecutor said Rahimi then entered the cubicle, followed by the girl.

Jurors heard this was when a third alleged rape took place.

The teenager later told police: “He done front sex with me.”

DNA matching Rahimi was subsequently found on the floor of the train toilet and in the girl’s underwear.



After leaving the cubicle separately, the men appear to exchange a few words before swapping seats.

Sadat then sits alongside the girl, who is positioned by the window.

Mr Witcombe said the footage appeared “almost as if Mr Rahimi was handing over the girl to Mr Sadat”.

At one stage, the teenager enters the toilet alone before Sadat follows her and tries unsuccessfully to open the door.

Later footage shows the two men following the much shorter girl off the train at London Bridge.



Sadat then boards another packed commuter service with her, heading towards Peterborough shortly after 4pm.

The girl had been reported missing earlier that day after running away from home.

Cops eventually found her at Peterborough Station shortly before 11pm and took her home.

Rahimi, of Southall, west London, denies three counts of rape, two of sexual assault, one of assault by penetration and six alternative counts of sexual activity with a child.

Sadat, of Cricklewood, north-west London, denies two counts of assault by penetration, two counts of causing a person to engage in sexual activity without consent and four alternative counts of sexual activity with a child.

The pair deny a total of 20 charges.

The trial is continuing and is expected to last three weeks.

News.title: Shock twist as tail of doomed Learjet are recovered four miles from site of fatal crash that killed nine people
News.content:
Next

THE tail of the doomed Learjet plane that nosedived at over 300mph and crashed in a residential area was recovered nearly 4 miles from the impact site.

The National Transportation Safety Board revealed the grim finding two days after the $2million private aircraft crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday, leaving a giant crater.



Days after the wreckage that displaced hundreds of residents, pieces of debris from the Learjet 60 have been recovered miles away from the original crash site.

NTSB member Tom Chapman said that early evidence suggested the plane was breaking apart before it smashed and erupted into a fireball on a busy roadway in Greenacres.



On Tuesday, Chapman said investigators located the plane’s tail elevator about 1.3 to 3.8 miles away from the crater site.

Chapman said the tail elevator was located in three pieces.

Read more in The U.S. Sun NO ESCAPE Minute-by-minute timeline of doomed jet's final moments before 9 killed in crash

He again urged residents who come across pieces of the Learjet plane to not touch or move the debris and instead call NTSB or local authorities.

The NTSB is investigating the incident and what caused the crash.

The Learjet 60 plane was en route to the Bahamas when a mayday call came from co-pilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, who told air traffic control that the aircraft was descending rapidly after experiencing ice and moderate turbulence.

The horrific audio recorded the Learjet crew’s final moments as they desperately attempted to regain control of the aircraft.



Filgueiras, 20, is heard screaming, “We are in an overspeed condition, descending 20,000ft per minute.”

As the crew struggled to regain control of the plane, Filgueiras continued to plead for help, “We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday – we’re descending 10,000ft per minute.

“We’re going to crash into the ground. We are descending 2,000ft and we are banking 60 degrees.”

As Filgueiras desperately pleads for help, captain Jeff Gregory, 55, is heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the background.

“Holy f**k we’re out of time,” Filgueiras said before the audio from the Learjet 60 went silent.



The Learjet 60 disintegrated on impact, killing all seven passengers and both pilots on board.

The passengers were identified as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, his wife Helen Sharp, 40, and their two children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2.

The family was traveling with two close friends, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and their nanny, Antia Maria Apellido Cetina.



Limerick Chapel, the church in Limerick, Pennsylvania, where captain Gregory grew up, sent out an email about his death, saying that he “went home to be with the Lord when the plane he was flying crashed.”

David Peters, Gregory’s former neighbor, mourned his old friend to The U.S. Sun, remembering him as “very diligent and dependable.”

Peters said Gregory had wanted to become a pilot from a young age and recalled that he “loved wearing his leather bomber jacket.”

“I know he worked hard to become a pilot and it was something he truly loved and poured his life and heart into,” Peters said.

Gregory is survived by his wife Cheryl, 53, and their children.



The captain’s young co-pilot was a stellar aviator who earned her wings as a 17-year-old senior in West Boca Raton High School in October 2023.

Filgueiras, who grew up in Palm Beach County, was featured in a news segment on CBS affiliate WPEC where she revealed she had earned private pilot’s certificate before getting her driver’s license.

“I definitely do brag because people say, ‘Oh, you can’t drive,’ and I’m like, ‘yeah, but I can fly,’” she said at the time.

“I like being different than everyone, so to me, I think it’s cool that like it’s not really an opportunity, I just didn’t do it, and this is how it ended up.

“But I think it’s cool. Some people think that it’s weird that I can fly planes, but I can’t drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it’s funny.”



Filgueiras started Ground School in 2020 during her sophomore year, but gained firsthand aviation experience from her father, who picked up recreational flying in 2018.

The young pilot explained that she had clocked air miles daily since she entered Ground School, and built 88 hours of flight time on top of passing the knowledge test students need to earn their private pilot’s license.

The Palm Beach County school district paid for Filgueiras to get her license through their Aviation Academy.

At the time of her death, Filgueiras had logged 1,300 hours of flight experience, her stepfather Thiago Corteleti told the New York Post.

Corteleti said his stepdaughter had texted her boyfriend 10 minutes before the crash saying the crew was experiencing turbulence and ice.



Camila Corteleti, Filgueiras mother, said her daughter was passionate about flying since childhood, but feared her dream would eventually take her away from her.

“I wanted her to live her dream, but I knew that her dream was going to be the thing that would take her away from me,” Camila told the New York Post.

News.title: Ketchup and mayo sachets face ban in pubs and restaurants as Labour moves to align with EU rules
News.content:
Next

KETCHUP, mayonnaise and vinegar sachets could be banned from cafes and restaurants as Andy Burnham tries to align the UK with the European Union.

The EU has outlawed single-use plastic packaging for condiments in the catering sector on environmental grounds from January 1, 2030.



The regulations will forbid European restaurants and hotels from offering ketchup and mayonnaise sachets to dine-in customers from January 2030, to cut down on “unnecessary” waste.

The packets are also going to be banned in Northern Ireland under post-Brexit arrangements that require the country to follow some EU rules.



Ministers have now signalled plans to extend the ban to England, Scotland and Wales to create “alignment” across the UK after Andy Burnham’s EU reset.

Environment minister Emma Hardy said the government would launch a consulation “UK alignment” with the new EU roles on packaging waste.



In response to a Tory question, environment minister Emma Hardy confirmed: “A consultation regarding UK alignment is being planned.”

Earlier in the week, Labour’s Brexit row deepened as two Cabinet ministers distanced themselves from Andy Burnham’s aim to rejoin the EU.

Chancellor John Healey and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds both failed to back the PM’s wish to return to Brussels within his lifetime.

Mr Reynolds suggested he would be uncomfortable returning to a Europe swept by right-wing populism.



Asked if he shared the PM’s dream, he told The Sun: “I genuinely can’t answer that, because I don’t know what the future of the EU is — because some of the very strong political currents in member states.

“For me, it’s an approach to issues. What is their approach to how they regulate technology, AI? How dynamic will the economy be?”

Meanwhile, the Chancellor seemed just as reluctant. On the UK joining the EU in his lifetime, he told Channel 4: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”

News.title: Taxpayers burdened with bill for billions because of Burnham’s ‘catastrophic’ capitulation on benefits, Brexit & borders
News.content:
Next

TAXPAYERS are on the hook for billions of pounds because of PM Andy Burnham’s capitulations on benefits, Brexit, borders and bungs for ex-colonies.

A flurry of Labour climbdowns in recent days come with mega price tags that will add to a surging debt pile, ­which economists yesterday branded “catastrophic”.



The U-turn on migration reforms alone could cost up to £10billion after Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood spared hundreds of ­thousands of careworkers from tougher curbs.

She yesterday admitted it would increase the already blistering welfare bill by making them eligible for benefits much quicker.



She was also slammed for sneakily dropping proposals to raise the bar on migrants who can claim social security.

Ms Mahmood axed plans to save money by restricting welfare to British citizens, instead letting immigrants access funds after gaining residency.



Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp ­yesterday said: “Hard-working ­taxpayers toil all day to make ends meet and Labour wants to take their hard-earned cash to fund migrant benefits.”

While most migrants will now have to wait ten years instead of five to settle here ­permanently, nearly 300,000 foreign care ­workers and their families could still qualify after five.

That is despite ­original plans to force lower-skilled migrants to wait up to 15 years before securing settlement rights.

Ms Mahmood conceded the care worker exemption would have an “impact” on the welfare bill — but could not say how much money would now be lost from the projected savings.



Her own department ­previously warned that care workers and their adult dependents expected to settle here by 2030 could cost taxpayers a whopping £10billion over their lifetimes.

Following the U-turn, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch fumed: “Britain can’t afford the cost of Burnham. His retreats on borders, benefits and Brexit are landing taxpayers with an enormous bill.

“Labour are feeding their welfare addiction, whilst businesses are being hammered by taxes and our armed forces desperately need funding.

“We can’t afford it any more.



“He’s running up the bill to keep his own party happy and expecting the British taxpayer to pick up the tab.”

Mr Burnham also risks slapping Britain with a massive bill as part of his bid to get closer to the EU.

This reportedly involves caving to Brussels’ demands to subsidise EU ­students at British universities.

Slashing tuition fees for students from the continent could sting taxpayers for £450million a year.



The PM hopes to use the EU-UK summit on November 20 as a launchpad to forge much closer ties with the bloc Britain voted to leave in 2016.

He has touted a return to freedom of movement and even opened the door to rejoining completely in a fresh referendum.

But as part of the talks, Brussels is demanding Mr Burnham scraps plans to deport EU criminals as soon as they are sentenced to jail in the UK.

Thousands of EU citizens are currently behind bars in Britain, at a rough cost of around £60,000 each per year.



No 10 yesterday did not deny they could agree to the EU’s demands, although stressed it was up for negotiation.

Mr Burnham has also been slammed for handing £40million to Caribbean projects amid the slavery apology row.

The PM — gifted a South Sydney Rabbitohs cap by Aussie counterpart and fellow rugby league fan Anthony Albanese — announced the cash would cover infrastructure improvements over the next three years.

Mr Burnham is open to offering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade.



But Reform UK MP Suella Braverman said: “This is a disgraceful betrayal of the British people that once again shows Labour don’t live in the real world or care about hard-working British people.

“We need to scrap foreign aid and support our own. How about this money goes to British young people who are out of work and to funding our armed forces and our brave veterans instead?”

Britain is committed to £350million for major projects in the Caribbean over ten years.

Taxpayers’ cash is being spent on climate-resilient economic infrastructure in countries such as Jamaica, Guyana, Belize and Grenada.

Meanwhile, Britain’s spiralling debt interest bill was blamed for a “really catastrophic” squeeze on living standards by Resolution Foundation boss Ruth Curtice.



Taxpayers are being forced to shoulder almost all of the burden of servicing the nation’s £3trillion debt, her think-tank warned.

The annual interest bill is set to hit a staggering £155billion by 2027-28 — more than the entire education budget.

Ms Curtice told MPs the soaring costs had made Britain “much, much poorer as a country”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She added: “The choice the Government faces is the extent to which public services or households absorb that cost.

“The reason we’ve seen these grim living-standards forecasts through the 2020s is because they have chosen to ask households to bear almost all of that burden.”

News.title: Burnham ducks any hard decisions and spends your money like water – Britain cannot afford to have him in charge
News.content:
Handout Andy







Next

BRITAIN cannot afford to have Andy Burnham in charge.

It’s only Wednesday and already this week our unelected Prime Minister has burned through billions of pounds of YOUR cash.



The immigration climbdown he’s forced on the Home Secretary to appease the unions and Labour back-benchers could cost up to £10billion.

Humiliated Shabana Mahmood won’t say exactly how much exempting almost 300,000 care workers and their dependants from new settlement rules will cost — but it will be eye-watering.



And that’s before we see the bill for allowing migrants to claim handouts WITHOUT first having obtained British citizenship.

The PM plans to blow another £450million subsidising UK university places for EU students as a sweetener to Brussels, as he begins to dismantle Brexit without any mandate to do so.

He’s so desperate for a “reset” that he could also shelve plans to deport foreign criminals back to Europe immediately — despite it costing a fortune to keep them in our overcrowded prisons.

He’s working, too, on using British taxpayers’ cash to fund development projects — like roads, airports and nice new green energy facilities — across the EU’s poorer member states.

Cash-starved poorer regions of this country will just have to wait.

Then there’s the foreign aid bungs he’s prepared to give to Commonwealth countries — along with an official apology — to keep them on side as they demand slavery reparations.



That’ll be another £40million for you to find, just for starters.

And all of this before we get to the cost of what he ISN’T doing. Namely, sorting out the ballooning benefits bill, which is due to cost £430BILLION a year by 2031 — devouring the funds needed to sort out our nation’s threadbare defences.

Times are tough and we need a serious politician at the helm.

What we’ve got is a TikTok-loving PM so desperate to be liked that he ducks any hard decisions and spends your money like water. All in order to make all the wrong people like him.

Justice served

MENTAL health problems are a serious issue — but they should never be used as an “automatic veto” to stop the media reporting claims of wrongdoing which are overwhelmingly in the public interest.



Such a gagging order could open the gates for every wealthy, corrupt or powerful person to buy anonymity by claiming mental distress, real or not.

The High Court decision to deny a well-known celebrity an injunction against reporting multiple accusations of exploitative sexual behaviour was a victory for open justice, a free Press and for the right of the alleged victims of his behaviour to tell THEIR story.

News.title: Reform vows to axe DEI in Army Cadets as it claims volunteers face pressure to push Left-wing views on young people
News.content:
MARCHING ORDERS Reform vows to axe DEI in Army Cadets as it claims volunteers face pressure to push Left-wing views on young people







Next

REFORM has vowed to axe DEI in the cadets after claiming volunteers face pressure to push Left-wing views on young people.

Army cadets openly support “race-based” discrimination from the recruitment process, the party claimed.



The cadets’ website says recruiters should seek young people from all backgrounds, especially groups under-represented in the organisation.

Reform leader Nigel Farage blamed Labour for allowing DEI to rip through the organisation while Whitehall continues to “indoctrinate” young people.



Mr Farage told The Sun: “As a former cadet myself, I know the crucial role they play. Instead of supporting them, Labour have slashed their funding and allowed DEI to run rampant.

“Reform UK will ensure that meritocracy is restored to the army cadets as well as the armed forces and stop pen-pushing civil servants from indoctrinating young people with DEI.”



Reform claimed MoD personnel are breaching their vital duty of care and abusing their positions to indoctrinate young people with left-wing dogma.

Labour slashed cadet force funding in real terms by 50 per cent in 2024-25 compared with figures between 2019-2020, according to Reform.

It also axed funding for school staff teachers which funds adult instructors for the cadets.

More than 137,000 young people in 2025 were part of around 3,500 cadet units across the UK, supported by 28,000 adult volunteers.



Reform has said every town will have at least one branch of the cadet forces open.

Plans will be funded by reversing cuts made by Labour which were £49million a year, the party claims.

Reform will offer every state secondary school the chance to have a Combined Cadet Force if they want one.

An MoD spokesperson said: “The Cadet Forces are a non-political organisation and are open to cadets from all backgrounds regardless of race, ethnicity, religion, gender or socioeconomic status. It brings together young people from all backgrounds and giving them the confidence, skills and sense of purpose that benefit their communities and our country as a whole.”

“This government has confirmed additional funding to modernise the organisation and set the conditions for sustainable growth now and into the next parliamentary period”.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch gives Conservatives biggest polling boost since election as party moves within touching distance of Labour
News.content:
Next

KEMI Badenoch has given the Conservatives their biggest polling boost since the General Election — putting them within touching distance of Labour.

Support for the Tories has jumped to 24 per cent.



Labour slipped one point to 26 per cent while Reform UK trailed in third place on 21 per cent.

The YouGov poll, the first since last week’s Budget, suggests Labour’s surge since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister in July could be starting to level off.



The Tories have now been ahead of Reform for three consecutive weeks after trailing for months.

A Tory source said: “The choice at the next election is becoming increasingly clear — a Conservative Party prepared to take the tough decisions to get Britain working again, or a Labour Party too weak to stand up to its own left-wing backbenchers.



“While Conservatives have a plan to get welfare spending under control and fund our defence, Labour will keep putting up taxes rather than make the difficult decisions.”

The Tories’ latest poll rating is a huge improvement on the 17 to 19 per cent support they were on for much of this year.

But it only puts them back at roughly the same level as their disastrous 2024 election result under Rishi Sunak when they secured 23.7 per cent of the vote.

The figures are still a boost for Tory leader Mrs Badenoch following last month’s party conference.



There are signs she is winning back voters who had jumped ship.

Some 67 per cent of those who voted Tory at the last election say they would do so again, while 23 per cent now back Reform — down from 28 per cent in April.

The Conservatives are also attracting younger voters, with 17 per cent of those aged 18 to 24 backing the party.

This is more than Reform and the Lib Dems combined among that age group, although Labour is still in front on 29 per cent.

The poll for The Times and Sky News has the Lib Dems unchanged nationally on 11 per cent and the Greens remaining on ten per cent.

News.title: A simple guide to the midterms
News.content:
Americans will choose members of Congress, which is made up of two parts - the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Elections take place every two years, and when they happen in the middle of the president's four-year term of office, they are called the midterms.

A key task of Congress is to create and pass federal laws - laws that apply nationwide.

The outcome of the midterms will decide which political party - Trump's Republicans or opposition Democrats - controls Congress and how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.

The results are also seen as a measure of how happy people in the US are with the president's performance so far.

News.title: When will we know the results?
News.content:
Congress is made up of two parts - the lower chamber, the House of Representatives and the upper chamber, the Senate.

To win a majority in the House, a party needs 218 seats. In the Senate, a party needs 51 seats for an outright majority. But if the upper chamber is split 50-50, the vice-president has a tie-breaking vote, which gives their party control of it.

First results will start to come in after 18:00 EST (23:00 GMT). They won't tell us much about the overall result because these races are in places considered safe bets for Republicans (Kentucky and Indiana) or Democrats (Vermont).

Throughout the night, BBC analysts will focus on the competitive races which will give an indication of how well things are going for Trump.

There are several tight Senate contests in the Eastern Time zone - like Ohio, where polls close at 19:30 EST (00:30 GMT) and Maine, where they shut at 20:00 EST (01:00 GMT). These could provide early indications of the electorate's mood.

Some key contests might start to be "called" by US media outlets. They use models to project which way a state has voted, even before the full vote count has been completed.

This happens when they believe a party or a candidate has gained a lead that cannot be beaten. But in some closely-fought states, outlets could take a long time to make their projections.

The overall timing of the result will depend on how tight the races are and which races end up being decisive.

News.title: How the US midterm results could unfold - as millions of Americans head to the polls
News.content:
After months of campaigning and billions of dollars spent on the US midterms, election day is finally here.

According to the latest public opinion surveys, Democrats appear to have the upper hand - but polls haven't always been reliable, and this year could have its own share of surprising results.

In broad strokes, however, there are three possible outcomes after Americans have their say.

Here's a look at what they could be, what the early signs might be as results come in (which you can follow later on our results page) and what it could mean for the country.

News.title: The key US Senate races to watch
News.content:
Millions of Americans are deciding the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.

All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber.

A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration.

Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.

For much of the race, independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external has characterised seven Senate races as toss-ups.

Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.

News.title: The elections that could define Trump's closing chapter
News.content:
Winning the Senate on Tuesday is likely to be a much harder task for Democrats.

Thirty-five seats are up for election, and they will need a net gain of four to win control. If they lose in Michigan - a battleground seat they already hold - they will need a net gain of five seats to win it.

Most of the battleground races are close and several sit within the margin of error for pollsters. The crucial Senate races to watch are in Michigan, Texas, Ohio, Iowa, Maine, Alaska and North Carolina.

This is, in reality, where these midterm elections will be won and lost.

There is, as always with American elections, an important caveat around the polls. They have historically overestimated the Democratic Party and underestimated President Trump, who appears convinced that he can once again defy them.

But if the polls are close to correct about the suggested surge of support for Democrats, then he could be looking at painful defeats in states that have been reliable Republican strongholds for decades.

How Trump may respond to any stinging losses is an open question. He has repeatedly questioned the integrity and security of these elections, and the possibility that he does so again as votes are still being counted or when results are declared is a very real one.

These elections, however, represent a hugely significant moment for Americans, many of whom want to see real change over the next two years.

For both parties, they will serve as the final electoral test before a 2028 presidential election that will determine what a post-Trump politics looks and feels like. And for the president himself, they are an opportunity for voters to cast judgement on how he and his party are performing.

As Trump looks to shape his legacy in the next two years, the question is whether a change in control of Congress, which he has largely bypassed, would really curb his presidency at all.

News.title: King calls slave trade a 'shameful chapter' during Commonwealth address
News.content:
King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.

He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.

There have been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also at the summit, has said that he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations.

While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.

He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."

King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.

"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures â the good they did as well as the wrongs."

The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.

The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.

The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.

Speaking on Tuesday, Burnham said his government was bringing a new approach, aiming to "revitalise the Commonwealth", despite turning down demands for reparations.

"I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," he said.

"But it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they've got, green finance.

"That's what we've done under all governments and in my view we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth."

The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.

On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".

In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

News.title: Celebrity loses injunction bid but will stay anonymous pending appeal
News.content:
The case raises highly unusual legal issues concerning whether a court should stop publication when an individual claims that a media investigation would lead to them inflicting harm on themselves.

The celebrity first asked the court in the summer to stop the publication of the investigation after journalists contacted him with allegations about this sexual activities with a large number of young women.

ITN and the Guardian said their investigation had uncovered how the celebrity had allegedly abused his "power and status".

During last week's application for a permanent injunction, Mansoori said making the allegations public would have a "potentially fatal impact".

The barrister told the court that the man had tried to kill himself after he had been contacted by the media organisations and was later detained in hospital for his own protection - but later absconded and tried a second time to end his life.

Those incidents of self-harm had not been because of the allegations themselves but the result of "long-term trauma and the fear of trial by media", she argued.

"The only reason [suicide attempts] would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life," she said.

Lawyers for the media groups argued that there was a strong public interest in allowing their investigation to be publicised because of the serious nature of the allegations.

In his judgment, Nicklin wrote: "The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the conduct of a prominent person and the alleged use of status, influence and access in dealings with women and girls.

"The subject matter includes alleged abuse of power, sexual misconduct and inappropriate conduct towards younger or vulnerable persons.

"Those are matters capable of making a significant contribution to public debate."

The celebrity argued that publishing the allegations would breach his protections under the European Convention on Human Rights, including articles that guarantee the right to life and protection from inhuman or degrading treatment.

However, the judge rejected the claim that publication would violate the man's right to life, writing: "No prior case establishes that the Court's knowledge of a suicide risk, together with its power to prohibit the event expected to increase that risk, is by itself enough to require the Court to act."

The judge accepted that publishing would cause the man "acute and potentially prolonged mental suffering" â but said "established law did not impose a positive obligation upon the Court to prevent that suffering by restraining publication".

The man also cited the right to private and family life.

While the judge acknowledged that publication "would interfere exceptionally seriously with the Claimant's private and family life", he also rejected that claim, saying a permanent injunction "would have been an exceptionally serious restriction upon freedom of expression".

The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

News.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor called to give evidence in fraud trial in December
News.content:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons compelling him to give evidence in a fraud trial in the High Court on or around 15 December, the BBC understands

The witness summons will see him giving evidence and taking questions, in a case in which a wealthy woman alleges she was cheated by her former financial adviser.

Mountbatten-Windsor is not accused of wrongdoing, but he could face difficult questions about his financial arrangements as it is said that he was in receipt of some of the disputed payments, including a transfer to him of Â£750,000.

His court appearance will be the first public questioning Mountbatten-Windsor has faced since his BBC Newsnight interview in 2019.

It is also believed that Mountbatten-Windsor is the first royal since the 19th Century to be sent such a witness summons.

Such an unusual royal moment is likely to receive widespread media coverage - not least for the opportunity to hear the former Duke of York's first public comments since being stripped of his titles.

Last month, a judge gave permission for Mountbatten-Windsor to be called as a witness.

The summons was issued this week, with the case set to begin from mid-November and with Mountbatten-Windsor to appear as a witness around the 15 December, which is usually in person, but could be on video.

There have been many questions in recent years about Mountbatten-Windsor's personal finances - and challenges about a lack of transparency - and this case promises to give a rare opportunity to hear his own explanations about his financial dealings.

The case will hear allegations made by Nebahat Isbilen, an elderly Turkish woman, who says her former adviser Selman Turk misled her and used her wealth to his own advantage.

Turk has strongly denied dishonesty.

Mountbatten-Windsor will be asked to give evidence related to disputed questions about the handling of Isbilen's money.

According to court documents, Isbilen claimed she was misled by Turk into paying Â£750,000 to Mountbatten-Windsor, believing it was for help with a passport.

Turk has denied the allegation and says this payment was a gift made on Isbilen's own initiative to create goodwill with the then duke and had nothing to do with a passport.

The case covers payments made at the very end of his time as a working royal.

The transfer of money came the day after Mountbatten-Windsor recorded his BBC Newsnight interview, which was then broadcast the following night, and was soon followed by the then Duke of York stepping down from royal duties.

In 2021, Isbilen's lawyers contacted the then Prince Andrew and the money had been paid back, but the forthcoming court case will consider claims about Turk's behaviour, with Mountbatten-Windsor set to be a significant witness.

Court documents show there will be questions about another significant sum of money paid from Isbilen's account - around Â£768,000 in January 2020.

Turk has claimed it was a loan to Mountbatten-Windsor for the purchase of a chalet in Switzerland - a suggestion which is contested by Isbilen and had been challenged in previous court hearings.

Turk had met Mountbatten-Windsor in autumn 2019 through the Pitch@Palace project, a Dragon's Den-style pitching event run by the former duke.

That had led to social gatherings, bringing together Turk and his family, Isbilen and the then Duke and Duchess of York.

Justice Adam Johnson has said that, given the seriousness of the allegations, Turk should have access to "the evidence he considers relevant and material".

That meant that Turk wanted to use Mountbatten-Windsor's evidence and has been successful in summonsing him for that purpose.

Turk's representatives, Janes Solicitors, said he denies the claims of dishonesty and looks forward to being vindicated in court.

Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for a response.

The trial at the High Court is expected to begin later this month.

News.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
News.content:
The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.

The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.

The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see Â£5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.

The deal could have the following impact:

Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume

It should remove the need for Â£200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to

It should also end the need for Â£25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases

Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed

It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU

In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".

Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.

Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.

At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."

Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.

"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.

"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."

News.title: Scientists detect signals at the smallest scale ever explored
News.content:
Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.

Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.

So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.

One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.

The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.

Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.

Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.

"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.

He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.

"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.

News.title: UK meat industry hit by cyber-attack which targeted European supermarket freezers
News.content:
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.

Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.

AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.

The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.

On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.

The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.

Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.

Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.

But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.

Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.

But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".

"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.

"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."

News.title: Jury in Russell Brand rape trial begins considering verdicts
News.content:
The jury has begun considering the verdicts in Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial.

The media personality, 51, has been on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London for three weeks, facing three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

He has pleaded not guilty to all the charges. Giving evidence, he told the court he had been "obsessed" with sex in the past, but insisted it was always consensual.

The charges relate to allegations from six women spanning a decade between 1999 and 2009. Prosecutors said the complainants described him as someone who "didn't listen" when they said no, and "didn't care".

On Tuesday, judge Mr Justice Bennathan told the jury of eight men and four women he can only accept a verdict they all agree on.

Brand was one of the UK's most high-profile comedians, presenters and actors during the 2000s.

At the trial, he admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access", which he now said was wrong, but denied ever doing anything criminal.

His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

He also said none of the women reported the alleged incidents to police at the time, and that allegations in a 2023 TV and newspaper investigation had "poisoned the well of justice" by prompting women to come forward afterwards.

Meanwhile, prosecutors depicted Brand as someone who saw women as a "disposable commodity" who "didn't matter to him" and were simply a "means to an end".

Barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told the jury that the women said his personality changed "from charming to frightening to nasty" during the alleged attacks.

She said the women, who do not know each other, had been "haunted for years" by their experiences.

One woman accuses Brand of raping her after they had met at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999.

She claimed he turned from "camp, friendly and effeminate" to "monster-like" before the alleged assault.

When asked if there was any truth in the allegations that he raped her, he told the court: "No."

Another woman claims that the entertainer grabbed her breasts at a bar in London in 2004 before dragging her into a toilet, where he allegedly orally raped her.

Brand said he remembered going into the toilet with the woman but did not drag or force her there, or force her to perform oral sex.

A third woman had a consensual sexual encounter with Brand and another fan in his dressing room at the Hammersmith Apollo theatre in London in 2009.

She accuses the star of later raping her after he invited her to his house in Hampstead.

She said she had agreed to vaginal sex but did not consent to anal sex. After he texted her six months later, she said she told him he had "treated me like an animal".

Brand told the court they had consensual sex, and denied committing anal rape.

The other allegations come from a woman who says she was pinned against a wall and groped; another who claims he put his head into her lap when she had been forced to give him a massage; and a complainant who says he tried to drag her into a toilet. Brand also denies these charges.

Brand's wife Laura gave evidence in his defence at the trial, describing him as "caring, kind and a wonderful father to our children".

Allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand were first made in a Channel 4 documentary and a Times and Sunday Times investigation in 2023.

He denied those allegations, which related to different women than those involved in the criminal trial.

Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

In recent years Brand has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

News.title: Lorry driver electrocuted after vehicle hit overhead power line
News.content:
A driver of a tipper lorry was electrocuted after part of his vehicle hit an overhead power line, an inquest has heard.

Andy Lloyd, 56, who ran a family business, was delivering a load of hardcore to a farm with his 14-year-old son when the grab arm on his truck came into contact with the 11,000-volt overhead cables.

Ruthin Coroner's Court heard Lloyd, from Bod Elian, Llanelian in Conwy, climbed down from the cab and was electrocuted when he came into contact with the metal step.

He was pronounced dead at the scene in Tan y Dderwen Farm in Betws-yn-Rhos, Conwy on 1 May - less than a month before he was due to get married.

The inquest heard that Lloyd's son, who cannot be named for legal reasons, had joined his dad in the lorry that day to gain work experience.

Senior coroner John Gittins for North Wales East and Central read from the teenager's statement.

He said his dad had moved the lorry closer to where contractors were erecting a shed to tip the load when the grab arm hit the power line.

The court heard the teenager had tried to tell his dad, but Lloyd had already exited the cab.

Contractors who witnessed the incident described seeing flames coming from the rear tyres of the lorry and Lloyd's boots before he collapsed.

One of the men then noticed the teenager in the lorry and helped him exit safely.

Another performed CPR on Lloyd while the third called an ambulance.

The inquest heard that Devon Locke, a Scottish Power engineer, had been dispatched to the area to investigate after the supply had been tripped.

When he saw the emergency vehicles at the farm he learned what had happened and saw the lorry was still in contact with the cables running above the field.

Although the power had been tripped plans were made to make the line safe.

The coroner concluded that Lloyd died as a result of an accident and offered his condolences to his family.

Lloyd's partner, Hayley Lloyd, said in her statement that his "last moments were spent in his truck with his son beside him" and that he "cared quietly but fiercely for those around him."

News.title: Cambridge scientist killed in Spain train crash was 'a light for all of us'
News.content:
The aunt of a University of Cambridge scientist killed in the Spanish rail disaster has paid an emotional tribute, describing her niece as "a light for all of us".

Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to collect a prize for scientific excellence in Andalusia on 28 October, when her train crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.

MarÃ­a JosÃ© Alonso told the BBC a funeral had been held in Madrid on Monday for the mother of two.

"Hundreds of friends came from all over the world... because Marta was an amazing lab mate and amazing friend," she said. "She was the friendliest person you can imagine, with lots of energy. She was a light for all of us."

Shahbazi, 41, had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development.

She was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.

Alonso said her niece had originally intended to travel to the ceremony by car with her family, but decided to take the train.

"Her family was here in Madrid, and they could have gone together by car - but she said 'no, stay here'," she said.

News.title: Rape accused 'told woman would pretend to be asleep'
News.content:
A man accused of raping a woman after he answered an advert for sex online said he was told she would "pretend to be asleep" by her then husband.

Richard Wilkins, 62, is one of four men accused of sexual offences against Joanne Young, who was drugged and raped by Philip Young over 13 years at their Swindon home.

Giving evidence, Wilkins said he was told to "come in, have sex and leave" after answering a Craigslist post in 2016 that he thought was placed by the couple but was actually placed by Young alone.

Wilkins is on trial with Norman Macksoni, 48, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38. They all deny sexual offences against Joanne, who was waived her right to anonymity.

News.title: Speeding driver jailed for fatal Lamborghini crash
News.content:
A driver who caused the death of her friend when she lost control of a rented Lamborghini and crashed into a motorway barrier has been jailed for 10 years.

Mohammed Shaan Hussain, 20, died when Humaira Batool crashed the Â£200,000 supercar on the M62, near Ripponden, in West Yorkshire, in December 2022, causing it to flip over and burst into flames.

During her trial, jurors heard Batool, 26, from Bradford, had been driving at speeds of up to 140mph (230km/h) in wet conditions shortly before the crash.

Passing sentence, Judge Ray Singh said Hussain died as a result of Batool's decision to drive the "powerful performance vehicle" at "eye-watering extreme speeds on a damp motorway in darkness".

The judge said: "This was not a momentary lapse of concentration. It was a conscious decision to drive at extraordinary speed in conditions that made such driving especially dangerous.

"You deliberately exposed your passenger, yourself and other road users to an obvious and grave risk of death or serious injury. Tragically, that risk materialised."

During the trial, the court heard Hussain, also from Bradford, had rented the vehicle and was driving to HMP Leeds with Batool to collect a friend.

The pair switched places en route and the car crashed off the carriageway within eight seconds of Batool taking the wheel.

In court, Batool tried to blame Hussain, saying he had "reached over" while she was driving and touched something, causing the car to surge, but this was rejected by the jury.

The judge said: "During the trial, various alternative explanations were advanced on your behalf, all of which were rejected â the possibility of mechanical failure, aquaplaning and your suggestion that, just prior to the collision, the controls of that vehicle had been tampered with by Shaan.

"The jury rejected those explanations. I do likewise.

"The sole cause of this collision was the manner of your driving."

Hussain died as a result of the injuries he sustained in the crash, while Batool suffered serious injuries, including burns to around 10% of her body and a shattered tibia.

Batool was found guilty of causing death by dangerous driving in September.

News.title: Champions League round-up: PSG thrash Villarreal as Harry Kane fails to equal Cristiano Ronaldo record
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

PSG established a three-point lead at the top of the Champions League table after a comprehensive 6-0 victory against Villarreal.

Luis Enrique’s side registered a 10th successive win in emphatic style, going 4-0 ahead within 17 minutes through Joao Neves, Desire Doue, Senny Mayulu and Fabian Ruiz. Ruiz struck again early in the second half, before substitute David Boly rounded off the scoring in the 78th minute.

Meanwhile, Harry Kane missed the chance to match Cristiano Ronaldo’s milestone of scoring in 11 consecutive Champions League games.

Appearing in his first European fixture since winning the Ballon d’Or, the England skipper drew a rare blank, but second-half goals from teenager Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer secured a 2-0 win for Bayern Munich at Atletico Madrid. Kane registered an assist for Laimer’s goal that wrapped up the victory for the German giants.

Over in Spain, Barcelona moved up to second place by bringing Aston Villa’s 100 per cent record to an end with a 3-0 win at the Nou Camp.

open image in gallery Harry Kane did not get on the scoresheet on Tuesday ( Getty )

Lamine Yamal provided an early opener, and after Villa’s Matty Cash, Victor Lindelof and Johan Manzambi missed chances, a second-half double from Raphinha sealed Barca’s third victory in four European matches to keep them on course to reach the knockout stages.

At Old Trafford, Manchester United ended a nine-game winless run across all competitions, staging a remarkable comeback from 2-0 down to beat Roma 3-2.

The current slump has left head coach Michael Carrick’s future uncertain, and his team faced a bleak half-time reality following Matias Soule’s opener and a Donyell Malan penalty.

United captain Bruno Fernandes converted a twice-taken spot-kick to spark the recovery, before Bryan Mbeumo saw a shot strike both posts and Matheus Cunha scored twice before receiving a red card in stoppage time.

Elsewhere, Inter Milan claimed a 3-0 victory at Feyenoord, while Galatasaray, Sporting and LASK also picked up wins. Bodo/Glimt and Lille played out a 0-0 draw.

There will be nine more Champions League matches on Wednesday night, with Arsenal taking on Slavia Prague, Liverpool facing Dirk Kuyt’s Fenerbahce and Manchester City playing RB Leipzig

News.title: Learjet debris found nearly four miles from Florida crash site, investigators reveal
News.content:
Parts of the private jet which crashed in Florida killing all nine on board have been found nearly four miles away from the impact site, air investigators say.

In an update to the media on Tuesday (3 November), a National Transportation Safety Board spokesperson revealed the Learjet’s left elevator - a control surface located on the the tail of the aircraft which controls its vertical pitch - had been found in three pieces between 1.3-3.8 miles away from the crash crater.

Spokesperson Tom Chappell confirmed investigation of the crater, which had been delayed due to debris obstructing access, would likely begin tomorrow, with other ‘critical components’ of the aircraft expected to be found.

News.title: Man United latest: Michael Carrick’s job saved by brilliant Champions League comeback against Roma
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Michael Carrick saw his job saved in the most remarkable way as Manchester United fought back from 2-0 down against Roma in the Champions League to snatch the unlikeliest of 3-2 wins at Old Trafford.

Carrick, who had seen United go winless in nine games for the first time in 40 years, was desperate for a change of fortunes to save his skin but his time at Old Trafford appeared to be coming to an end as the hopeless Red Devils were 2-0 down inside 20 minutes as part of a diabolical first-half display.

But they were a different team in the second half and were given a lifeline when Bruno Fernandes scored a re-taken penalty – with a Roma player encroaching into the area during the initial miss – after Matheus Cunha was fouled.

Cunha then became the hero when he capitalised on a Roma error seven minutes from time to equalise before firing a winning goal in style shortly after, although he was booked for his celebration and then sent off injury time after an clumsy lunging tackle earned a deserved second yellow.

There was huge relief for Carrick who will head into a crunch clash with Aston Villa on Sunday with at least a little bit of confidence restored as he looks to come back from the brink. Follow all the reaction from Man United’s remarkable comeback win over Roma in our live blog below:

News.title: Bruno Fernandes admits Michael Carrick was right to drop him in fiery interview
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Bruno Fernandes denied that Manchester United’s remarkable comeback win against Roma saved Michael Carrick from the sack but admitted the manager was right to drop him for criticising his tactics last month.

The United captain scored their first goal with a twice-taken penalty as they came from 2-0 down to beat Roma 3-2 and record their first victory in 10 matches.

But after their previous Champions League game, a 4-1 thrashing by Como, Fernandes had blamed Carrick for United’s lack of pressing in a post-match interview – and the United manager responded by leaving him as an unused substitute for their next match, a 3-0 loss to Bournemouth.

open image in gallery Michael Carrick had dropped his skipper Bruno Fernandes ( Reuters )

And Fernandes addressed the issue in another fiery post-match interview following the Roma comeback.

Speaking to Amazon Prime Video, he said: “The manager took a decision of making myself be on the bench because I wasn’t performing, and that’s fair.

“Everyone felt that was a punishment for the words that I had said. And if it was, it was right. The manager is the one that makes the decisions. I have to accept them. I have to go forward with that.

“It doesn’t change the belief I have on the manager and on the staff and and every player that is in this club, and it doesn’t change my aim to win every f***ing game that I have ahead of me.”

open image in gallery Fernandes scored a re-taken penalty and helped inspire United to a comeback win over Roma ( Reuters )

Fernandes and Carrick subsequently held talks before the Portuguese was brought back into the team on Saturday against Chelsea.

And as he got increasingly passionate, Fernandes added: “It’s been tough. It’s been a lot of speculation in the media, a lot of lies around many things that have happened in this club between me and the manager, like that we had cleared the air then after when nothing of that happened.”

Carrick has been under pressure as United have only taken seven points in the Premier League this season and had lost their three previous matches in all competitions.

But Fernandes said: “We don’t need to save anyone’s job. But it was important, he needed that win tonight. The club needed that win, the players needed that win. It’s something that we needed as a group of players together with the staff.”

News.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor ‘summoned to give evidence’ in High Court fraud trial
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been served with a summons to give evidence in a £40m fraud trial in the High Court, it has been reported.

The former Duke of York, who is not accused of any wrongdoing, is caught up in a legal battle involving a wealthy Turkish woman who alleges her former financial adviser misled her over a £750,000 payment made to Mr Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.

It will be the first time Mr Mountbatten-Windsor has faced public questioning since his disastrous Newsnight interview in 2019, as well as an opportunity to hear his first public comments since the King stripped him of his titles last year.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor is also thought to be the first royal to be sent a witness summons since the 19th century.

It is understood he will appear in court on or before 15 December to give evidence on behalf of Selman Turk, who is being sued by Turkish national Nebahat İşbilen over allegations that he misled her and used her wealth for his own interests.

Mr Turk has strongly denied dishonesty.

open image in gallery A businessman made a bid to be allowed to call Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor to give evidence at the trial (PA) ( PA Wire )

His representatives, Janes Solicitors, said: “The Judge concluded that the proposed evidence that Mr Turk wishes to adduce from Mr Mountbatten-Windsor appears relevant to allegations of dishonesty advanced against Mr Turk and that, in the circumstances, it would be unfair and unjust to prevent him from seeking to adduce that evidence at trial.

“Mr Turk continues to strongly deny the allegations made against him and looks forward to vindicating his position at the forthcoming trial.”

The judge gave permission for the former prince to give evidence last month and the case is due to begin in mid-November.

Mr Turk has claimed that the £750,000 payment sent to Mr Mountbatten-Windsor was a loan for the purchase of a chalet in Switzerland.

He alleges that Ms İşbilen had arranged to make the gift as she wanted to create goodwill with Mr Mountbatten-Windsor.

Mr Turk claims Mr İşbilen believed that the former duke might be able to assist her husband, who was in prison in Turkey, through his connections in the country.

open image in gallery The payment was made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor the day after his disastrous Newsnight interview ( PA Archive )

But Mr İşbilen has alleged that Mr Turk misled her into making the payment by saying she needed to make a purported “gift” for assistance that the then Duke of York had provided in relation to Ms İşbilen’s Turkish passport.

She says Mr Turk knew this representation was false.

The former duke will be asked to give evidence related to this dispute.

Mr Turk said he first came into contact with the then duke through the Pitch@Palace initiative, a Dragon's Den-style startup founded by Mr Mountbatten-Windsor in 2014.

The money was sent to Mr Mountbatten-Windsor’s personal bank account on 15 November 2019, the day before his car crash BBC Newsnight interview.

Mr Mountbatten-Windsor revealed he was stepping back from public duties four days after the interview amid scrutiny over his relationship with convicted paedophile Jeffrey Epstein and claims he slept with Virginia Giuffre when she was 17-years-old.

He was later stripped of his military titles and royal patronages by the late Queen in 2022, and forced to remove his remaining titles, including the Duke of York, in October last year.

The Independent has approached Mr Mountbatten-Windsor for comment.
