Chief Superintendent Mel Adams said everyone who witnessed the violence would carry some trauma from the night.

'This could have been your family member,' she said.

'This was a random group of people at the front of a popular hotel that became victims.'

The three other victims, men aged 27, 37 and 38, all suffered gunshot wounds to their abdomens. The 38-year-old was also shot in the arm.

All three remained in serious conditions on Monday but were improving, Adams said.

Police have not confirmed whether the men knew one another.

Police believe the attack involved pre-planning but say it remains premature to speculate about gang or organised crime involvement.

The Mitsubishi was found burnt out at Waterford West shortly after the shooting.

CCTV from nearby homes showed its occupants being collected by another vehicle after the car was torched. Police believe one of those involved may have suffered burns or another injury.

A ute was also found burnt later that night, with investigators still examining whether it was connected.

Adams urged anyone who knew or suspected who was responsible to come forward.

'There will be people out there who know who did this or suspect who did this,' she said.

For Austin, who has a son the same age as the critically injured teenager, the shooting has hit particularly hard.

'I've got a son her age, so it's really, really hit home hard,' he said.

He offered the federation's support to the victims, their families and friends.

'This is an awful, awful time for everyone,' he said.

'Let's just hope this girl recovers. It's just awful.'

Sports.title: Conor Benn calls out Conor McGregor for lucrative crossover fight - as he looks to bounce back from brutal second-round knockdown by Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
Conor Benn has called out Conor McGregor for a potential crossover fight, just weeks after suffering a devastating defeat by Ryan Garcia.

Benn was stopped in the second round of his world title challenge against Garcia in Las Vegas, with a brutal right hand sending the Briton crashing to the canvas before the American finished the job.

It was the first knockout defeat of Benn's professional career and left serious questions over what comes next for the 30-year-old.

But he appears to have an unexpected opponent in mind.

Benn took to social media to share a fight poster featuring himself and McGregor, accompanied by the caption: 'Benn vs McGregor coming soon, 2027'.

He added to the speculation by responding: 'Any day of the week.'

Conor Benn (pictured above) has called out Conor McGregor for a potential crossover fight, just weeks after suffering a devastating defeat by Ryan Garcia

Benn is understood to be interested in making the fight happen and is expected to explore potential terms with the Irishman.

Benn has previously been tipped to face McGregor in a lucrative crossover bout, with boxing legend Roy Jones Jr suggesting that the fight would make sense.

He said the crossover bout would be one of two major paydays for the Brit before he considers bringing his career to a close.

Jones also suggested such a contest could help Zuffa Boxing recoup its investment in Benn.

The prospect would offer Benn the chance to headline another major event without the pressure of a world title being on the line, while a fight against McGregor would attract an audience well beyond traditional boxing fans.

McGregor is one of the biggest names in combat sports, having become a global superstar during his time in the UFC before stepping into the boxing ring to face Floyd Mayweather in 2017.

The Irishman is also coming off a difficult period of his own, having suffered a fresh setback on his return to the Octagon against Max Holloway.

A fight with Benn would undoubtedly attract huge attention, although there is no indication yet that the pair are close to agreeing a deal.

Roy Jones Jr has said such a contest could help Zuffa Boxing recoup its investment in Benn

Benn's call-out comes after a brutal night in Las Vegas, where his hopes of becoming a world champion were ended in devastating fashion.

The British fighter had talked up his chances of upsetting Garcia, but the American's speed and power proved too much.

Garcia caught Benn with a vicious right hand in the second round, dropping him heavily to the canvas. Benn managed to get back to his feet, but Garcia immediately went on the attack again, forcing referee Thomas Taylor to step in after just one minute and 25 seconds of the round.

It was a crushing result for Benn, who had worked his way back into contention following his two-fight rivalry with Chris Eubank Jr.

Benn lost their first encounter by decision in April 2025 before getting his revenge with a points victory in November.

He subsequently returned to welterweight to challenge Garcia for the WBC title, but the American proved a step too far on the night.

The defeat also raised fresh questions about Benn's future at 147lbs, with making the weight having been a talking point in the build-up.

After the fight, Benn admitted he was unsure what came next and spoke about the sacrifices his boxing career had demanded of his family.

Benn was beaten inside two rounds by Ryan Garcia in their welterweight championship fight

It was the first knockout defeat of Benn's professional career and left serious questions over what comes next for the 30-year-old

He made it clear that spending time with his children was his immediate priority, leaving his next move uncertain.

A lucrative showdown with McGregor would offer a very different route back into the spotlight from another world title challenge.

McGregor, meanwhile, has endured his own difficult return to competition.

The former two-weight UFC champion had been out of action since breaking his leg during his trilogy fight with Dustin Poirier in July 2021.

His long-awaited comeback against Holloway was supposed to mark the start of a new chapter, but things quickly went wrong.

McGregor injured his knee after attempting a jumping kick in the opening seconds of the fight. Unable to continue, he was forced to withdraw after just 69 seconds, handing Holloway the victory.

The result was a frustrating setback for the Irishman, whose return had generated enormous interest among UFC fans.

McGregor subsequently announced plans to undergo surgery, leaving his immediate and long-term future uncertain once again.

McGregor's long-awaited comeback ended in disaster at UFC 329 in Las Vegas (above)

The Irishman blew his knee out after throwing a kick within the first seconds of the bout

At 38, he remains one of the most recognisable figures in combat sports, but another comeback will depend on his recovery and whether he can return to full fitness.

A boxing match with Benn would be a different proposition from another UFC appearance, though it would still require McGregor to make a significant commitment to training and preparation.

McGregor is no stranger to a crossover fight.

His most famous venture outside MMA came in August 2017, when he faced Floyd Mayweather in one of the most heavily promoted boxing matches of all time.

McGregor had never competed in a professional boxing bout before, but that did little to dampen interest in the contest.

The pair embarked on an extraordinary promotional tour, trading insults in front of huge crowds as the fight became a global spectacle.

McGregor made a competitive start, but Mayweather quickly took control before stopping him in the 10th round.

Mayweather improved his professional boxing record to 50-0, while McGregor returned to the UFC having secured a huge payday and further cemented his status as one of sport's biggest commercial attractions.

Sports.title: Boxing world champion Adrien Broner back in hot water as video shows him being handcuffed and hauled into police car in Beverly Hills
Sports.content:
Boxing world champion Adrien Broner back in hot water as video shows him being handcuffed and hauled into police car in Beverly Hills

Adrien Broner, the troubled former boxing champion once seen as the future of the sport, had another run-in with police over the weekend in Beverly Hills.

Now more than two years removed from his last fight, the 37-year-old Broner was among a group of men recording content on the streets of Beverly Hills for the social media platform, Kick, when local police arrived.

Viral footage from the incident shows the group recording what appears to be a music video involving both Broner and his fellow content creator, Deen The Great.

A separate clip shows Broner with his arms raised and walking backwards towards a pair of officers, who ultimately placed him in handcuffs. Broner is seen trying to poke fun at the situation by doing a funny walk for the officers' benefit, but they did not seem amused.

'Broner was detained during a traffic stop as part of an investigation into a large street gathering in a residential area,' Beverly Hills police told TMZ in a statement. 'He was released from the scene and a citation was not issued.'

The Daily Mail has sought further information from Beverly Hills police.

Adrien Broner dancing while getting put in handcuffs by the police 💀 pic.twitter.com/h9SZlIYfdM — Happy Punch (@HappyPunch) October 26, 2026

Viral footage shows the group recording what appears to be a music video involving both Broner (center, open gray sweatshirt) and his fellow content creator, DeenTheGreat

A separate clip shows Broner with his arms raised and walking backwards towards a pair of officers, who ultimately placed him in handcuffs on the streets of Beverly Hills

Adrien Broner and Deen The Great attend the Internet Ball on August 19, 2026

Broner is currently among several defendants being sued in Los Angeles County over allegations of sexual battery, battery and assault.

'Plaintiff alleges that Broner repeatedly pressured Plaintiff for sexual activity after repeated refusals, attempted to isolate Plaintiff, repeatedly pressured Plaintiff while intoxicated, attempted unwanted physical contact, publicly humiliated Plaintiff, and made false sexual statements about Plaintiff to a livestream audience,' read the complaint, obtained by The Daily Mail.

Broner has denied any wrongdoing in the case.

Previously, in September of 2025, Broner was kicked off rapper Cam'ron's popular podcast after ignoring the host's warnings to stop flirting with his on-air co-host.

Sporting a greying beard and speaking in an increasingly raspy voice, Broner repeatedly interrupted the interview to make passes at Treasure 'Stat Baby' Wilson, who co-hosts It Is What It Is with Cam'ron and Ma$e.

Adrien Broner and Deen The great attend Sold Out Saturdays on August 15, 2026 in Atlanta

Adrien Broner punches Gavin Rees during their WBC Lightweight Title fight at Atlantic City Boardwalk Hall in 2013. Broner won the WBO Super Featherweight title at just 22 in 2011

At one point, Broner responded to a question about boxing's welterweight division by telling Wilson: 'Stat, I love you.'

Things ultimately boiled over during a discussion about Sunday's NFL action when Broner appeared to stop himself from making another comment about Wilson: 'I can't talk… You told me to stop.'

Cam'ron took the moment to end his interview with Broner.

'Hey, we going to have to ask you to go, my n*****,' Cam'ron said before pulling a stack of cash out of a small bag to give to his guest.

'I don't have no problems with you, but I'm gonna pay you for your time,' the rapper said, adding: 'You can't violate, bro.' Cam'ron went on to explain that Wilson's boyfriend was on set.

A native of Cincinnati who won the WBO Super Featherweight title at just 22 in 2011, Broner enjoyed a meteoric rise in the boxing world before his career was derailed by a series of arrests, upset defeats and mental health issues.

Sports.title: Aussie boxing legend Jeff Fenech hospitalised as he faces fresh new health battle: 'He's always a fighter'
Sports.content:
Aussie boxing legend Jeff Fenech hospitalised as he faces fresh new health battle: 'He's always a fighter'

Australian boxing legend Jeff Fenech has been hospitalised with heart problems, with his NRL star son-in-law Bradman Best revealing the family’s concern ahead of his Kangaroos debut.

The four-weight world champion, 62, was admitted to Strathfield Private Hospital around 10 days ago after suffering severe fatigue, breathing difficulties and feeling unwell.

Fenech has since had a blood clot removed from his wrist and undergone tests to investigate whether a potentially life-threatening staph infection has returned.

A recurrence has not been confirmed.

Best, who has a baby daughter with Fenech’s daughter Kayla, disclosed the hospital stay while discussing the boxing great’s influence on his career.

The Newcastle centre is preparing to make his Australian Test debut against Fiji on Sunday, but took time to acknowledge Fenech’s health battle.

Jeff Fenech, 62, has been hospitalised after suffering heart problems, fatigue and breathing difficulties

Bradman Best paid tribute to his father-in-law ahead of his Australian Test debut

Fenech has reportedly had a blood clot removed from his wrist and undergone tests for a possible recurrence of a serious infection

‘Jeff has been massive for me, I just want to give a quick shout-out to him,’ Best said.

‘He’s actually in hospital at the moment.

‘I’m thinking of him. He’s tough, he’s always a fighter.’

Best said Fenech had become an invaluable source of advice as he worked towards representing Australia.

‘Jeff has done a lot for me in my career,’ he said.

‘I was visiting him last week and he’s always giving me tips on what to do and how to be better.

‘It’s special having a father-in-law like that who’s a four-time world champion.

‘He’s an icon in Australia and it’s special having a bond like that with him.’

Tim Tszyu’s preparations for his world-title clash with Erislandy Lara have been disrupted by his trainer’s hospitalisation

Fenech became one of Australia’s greatest boxers, winning world titles across four weight divisions during a career that earned him the nickname ‘The Marrickville Mauler’

Asked whether Fenech’s condition was serious, Best remained hopeful.

‘Yeah, he will be right. He’s always a fighter. He’s been in there with a few heart problems and stuff, but he’ll be good.’

The hospitalisation has also interrupted Tim Tszyu’s preparations for his planned WBA middleweight world-title clash with Erislandy Lara.

Fenech became Tszyu’s head trainer in July, helping guide him to a unanimous decision victory over American star Errol Spence Jr.

Tszyu credited the veteran trainer with helping inspire that result, which set up his pursuit of a world championship in a second weight division.

With Fenech sidelined, fellow trainer Basil Nassis has taken charge of Tszyu’s work in the gym.

The Lara bout is expected to take place in Australia in November or December, according to the reports.

Fenech hopes to recover in time to be involved, although the Telegraph reported he is unlikely to perform padwork during the build-up.

The latest scare follows two major heart operations.

In October 2019, Fenech underwent emergency open-heart surgery in Thailand while preparing Jack Brubaker for a fight against Tszyu.

He needed another six-hour open-heart operation in 2024 during a serious infection.

Sports.title: British boxing has a world beater in the ascendancy. Daniel Dubois is starting to look like a monster - and he's ready for Oleksandr Usyk, Anthony Joshua, Tyson Fury or anyone else, writes JEFF POWELL MBE
Sports.content:
'Bring him on,' roared Daniel Dubois when asked if he would like a third fight against the greatest boxer of his generation who has beaten him twice.

Oleksandr Usyk, who is in a state of limbo somewhere between vacating all the heavyweight tiles and semi-retirement, is a genius so may not fall readily into the trap baited on the banks of the Thames in the dark hours of this Sunday morning.

Ukraine's war hero will have watched Dubois annihilate the gallant Fabio Wardley and recognised that Dynamite Daniel is no longer the callow youth he wiped the canvas with a couple of times during his reign as the undisputed world champion.

Promoter Frank Warren is not given to understatement but when he said 'Daniel has matured now' he was only scratching the surface of the transformation.

It may be a stretch to compare Dubois with the once terrifying Sonny Liston but to those rivals wearing the other belts he needs if he is to become undisputed then he is starting to look like a monster.

'I want them all,' said WBO champion Dubois. He was referring to the winner between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua in December, who will thereby hold a WBA title, as well as IBF and WBC champions Filip Hrgovic and Ajit Kabayel.

Daniel Dubois knocks down Fabio Wardley during his annihilation on Saturday night

Dubois has declared himself ready to fight anyone in the heavyweight division

Their availability, especially that of AJ or the Gypsy King, will be determined no doubt by there being many more millions in the Aladdin's Cave from which Saudi Arabia has helped finance the welcome flux of mega-fights of late.

If so then Warren is promising a 2027 bursting with monthly heavyweight spectaculars as lustily anticipated as Dubois' second demolition of Wardley . At the rapid conclusion of which another packed O2 crowd was switching its allegiance from a love affair with Fabio's romanticised emergence from white collar boxing to realisation that Britain has a world beater in the ascendancy.

One who may be growing, also, into more of a box office star than the monosyllabic Liston ever was. If his accurate bravura prediction of a 'bash and smash' slaughter of Wardley and his most jovial media conference yet which followed are anything to go by.

Having nursed his confidence in the Dubois family cocoon Daniel now has a mansion of his own to live in and a selection of race cars to drive. No more Mister Shy Guy but none the less likeable for that.

The transition to full manhood was rounded off over the two fights with Wardley. This included recovery from two early knockdowns in the first Fight Of The Year battle to a brutal 11th round stoppage victory.

And now the onslaught triggered by a staggering right hand blow only 17 seconds after the first bell which imposed an eight count on the ropes. Followed by an overwhelming TKO in round two. Wham, bam and thank you man. No criticism this time of a delay in calling it off. In flew the white towel, in jumped referee Steve Gray.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua fight each other in December - and Dubois wants the winner

There has been some nagging at the edge of Dubois' triumph. Suggestions that Wardley came back too soon after the second-half beating in May. But if five-and-a-half months is not sufficient time to recover then how long would be? The immortal Joe Louis used to fight once a month, for heaven's sake.

Wardley, honest man that he is, blamed himself. Having lived to fight another day he vows to do better enough to launch a comeback campaign for another world title. Meanwhile Dubois, at 29 last month, heads for the stratosphere as champion of the next generation of heavyweight boxing.

As the new monster of the prize-ring? It took The Greatest Of All Time to stop the Liston beast In his awesome tracks. Might Usyk be the Muhammad Ali in waiting for Dubois? Maybe. Perhaps not since he is the older legend now. It would be fascinating finding out.

The tombstone on Sonny Liston's grave in Las Vegas describes him simply as A MAN. Frank Warren is right about Dubois becoming exactly that.

Sports.title: Rafa Camara to debut in F1 Brazil GP as Esteban Ocon out at Haas
Sports.content:
The Haas F1 team has decided Esteban Ocon will not race again for the squad, with 2027 debutant Rafa Camara getting an early debut this weekend on home soil.

Following increasingly strained relations between Ocon and the team, a heated argument in Mexico proved the final straw that made team principal Ayao Komatsu decide to bench the Frenchman. Reserve driver and Toyota protege Ryo Hirakawa replaced Ocon from Saturday onwards in Mexico, going on to score a point on debut in 10th place. The team has now confirmed Ocon, who is a free agent next year, will not return.

"We have now notified Esteban Ocon that he will not return to a race seat with TGR Haas F1 Team this season," Komatsu explained.

"Such decisions are never made lightly, as was the case in Mexico City - but then, as now, we feel this is firmly in the best interest of the team moving forward. The conversations that ultimately unfolded between the team and Esteban remain an internal matter, and we will continue to respect the private nature of closed-door situations."

Ferrari junior Camara, who had already been signed by Haas to replace Ocon for 2027, will take the wheel of the VF-26 at Interlagos. The Brazilian, who currently leads the Formula 2 standings and made a stellar impression on Haas in private testing, will have the opportunity to begin his F1 career several months ahead of schedule.

The final green light came on Tuesday afternoon, although Camara had already been placed on standby during the Mexican Grand Prix weekend following Ocon's sudden removal from the Haas line-up. At the Autodromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the American team fielded Ryo Hirakawa as a temporary replacement while assessing its options for the remaining races of the season.

It is not yet confirmed whether Camara or Hirakawa will race for the team in the remaining rounds at Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi, with it likely being a combination of both drivers.

Rafa Camara has conducted private testing in older machinery with both Ferrari and Haas. Photo by: Davide Cavazza

Camara has never driven a 2026 F1 car, but will not arrive at his high-pressure home debut unprepared. Alongside. During the season, he has completed five Testing of Previous Cars (TPC) outings, four at the wheel of Ferrari's SF-25 and one driving the Haas VF-25.

The latter took place in August at Portimao in Portugal and played a crucial role in convincing the US-owned team of his natural ability.

"Looking ahead, we've chosen Rafael Camara to drive alongside Ollie Bearman at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix," Komatsu confirmed.

"Having excelled in his TPC outing in August, we know Rafa's capabilities and we're looking forward to welcoming him into the team this weekend and working with him through his Formula 1 debut driving the VF-26 in Brazil."

The change of plans will also have consequences for Ferrari. Friday morning's FP1 session, originally allocated to Camara, will instead be handed to Dino Beganovic, giving the Swedish driver another opportunity to get behind the wheel of the Maranello team's car.

Sports.title: Why Bearman is yet to be announced as a Haas driver for F1 2027
Sports.content:
With Oliver Bearman firing on all cylinders in his sophomore Formula 1 campaign, it feels odd that Haas has been able to confirm the identity of Esteban Ocon's replacement in the second seat for 2027 before announcing Bearman is staying put for a third year.

There is no real doubt that Bearman will stay where he is, with both parties keen to continue for another season into 2027.

“I think it's very clear. I want to continue with Haas and that's definitely my goal," Bearman said in Mexico on Thursday. "It's not really in my hands. If it was up to me, it would have already been announced a long time ago, but there are a few bigger picture things that we're working on."

Team principal Komatsu added: "I don't like to go into the details of our contract, but Ollie is showing amazing potential. He's contributing a lot to the team's success and we want to grow together. We want to move up the grid as a team.”

And while Komatsu had to dismiss unsubstantiated rumours over Bearman's pay demands, holding up a deal as "absolute nonsense", the real reason behind the delay is not about 2027, but about what happens next.

Autosport understands that should Ferrari be unable to guarantee him a seat in 2028 - after three years of being loaned out to customer team Haas - then Bearman will have the freedom to part ways with Maranello. It is this "bigger picture" that Bearman was referring to in his answer, and a picture that has become increasingly clouded in recent months.

Oliver Bearman, Scuderia Ferrari, Jeddah 2024 Photo by: Mark Sutton

Bearman is still on course to complete the full Ferrari Driver Academy pathway, all the way from F4 to a race seat with the Scuderia - Charles Leclerc being the only driver thus far to have completed the entire trajectory.

But a new road block has emerged in the shape of Lewis Hamilton, who has regained form this year and exercised the contractual option that secured his place at Ferrari for 2027. While Bearman initially looked like a perfect successor to Hamilton, the seven-time world champion's recent comments in the media about his longevity do not portray a man who is walking away from Ferrari and F1 anytime soon. Leclerc, meanwhile, has already agreed a long-term contract extension until at least 2030.

So, if Ferrari isn't able to guarantee Bearman a seat for 2028 and the 21-year-old Briton would be free to explore other options, it makes sense that there is a need right now to clarify certain aspects of his long-term future before formally announcing an extension with Haas.

Komatsu stressed that there is no disagreement regarding the desire to continue the partnership. “I don't think I can go into the details of the what's the hold up, but it's very clear from both parties that they want to continue working together,” he said.

"We work really well together, push each other. He brings a lot to the team and then we are growing together so our intentions from both parties are fully aligned. We're trying to find a solution to work together next year and I'm sure we will”.

The Bearman camp's priority, then, seems to be about ensuring that another year at Haas does not tie him down longer than necessary and potentially limit future opportunities. The paradox is that all parties involved appear to be pursuing compatible objectives. Haas wants to retain Bearman, the driver wants to keep racing, and Ferrari has every interest in protecting a young talent in whom it has invested for years.

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

What complicates the picture is the impossibility of guaranteeing today what might happen two seasons from now. For Bearman, therefore, the issue is not finding a seat for 2027. The real challenge is ensuring that the seemingly inevitable decision to remain at Haas does not become an obstacle to his prospects for 2028.

That delicate balance is what is currently being worked out behind closed doors. And it is probably the most likely explanation for an announcement that, only a few weeks ago, appeared to be nothing more than a formality.

Sports.title: McLaren to bring upgrades to Brazil GP with F1 2027 in mind
Sports.content:
McLaren will introduce upgrades to its MCL40 Formula 1 car at this weekend’s Brazil Grand Prix, featuring a front wing concept which is expected to feature on its 2027 challenger.

The team had surged to the front when it substantially updated the MCL40 in Hungary, with Lando Norris winning that race and the following one at Zandvoort, but it has since slipped back in the pecking order despite introducing another comprehensive upgrade package in Baku and further new parts in Austin.

McLaren had the fourth-quickest car in the last four qualifying sessions, with a 0.511s deficit to pole position and a 0.236s gap to the third-fastest challenger on average, but is still working away at improving the MCL40 – with an eye on 2027.

“We’ve got some updates coming to the car across the front wing, rear wing and some floor components as part of our normal development cycle,” said Peter Prodromou, chief technical officer, aerodynamics. “The aim is to make up ground, improve our performance over the remaining races and build momentum into next year.

“Sao Paulo has been a good circuit for us in the past and is a fairly representative track, so we’re hopeful these upgrades can help us take another step towards the front.

“The season isn't over yet: these upgrades are designed to improve the car now and help us in our fight for third in the championship. While the learning we take from these upgrades will feed into next year’s development, we also expect to carry over the concept of the new front wing into the launch specification of next year’s car.”

Peter Prodromou, McLaren Technical Director Aerodynamics Photo by: McLaren

McLaren has a 17-point deficit to third-placed Red Bull but has scored just 59 points to its rival’s 152 across the last five rounds.

The Mexican race was still encouraging, with Norris taking fifth just 12 seconds adrift of race winner Max Verstappen, yet the reigning world champion wasn’t optimistic for the next few rounds.

“If we look at Baku and stuff, I think we're still going to be struggling for pace,” he said on Sunday evening. “So we need to improve the car in certain tracks and certain areas still a lot more.

“Today it was good, but I'm not convinced that if we go back to the tracks we struggled at we'd be good all of a sudden. It's just today suited us, but I don't want to rely on a bit of hope and luck on performance.

“We know what we need to improve on, it just takes time, and hopefully we can have a better day in Brazil.”

Sports.title: The reason behind Honda’s power unit lasting five laps in Mexico GP
Sports.content:
In its Mexico Grand Prix preview, Honda’s Shintaro Orihara had described Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez as “a very challenging track for the power unit”, but he perhaps didn’t expect Aston Martin’s weekend to go so awry.

Despite decent pace and mileage in free practice – Fernando Alonso was just 0.769s down on pacesetter Charles Leclerc in FP2, with the AMR26s covering a whopping 144 laps across all three sessions – it all went wrong in the competitive sessions.

Honda did fix some driveability and turbo lag issues between FP3 and qualifying, but Alonso encountered “abnormal signals on the water systems” on Saturday afternoon, which didn’t prevent him from outqualifying Lance Stroll; still, both cars were out in Q1, four tenths down on the Q2 cut-off time.

In the race, the pair retired after five laps due to cooling issues.

“We knew that with the special high-altitude circumstance of Mexico City, we would face some additional challenges compared to other racetracks for the cooling,” said Orihara, Honda’s trackside general manager and chief engineer, following the race.

“However, we found that our ERS cooling circuit was under heavier stress than anticipated and this is why we had to stop the car in different sessions.

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

“Despite completing a series of laps during the practice sessions, the issue occurred today and during qualifying yesterday.

“At each race this year, we need to learn for 2027, even the hard lessons. We have a lot of data that we can bring back to this circuit next year, including on the turbo lag, and we will work on the solutions.”

Orihara pointed out on Thursday that in previous years the MGU-H supported the turbo, therefore reducing lag, but the new, simpler power units no longer feature that device – and that too was a problem with the thinner air at Mexico City’s high altitude.

While a frustrated Stroll only gave laconic answers to the media at the end of the weekend, Alonso was slightly more loquacious and underlined the scale of the challenge for Aston Martin and Honda.

“The car is very good,” the Spaniard said. “The problem is just, we cannot do more laps than a certain number, apparently, with the engine. Hopefully we learned a lesson and we come next year more prepared.”

But the Adrian Newey-designed machine had potential – even in Mexico. It’s fair to say Alonso and Stroll didn’t get much of a chance to show what they could do in the race; yet, putting the Spaniard’s quickest three sectors together on Sunday (he pitted on lap three, which prevented him from completing a decent lap), he was nearly as quick as Williams’ Carlos Sainz, despite presumably having a much heavier car with a full tank of fuel.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

“On Thursday, when we sat together, we said this is a track that has a lot of low-speed corners,” Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack said. “And if we get the driveability under control, that we can be competitive. For example, corners like the stadium section, [Turns] 4-5-6, low-speed stuff.”

Reliability therefore is the crux of the issue – as well as keeping morale up. “It's difficult for everyone to keep the motivation high in such situations, and we are struggling all year already,” Krack admitted.

“We had a very difficult start of the year, then the period when we introduced the upgrades and the ADUO, we [had] a bit better results. Now, we have more trouble in terms of reliability. In Texas, we had different issues with incidents. You know, it's part of racing.

“The thing is, everybody tries his best, everybody is motivated to do better, and I have no doubt about the motivation. We don't have to motivate them, it's motivating them the highest possible.”

And if anyone is staying motivated, that will be Alonso. “I’m doing my best every time, every lap I do, every morning I wake up, every preparation I do, every food I take – everything is focused on performing at my best behind the wheel,” he insisted again, despite his seventh retirement of the season.

Additional reporting by Luis Ramirez

Sports.title: Red Bull's key strategy call behind Verstappen's Mexico win
Sports.content:
Although Sunday at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez was above all Kimi Antonelli's day, there were naturally two other major storylines in the Formula 1 paddock: the tensions at Ferrari and how Fred Vasseur will manage them, plus Max Verstappen's sixth victory in Mexico.

When the latter came up in the post-race press conference, the Dutchman immediately joked: "Yeah, they should actually call it the ‘Maxico’ Grand Prix. That would be great."

On a more serious note, there are several factors behind Verstappen's track record in Mexico. During Red Bull's Honda years, the Japanese manufacturer had a highly effective turbo at altitude – partly based on knowledge from the aviation industry – which often made Red Bull competitive in terms of engine performance.

In addition, Verstappen himself is particularly adept at dealing with the low-downforce conditions that traditionally make Mexico a slippery affair, with drivers sliding around even more than normal.

In 2026, however, another factor also played an important role: strategy.

Red Bull immediately puts lessons from Austin into practice

While Red Bull made mistakes in Austin and, according to its drivers, stuck too stubbornly to the softer compounds and was not open-minded enough to react to what was happening during the race, the opposite proved to be the case in Mexico.

Due to Charles Leclerc's five-second penalty, Red Bull immediately decided to pit at the same time, even though this was not entirely in line with its own pre-planned tyre strategy. After all, Verstappen had started on mediums and would normally have gone longer, but Red Bull understood that track position was crucial at the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez, where the effect of dirty air was significant and overtaking was also difficult because of the power unit regulations.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

Red Bull knew that if it stayed out longer, it would give Leclerc the advantage of several laps on fresh rubber. With a later pitstop, Verstappen would therefore have rejoined the track behind Leclerc. The four-time world champion would then have had the tyre advantage, but Red Bull opted for track position, much to Verstappen's satisfaction.

"I think Charles just pulled away. I could not really stay with him,” said Verstappen. “I did not have the pace to follow him, but at the same time, I was still around that five-second window. So, then the team, I think, did a really good job to follow him in."

Aside from the aforementioned danger posed by Leclerc on fresh tyres, Verstappen said another factor also played a role: "It's always very tough when you have a five-second penalty to actually make it exactly five seconds, so I jumped him."

In practice, pitstops involving a five-second time penalty often take even longer, as mechanics do not want to touch the car too early and therefore build in a certain margin. Red Bull knew it could benefit from that if it pitted on the same lap.

The only downside to the decision was that Verstappen faced a particularly long stint on softs, prompting race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase to say over the team radio that Red Bull would need one of Verstappen's “magical Mexico stints”.

That also appeared to work in practice, although Verstappen feared he would be the one to lose out when he saw the safety car come out.

"Charles was very close, but at the same time, it's very hard to follow around here because everything overheats,” he said. “That probably helped me as well because I think, at one point, Charles had to back off just for cooling. That was quite nice for me.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

"But when I saw the safety car come out just out of the last corner and I couldn't box, I was like, ‘there's no way this is happening now’, because that was probably game over for me."

A subsequent red flag gave Verstappen the opportunity to change tyres as well, although it also meant there would be another standing start – not necessarily Red Bull's strongest point this year.

"It ended up being a red flag, so then it reset everything,” said the world champion. “I was a bit worried because our starts this year have not been amazing, but luckily today, twice, they have actually been good, and that then made my way ‘til the end."

Red Bull surprised by lenient penalty for Leclerc

Team principal Laurent Mekies also praised the strategy team post-race and acknowledged that they had immediately made amends for the US Grand Prix, where its execution had not been at the desired level.

"It was once again an extremely strong execution,” said Mekies. “The team is so strong when race day comes and they are taking a lot of risks in every race. The striking rate is pretty impressive, even though, as you said, not everything was perfect in Austin.

"It's the usual suspects with the strategy group and the people on the pit wall that came up with that when we heard Charles was coming in. That was the best option. We had just about the gap to him considering the penalty. We took the shot and it worked."

Laurent Mekies, Red Bull Racing Team Principal Photo by: Jayce Illman / Getty Images

Red Bull also felt that the penalty itself was rather lenient, as Mekies admitted: "The first thing that comes to your mind is that should be a penalty. And therefore we were certainly a bit surprised by how long it took to see the penalty confirmed.

"And in some respects, we were also surprised that it was only five seconds. Because probably at the time they had given that penalty, I think Charles was already five seconds clear from Lewis anyway.

"So it felt a bit light, but it's what it is. We race with what we have."

Ultimately, it still proved enough for Verstappen's third victory of the 2026 season, which also moved him up to second place in the world championship standings.

However, the Dutchman has already told Autosport that finishing second or third in the final standings would mean "nothing" to him, as he only cares about winning the world title.

Sports.title: What was Antonelli’s best moment of his F1 title-winning campaign? Our writers have their say
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli’s record-breaking Formula 1 world championship triumph was highlighted by many superb performances. But which one was his best?

Antonelli duly wrapped up his maiden F1 crown in Mexico with four rounds to spare – becoming the youngest-ever world champion in the process.

Our writers have picked out the moments they believe turned the Italian from a contender into a world champion in waiting.

Melbourne crash response offered first glimpse of new Kimi – Filip Cleeren

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

It may sound odd to pick one of Antonelli's few defeats against Russell, but his runner-up spot to the Briton at the season opener in Melbourne showed me the first tranche of evidence that the Antonelli who had rocked up Australia wasn't the same insecure rookie who had struggled through spells of 2025.

The Albert Park weekend was actually one of Antonelli's more challenging weekends, suffering a heavy 25G crash in FP3 that looked set to derail his weekend. It may have done a year prior, but this time the young Italian stayed cool and collected. And as Mercedes was able to pull off a full rebuild just in time for qualifying, Antonelli was able to shake off the incident and take second on the grid behind Russell despite not being able to finetune the car's set-up.

In the race Antonelli then suffered from a poor getaway with no battery power as he was swamped and dropped to sixth, but Mercedes' pace advantage was thus that he was able to make a controlled recovery to second.

"If something like that had happened to me last year, the rest of the weekend would probably have been very compromised," Antonelli reflected in Austin. "When you have one year of experience, one full year in Formula 1, you come back the next year and you just feel better. Things happen a bit more easily, let's say, also because you're not forcing them to happen as much.

"I kind of took a step back in that regard and just tried to focus on the important things and enjoy the process as much as possible. Definitely, mentally I've been in a much happier place this year compared to last season. And especially when you've been working with the same group of people for one year, going into year two is a big difference as well. You know how to move on together as a team, especially from difficult situations."

Canadian GP:Antonelli's real statement drive – Ewan Gale

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

By the time F1 had rocked up to the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve, Antonelli had already proven that he possesses some of the traits needed to be successful.

Yet this was the first real ding-dong battle we had seen between the Italian and an adversary that meant something. Fighting for the lead with Russell throughout the first half of the race, we saw that Antonelli was not going to be a pushover for his more experienced team-mate in the race for the title.

Let's not pretend that it was perfect racecraft - far from it. Both drivers left the road and came close to taking each other out - crucially avoiding what would have made for an angry Toto Wolff.

Antonelli grabbed track position off the line in damp conditions and initially fended off Russell's advances, only for the Briton to sweep into the lead on lap six, almost being swiped off-track by the #12 as the now-trailing Mercedes locked up into the final chicane.

What was impressive was that Antonelli put that to one side and kept up his assault. He didn't shy away after such a sizeable mistake that could have ended in disaster, it was a real show of the tenacity and exuberance we have come to love from him.

This was showcased best by an ultimately unsuccessful dive up the inside at Turn 1 on lap 13 as this regulation set's yo-yo racing showed its head. Side-by-side into the last chicane on lap 24 and inches - perhaps centimetres - from contact, Antonelli stayed in the fight for as long as possible before bailing, and then complaining on team radio, much like we often here from four-time champion Max Verstappen.

The fight was brought to an early end when Russell suffered a mechanical failure on lap 30 while still ahead and whether he would have won or not had his team-mate remained in the race - and reminiscent of how Nico Rosberg came out fighting against Lewis Hamilton in 2016 - Antonelli had set out his stall and delivered a statement; 'I can stand up to Russell one-to-one'.

His most perfect performance of his championship triumph? Nowhere near. But the message sent to team-mate Russell and those watching on spoke loud enough.

Monaco magic showed Antonelli could match aggression with precision – Stuart Codling

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

From his maiden appearance in FP1 at Monza in 2024 onwards, Antonelli has been among the most exciting drivers to watch. Often you could argue that he has tended towards a harum-scarum style, perpetually on the limit and sometimes beyond it.

In the year that he became the first Italian world champion since Alberto Ascari, Antonelli showed another element of his craft which aligned him more closely with his predecessor. In an era of flexing chassis suspended on leaf springs and riding on skinny tyres, Ascari was a beacon of consistency. Lap after lap he would hit the same line through each corner with unruffled finesse.

Monaco, a track where taking liberties with the barriers results in rapid elimination, was where Antonelli noticeably stepped up his game. On a weekend where Ferrari was expected to be dominant, Antonelli set pole position and raced to his fifth consecutive victory, pressured constantly from behind.

“We were surprised ourselves about that speed,” Wolff said after the race. “The laps he was pulling, the times, they were two seconds faster than the McLarens, and a solid plus one second faster than Ferrari. And it was like clockwork. Why that is on a track that we would have not considered to be our strengths before the weekend, I don’t know.”

The Spa weekend that Antonelli stopped any momentum Russell was starting to build – Ed Hardy

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

For the early part of the 2026 season, even during Antonelli’s winning run, I was still adamant that George Russell would become world champion. I found it hard to believe that Antonelli really had overturned such a large gap between the pair - 169 points in 2025 - over just one winter and that when faced with adversity, the Italian’s lack of experience would show.

Those doubts were removed in Belgium: arguably the first time he’d arrived at a grand prix this year on the back foot. In two of the prior three races - Austria and Britain - Antonelli had suffered non-scores due to car problems, while Russell took a win and two runner-up finishes to close the gap to 25 points.

The Briton had the momentum and with 14 rounds still to play, his deficit was hardly anything. Just look at last season, when late on Oscar Piastri flustered a larger gap of 34 points at the sudden moment he lost momentum to Lando Norris.

But in Belgium, Antonelli stayed calm and restored the order. He topped two of three practice sessions, took pole, and overcame an untimely VSC by overtaking brief leader Charles Leclerc for victory.

For Russell, he qualified five tenths off Antonelli in fifth and retired after a lap one clash with Hamilton’s Ferrari. The deficit to his Mercedes team-mate rose to 50 points and from there, it was quite obvious where the title would go.

It is not about how one falls, but about how they get back up, and Antonelli did that perfectly at Spa. A true champion-like weekend.

Monza: A recovery for the ages – Ben Vinel

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

Of Antonelli’s stellar drives in 2026, this likely was the most formidable.

The odds really weren’t in his favour. Norris had driven the upgraded McLaren to victory in the previous two rounds; Mercedes decided to give Antonelli a new power unit for his home race, taking the brunt of a back-of-the-grid start at a Monza track where overtaking theoretically is easier than anywhere else.

Antonelli qualified just seventh as Pierre Gasly took a shock pole, but that was simply down to the Italian giving team-mate Russell a tow in Q3, as his own result didn’t matter in light of the grid penalty.

Antonelli climbed to 12th within the opening two laps of the race, after which it was red-flagged for Leclerc’s high-speed crash; he gained another four positions at the second start, then passed Arvid Lindblad and Norris on the next lap.

Subsequent moves on Gasly, Hamilton and Piastri meant Antonelli was hot on Verstappen’s and Russell’s tails by lap 15. He made short work of them both, snatching the lead in Turn 1 on lap 18.

Russell did put up a decent challenge thereafter with a breathtaking battle, but the race was neutralised by the virtual safety car on lap 28. Antonelli, on mediums, pitted for another set of the yellow-walled compound; Russell, on hards, didn’t.

Antonelli rejoined 14 seconds adrift of his team-mate; again, he made his way past Gasly, Norris, Hamilton and Piastri, catching the sister Silver Arrow with six laps remaining. A trip through the gravel in wheel-to-wheel combat only briefly delayed the 20-year-old’s triumph, and he took victory from 19th on the grid – only John Watson ever did better than this, winning the 1983 United States Grand Prix West from 22nd. Antonelli’s fastest lap was seven tenths quicker than anyone else’s.

“After the second restart I was up there and I knew I could have a shot for the win,” he said. “So, definitely I believed in it, especially when I was behind George.

“But it was really difficult to break away, with the tow being so strong. At the end, we pitted and he stayed out and he struggled a bit with his tyres, while with fresher tyres I was able to increase the pace and, yeah, managed to win it.”

Was this the best race of his career? “The best one has yet to come, but I feel like, yeah, it was one of the best races I’ve done so far, and one that I will remember forever.”

Bouncing Baku: Antonelli fell in Azerbaijan, but quickly got up – Jake Boxall-Legge

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Gabriel Bortoleto, Audi F1 Team, Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Selecting the race where Antonelli made his own life incredibly difficult is, without context, a seemingly odd choice to make. Nothing is ever context-free, however.

When he clipped the inside wall at Turn 1 during the first stage of qualifying for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, Antonelli had already guaranteed himself a path to Q2 - but no further, as Mercedes knew the damage couldn't be repaired in time. He was guaranteed to start 16th, and with clear parallels to the horror-show weekend Piastri had endured a year before. That race is generally regarded to be the turning point in the championship, as Piastri unceremoniously dumped himself out of qualifying and, a day later, the race on the first lap.

But Antonelli was of no mind to entertain such parallels. He knew that the Baku weekend was now about mitigating the damage to his title lead, since Russell had uncovered a rich vein of performance and on course to win the grand prix. To limit Russell's victory prize, Antonelli had to stay in the race and made the decision to drive within himself and take plenty of margin in the opening laps. After that, he could let the Mercedes chassis underneath him do the work in bringing him through the field. He even lost a position at the start but, unlike Piastri's self-immolation in 2025, he remained in the race.

With care, Antonelli mounted a series of slide-rule passes on the midfielders to ease into the top 10, and the second-half safety car produced by Alex Albon presented Antonelli with an opportunity to close up to the rest of the pack and reclaim further points. His cause was helped further by the restart fracas, produced by Franco Colapinto, which took Norris and Gasly out of Antonelli's way; Hamilton then fell prey to Antonelli a few laps after the restart.

It was a masterclass in damage limitation, one admittedly helped by drivers ahead coming into strife, but Antonelli could easily have been claimed by an incident over the 50-lap tour around the Baku streets. That he didn't, and ultimately limited Russell to only a 15-point gain on what could have been a disastrous weekend, ensured Antonelli had dug himself out of a pretty big hole.

F1’s new star showed what he’s really made of in the Lone Star State – Ronald Vording

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Although his charge through the field at Monza was his most memorable performance of the year – one of those days when simply being at the track already felt special – the US GP was probably his most impressive race.

In Austin, the entire media day revolved around just one subject: the possibility of clinching the world title in the Lone Star State. Admittedly, it was hardly Abu Dhabi 2021, and yes, Antonelli's enormous lead took away much of the pressure, but there was still pressure on the shoulders of a 20-year-old who was only in his second F1 season.

It would have been very easy to lose his head during the weekend of his first opportunity to clinch the title, and given his enormous lead, it would not even have had any consequences. But the fact that Antonelli delivered his best performance precisely that weekend says a great deal about what he is made of.

To be precise, Sunday in Austin was revealing for three reasons. The first moment came on the grid. This writer spent some time standing next to Antonelli's Mercedes W17. The world champion-in-waiting looked up at the big screens, where he spotted himself and some of his fans. It brought a smile to his face and prompted a friendly wave. It is characteristic of his youthful enthusiasm and, as Verstappen rightly pointed out in Mexico, perhaps his greatest quality as a person is that he remains his friendly and playful self despite the success and pressure. Let's hope that aspect never changes.

The second way in which Austin was revealing is even more important: his pure performance, and therefore how Antonelli delivered on track. Despite the pressure and perhaps the nerves surrounding his impending world title, the Italian delivered flawlessly. In fact, on the slightly uphill grid at the Circuit of the Americas, the youngster arguably made his best start of the year. His pace afterwards was equally impressive, and he had made it his personal mission not to pick up a single-track limits infringement, something he duly managed apart from one little moment involving Carlos Sainz.

The overall package resulted in his most complete and mature F1 race to date, on the very weekend of his first opportunity to clinch the title. It says a great deal about his capabilities, but that leads to the third point: Antonelli refused to take the credit himself. When I asked him in the post-race press conference exactly how he deals with the pressure, Antonelli did what he always does: rather than pointing to himself, he pointed to his father, the rest of his family and the people around him at Mercedes.

It is highly commendable and modest, but Austin made one thing clear: Antonelli himself deserves considerably more credit than he was willing to take. Modesty is a good quality, however, so he doesn't need to say it. We'll do that for him.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Sports.title: Hamilton slams Leclerc for "do or die" attitude after Mexico GP clash
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has criticised team-mate Charles Leclerc for his “do or die” attitude after Ferrari lost a straightforward victory at the Formula 1 Mexico Grand Prix.

The seven-time world champion started on pole at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez with Leclerc third, but he rose to second when George Russell lost momentum into Turn 1.

It was there that the Monegasque attacked Hamilton on the outside with the hope of completing it down the inside of Turn 2, but he instead ran over that kerb and remained second.

But it continued as Leclerc again made a move on his team-mate at the outside of Turn 4, yet space quickly disappeared and he took evasive action by cutting Turn 5 to gain the lead.

Hamilton was consequently overtaken by Max Verstappen, who subsequently took first due to Leclerc’s five-second penalty for the lap one fiasco, leading to the Red Bull driver winning.

The Briton ultimately finished second ahead of new world champion Kimi Antonelli, while Leclerc took fourth, meaning Ferrari remained on just two wins across the 2026 campaign.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

A furious Hamilton said: “When I was at Mercedes, I watched and witnessed the back and forth between Charles and Carlos [Sainz] several races, where they were battling so much that the person ahead just pulled away, and they had the pace to actually win.

“But it is one thing when that's happening in fourth and fifth, as opposed to first and second, and you lose the win. That's significant.

“The guy is 28 years old [sic], so I don't think it's an age thing. I think it's a mentality thing.

“It's like, ‘Do or die. Either I win or none of us do’, and it shouldn't be that. It should be us getting that 1-2.”

Sunday was the latest in a series of heated moments between Leclerc and Hamilton recently, starting with Zandvoort where the Briton was held up and criticised the lack of team orders.

Then the following race at Monza, Hamilton lost positions after being forced onto the gravel at Turn 2, which Leclerc took responsibility for, so the Briton reckons “serious talks” are needed.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

But he’s unsure how much of a difference that will make and after Mexico on Sunday, Leclerc told Sky Sports that “there was a gap and when you are fighting for a win, I will always go for it”.

“I don't know what needs to happen now, how we discuss things when we go back,” said Hamilton.

“I'm not quite sure how I want to engage in that. Of course, the frustrations are today. I'm happy because this guy just won the championship, so I'm really torn because, on one side, I'm happy, and on the other side, I'm really pissed.

“We lost valuable points, and we, as a team, worked so hard. We could have easily had a 1-2 today. Really, we had the pace to do so.

“We're going into Turn 4 first and second. If we just hold position, I think anything can happen in the race. But when your team-mate works against you and then you lose positions like that, it's definitely tough.

“So, we'll just talk about it offline, and it's not really worth saying too much more. We don't have rules of engagement, and whether or not that will change anything from Charles' side, I don't know.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“We've just got to figure it out, but something needs to change for sure.”

Hamilton’s comments were made with the staff at Maranello in mind amid it going yet another year without a world title, as it trails champion-elect Mercedes by 126 points.

“Fred's doing his best,” said Hamilton of team boss Fred Vasseur. “I think Fred came and spoke to me before the race, and I think he was nervous.

“He just wanted us... Of course, he wants these two drivers to do well. From my side, if I'm coming from behind and I'm taking all the risk and it ends up that we lose as a team, then I think I have some answering to do, because it impacts a lot of people.

“But the other way around, I'm in the lead, and it was just unnecessary. I think we could have easily, as I said, had that 1-2 today, which would have been huge for the team and for everyone back at the factory who's worked so hard to bring us these upgrades.

“I don't really know what will be done because up until now nothing really has been done. So, yeah, we'll see.”

Sports.title: Piastri out of F1 Mexico GP points after post-race penalty for Lindblad clash
Sports.content:
Oscar Piastri’s tough Mexico Grand Prix weekend has ended in point-less fashion, after the McLaren Formula 1 driver copped a penalty for his collision with Arvid Lindblad.

Piastri’s 60-strong streak of Q3 appearances (including sprints) ended at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez as he qualified a lowly 12th, which paved the way for his troubles in the midfield.

Piastri did gain three spots at the start, subsequently overtaking Franco Colapinto and Lindblad to grab seventh place. The Australian led the rookie by 13 seconds when Valtteri Bottas crashed out, but the subsequent safety car and standing start reduced that gap to next to nothing – and Lindblad actually moved ahead at lights out.

Piastri pressured his rival for 12 laps before attacking him around the outside in Turn 1; now on the inside line for Turn 2, he didn’t back off early enough and hit the Racing Bulls’ rear-left wheel with his front-right. Lindblad ended up in the wall.

“I tried to go up the inside actually, and then he shut the door very, very late,” the McLaren man recounted. “So I had to kind of avoid him and end up on the outside.

“I tried from there, and obviously he pushed me pretty wide, and at that point I knew I was not going to completely overtake. So I was trying to get out, but he pushed me so far wide that I couldn't go any further left, and we just interlocked wheels, and that was the end result, of course.”

Oscar Piastri, McLaren, Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Asked if he was far enough alongside that he should have been given racing room based on driving guidelines, Piastri responded: “It's always tricky. I was very close to alongside, and I was kind of there because I was avoiding a crash in the first place.

“A tricky one, but I think when we actually made contact, we were both going straight. It wasn't like I tried to stick my nose into Turn 2 and stuck my nose where I shouldn't. I was trying to concede the position, and I was already off the track, so I couldn't really do much more than that.”

Meanwhile, Lindblad wouldn’t comment on the incident, having not been able to watch a replay, but still made his thoughts clear: “In the end, we were fast, I was in a genuine race with him, he was stuck behind me for over 10 laps. I was committed for racing for the position, and I wasn't just going to let him easily drive around the outside of me.”

The FIA’s stewards took a dim view of Piastri’s driving, handing him a 10-second penalty that dropped him from seventh to outside the points-scoring positions.

“On the approach to Turn 1, the driver of Car 81 attempted an overtake on the outside of Car 41,” the stewards’ report read. “Car 81 was never fully alongside Car 41 so was not able to claim the right to the corner. Through Turn 1, the driver of Car 41 defended his position by releasing the brakes, however does not force Car 81 off the track, allowing racing room on the outside – which he is not required to do.

“The Stewards determined that the collision could have been avoided if the driver of Car 81 had moved further to the left after Turn 1, even if this involved leaving the track prior to Turn 2.”

Having endured a tough season, Piastri will be disappointed – all the more after nursing a damaged McLaren to the finish line.

“I tried to get a number on how much damage I had,” he said. “I could kind of sense in Tom [Stallard, race engineer]'s voice that we had a lot of damage. When I looked at the car afterwards, it was pretty significant, so it was hard work. I think we had enough pace to be able to hang on reasonably comfortably in the end, but yeah, not the easiest last 10 laps for sure.”

Additional reporting by Stuart Codling and Ronald Vording

Sports.title: Official: Ocon will not return to drive for Haas, Camara to take over in Brazil | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Haas has confirmed Esteban Ocon will not return to drive for them following his shock ousting for the team last weekend.

Rafael Camara , who was due to make his Formula 1 debut for the team next year, will take over Ocon’s car from this weekend’s round in Brazil.

Ocon participated in Friday’s second practice session in Mexico and was due to remain in the car for the rest of the weekend. However Haas unexpectedly announced on Friday morning that Ocon’s place had been taken by Ryo Hirakawa, the team’s test driver who participated in the first practice session driving Ocon’s car.

Ocon subsequently issued a statement confirming there had been a difference of opinion between him and the team but strongly denying any claims “physical violence was used to resolve any differences”. He challenged race engineer Laure Mueller’s instruction regarding tyre strategy during second practice.

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu has not explained the team’s reasons for dropping Ocon.

“We have now notified Esteban Ocon that he will not return to a race seat with TGR Haas F1 Team this season,” he said in a statement issued by the team. “Such decisions are never made lightly, as was the case in Mexico City – but then, as now, we feel this is firmly in the best interest of the team moving forward.

“The conversations that ultimately unfolded between the team and Esteban remain an internal matter, and we will continue to respect the private nature of closed-door situations.”

Haas announced last month that Ocon won’t return to drive for the team next year. Camara will therefore make his debut at his home race this weekend.

The team has not given any indication who will drive for them at in the final three rounds of the championship. Komatsu said Camara “excelled in his TPC [Testing of Previous Cars] outing in August.”

“We know Rafa’s capabilities and we’re looking forward to welcoming him into the team this weekend and working with him through his Formula 1 debut driving the VF-26 in Brazil,” he added.

Sports.title: “Silly” power unit rules prevent passing, says Hamilton: “The engine can go faster” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1’s power unit rules made it harder for drivers to race at the Mexican Grand Prix, according to Lewis Hamilton.

The Ferrari driver spent the final laps of the race trying to attack race leader Max Verstappen . He said he was unable to do so because of the limits on energy deployment. This causes the effect known as “clipping”, where the amount of power being delivered drops.

“You can’t overtake here,” said Hamilton in the post-race press conference with Verstappen and Andrea Kimi Antonelli. “I think it’s something the FIA need to [address]. It’s just quite bad, I’m sure these guys would agree.

“We have this clip at the end of the straight where you can’t go past a certain speed, so everyone just follows. It’s the silliest thing when you are behind and you have a little bit more power in the slipstream. You should be able to go past that to have a chance to overtake.

“The engine can go faster, it’s just they have these silly clips. It’s the worst engine profile setting that I think they’ve probably ever had in this sport and it doesn’t provide great racing. So today you probably didn’t see much overtaking, unfortunately, because of that.”

Other drivers warned before the race that the “speed limiter” would inhibit overtaking. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali has rejected criticism of the series power units and said fans “don’t understand” what clipping is.

Hamilton acknowledged other factors make overtaking especially difficult in Mexico. The high altitude means the air pressure is lower which makes it harder to keep cars cool when running in traffic. He also thinks the track’s configuration could be improved.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Obviously the starts were fun, but it’s a very hard track to follow [other cars at] with the thin air and low downforce. I gave it everything to try and get close to Max.

“I don’t know if they need to change the last corner because it’s so quick. I don’t know, there could be a change to the track, maybe, to enable us to have a little bit better racing.

“But everyone having this [clipping] this year just diminishes any opportunity of that.”

Sports.title: Antonelli says doubters “added fuel to the fire” in his world championship pursuit | Formula 1
Sports.content:
New world champion Andrea Kimi Antonelli says he was driven to disprove those who said he wasn’t ready for Formula 1.

Mercedes brought him up through the junior ranks quickly, skipping Formula 3 entirely and only spending a single season in Formula 2. Antonelli made his F1 debut last year, aged just 18, with Mercedes’ works F1 team rather than one of their customers.

Antonelli’s first season did not go entirely smoothly. He endured a nine-round spell during which he failed to score on seven occasions.

However he was competitive right from the start of his second season and quickly overtook team mate George Russell in the championship. Antonelli clinched the title yesterday with four rounds to spare.

He said that had been a satisfying response to those who suggested he wasn’t ready for F1.

“It’s always good to shut off some of the noise,” said Antonelli. “I think in many ways it does help to add fuel to the fire, the fact that some people said that I didn’t belong in Formula 1 or I wasn’t ready for it.

“At some points last year, it probably looked like that I wasn’t ready for it. But I think last year, being able to experience those moments made me much more ready ahead of this year. Experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year, and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver and as a person.”

Antonelli clinched the title with nine grand prix wins, the most of any driver. But he admits there was room for improvement in his performance. “I’ve had moments where I could have done better, a lot better. It’s just a constant learning process.

“But I think last year, being able to race [with] Mercedes, obviously [going] straight under the spotlight, made me grow much, much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example.”

Sports.title: Social Media: Russell vows to rediscover his performance after “more bad days than good” in 2026 | Brief

He also offered his congratulations to team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli , who won the title yesterday.

It’s been the first proper season of my career where I’ve had more bad days than good.

“Has it been tough to deal with? Yes, very. Has it been tough to pick myself up week in, week out? Yes, very. Confusion at times? Often. All I know is that I’ve given it my all and 2026 was not meant to be my year.

“Now, all I can promise is that for the rest of this season, and into the next one, I will be giving my absolute all to rediscover the performance I have been capable of producing for the majority of my career and fingers crossed a little bit of luck returns.

Sports.title: Leclerc has wrong mentality, says Hamilton: ‘It’s ‘do-or-die, either I win or none of us do” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari would have lost more wins this year if he had the same “kamikaze” mentality as team mate Charles Leclerc.

The seven-times world champion blamed his team mate for costing Ferrari victory in yesterday’s Mexican Grand Prix. Both he and Leclerc went off at turn four while fighting over the lead on lap one.

Hamilton said he’d noticed Leclerc’s battles with his predecessor Carlos Sainz Jnr cost Ferrari points in the past.

“Before I joined this team, when I was at Mercedes, I watched and witnessed the back and forth between Charles and Carlos several races, where they were battling so much that the person ahead just pulled away, and they had the pace to actually win,” he said. “But it is one thing when that’s happening in fourth and fifth, as opposed to first and second, and you lose the win. That’s significant.

“The guy [Leclerc] is 28 years old, so I don’t think it’s an age thing. I think it’s a mentality thing. It’s like, “Do-or-die. Either I win or none of us do,” and it shouldn’t be that. It should be us having, getting that one-two.”

Hamilton pointed out he did not compromise Leclerc’s race when he won at Silverstone earlier this year. “In Silverstone, I could have gone all kamikaze on him and taken him off and lost us the win, but instead the one-two was there.” They finished first and third but were holding the top two positions before Hamilton pitted when the Safety Car was deployed.

“For me, I’m happy for the team to have experienced that, but I’m hopeful we’ll work towards a better working place in the future.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

In remarks similar to those of Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur, Hamilton said the result did not do justice to the effort made by the team.

“I think the core thing to remember, which maybe comes with age, is that every decision you make in the car impacts all the people that work in the background for the whole team,” he said. “So, working as a team is a part of our job and a part of our contract.

“We have to work as a team, which we could have easily done today. So, it’s a shame to see us lose this, as we did. That will just continue unless action is taken, if a real deep, serious conversation is had. So, it shouldn’t happen [again] moving forward.

“Of course, I’ve had close battles with team mates in the past, and you can’t always get it right, but nine times out of ten we should be able to. So, I think we’ll take it offline and we’ll have some good conversations, hopefully. For sure, it won’t be easy, but it must be done.”

However Hamilton admitted he’d experienced tougher situations previously at other teams, such as at Mercedes, where he and team mate Nico Rosberg once took each other out at the start of a race.

“I’ve had way worse times at Mercedes. There were some really bad moments. I don’t really see there being huge differences. I think it was managed well at Mercedes, and I think Fred’s doing his best.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Fred came and spoke to me before the race, and I think he was nervous. Of course, he wants [his] two drivers to do well.”

He said he would have had to explain his actions had he attacked his team mate from behind the way Leclerc did.

“From my side, if I’m coming from behind and I’m taking all the risk and it ends up that we lose as a team, then I think I have some answering to do, because it impacts a lot of people. But the other way around, I’m in the lead, and it was just unnecessary.

“I think we could have easily had that one-two today, which would have been huge for the team and for everyone back at the factory who’s worked so hard to bring us these upgrades. I don’t really know what will be done because up until now nothing really has been done.”

Sports.title: Antonelli “lost two seconds because I was crying” at end of Mexican GP | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli admitted he was already crying before he took the chequered flag to win the world championship.

The Mercedes driver finished third in Mexico, clinching the title in his second season as a Formula 1 driver. The 20-year-old was so emotional he was struggling to see the track and he lost 1.8 seconds to the leaders on his final lap.

“I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying, basically,” Antonelli admitted. “I couldn’t see clearly ahead.

“I could see two Ferraris, somehow, with the tears. So it was very special.”

Antonelli became the youngest world champion in F1 history, just five years after moving from karts to cars. “A lot of memories went through my mind in that moment,” he said, “all the memories since karting all the way to here.

“It was a very special final lap, and definitely when I crossed the line, I let it all out because it was just achieving one of my biggest dreams. It was very special.”

The championship outcome was a foregone conclusion before the weekend began: Antonelli needed to score only two points to be certain of the title even if his closest rival won all the remaining rounds. Nonetheless he felt the weight of expectation during the weekend.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I knew I was very close. However, I still needed to get the job done, and, of course, you still want to do a good race. You want to do a good performance, so that was the goal.

“But it hasn’t been the easiest weekend either. Physically, I haven’t been in the best shape, but also yesterday we had a bad qualifying execution, and emotions were a bit high overall.

“But I’m really happy that today we did a strong race and really happy that we managed to finish the job. And then now we’ve got a few races to go, and we’re just going to enjoy all the way and try to finish on a high.”

He made a careful start to the race, ceding a position to eventual winner Max Verstappen on the run to turn one. However he decided to risk more at the second standing start following a red flag period.

“At the start I was very cautious, and I gave a lot of room. So I was probably playing it very much on the safe side.

“But then I saw I had the pace, and especially that first stint, I knew we would be in the fight because the pace was very good on used tyres.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Then with the red flag, it kind of all went back to zero. And in that moment I was like, ‘You know what? I’m just going to take more risks.’

“I had the opportunity to gain a few places, and that move on Charles [Leclerc] was crucial to get on the podium. I tried until the end to stay close, and it was very fun, the last stint, because we were all, I think, the three of us within two seconds, and we were all pushing. It was just difficult, of course, to overtake, but it was high intensity, and it was fun.

“Then on the last lap I just backed off because I just couldn’t see the track. I was getting emotional, and I said, ‘I’m just going to back off because otherwise I crash here.’ So it was just good to bring it home.”
