World.title: Nigeria: The Assassination of a Peacemaker
World.content:
blog

An Islamic preacher's brutal after-dark execution is a tragic reminder of what is at stake in the struggle to vanquish jihadism in northern Nigeria.

It tells you everything you need to know about the moral confusion surrounding the jihadist insurgency that has throttled vast swaths of northern Nigeria that Sheikh Yahaya Masussuka, the respected Islamic cleric who was gunned down outside his Dutsin-Ma, Katsina state residence last week by two armed men on a motorcycle, is being described by sections of the media as "controversial." For, if Malam Masussuka was "controversial," it raises the legitimate question of what to call his assassins.

Prior to his assassination (a friend of the cleric, one Adamu Abubakar, also lost his life), Mr. Masussuka had received numerous death threats, including on social media, from those who wanted him to stop doing what he was doing: preaching against extremism, contesting conservative interpretations of sections of the Quran and Hadith, and generally being a voice for theological moderation and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians in the northern region of the country. In June 2025, Mr. Masussuka was honored for his efforts with a Peace Ambassador award by the Abuja-based Network for Good Governance and Transparency. Receiving the award, Mr. Masussuka reiterated the keynote of his advocacy as reorienting Nigerians "to embrace peace and unity" and challenging "hate speech and extremist ideologies."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

If Mr. Masussuka's message of peace and tolerance was music to some ears, there were others who bitterly resented what he stood for and were desperate to have him removed from the scene. For example, in November 2025, just five months after he was honored for his peacemaking interventions, Mr. Masussuka received an official summons from the Katsina state government "for questioning over allegations that his sermons contravene established principles of Islamic law." At the time, Mr. Masussuka had also complained to the government that he was being insulted by members of Jama'atu Izalatil Bid'ah wa Ikamatis Sunnah--commonly known as Izala or 'Yan Izala.

Last week, though, it wasn't an Izala member who finished off Mr. Masussuka and his friend. Rather, it was gunmen deputized by a different extremist group, Jama'atu Ansarul Muslimina Fi Biladis-Sudan (meaning "Vanguard for the Aid of Muslims in Black Africa"), popularly known as Ansaru, who did. We know this because the group has claimed responsibility through a four-minute video obtained by Premium Times, a leading Nigerian newspaper. In the video, the terror group did not mince words about why they decided to eliminate Mr. Masussuka: because he was "an (arnai) infidel, not a Muslim. He was contracted to disrupt Islam and confuse Muslims." While it is not clear from Ansaru's video who or what entity they believed had "contracted" Mr. Masussuka, what is beyond dispute is the group's bloodcurdling warning to "other infidels" who "belittle the Hadiths of the Prophet": "You should repent. You should stop, or else we are coming for you." Translation: Ansaru is coming for you if you dare insist that (Nigerian) Muslims and Christians should peacefully coexist.

For some time now, the origins of the decadeslong jihadist violence in northern Nigeria and much of the Sahel have been a subject of intense litigation. While some scholars and analysts have insisted that the violence has nothing to do with religion and that it is best seen as an expression of legitimate grievance against failing states, others (I belong to this group) have argued that not only is the violence mobilized by various terror groups ultimately religious in essence, neither the violence nor the totality of their praxes can be understood without recourse to this basic and inextricable religious factor. The latter position does not dispute the need for investment in good governance, or that such will not work to vitiate the appeal of terror groups to disaffected young men; the argument has always been that after all is said and done, we need to face the reality that there are those who engage in violence because they see it as a religious obligation. For such people, no amount of investment in good governance or infrastructure will do. If that were so, there would be zero extremism in societies where social opportunities are abundant, relatively speaking. As a matter of fact, part of what Islamist groups take exception to (and they could not be more transparent about this) is the very apparatus of the modern state that seeks to pacify and draw them into its fold. Their grouse, not to put too fine a point on it, is unbelief, not the poverty of good governance.

This is where the late Malam Masussuka comes in. The reader will notice that he was abused, threatened, and ultimately assassinated, not for his extremism, but because he disavowed extremism. In other words, Mr. Masussuka lost his life because he preached moderation and peaceful coexistence, and we need no further confirmation than the video message from Ansaru. How in the world this makes someone "controversial" (looking at you, BBC) is beyond me.

For context, Mr. Masussuka is not the first Islamic cleric in northern Nigeria to be silenced for good by armed gunmen. In May 2025, Islamic scholar Sheikh Mustapha Aliyu was brutally murdered by armed bandits who had earlier abducted him. Around the same time, Chief Imam Alkali Salihu Suleiman was killed by his abductors in the northwestern state of Zamfara. Sheikhs Jaafar Mahmud Adam and Auwal Albani Zaria, both respected Salafi scholars, lost their lives in similar circumstances in 2007 and 2014, respectively.

Nor, crucially, is this Ansaru's first rodeo as far as eliminating its ideological adversaries is concerned. Since its emergence as a splinter faction of Boko Haram in 2012, the group has been linked to several high-profile attacks and kidnappings across the country. These include the 2012 prison break in Abuja, the ambush of a Nigerian military convoy in 2013, the kidnapping and subsequent execution of seven foreign construction workers during the same year, and assaults on military bases leading to the execution of dozens of Nigerian army personnel in August 2020 and April 2022.

Ansaru is officially proscribed and designated as a terrorist organization by Nigeria, the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union.

All of which raises an interesting question: If Ansaru and the many cognate terror groups currently active in Nigeria and across the Sahel have not been shy about their aims, why is it that many commentators continue to play the ostrich, attributing to terror groups moral and political objectives that they unambiguously deny? One reason is that many are wary of antagonizing Muslims--especially Muslim minorities in Western countries. Such people wrongly equate condemning the rampages of Islamists with taking sides with alleged Islamophobes. Nothing could be further from the truth. Indeed, refusing to back moderates like Malam Masussuka only allows religious bigots in northern Nigeria--and elsewhere--to avoid confrontation with their own demons.

Close 

Failure to decisively champion the Masussukas of this world has another regrettable consequence. It lets bigots get away with not just bad but objectively regressive arguments. Those of us who care about modernity and its amenities can ill afford not to speak up against the plague that is Islamist terror, which, drilled down to its essence, is a rejection of life, value pluralism, and the right of the individual to choose what is best for him (and vitally, change his mind) in matters of faith. What this means is that, from the standpoint of the Islamist terrorist, we should all be "infidels." This particular point bears emphasizing because, if past experience is anything to go by, it really does not matter whether or not we are interested in Islamism. Islamists are interested in us, and there is no better antidote to their poisonous ideology than standing our argumentative ground and taking sides with and empowering moderates and peacemaking agents like the late Mr. Masussuka.

In the meantime, one would hope that this tragedy is the final nail in the coffin of the risible argument that violence in northern Nigeria has nothing to do with religion. As should be obvious by now, no amount of wishing Islamism away would make it disappear.

World.title: Africa: Women Still Shut Out of Power As Gender Bias Undermines Africa's Democracy
World.content:
Discriminatory social norms, unequal power relations and growing gender-based violence continue to undermine women's participation in political leadership across Africa, despite progress in representation and the adoption of laws promoting gender equality, United Nations and European Union officials have warned.

Speaking at the opening of a two-day Inter-Regional Dialogue on Advancing the Transformation of Gender Social Norms to Enhance Women and Youth Participation and Representation in Leadership and Decision-Making in Zanzibar, UN Women Representative in Tanzania, Julia Broussard, said women's political representation remained disproportionately low, with entrenched attitudes continuing to influence who gets opportunities to lead.

Broussard said women occupy just over a quarter of parliamentary seats across sub-Saharan Africa, while in Tanzania they account for approximately 38 per cent of Members of Parliament.

However, she warned that progress in representation had not necessarily translated into equal influence in decision-making spaces.



"Beyond the numbers, discriminatory social norms and unequal power relations continue to shape who is seen as a legitimate leader, whose voice is heard and whose contributions are valued," she said.

Citing the OECD's 2023 Social Institutions and Gender Index, Broussard said 43.9 per cent of Tanzanians believed men made better political leaders than women, highlighting the attitudes that continue to reinforce gender inequality in public life.

She said such perceptions had practical consequences, affecting the opportunities women receive, the support they can mobilise and their ability to influence decisions.

Women who venture into politics also face violence and intimidation, including technology-facilitated gender-based violence, which further discourages their participation.

Tanzania's Minister for Community Development, Gender, Elders and Children, Saada Mkuya Salum said women aspiring to political leadership continued to face social scrutiny and criticism that often left them with little opportunity to defend themselves.

"It's not easy at all. They will write. They will comment. They will do everything. And you don't have a chance actually to explain," she said.

She added that although progress had been made in empowering women, the systems and attitudes that historically excluded them remained firmly entrenched.

"So even the journey, women journey much as enhanced, are empowered somehow, but the journey has never and I believe it's not going to be that easy because of these systems that have been rooted," Mkuya said.

The Minister said Tanzania was proud of the progress made but warned that discriminatory social norms, weak institutional support and inadequate assistance for female candidates continued to undermine meaningful participation.

"We're proud of progress but they also tell us that when we are heading into the right direction we are not there yet and we will not get there as long as deep-rooted discriminatory social norms, institutions that support women's advancement and inadequate support for women candidates continue to restrict their participation," she said.

Mkuya also highlighted the additional burden placed on women by traditional household and caregiving responsibilities, which often leave them with less time and resources to build political networks, mobilise support and pursue leadership positions

European Union Ambassador to Tanzania and the East African Community, Jean-Marc Pisani, echoed the concerns, arguing that women's underrepresentation was not primarily a question of legal frameworks or leadership capabilities, but of deeply rooted social attitudes and the failure to translate commitments into practice.

Pisani said women held an average of 27 percent of parliamentary seats and 26 percent of local government positions across sub-Saharan Africa.

Regional disparities remain significant, with women accounting for approximately 31 percent of parliamentary representation in East and Southern Africa, 20 percent in Central Africa and 16 percent in West Africa.

Rwanda, where women hold 64 percent of parliamentary seats, demonstrates what can be achieved through political will and strong institutions, he said.

"Norms are not a cultural footnote to democracy. They determine who can take part in it," Pisani said, pointing to research showing that about half of the world's population still believes men make better political leaders than women.

He warned that violence against women in politics was increasingly moving into digital spaces, where abuse, threats and disinformation targeting female candidates and leaders were becoming additional obstacles to their participation.

"These are not private harms. They are attacks on democracy itself," he said.

Both officials called for a broader approach to gender equality, arguing that increasing the number of women in political institutions would not be enough without addressing the social and institutional barriers that limit their influence.

Broussard called for more inclusive political institutions, gender-responsive media coverage and the active involvement of men and boys in challenging discriminatory attitudes.

She also highlighted the importance of recognising young people, particularly young women, as agents of change rather than merely future leaders.

Pisani similarly urged men to take an active role in dismantling barriers by supporting women's political ambitions, speaking out against harassment and sharing decision-making power.

He also challenged journalists to examine how media narratives shape public perceptions of leadership and influence what girls believe they can achieve.

Close 

"The stories a society tells about leadership shape what its girls believe they can become," he said.

The two officials also pointed to ongoing interventions aimed at translating gender equality commitments into tangible improvements.

Broussard highlighted Tanzania's legislative reforms, including the recognition of violence against women in politics as an electoral offence under the Presidential, Parliamentary and Councillors Election Act.

She also cited initiatives supporting women parliamentarians through partnerships involving the Uwongozi Institute and the European Union, as well as community engagement programmes with the Tanzania Media Women's Association (TAMWA).

Pisani said the European Union had committed €90 million to its Gender Transformative Action programme, Breaking the Glass Ceiling, which supports gender-responsive policies, legal empowerment and community-level efforts to challenge discriminatory social norms.

The dialogue, bringing together participants from 23 countries, including journalists, women in politics and community leaders, is being convened by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA), with support from the European Union and UN Women.

The meeting seeks to facilitate exchanges on practical strategies for transforming gender norms and strengthening women's and young people's participation in leadership and decision-making.

World.title: Kenya: IG Kanja Denies Police Custody of Missing Tanzanian Activist Twaha Mwaipaya
World.content:
Nairobi — Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja has denied that security officers arrested or detained missing Tanzanian activist Twaha Mwaipaya, even as he faced questions in the High Court over investigations into a wave of abductions.

Appearing before the Milimani High Court on Tuesday, Kanja told Justice Alexander Muteti that Mwaipaya had never been in police custody anywhere in the country, distancing the National Police Service from his disappearance.

"My Lord, I'd wish to inform this court we don't have the subject in our custody throughout the Republic of Kenya," Kanja said.

He also denied knowledge of any arrest involving the activist by officers from the National Police Service, insisting that police could not have removed someone they had never detained.



However, Kanja confirmed that a report on Mwaipaya's disappearance had been lodged at Ruai Police Station and that investigations were ongoing.

The Inspector General's appearance came amid mounting pressure on security agencies to account for the activist, who was reportedly abducted on October 25 in Kamulu, Machakos County.

The court had directed police to produce Mwaipaya, dead or alive, following an application by human rights organisations led by Vocal Africa.

Kanja maintained that police treat reported abductions as criminal offences and initiate investigations whenever such incidents are reported.

"Not at all, we don't abduct and make people disappear," he told the court when questioned about allegations of police involvement in enforced disappearances.

"Any abduction is to be treated as an act of criminality," he added.

However, his assurance that investigations were underway faced questions over whether authorities had made progress in identifying and prosecuting those responsible for abductions.

During cross-examination, lawyers challenged Kanja to name individuals who had been arrested and brought to justice over abductions reported in the country.

Asked whether he could identify any perpetrators who had been held accountable, the police chief said several investigations were still ongoing.

"We have got many cases that are running even now. Investigations are still ongoing," he said.

Pressed further on whether any suspects had been brought to book, Kanja described the investigations as tedious, saying they involved extensive work.

He acknowledged that some cases could have been concluded but said he would need more time to provide details.

Close 

The police chief nevertheless maintained that Kenyans had confidence in his leadership, arguing that the country remained safe and secure.

"From north to south, from east to west, this country of ours is safe and secure. The properties of people are safe and secure. That is why Kenyan people are confident in the Inspector General," he said.

The activist was reportedly seized at around 2pm on October 25 while travelling in a taxi to visit friends in Kamulu.

Amnesty International Kenya and the Defenders Coalition said the individuals involved were travelling in three vehicles, including a Toyota Land Cruiser hardtop, and called on authorities to urgently establish his whereabouts and guarantee his safety.

The High Court is expected to give further directions on the petitioners' application as the search for Mwaipaya continues.

World.title: Uganda: Uganda Arrests Former Army Deputy Chief
World.content:
Former deputy chief and presidential adviser Peter Elwelu has been arrested over allegations of destabilising the country.

The Ugandan military has announced the arrest of its former deputy chief and presidential adviser Peter Elwelu over allegations of destabilising the country.

In a post shared via X, Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF)'s acting spokesperson Chris Magezi said Elwelu had been arrested on Monday, November 2, describing him as a "renegade" officer who was involved in subversive activities.

ALSO READ: RDF, UPDF hold proximity commanders meeting in Mbarara

Recently, Uganda's defence chief, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said he had stripped Elwelu of his Lieutenant General rank and demoted him to a private.

According to Magezi, security forces recovered 15 guns in Elwelu's possession, military fatigues, and two pick-up trucks.

"Elwelu has been on the run over involvement in subversive activities and plans to destabilise Teso," Magezi said.

ALSO READ: EASF military exercise tests region's readiness for crises

Last week, Kainerugaba accused Elwelu of stockpiling weapons and organising activities against the government. He ordered him to surrender, warning that anyone helping him evade arrest would face "serious consequences".

World.title: South Africa: South Africa Responds to U.S. Decision On AGOA Benefits Withdrawal
World.content:
From next year, South Africa will no longer be eligible for benefits under the AGOA trade pact.

Government says it has acknowledged the announcement by the United States government regarding its intention to withdraw South Africa's benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective from 1 January 2027, with a 60-day advance notice period.

Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau addressed the implications of the recent trade decision involving South Africa and the United States, affirming the country's commitment to a constructive and balanced partnership.

"This decision does not define the broader relationship between South Africa and the United States, however, a solution depends on the willingness of both parties to find solutions," Tau stated, highlighting the importance of ongoing dialogue to resolve trade challenges.

He assured that the South African government is focused on protecting the interests of sectors affected by the decision.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"At the same time, government will support affected sectors, protect South Africa's national interests and continue pursuing trade, investment and shared economic opportunities with the United States," Tau said.

Acknowledging the significance of the US as a key trade and investment partner, the Minister reaffirmed South Africa's dedication to a balanced and mutually beneficial partnership.

"South Africa has affirmed its commitment to a balanced and mutually beneficial partnership that supports preferential trade, beneficiation of critical minerals at source and investment promotion."

Tau reiterated South Africa's sovereign responsibilities and goals. "As a sovereign constitutional democracy, South Africa will uphold its constitutional responsibilities, transformation objectives, and international obligations, while seeking practical solutions to expand trade and investment," he affirmed.

This stance underscores South Africa's commitment to advancing economic growth through strategic partnerships, while safeguarding national interests and fostering equitable development.

Mutual benefit

The South African Government says it remains engaged in efforts to navigate trade challenges and strengthen cooperation with the United States.

Government also recognises the concerns this decision raises for workers, exporters, businesses, and communities connected to AGOA-supported value chains, and that the impact will vary across different sectors.

Government is actively collaborating with affected industries to assess the full implications.

Despite extensive efforts by South Africa to respond constructively to US concerns, including offering additional concessions beyond those agreed in 2015 through the proper channels, the US has introduced new issues outside the scope of the ongoing negotiation process that began in 2025.

"These concessions respect due process, safeguard South Africa's biosecurity and constitutional imperatives and its obligations under World Trade Organisation rules. It is, however, unfortunate that the US is now raising new issues that have not been the basis for discussions as part of the negotiations process that commenced in 2025.

"AGOA still holds significance for South Africa but does not represent the entirety of the economic relationship between the two countries," government said in a statement.

In 2025, about 89% of South African exports to the US were under ordinary World Trade Organisation most favoured nation terms, while only approximately 10% were AGOA exports -- a decline from 28% in 2024. AGOA exports totalled nearly US $1.7billion in 2025, down from US $4 billion in 2024, and accounted for roughly 1% of South Africa's total global exports.

Bilateral trade reached US$28.8 billion in 2025, with over 600 American companies operating in South Africa and supporting approximately 134 600 jobs. Trade relations between the two are complementary and mutually beneficial.

Close 

South Africa plays a critical role in supplying key minerals to the US, including 12 of the 50 minerals deemed critical by the US, and 70% of US isotopes used in cancer treatments. Additionally, South Africa sources inputs from the US for goods manufactured for export under AGOA, such as automobiles and boat building.

South African investments in the US economy may be adversely affected by the AGOA withdrawal, potentially undermining existing value chains.

Government said it remains committed to diversifying export markets aggressively. Its Cabinet-approved Industrial Development Strategy and Butterfly Strategy are targeting new opportunities across the African Continental Free Trade Area, India, SADC, the European Union, the United Kingdom, ASEAN, MERCOSUR and China. New markets have also opened up for South African citrus, avocados, grapes and apples.

World.title: Somalia: Indian Navy Rescues 20 Crew Members From Hijacked Fishing Vessel Off Somalia
World.content:
Mogadishu — The Indian Navy has rescued all 20 crew members of a hijacked Iranian fishing vessel off the coast of Somalia following a 48-hour military operation involving naval forces and the Indian Air Force, India's Defence Ministry said on Tuesday.

The operation, completed on November 2, involved locating and intercepting the vessel, identified as Azini, which had been seized by armed pirates off Somalia's northeastern coast last month.

The ministry said all 20 crew members were freed safely, with no casualties or injuries reported.

The fishing vessel had been hijacked on October 29, raising concerns that it could be used as a so-called mother ship to launch further attacks on commercial vessels travelling through the strategically important shipping routes in the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Aden.



In response, the Indian Navy deployed a warship supported by maritime surveillance aircraft to locate and intercept the vessel.

According to the Defence Ministry, the naval platforms maintained persistent surveillance, tracked the vessel's movements and used calibrated non-kinetic measures to restrict its movement and prevent it from escaping.

Indian Marine Commandos, known as MARCOS, were subsequently deployed in a precision airdrop operation from an Indian Air Force C-17 military transport aircraft.

The commandos boarded and secured the fishing vessel, overcoming the pirate threat and freeing all the hostages.

India's Defence Minister Rajnath Singh congratulated the navy and other personnel involved in the operation, describing it as a demonstration of the country's ability to respond to maritime security threats far from its shores.

"The swift localisation, interception and safe release of the crew and vessel from significantly-armed pirates, with timely support from the Indian Air Force, speak well of the Indian Navy's high operational readiness and ability to respond decisively to maritime threats across the region," Singh said in a statement posted on X.

He added that the operation demonstrated India's commitment to protecting seafarers, securing maritime trade routes and maintaining stability across the Indian Ocean.

The rescue took place more than 3,000 kilometres from Mumbai, highlighting the operational reach of India's naval forces.

The incident comes amid renewed concerns over piracy off Somalia, where armed groups have stepped up hijackings of fishing vessels and commercial ships after years of relative calm.

Somali piracy reached its peak between 2008 and 2012, when armed groups seized numerous vessels and held crew members for ransom. International naval patrols and improved security measures subsequently helped reduce attacks.

Close 

However, a resurgence in piracy since late 2023 has raised fresh concerns about the security of international shipping routes connecting the Indian Ocean, the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea.

The Indian Navy said it remained committed to protecting maritime trade and ensuring safe passage for vessels operating across the Indian Ocean region.

World.title: Why isn’t Angel Reese held to the Caitlin Clark standard when fans attack her teammates?
World.content:
The WNBA media constantly demands that Caitlin Clark answer for internet trolls. They tell her she needs to condemn "racism, misogyny and homophobia," even though she has nothing to do with the messages other players receive on social media.

But does that standard change when the players facing online trolling are being attacked due to their proximity to a different WNBA star, one who receives very different treatment from those same commentators?

ANGEL REESE, ATLANTA DREAM DISAPPOINTED AFTER WNBA FINALS GAME 7 LOSS: 'WE'LL BE BACK'

Atlanta Dream players Jordin Canada and Rhyne Howard are now on the receiving end. And the hate isn't coming from supposed Caitlin Clark fans; it's coming from supposed Angel Reese fans.

Will the commentators who keep assigning Clark responsibility for other people’s behavior apply their standard to Reese?

Don't hold your breath.

For the record, I don’t think either player owes anyone a statement. Neither Clark nor Reese is responsible for what other people do or say online. However, I do think the people who keep demanding condemnations from Clark owe us an explanation as to why they aren't keeping up that energy when it's Reese at the center.

The responsibility assigned to Caitlin Clark

The list of WNBA media members who have openly called for Clark to denounce online hate, something Clark has done multiple times by the way, is almost too long to count. But let's recap a few of the biggest ones:

Nancy Armour: The USA Today columnist called on Clark "to publicly call out the racist and homophobic trash purporting to be her fans." Armour acknowledged Clark had already condemned the behavior but discounted that response because it came after a question rather than on Clark’s own initiative. Her conclusion: "She at least needs to try."

The USA Today columnist called on Clark "to publicly call out the racist and homophobic trash purporting to be her fans." Armour acknowledged Clark had already condemned the behavior but discounted that response because it came after a question rather than on Clark’s own initiative. Her conclusion: "She at least needs to try." Sarah Spain: On her podcast, Spain praised Armour’s column and said, "Caitlin didn’t ask for any of this, but she is still sort of responsible for helping shut it down."

On her podcast, Spain praised Armour’s column and said, "Caitlin didn’t ask for any of this, but she is still sort of responsible for helping shut it down." Elle Duncan: Duncan wanted Clark to tell supposed supporters: "stop that s--t, I don’t want it, I’m tired of it."

Duncan wanted Clark to tell supposed supporters: "stop that s--t, I don’t want it, I’m tired of it." Charlotte Wilder: The podcast host acknowledged Clark had spoken out but wanted "something a little more forceful." She suggested telling abusive supporters, "You are not a fan of mine if you are perpetuating this behavior and these actions."

The podcast host acknowledged Clark had spoken out but wanted "something a little more forceful." She suggested telling abusive supporters, "You are not a fan of mine if you are perpetuating this behavior and these actions." Etan Thomas: The Guardian columnist argued Clark should keep condemning fans, writing that "staying silent just isn’t an option."

Those examples span from 2024 through this season. So, this isn't new. These people have been making demands of Clark for three seasons, despite her repeated condemnations of the behavior.

CAITLIN CLARK SAYS SHE BLOCKS SOCIAL MEDIA HATE AND ENJOYS HOSTILE WNBA ROAD CROWDS

On July 3, Clark once again delivered a lengthy statement condemning online hate. She explicitly extended that condemnation to the treatment of opponents, teammates and coaches.

"The harassment, the hate, none of that is okay. … There should never be question of character. Like I’ve always stood up here and said that and that’s truly what I believe. That’s how I was raised. … none of that is okay. And I don’t want anybody to ever experience that," Clark said.

A reporter raised the subject again at her October 8 season-ending news conference. Asked about Kelsey Mitchell’s comments on the treatment she receives, Clark was also asked to address "the attention this team receives because of you, but maybe not attention that you necessarily asked for."

There’s that familiar framing again. Other people send the messages, but Clark gets asked to account for the attention surrounding her teammates.

So she answered. Again.

"As far as people that have used me to demonstrate racist rhetoric or hate or discrimination, that’s not something I stand for," Clark said.

The expectations come from commentators, the questions come from reporters, and Clark keeps giving them an answer.

But apparently, that still wasn’t enough.

On October 23, ESPN analyst Monica McNutt said: "There is no way that someone would use my likeness to support causes that I am against."

Clark has already told people she opposes that behavior. Repeatedly. How many more statements would satisfy McNutt?

And now that people defending Angel Reese are attacking Reese’s own teammates, does McNutt expect the same response from her?

My guess? Not a chance.

Where are the calls for Angel Reese to condemn online trolls?

Jordin Canada returned to social media after avoiding it during the playoffs and immediately found a reminder of why she had stayed away.

"It blows my mind that as fans yall CHOOSE to say the hurtful and cruel things out loud and on here," she wrote, describing the comments as "heartless, rude, insensitive."

Some of the posts targeting her and Howard make their allegiance clear. One account accused Howard, coach Karl Smesko and the Dream’s owners of selling Reese out in a supposedly rigged Finals. Another defended Reese while calling Canada and Howard "BOTH selfish players and human beings" and accusing them of not caring about winning. And some of the attacks were explicitly racist, including posts using the N-word.

So where is the insistence that Reese address online trolls "invoking her name" as an excuse to attack other players? So far, the WNBA media has been silent.

WNBA FINALS TEAMS END SEASON WITH ONE FINAL NATIONAL ANTHEM SNUB AS DREAM, VALKYRIES LEAVE COURT

Reese, meanwhile, outlined her plans for the next six months. In an Instagram post (on her private secondary account), Reese announced she is pausing her podcast for the offseason, plans occasional YouTube vlogs and will spend time resting and working out in Florida.

Her explanation: "i’m dedicating this off season to myself."

Can you imagine Caitlin Clark announcing that she's taking the next six months to focus on herself while her teammates are complaining about receiving nasty messages on social media? The WNBA media might never recover from such a scenario.

We’d get days, probably weeks and maybe even months of lectures about leadership, accountability and whether Clark was abandoning the teammates receiving online abuse.

Think pieces would be plastered all over The Guardian, The Athletic, ESPN and other left-wing sites explaining how White women have the privilege of focusing on themselves while Black women have no choice but to always worry about everyone else in their "community."

They would all demand that Caitlin Clark issue yet another statement. Then, they would complain that the statement wasn’t enough. The whole cycle would fuel the WNBA media ecosystem through the entire offseason.

So, where are the lectures for Angel Reese? Anyone see any think pieces about how Reese is being selfish? Didn't think so.

The WNBA’s obsession with online trolls

All of this unfolds in a league that spends an extraordinary amount of time talking about what people (and bots) say on the internet.

In August, after Sophie Cunningham’s comments about "biological men" competing in women’s sports sparked a debate over eligibility, WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert told teams an upcoming meeting of the league’s anti-hate task force would address whether males should be eligible to play in the WNBA.

Yahoo Sports reported that meeting instead largely focused on online hate directed at players. Even with eligibility rules on the agenda, the WNBA couldn’t stop talking about internet trolls.

USA SPORTS, NBC CLAIM RECORD WNBA FINALS RATINGS, BUT COMPARISONS LEAVE OUT IMPORTANT CONTEXT

That’s what I wanted to ask Engelbert about when I attended her October 17 press conference before Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. Why does online commentary warrant so much of the league’s time and attention? And does repeatedly highlighting negativity overshadow the positive things happening with attendance and television audiences?

I wasn’t called on.

Engelbert nevertheless returned to the subject in her final answer, condemning people who sit "behind a keyboard to spew vitriol and hate and racism and misogyny at our players."

After all those meetings, statements and lectures, you’d think the reporters, analysts and commentators demanding more from Caitlin Clark would recognize a familiar situation in Atlanta.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Where are you, Elle Duncan, Monica McNutt, Sarah Spain, and Nancy Armour? Where are your demands for Angel Reese to defend her teammates?

Again, I don’t think Reese owes anyone a statement. Clark doesn’t, either.

But the people who have spent three seasons assigning that responsibility to Clark should explain why their standard apparently disappears when applying it would require them to make demands of Reese.

In the WNBA media’s world, Caitlin Clark has to answer for the internet.

But Angel Reese gets to focus on herself.

World.title: 'Grand Theft Auto' community organizing 'last ride' on old game before release of 'GTA VI,' but why?
World.content:
November is finally upon us, and aside from setting our clocks back an hour, that also means we are a little more than two weeks away from the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI."

The hotly anticipated title is set to drop on November 19, and the gaming community at large can hardly wait, which is understandable considering they've gone 13 years between installments.

Yes, hard to believe that, as of September 17 of this year, "Grand Theft Auto V" would be old enough to see a PG-13 movie in theaters.

UNKNOWN HACKER ALLEGEDLY LEAKS SEVERAL MINUTES OF GRAND THEFT AUTO VI GAMEPLAY AHEAD OF NETFLIX REVEAL

Given the large time gap between games, you would expect there to be equal parts yearning for the new game as there is nostalgia for the old one, and from that nostalgia comes the "Last Ride."

The "Last Ride" was pitched by the GTA community, and will see thousands of players take one last lap around the map of Los Santos — the in-game world for "GTA V" based heavily on Los Angeles — the night before "GTA VI's" big release.

It's been trending heavily on social media, with gaming outlets all over the world picking up on it.

As a particularly nostalgic person myself as well as a fan of the "Grand Theft Auto" series, I can see where these guys and gals are coming from with the "Last Ride," but it doesn't make a whole lot of sense when you peel the layers back a bit.

For starters, "GTA V" isn't going anywhere.

On November 20, you will still be able to pop the disc into your Xbox or Playstation and ride around Los Santos in your vehicle of choice to your heart's content.

Hell, I still play "GTA IV" about as much as I play its predecessor, and I doubt I'll stop playing either once VI comes around.

If you love the game that much, I guarantee you November 18 won't be the last time you ever play "GTA V."

I appreciate the symbolism, but let's not get melodramatic here.

When "Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask" came out, do you think everyone just immediately chucked their copies of "Ocarina of Time" in the trash?

NINTENDO OF AMERICA RELEASES TEASER TRAILER CONFIRMING LEGEND OF ZELDA: OCARINA OF TIME REMAKE IN 2026

No, and as a matter of fact, the demand for "Ocarina of Time" has remained so high over the last 28 years that a remake is coming to the Nintendo Switch 2 later this month.

This isn't "Madden" or "FIFA," where an updated version makes last year's game immediately obsolete.

"GTA V" is unique because of the world the developers created as well as the memories those who played the game created for themselves.

I'm not here to yuck anyone's yum; take the "Last Ride."

Enjoy it.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Reminisce on all the good times you had these last 13 years, but let's not act like "GTA V" is being relegated to the shelf for all of eternity come November 19.

World.title: NTSB finds 'no evidence' of Mar-a-Lago connection after Florida jet crash kills nine people
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A critical piece of the private jet that plunged into a Florida neighborhood was found miles from the impact site, federal investigators revealed Tuesday as crews prepared to drain the crater left by the crash that killed nine people.

Asked about the crash occurring less than 10 miles from President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago home and any potential connection to Secret Service operations, National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman dismissed a link.

"There is no evidence of connection. Purely coincidence," he said.

FORMER NFL STAR SAYS HE PREVIOUSLY FLEW ON PRIVATE JET THAT CRASHED IN FLORIDA: 'ABSOLUTELY DEVASTATED'

Most of the Learjet 60’s left elevator was recovered between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the crash site in Palm Beach County, Chapman said during the agency’s final onsite briefing.

The discovery adds to evidence that the aircraft began breaking apart before impact. The elevator is a movable surface on the aircraft’s tail that helps control whether its nose points up or down.

TEXAS FAMILY OF 4, 20-YEAR-OLD COPILOT AMONG 9 KILLED IN FIERY FLORIDA JET CRASH

But Chapman said he did not believe the component would have enabled the aircraft to recover even if it had remained attached, given the speed of the jet’s descent.

The Learjet was carrying seven passengers and two crew members from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas when it crashed Sunday, killing everyone aboard.

FAA SEEKS PERMANENT AIRSPACE RESTRICTIONS NEAR TRUMP’S MAR-A-LAGO AS EXPERT WARNS RULES ARE ‘NOT GOOD ENOUGH’

Investigators are now preparing to remove water from the impact crater, where Chapman said they expect to recover additional aircraft components. Given the force of the crash, pieces buried there will likely be small.

Severe weather has hampered some recovery efforts, and weather remains a key focus of the investigation. The cause of the crash has not been determined.

FAA, NTSB INVESTIGATING POSSIBLE VIOLATION OF SAFETY PROTOCOL INVOLVING TRUMP, MARINE ONE

Investigators have also obtained dashcam footage to help reconstruct the aircraft’s final moments, Chapman said. Recovered wreckage is being retained for analysis, and officials urged anyone who encounters debris to leave it untouched and notify authorities.

The crew had reported light clear ice and moderate turbulence while flying at about 35,000 feet before requesting permission to climb to 37,000 feet. Less than 30 seconds after controllers approved the request, the crew reported they were descending and issued a mayday call.

Roughly 600 residents near Military Trail and Cresthaven Boulevard were evacuated after the crash, according to The Palm Beach Post.

Between 40 and 50 people were staying at the Greenacres Community Center, Palm Beach County spokesperson John Jamason told the outlet. County officials were seeking state funding to help displaced residents with housing and transportation while authorities worked at the crash site.

TRUMP HELICOPTER’S RADIO WARNINGS WENT UNHEARD BEFORE CLOSE CALL WITH PASSENGER JET, REPORT SAYS

Officials said during Tuesday’s briefing that Military Trail remained closed in both directions between 10th Avenue North and Purdy Lane. They did not provide a timeline for reopening the road or allowing displaced residents to return home.

Among those killed were Austin technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, his wife, Helen Sharp, 40, and their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2.

NORAD FIGHTER JETS INTERCEPT 2 AIRCRAFT NEAR TRUMP’S GOLF CLUB, 3RD PLANE DELAYS HIS NJ DEPARTURE

Robinson, CEO and co-founder of Retention.com, had celebrated a business milestone in his final LinkedIn post the day of the crash, announcing that RB2B had reached $10 million in annual recurring revenue. He was also preparing for a live business debate scheduled for Tuesday.

"Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives. Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever," the families said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

"Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return."

Chapman expressed confidence that investigators would determine what happened and thanked Florida and Palm Beach County authorities and first responders for their assistance.

Officials added that further investigative updates will be posted on the NTSB’s website.

People will be radicalized against corporate, pro-Israel Dems. There will be a reckoning. If, when, he wins, it will be a watershed moment. And that reckoning will still come."

After facing backlash, Ali posted another message Tuesday morning, expressing no regrets and instead scolding critics for alleged bigotry. "Ah, that Islamophobia and anti-Arab bigotry are so pure and naked," Ali wrote. "People are just coming out in the open about how they’ve always felt. Great. Please, be honest. Just share the ugliness with the world so we can all see."

Ali didn't respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

A Fissure Among Muslims

Reform-minded Muslim leaders aren't buying Ali's rhetoric.

The divide with Muslim reformers reflects a broader fissure within American Muslim politics: between establishment organizations and leaders who accept political Islam, or Islamism — the idea that religion should shape government and political life — and reform-minded critics who challenge orthodoxy, reject anti-Israel and anti-Western rhetoric and support secularism, including the separation of mosque and state.

"What Wajahat Ali said on the eve of elections is actually the language we’ve seen Islamists use before elections in countries in the Middle East, including Egypt," Dalia Ziada, an Egyptian Muslim reformer and critic of political Islamism, told Fox News Digital.

"The threat is usually: If you don’t choose us, this will lead to radicalization, and this will lead to violence," added Ziada, who is Washington, D.C., director at the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy. "Maybe we need to expect troubles coming up."

EL-SAYED'S PAST MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD COMMENTS RAISE RED FLAGS AS HE EYES POWERFUL ROLE

Soraya Deen, a Muslim reform activist, attorney and co-founder of the Los Angeles Women's Multifaith Alliance, said Ali’s language shouldn't be treated as a routine social-media outburst.

"His words are deeply troubling," Deen told Fox News Digital. "His warning that ‘the fire will rise,’ that people will be ‘radicalized,’ and that a ‘reckoning’ is coming deserves serious scrutiny."

"Losing an election is not a license for radicalization," added Deen, . "We must reject intimidation, political extremism and the politics of perpetual grievance."

EX-DSA MEMBER RIPS ABDUL EL-SAYED AND WARNS FAR-LEFT ADOPTING POLITICS OF FOREIGN TERROR ORG

'Jihad First' Lens

Dr. Zuhdi Jasser, a Muslim reformer and founder of the American Islamic Forum for Democracy, said Ali’s comments reflect what he describes as a "Jihad First" lens for viewing political conflict.

"Wajahat Ali, like Abdul El-Sayed, proves yet again their decades of anti-American Islamist obsession and the ‘Jihad First’ lens through which they view every cultural, social, military and political conflict," said Jasser, who is running for Congress as a Republican candidate in Arizona’s 4th Congressional District.

Jasser’s comments were directed at what he described as the political rhetoric surrounding El-Sayed’s campaign. The reformers didn't accuse Ali of belonging to an Islamist organization. Their criticism focused on language they said resembles tactics used to pressure voters by warning that rejecting a candidate could produce violence or radicalization.

EL-SAYED TRIES TO MAKE PEACE WITH JEWISH DEMOCRATS BUT DRAWS LINE AT DUMPING HASAN PIKER

El-Sayed’s Political Network

Ali’s comments came as El-Sayed’s campaign draws support from a wide network of Muslim advocacy groups, Palestinian activist organizations, progressive groups, labor organizations and political influencers.

A Fox News Digital review of campaign endorsements, public statements and voter-mobilization efforts identified 70 Muslim groups and influencers supporting El-Sayed’s political orbit one way or another. The records include formal endorsements, campaign-listed support, voter mobilization and public amplification. Not every organization has the same relationship with the campaign.

They include CAIR Action, Americans for Justice in Palestine Action, Bangladeshi Americans for Political Progress, Emgage Action and the US Campaign for Palestinian Rights. El-Sayed's official website includes endorsements from "Muslims for Abdul," the Yemeni American Michigan Democratic Caucus, the Michigan Bangladeshi American Democratic Caucus and Palestinian American political operative Linda Sarsour's MPower Action, among others.

ABDUL EL-SAYED REPORTEDLY CALLED HASAN PIKER WARNING HIS RHETORIC WAS 'COSTING' VOTES

The broader coalition supporting El-Sayed includes Democratic Party organizations and Democratic Socialists of America chapters, as well as online commentators and political figures including Hasan Piker, Linda Sarsour, Rep. Ilhan Omar and Rep. Rashida Tlaib.

The organizations and individuals have overlapping priorities, including opposition to U.S. support for Israel, demands for an arms embargo or cease-fire, support for Palestinian activism, criticism of Democratic moderates and efforts to mobilize Muslim and progressive voters.

The coalition’s critics have described it as a "red-green" alliance involving "red" left-wing political organizations and "green" Muslim advocacy groups.

"Their red-green ‘Jihad First’ filter — threatening fire and radicalization — is simply an unmooring of their own dreams to live the jihad of Islamism and destroy the American dream and everything for which it stands," Jasser said. "Patriotism is not in their vocabulary."

TRUMP SAYS ISRAEL WILL STOP RECEIVING $4B IN US AID BY YEAR'S END, CAN STILL BUY WEAPONS

A warning about political intimidation

For Ziada, the significance of Ali’s post lies in the suggestion that an election loss could trigger radicalization.

"Muslims like Wajahat Ali are just using the political movement backing Abdul El-Sayed as a staircase to bring them to the power of a chair they want to claim," Ziada said. "Once they get there, they don’t care what they may have promised. And if they don’t get there, they will turn it into fire."

Ziada also criticized El-Sayed’s campaign rhetoric about Israel, comparing what she described as repeated attacks on Israel to political tactics used by leaders in the Middle East. Tuesday morning, President Donald Trump announced that he would cut off $4 billion of aid to Israel, one of the network's demands, designed to isolate the nation.

"The demonization of Israel that we saw very prominently in the campaign of El-Sayed is a tactic that we saw Middle Eastern dictators resorting to every now and then," Ziada said.

"Whenever they are stuck with economic issues or politics, they just bring up the ‘Israel is bad’ card," she added. "Again, he is just copying dictators in the Middle East."

Jasser said the episode should prompt Muslim voters and Democratic leaders to examine the language used by political influencers who claim to speak for Muslim communities.

"Any honest Muslim who reads that post will see ‘Jihad First’ and everyone else be damned, including patriotic Muslims," Jasser said.

Ali has emerged as a prominent media figure over more than two decades, writing for and appearing on outlets including The Daily Beast, The New York Times, CNN and The Guardian. He also hosted programming for Al Jazeera America.

His political activism began after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, when he became involved in campus protests at the University of California, Berkeley. He later worked with Democratic operative Faiz Shakir, who became campaign manager for Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign, at the Center for American Progress, a nonprofit established by former Clinton administration chief of staff John Podesta.

Ali has continued to weigh in on Israel, Democratic Party strategy and Muslim political activism, regularly drawing fire. Earlier this year, in a broadcast with former MSNBC host Joy Reid, the two decried "weak White mean" in a heated anti-Trump rant.

Most recently, Ali hosted a speaker who criticized Democratic House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries for receiving political contributions from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, calling him an "AIPAC monkey." The smear drew cries of racism against Jeffries, who is Black.

Now, Muslim reformers are scolding Ali for making comments that seem to threaten voters with "fire," a "reckoning" and a "radicalized" citizenry if his preferred candidate loses.

Deen said the response to an election should be political disagreement, not warnings of unrest.

"Losing an election is not a license for radicalization," Deen said. "We must reject intimidation, political extremism and the politics of perpetual grievance."
