World.title: Democrats have polling and history on their side in House races
World.content:
The House of Representatives is up for grabs Tuesday as Democrats try to wrest control from Republicans, who have enjoyed power in the chamber for the past four years but are facing formidable political headwinds.

The outcome will set the tone and sway the direction of the final two years of President Donald Trump’s tenure in the White House, with Democrats vowing to aggressively investigate his administration if they win control of the House. And while Republicans were able to advance signature Trump priorities on party-line votes over the last two years, Democrats would have a say in any major congressional action if the House flips.

Democrats must flip a net of three seats to win the 218 needed for a majority. Republicans attempted to give themselves some cushion by redrawing congressional maps around the country over the past year and a half.

Follow live election coverage here.

But historical trends are working against them, as the president’s party typically loses seats in a midterm year. And polls leading up to Election Day showed deep voter dissatisfaction with Trump overall and across a range of issues, most notably his handling of the economy and the cost of living amid the Iran war and the administration’s tariff agenda.

While House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who could become the first Black speaker if Democrats win control of the chamber, has tried to tamp down expectations of a blue wave, he has predicted his party will emerge from the election with a majority.

“I also refer to Nov. 3 not simply as Election Day, but as judgment day,” Jeffries said at a weekend campaign rally for former Rep. Elaine Luria, who is trying to win back her old seat from GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans in Virginia. “The American people are going to judge these MAGA extremists and run them out of town for what they’ve done to our economy, to our military, to our families, our farmers and to the American people all across the country.”

Still, Democrats have had to navigate challenging terrain in an unpredictable election cycle. In addition to Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, which Democrats were able to partially counter with a redrawn map in California, many of the seats Democrats are targeting are in districts that Trump won in 2024. After those redistricting changes, just eight Republicans represent districts that then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried two years ago, while 21 Democrats sit in seats in districts that Trump won.

Yet, in the closing stretch of the campaign, top Republican outside groups threw in the towel on a handful of once-competitive races.

In mid-October, Republicans nixed millions of dollars in ad reservations meant to support vulnerable Reps. Tom Kean Jr., R-N.J., and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who represent battleground districts that Trump carried in 2024. Instead, they shifted the money to other races.

GOP groups also slashed hundreds of thousands of dollars in ads last month from Nebraska’s 2nd District, which Harris carried two years ago. Moderate Republican Rep. Don Bacon represents the district but announced his retirement, making it difficult for the GOP to hold the seat.

Down the home stretch, Jeffries criss-crossed the country, stumping with candidates in California, Texas, Florida, Ohio, Michigan, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., trying to protect his paper-thin majority, campaigned in many of the same battleground districts.

The speaker, a close Trump ally, warned that a Democratic victory would lead to nonstop investigations and a rollback of key pieces of the signature piece of legislation the Republicans passed during the first two years of Trump’s second term, the “big beautiful bill.”

“If this crazy group of Marxist Democrats took over, you can kiss your freedom goodbye. … They would spend every waking hour for the next two years investigating the president, the Cabinet, leaders in business and industry. It would be retribution,” Johnson said at a campaign event for Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., one of the cycle’s most vulnerable Republicans who represents a Harris-won district.

“We cannot go down that road,” Johnson added.

World.title: GOP fights to hang on to Senate majority
World.content:
Control of the Senate is on the line Tuesday following a midterm election cycle with races marked by betrayal, alleged ballot shenanigans and President Donald Trump’s incessant swooning over the backside of one Republican candidate.

Close races are expected in several traditional battlegrounds — including Georgia, Michigan and North Carolina — but also in states that have become more reliably red since Trump’s rise in politics, such as Ohio and Iowa.

There also are closer-than-expected races brewing in even redder states such as Alaska, Kansas and Texas. Underscoring the high stakes: More than $3.4 billion has been spent on television and digital s in Senate races across the country, according to tracking firm AdImpact.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the chamber, meaning Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to regain control.

Follow live election coverage here.

The consequences for Trump are significant. For the past two years, his own Republican Party has controlled both chambers of Congress, allowing him to pursue his agenda largely unchecked. But if the Republicans lose the Senate, he’ll need Democratic cooperation to move forward on legislation and appointments. Democrats will have increased power to pursue investigations into the administration.

Alaska has emerged late as a closely watched contest. Democrat Mary Peltola is under scrutiny after a New York Times report that her campaign and other Democrats recruited a candidate into the race — Dan J. Sullivan — with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The “ballot-stacking” tactic is seen as a way to sow confusion among voters in a state that uses ranked choice voting and has four Senate candidates on the ballot.

Peltola and her campaign have repeatedly denied allegations that they recruited the lesser-known Sullivan.

Polls close in Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.

Clarity about the fight for the Senate will come much earlier in states such as Ohio, where polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET, and Michigan, where the last polls close at 9 p.m. ET.

In Ohio, Republican Sen. Jon Husted faces a tough challenge from Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown in the race to serve the remaining two years on JD Vance’s unexpired Senate term. Husted was appointed to fill the seat temporarily last year after Vance was elected vice president.

Polls have shown a close race in Ohio, and the president held three rallies in the state in recent weeks — as well as one in the Cincinnati media market, in neighboring Kentucky — in an effort to boost Husted. Trump used the rallies not only to promote Husted’s work as a senator, but also to compliment his physique. Trump, who often gives the impression that he is casting for a movie, repeatedly praised Husted’s “ass” in Ohio and elsewhere down the stretch.

“If Husted wins,” one senior Republican official told NBC News last week, “it’s because Trump literally dragged his ass over the finish line.”

Then there’s the Michigan race, which is ending on an explosive note. The Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, scored a surprise last-minute endorsement Sunday from Rep. Haley Stevens, who in August lost the Democratic nomination to challenge him.

Stevens had vowed as late as Saturday, publicly and privately, to not break her promise to vote for Abdul El-Sayed. The Democrats had long clashed over his criticism of Israel, but Stevens’ criticism had intensified in recent days, prompting the El-Sayed campaign to signal that she was no longer welcome at his events. Stevens cited that in her decision to defect to Rogers, sparking outrage and accusations of betrayal from House Democratic colleagues.

Other key races to watch Tuesday include Maine, where polls close at 8 p.m., and where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is up against Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson.

And at 9 p.m. ET, the last polls will close in Texas, which hasn’t had a Democratic senator in 33 years. The race took on a heightened energy after the Republican incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, lost a primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton after a heavy push by Trump in favor of the latter.

Democrats are excited about their candidate, state Rep. James Talarico, who has maintained steady leads in polls, though within the margin of error. Trump ally and tech billionaire Elon Musk, meanwhile, has spent at least $150 million to back Paxton.

World.title: Nearly half of voters saw midterm election as a rebuke of Trump, NBC News Exit Poll shows
World.content:
Nearly half of voters say they view the midterm election as an opportunity for a major rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to early results from the NBC News Exit Poll.

Forty-three percent said one reason for their votes was to express opposition to Trump — far higher than the share who said the same in the 2018 midterm election during his first term.

The early results show that Trump’s midterm campaign blitz in support of Republican candidates in recent weeks has done little to lift his job approval rating.

A key frustration voters cited? The economy.

Most voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families, with the affordability of gas, food and utilities being a significant concern. Voters blamed Trump for high prices and said his policies are making the economy worse.

The poll was conducted as voters left polling locations across the U.S. on Election Day. Results also include extensive interviews by phone and mail and online with people who voted early or by mail.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

Trump’s sagging job approval rating

Thirty-eight percent of voters said they approve of Trump’s performance, according to the poll. That’s substantially lower than in his first midterm election in 2018 (when 45% of voters approved of his performance).

Trump’s dismal approval ratings have dropped in Senate battleground states, as well.

Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas all said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job — also up compared with 2018.

Voters have negative opinions of both parties

Voters expressed more unfavorable than favorable views of the Republican and Democratic parties, the poll showed. And almost 1 in 5 voters said they don’t have favorable opinions of either party — at least 5 percentage points more than the share who said so during the past two midterm elections.

Fifty-four percent of voters Tuesday said they have unfavorable views of the Democratic Party, while 46% have favorable views. For the Republican Party, 59% of voters today said they have unfavorable views, and 41% said they have favorable views. Voters expressed more unfavorable views toward both parties than they did in the last two midterms.

Voters were likelier to say the Democratic Party could better handle several big issues than the Republican Party, including the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, government corruption and policies about transgender people. The GOP held an advantage on immigration.

On policies related to AI and taxes, voters were split.

Economic pessimism

The economy — once Trump’s strongest issue — is no longer viewed positively by voters, the poll showed.

An overwhelming majority said the nation’s economy is in rough shape (75%) — and 65% said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. About half of voters casting ballots said the cost of living was crucial to their votes. That is the opposite of how voters viewed the economy in 2018 — a wave election for Democrats during Trump’s first term. That year, 68% of voters said the economy was in good shape.

Voters are driven by the economy

Voters rated the economy as the most important issue facing the country today (39%), followed by the state of democracy (32%), according to the poll. They voiced significant concerns about the prices of gas, groceries and utilities, blaming Trump for affordability problems.

Forty-four percent of voters said their finances are worse today than they were two years ago when Trump returned to office. Just 18% say they’re better off. These numbers are in line with the way voters characterized their finances during the 2022 midterms but much worse than in Trump’s first midterm election in 2018.

Driving voters’ financial concerns: the cost of living. Top issues include the cost of gas and diesel fuel (87% said they were “very” or “somewhat” concerned), food and groceries (88% concerned), utilities (86%) and healthcare (85%). All told, just under 8 in 10 voters said inflation is causing hardship for their families.

More than half (65%) say Trump’s policies have made the economy worse; 62% said he’s responsible for high prices.

Groups we’re watching closely as the night unfolds

We’ll closely watch several groups that helped propel Trump to victory in 2024 — but with particular interest in Latino voters and voters under 30.

After having fallen in every national election since 2018, the share of Latino voters who identify as Democrats ticked up this year to 43% from 39% in 2024, the poll showed.

The share of Latino voters calling themselves independents dropped slightly, to 30% from 32%. The share identifying as Republicans also dropped slightly, to 27% from 29% in 2024.

The results halted a steady erosion of the Democrats’ advantage among Latino voters in party identification, which narrowed from 33 points in 2018 to 10 points in 2024. This year, Democrats hold a 16-point edge.

Young voters also seem to be shifting back to the Democratic Party after Trump shrank the margin among them in the 2024 presidential election.

World.title: Routine voting issues fuel conspiracy theories and confusion
World.content:
SLEEPY HOLLOW, N.Y. — Westchester County ballot tabulators malfunctioned across the county Tuesday, alarming voters and fueling a flurry of conspiracy theories online.

The issue was discovered early in the morning, after ballot tabulators failed to scan voters’ hand-marked paper ballots in 44 out of 45 of the county’s municipalities. State election officials said in a post on X that the issue was due to a programming error.

Election officials directed voters to put their ballots in secure orange ballot bags, following standard contingency plans.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

The news has raised alarm among voters and onlookers. In text chains and Facebook posts viewed by NBC News, Westchester voters discussed the issue, with some expressing concern over whether their votes would be counted.

Tensions are high in part because Westchester is home to a key House race in the battle for control of Congress: In the 17th Congressional District, Republican Rep. Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a close race. The district narrowly leans blue, but Lawler has held it for four years by maintaining high popularity and campaigning aggressively on crime and affordability issues. Conley, a veteran and former Biden cybersecurity official, hopes to capitalize on President Donald Trump’s sagging approval ratings in her challenge.

In social media posts, both candidates urged voters not to be dissuaded by the tabulator issues.

Ken Jenkins, the Westchester County executive, said Tuesday afternoon that alternate tabulators are being rolled out, and that the ballots stored in secure bags will be counted after polls close at 9 p.m.

“Long-established emergency ballot procedures have been implemented, where completed ballots are secured, under bipartisan control, and will be counted,” the New York State Board of Elections said in a Tuesday statement posted on X. “While technical issues can be frustrating, contingency procedures exist for precisely these circumstances.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, told reporters that the ballots would be counted.

“Every vote will be counted; I think I need to say that three times. Every vote will be counted, every vote will be counted,” she said in Queens on Tuesday morning. “It’s being resolved in a bipartisan way that it’s supposed to. The backup plan is in place, so voters in Westchester should feel very confident.”

Isolated ballot scanner issues are routine, though the problems have been been particularly common in New York state. In 2018, scanners jammed across New York City, while Queens reported tabulator issues in 2024.

This year, ballot tabulator issues also occurred in other states including Florida and Oklahoma, while other issues like power outages and flooding shuttered some polling sites, including some in Maricopa County.

Online influencers supportive of the Republican Party and some officials saw an opportunity in the malfunctioning machines and polling location closures, framing them as a conspiracy against party candidates.

“The Democrats are already cheating,” posted Loomer Unleashed, a podcast associated with close Trump ally Laura Loomer, about power outages in Maricopa County. In reality, heavy rain and flooding have caused polling location issues across the county. The ballot counting issues in New York have sparked similar accusations, including from an elected official.

“The Democrats in NY will do anything and everything to cheat,” posted Rep. Claudia Tenner, R-N.Y., the chair of the House Election Integrity Caucus.

“Democrats are already trying to steal the election in New York today,” Loomer wrote on social media, her post garnering over 100,000 views.

“This is how the Left steals elections,” wrote Katie Miller, conservative podcast host and wife of White House adviser Steven Miller.

The nascent accusations echo similar narratives Trump and his supporters raised in past elections. The most famous of these false narratives claimed machines stole votes away from Republicans, costing them the 2020 presidential election. Yet technical failures are common, officials have warned, as are conspiracies about those malfunctions.

Researchers studying false online information have been worried about the potential for such accusations to recirculate as normal glitches get misrepresented. Such narratives could pave the way toward challenging the results of the election, several researchers told NBC News ahead of the midterms.

In Oklahoma City, the county’s top election official said normal issues were getting far more attention than usual.

“It’s not uncommon to have some voting machines cause us a few problems early in the day. It’s a common occurrence,” said Doug Sanderson, the county’s election board secretary. “Many times we wouldn’t hear about it other than from our precinct officials. I just think perhaps the climate and the sensitivity everyone has around this election causes people to be a little bit more on edge than they normally would be.”

Offline in Westchester County, voting at a Sleepy Hollow polling site at a social club called the Fraternal Order of Eagles appeared to be proceeding smoothly. A regular flow of voters trickled in and out through the lunch hour in the Hudson River Valley town, most having already heard via text message or from friends and neighbors that the scanners were not functioning.

As of 12:30 p.m. ET, of the 225 people who had voted at that location, only two walked away on account of the tabulators being down.

“One was pretty disrespectful,” a poll worker named Dennis told NBC News, declining to share his last name. “The other said maybe they’d come back later.”

World.title: Floods and severe weather beset parts of the U.S. on Election Day
World.content:
Flash flooding, heavy rainfall and tornadoes have forced election officials in three different regions across the United States to move polling locations, scrambling Election Day plans in hot-button races.

At least 21 polling locations were moved across eight Florida counties — including Brevard, Broward, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties — after intense rainfall caused flash floods Monday and into Tuesday morning.

Roads were impassable in several parts of the state’s Atlantic coast after a storm dumped as much as 22 inches of rain in 24 hours in a storm that “exceeded everyone’s expectations,” as one forecaster put it.

Severe storms were moving across Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas overnight. Forecasters issued a tornado watch that lasted until about 2:45 a.m. local time Tuesday.

Forecasters were also predicting possible flash flooding in parts of Alabama, Tennessee, Arkansas and Mississippi on Tuesday, as that storm system continued to travel east. A flood watch remained in effect in some parts of Florida, though rainfall rates were slowing.

“Areas affected by catastrophic flooding remain extremely sensitive to any additional rainfall,” forecasters wrote in a Tuesday morning discussion.

In Oklahoma, a tornado Sunday forced Cimarron County officials to change one of its polling locations. The tornado, which had peak winds of about 100 mph, snapped tree branches, damaged the roof of the Keyes Community Center and collapsed a wall, according to a damage survey report from the National Weather Service.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

In an emergency request, county election officials said the tornado caused “considerable structural damage” to the community center “rendering the polling location unsafe.”

And after historic flooding in the Four Corners region, Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre M. Henderson declared a state of emergency and issued a special accommodation that will allow voters registered in San Juan County who are isolated by floodwaters to request and return ballots electronically.

The Colorado secretary of state is allowing a similar measure for voters — allowing votes online — in La Plata and Archuleta counties, according to 9 News.

In Florida, Port St. Lucie resident Jessica Rendon said she spent hours trying to cast her ballot after the weekend’s severe flooding led to water-logged highways and polling location closures.

“I personally did not see one officer out in public helping any of us out,” Rendon said. “Voting or not voting.”

She said she only learned that her polling location changed from another resident who was also out trying to vote. Other residents who have located their polling stations are sharing the information via social media.

“Unfortunately many by me are still stuck in their homes,” Rendon said, noting that the only reason why she’s been able to get around is because she owns a truck. “Frankly I don’t think a lot can vote because of this.”

An overturned mobile home and other debris in the Verde River as severe flooding rushed through an RV park in Camp Verde, Ariz., on Monday. Ross D. Franklin / AP

More election day surprises could be in store.

Experts say inclement weather has suppressed voter turnout in past elections. In research of elections from 1948 to 2000, researchers observed a modest drop in turnout during unusually intense rain storms.

“What we found was that for every inch of rain that a county received above its average amount of rainfall, voter turnout went down about eight-tenths of 1 percentage point,” said Brad Gomez, an associate professor of political science at Florida State University.

But experts said the effect of rain on turnout is diminishing over time as more people choose to vote early or vote by mail, and they said it’s hard to predict what effect the inclement weather will have, if any, on key races.

In Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency in seven counties along the Atlantic seaboard that are being hit with flash flooding and extreme precipitation.

Damage in parts of Colorado remains widespread after heavy rain and flooding, with first responders searching for people who may be stranded across the area, including by helicopter.

A vehicle is submerged on the Piedras River in Arboles, Colo., on Monday. Gregory Bull / AP

People with homes along the Animas River in southwestern Colorado were also facing evacuation.

Record rainfall was also reported in usually dry Arizona, causing deadly flooding and power outages.

The brief closure of two voting centers in Maricopa County sparked a chorus of conspiracy insinuations online Monday. Two out of the 254 polling locations in the county had to be temporarily shuttered “due to power related issues,” election authorities announced on social media.

The two polling locations have since been reopened, authorities said, but some online used the shutdown to allege impropriety in the competitive swing state.

Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs issued a statewide emergency declaration Monday after recently issuing an emergency for Navajo and Coconino counties. The governors of New Mexico and Colorado also asked President Donald Trump to declare a major disaster to receive federal funding assistance.

World.title: In top Senate race states, gas and grocery costs are rising faster than the national average
World.content:
From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day.

In 2024, President Donald Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him win back the White House.

But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran have driven costs higher across the country, fueling deep discontent among voters.

These frustrations aren’t confined to voters who support Democrats. More than half of Republicans, 53%, are dissatisfied with the state of the economy, according to the latest NBC News poll.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

This has created an opening for Democrats to win majorities in both the House and the Senate. And while the House majority is widely expected to shift to Democrats after Tuesday night, the Senate is still very much a jump ball.

Veteran election data analysts are quick to remind the public that as Tuesday’s voting and later counting unfolds, any one of the competitive Senate races could tip either way.

Pain at the pump

In several of the states with close Senate races, voters face gas prices that have climbed higher, and more sharply, than the mean nationwide prices over the same period.

Across the country, the average cost of a gallon of gas has risen 40% since Feb. 28, the day Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched attacks on Iran that sent crude oil prices through the roof.

Right before the war, the average price of unleaded was $2.98 per gallon, according to NBC News’ gas price tracker. On Monday, it was $4.16.

In Iowa, however, the average price has climbed by significantly more, nearly 55% since late February. The same figure applies in Nebraska. In Kansas, gas prices are up by 53%.

All three states broke for Trump in 2024. But two years later, they are in play, and Democratic Senate candidates Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, as well as independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, will be very closely watched Tuesday night.

World.title: Inside the Decision Desk: When will we know Senate and House control?
World.content:
In 2024, Donald Trump’s election night wins in the presidential battlegrounds of Georgia, North Carolina, Texas and Florida meant that most Americans went to bed on Tuesday with a good idea of the result of the election — and woke up to the networks having called enough states to declare Trump the president-elect.

Two years later, control of Congress is at stake. Republicans are trying to hang on to slim majorities in both chambers as Democrats try to wrest power in Washington for the final two years of Trump’s term.

Follow live election coverage

Democrats are heavily favored in public polling in the House and in a number of key Senate contests — and if those numbers prove accurate, it’s possible that NBC News could project control of both chambers on election night. But it’s more likely that determining the winners in important races will take time.

Of course, no one, including the Decision Desk, will know what will unfold until election night, but we will have a good sense possibly early in the night of how the contests are trending. The answer of when we could call control in both the House and Senate depends not only on how states count their votes, but on how close the races will be.

When we could know Senate control

Senate control will likely come down to the eight races that NBC News rates as either toss-ups (Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, Texas) or lean Democratic (Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire).

Assuming that Democrats win the states NBC News currently rates as “Likely” Democratic (which includes flipping North Carolina’s Senate seat from red to blue, and keeping Georgia in their column), Democrats still need to win five of these eight contests.

Some of these states are quick to count their ballots, and others are perennially slow. If some of these Senate contests are as close as we expect, calling control of the Senate as a whole could take us into the early morning hours of Wednesday, regardless of who wins those individual races.

It is also a real possibility that Americans will wake up at a slightly more reasonable hour on Wednesday without a majority decided, even if we have a good sense of who will ultimately win. And if Senate control comes down to the outcome in Alaska, we’ll all be here awhile.

In that case, it will take a couple of weeks to know who won the majority thanks to the state’s ranked choice voting system. Past elections offer a useful guide to how quickly we expect to see votes counted in each of these states, even if the timing Tuesday night is not exact. Let’s look more closely at each of these categories — the fast-counting states, the slow-but-steady states, and the ranked choice wild cards.

The fast counters

Votes in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas were counted fairly quickly in 2024. We expect over 80% of the vote in those states to be counted by midnight Eastern time. If those historical patterns hold, there is a good chance that those Senate races will be called. And some of these calls may come in before midnight if there is some spread in the races as some recent polls suggest.

But remember, Democrats must win five of those eight Senate races we listed above to take a majority, which means that even if they win all four states in the fast-counting list, NBC News would still not be able to project control of the Senate.

The steady counters

In two of the key battleground states, New Hampshire and Michigan, nearly all votes will be counted over the course of election night, but more steadily and slowly than the fast counters. Here, elections are administered by towns and municipalities, not by counties. This results in a more decentralized and variable counting process that lasts until early morning, or even midday Wednesday. How quickly these races are called really depends upon the margin of the race.

Earlier in the election cycle, polls suggested both these races would be close. Recent polls favoring the Democratic candidates and what appears to be a Democratic advantage in the early vote in Michigan mean there’s a wide range of timing possibilities there.

If the nationwide Democratic momentum translates to results, New Hampshire could possibly be called before midnight. But that seems to be highly unlikely in a place like Michigan, where Wayne County, home to Detroit, often releases large batches of votes between midnight and 3 a.m. ET. This is such a significant source of ballots that statewide races in Michigan often cannot be called without Wayne County’s results.

The takeaway here is that if the Senate races in these states are close as the polls have indicated all along, it’s unlikely that calls will come before the early morning hours. But it all depends upon how far apart the two candidates are in the state, and we won’t know that until tonight.

The ranked choice states

Maine and Alaska are the slowest counters of the group. As in New Hampshire, Maine’s elections are administered by towns, each with their own schedule for tabulating ballots and releasing results. In Alaska, mail ballots from remote corners of the state can arrive up to 15 days after the election. If these historical patterns hold, there will not be enough votes counted on election night to call a close race in either state.

In 2024, the presidential race in Maine was called on Wednesday at 4:40 p.m. ET, and in Alaska on Thursday at 10 a.m. ET. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by about 7 points, while Trump won Alaska by 13 points. It’s possible the margins in this year’s Senate contests could be much closer.

There is a second complication in Maine and Alaska that could cause even more delay in knowing which party will control the Senate. These states both use ranked choice voting for their Senate races, in which voters rank the candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the first choice of more than 50% of voters, the winner will be determined by ranked choice tabulation, in which the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their votes are reallocated based on voters’ next-most preferred candidates.

In Alaska, the ranked choice tabulation occurs 15 days after Election Day. Maine does not provide official guidelines on when its ranked choice tabulation will occur, but in June, the ranked choice results were released 10 days after Maine’s primary election.

In either case, if one or both of these seats are needed to win a majority, we may not know until the next day, or even for several weeks, which party will control the Senate.

What about the House?

Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to flip control of the House, and they’re heavily favored to succeed. But the size of that majority depends on how much voters shift their support toward the Democrats and away from Republicans.

A recent NBC News Decision Desk analysis shows evidence that this nationwide shift could be big enough to produce a historically large majority for the Democrats — or it could be sufficiently small that either party could end up with a razor-thin majority. (The House is made up of 435 seats, all up for re-election every two years, and 218 seats are needed for control.)

The size of that majority for either party matters significantly to our ability to project control of the chamber. The smaller the final size of the majority, the longer it will take for the Decision Desk to be certain of who will control the House.

If current polls are overestimating Democratic support and the size of the House majority for either party is small, the 2022 and 2024 elections provide some idea of timing.

During the 2022 midterms, it took the NBC News Decision Desk eight days after Election Day to project that Republicans would win a slim majority. This call came as the Decision Desk projected the Republicans would win California’s 27th District, their 218th win. The ultimate size of their majority was nine seats.

In the 2024 election, the Republicans won an even smaller majority — just five seats. This election also took until the second Wednesday after Election Day for the Decision Desk to project the 218th seat for the Republicans.

If the size of the Democrats’ or Republicans’ majority this year is a single-digit number of seats, we expect it to take days or weeks for either party to reach 218 seats.

Just like the Senate elections, the House elections in Maine and Alaska use ranked choice voting to determine a winner. If control of the House hinges on Maine’s 2nd District or Alaska’s lone district, we may have to wait until ranked choice tabulation occurs 10 to 15 days after Election Day.

On the other hand, if current polls end up being close to accurate, Democrats would be poised to win at least 230 seats, according to the recent Decision Desk analysis. This could speed up when we know control.

Throughout the night, the NBC News Decision Desk uses a statistical model to estimate the total number of seats that the Democrats and Republicans will end up winning. It is possible that NBC News will report this estimate on election night. The House model relies on past and current vote counts; it does not use any polling, including exit polls, in its estimation.

Early House indicators with clues for timing

Elections in states with early polling close times or that count their ballots quickly can also provide an indication of where things may end up. Kentucky’s 6th District, which Trump won in 2024 by 15 points, is a good example of an early bellwether district. The Republican-held district has its polls close at 6 p.m. ET, and in 2024 it reported nearly 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m.

While the Democrats do not need their candidate, Zach Dembo, to win this district to earn a majority, a low-single-digit win by the Republican candidate, Ralph Alvarado, is a favorable signal for the Democrats’ chances of winning the House. If Dembo were to win this district, it would likely foretell a Democratic tsunami, as there are 267 districts nationwide where Trump performed more poorly on his way to the White House. And if Alvarado were to win by a margin close to or in the double digits, it may suggest that neither party will end up with a large majority.

Florida, which tends to report its votes quickly, also has several congressional districts worth paying attention to early in the night. One of these is Florida’s 25th, where Democrat Jared Moskowitz seeks re-election in a district that Florida Republicans redrew to favor Trump by 9 points. If Moskowitz loses to Republican Scott Singer, it would be a major victory for Republicans and may foreshadow the party holding on to House control. If Moskowitz wins comfortably, it may signal a large Democratic wave.

Florida’s 14th District and Florida’s 22nd District are also Democratic-held toss-ups that Republicans redrew to be districts Trump would have won by 10.5 points. Given how quickly Florida counts its ballots, these two districts may be the first toss-ups NBC News can project. If one party were to win both of these districts early in the night, that party could very well end up with the majority.

World.title: NBC News Exit Poll: How it works and how we use the results on election night
World.content:
Before votes are tallied on election night, exit polls offer an early look at who is voting and what is motivating their choices.

An exit poll is a survey of voters taken as they leave (or exit) their voting location. Unlike public opinion polls ahead of elections that predict whether respondents will vote, exit polls capture the views of voters in person on Election Day. The exit poll also reflects the views of people who voted early or by mail — we take steps to reach those voters by phone and by mail, as well as online.

Here’s how exit polls work, where they are conducted and how NBC News will be using the results on election night and in the days after.

Who conducts the exit poll?

For this year’s midterm election, exit polls are being conducted by SSRS, a survey and market research firm, on behalf of a group of news organizations: NBC News, ABC News, The Associated Press, CBS News, CNN, Fox News and MS NOW. The companies receive the same data, and NBC News then independently analyzes and reports on the exit poll results.

What questions are asked?

The national exit poll asks respondents whether they voted for the Democratic or Republican House candidate in their district, and in many states the poll also asks which candidates voters supported in Senate and governor’s races.

In addition, the poll usually includes a number of questions about voters’ views, such as, “What is the most important issue facing the country?”

Follow live election coverage

The other key component of an exit poll is asking about voters’ demographics, such as age, gender, race and education level.

These types of questions help illustrate how different groups of people voted and what mattered to them. Demographic data is also used to weight the exit poll — that is, to make sure the poll reflects the demographics of the electorate as well as the election results.

The national and state exit polls include some different questions, to capture voters’ views on local issues and candidates.

The news organizations jointly determine how the exit poll will be conducted and develop the questionnaire together.

How are exit polls conducted?

The in-person Election Day exit polls are surveys that voters in scientifically selected precincts are asked to fill out as they leave their polling place. The paper forms have about 25 questions.

This year, interviewers will be stationed at over 450 polling locations in 15 Senate battleground states. Each interviewer follows local rules about where they can stand outside the polling location.

The exit polls also include a pre-election survey to capture voters no matter how they participate, whether early, by mail or on Election Day. Before Election Day, respondents are surveyed through methods including mailed invitations, telephone and text interviews and online surveys. Interviewers then follow up with respondents to confirm that they voted and whom they ultimately voted for.

Respondents can complete the poll in English or Spanish.

On Election Day, interviewers count the people coming out after they have voted and are instructed to offer questionnaires to every third person or every fifth person, for example, from the time polls open until polls close.

Interviewers phone in the results from the questionnaires to a data center three times during the day. Those results are tabulated with the pre-election survey results, and the exit poll is updated throughout the day as new data is collected.

Are exit polls anonymous?

Yes. In person, voters fill out the questionnaires themselves and deposit them in boxes, so their answers, like their actual ballots, are secret. Interviews conducted by mail, by phone and online do not retain any personal information about the voter who was interviewed.

Which states will have exit polls?

In addition to a national exit poll, which captures voters in all 50 states, there are also state exit polls this year in 45 states that have consequential Senate and governor’s contests.

How many people are interviewed?

The national exit poll sample will include over 75,000 voters at voting locations, online and by telephone.

In 15 states, interviewers will be stationed outside at least 30 randomly sampled voting locations. In the remaining states, interviews are conducted via phone, online and mail.

The sample size in each of these states will be about 4,000 voters: Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas and Wisconsin.

The sample size in Alaska will be about 3,000 voters, and it will also include interviews from voters at early-voting locations before Election Day.

All other states with exit poll results for Senate and governor’s races will include between 500 and 3,000 voters.

How do we use exit polls?

The NBC News Decision Desk uses some exit poll data to help project race outcomes on election night, but the exit poll is primarily used to help tell the story of the election.

The data gives viewers and readers real-time insight into what motivates voters and how they feel about the country. It’s the nation’s first look at who is turning out to vote this year and what is driving their choices.

What does NBC News report and when?

NBC News does not report any exit poll results before 5 p.m. ET on election night, and no exit poll results that may indicate the outcome of a race are reported until after all the polls are scheduled to close in that state. As election night goes on and interviewers on the ground call in more exit poll results, the data is updated and reweighted in real time.

World.title: Oklahoma man charged with mailing hundreds of white-powder letters
World.content:
Washington — An Oklahoma man faces federal charges after allegedly sending hundreds of letters containing white powder to public officials and media outlets ahead of both the 2024 and 2026 elections.

According to charging documents unsealed on Tuesday, Robin Patrick Martin allegedly sent more than 700 envelopes to public officials of both parties across the country. Authorities said the powder contained in the envelopes was nontoxic and said the envelopes had messages written in UV-reactive ink, not easily seen by the naked eye.

Martin is charged with one count of conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and another count of mailing threatening communications. It wasn't immediately clear whether Martin had been taken into custody.

According to an FBI affidavit, Martin "described perceived issues with the 2020 election, claimed that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election."

Some of the messages were marked with return addresses related to previous headquarters for the Green Party of the United States and Democratic Socialists of America. The DSA has cooperated with the FBI in its investigation, the affidavit said.

In one envelope addressed to the Oklahoma State Election Board ahead of the 2024 election, Martin allegedly wrote "stay on the right side of history your life might depend on it!" Federal prosecutors allege that the handwriting in that message was matched with the new batch of letters through a handwriting analysis.

According to the affidavit, the content of the letters sent in 2026 "all pertained to the upcoming 2026 national elections" and Martin allegedly referenced an organization known as the United States Traitor Elimination Army in his writings, threatening the recipients with being arrested for treason "OR WORSE!!"

Federal investigators also intercepted a message allegedly from Martin to FBI Director Kash Patel.

Surveillance footage allegedly showed Martin dropping off the envelopes at a USPS facility in both 2024 and 2026, and records analyzed by federal law enforcement allegedly show Martin purchased items used for the mailing in August of this year, as well as the ingredients for the "invisible ink" that was used to write on the envelopes.

In October, Brendan Donahue, the deputy chief inspector at the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, confirmed that "suspicious mailings" were sent to "various addresses nationwide," including secretary of state offices and related election offices.

The Senate sergeant at arms also issued a notice to congressional staff informing them of the investigation. Dozens of members of Congress and election officials across the country reported being targeted by the mailings.

CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

World.title: Google will block search access for schools that ban AI use
World.content:
Google said on Tuesday that it will turn off artificial intelligence in its educational apps for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators expressly enable it.

The Alphabet-owned search giant said that after surveying school administrators and teachers, it wants educational institutions to control students' access to various AI capabilities.

Access to Google's AI features — Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Classroom — as well as Google search will be automatically turned off for K-12 student accounts until "school administrators explicitly turn them on," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post.

Schools that ban AI "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available," Phillips told The New York Times.

While Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will be turned off by default, schools can choose to turn on one, two or all three services, Google explained in a post on X Tuesday.

"We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach," Phillips wrote in the post.

New policy prompts outcry

Google's new policy immediately prompted criticism that it is seeking to pressure schools to use its AI apps. In a statement posted on social media, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the tech giant of "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

"No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margins of Big Tech," he added.

A Google spokesperson declined to respond to Mamdani's remarks.

Roughly 150 million students and teachers use Google Classroom, and many students use school-provided Chromebooks, according to Google. Google drew backlash in August when it activated its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.

In September, New York City schools said that AI would be banned until students reach high school and implemented a one-year delay on the use of generative AI for children in 2-K through eighth grade.

Lina Khan, who served as chair of the Federal Trade Commission from 2021 to 2025, said in a statement posted on X that Google is seeking to exploit its dominance in internet search.

"This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service," said Khan, who now chairs the board of the New York City Economic Development Corporation, a nonprofit group that promotes economic growth and investment in New York.

"Multiple courts have found Google liable for violating antitrust laws, and this latest move shows it remains unchastened," she added. "As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don't fall in line."

Josh Golin, executive director of children's advocacy group Fairplay, said Google's attempt to "strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire." He said Google's technology in schools is not about learning but about "developing lifetime brand loyalty" for its products.

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, accused Google of putting its business interests ahead of education. "Instead of working with teachers and parents to uphold privacy and ensure their tools are safe and useful, it throws the baby out with the bathwater and bans access to the tools altogether," she said in a statement.

World.title: U.S. launches strikes on Iranian targets in Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
The U.S. military launched limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News.

The strikes targeted Iran's Qeshm Island, a senior U.S. official said. It came after two incidents on Monday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards fired at an American fighter jet, leading it to return fire, according to two U.S. military officials. Later Monday, Iran fired a missile from Qeshm Island that threatened shipping, the officials said.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the strikes, which came on the eve of Election Day in the U.S. President Trump has been floating the idea of restarting hostilities with Iran after the midterms, at the same time as U.S. and Qatari mediators broker talks on a possible U.S.-Iran deal.

Qeshm Island, in the northern Strait of Hormuz, is crucial to the Iranian regime's efforts to monitor and exert control over commercial traffic through the waterway.

Map shows the location of Qeshm Island, off the coast of Iran in the northern Strait of Hormuz. Omar Zaghloul/Anadolu via Getty Images

Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tuesday that Tehran retained "the right to legitimate self-defense" after the new U.S. strikes, and would do so "until the military aggression has been completely and permanently brought to an end."

Iran has retaliated for attacks on its territory throughout the war sparked by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28 by targeting commercial shipping traffic in the strait and U.S. allies and interests across the Persian Gulf region.

As the war enters its ninth month, Mr. Trump's rhetoric has continued to swing back and forth between suggesting he could strike a deal to end the war with Iran, to warning that he could resume major attacks against the country.

In a Truth Social post earlier Monday, the president said a deal "could happen" and that "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible."

Later Monday night, however, in an appearance on Fox News, Mr. Trump said "we still have to take care of" several sites in Iran, including Pickaxe Mountain, which houses a suspected nuclear site. During his appearance on Sean Hannity's program, Mr. Trump said it was "not a big deal" and could be done in "an hour."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend call with Mr. Trump, pushed for further sustained strikes against Iran, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Trump acknowledged the call had taken place, saying he had a "very good talk with" the Israeli leader, but he did not elaborate on what he and Netanyahu discussed.

The war has loomed large over both the U.S. midterm and Israeli parliamentary elections. In the U.S., rising costs stemming from threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have led to cratering support for Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.

In Israel, Netanyahu's right-wing bloc lost its majority in the first parliamentary elections since Oct. 7, 2023.

As of mid-October, the Iran war had cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47.1 billion in military expenditure alone, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News.

CENTCOM said the cost of replacing spent munitions alone was about $29 billion, according to the latest estimate, which was provided to lawmakers. Another $6.1 billion was needed to replace lost equipment, and there has been around $11.9 billion spent on incremental costs including support for American service members.

The estimate does not include the cost of damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East, many of which have been targeted by Iranian drones and missiles.

World.title: Cruise canceled after Coast Guard detains ship in Miami, officials say
World.content:
MSC Cruises canceled the voyage of its MSC Poesia cruise ship after it was detained by the Coast Guard at the Port of Miami, the cruise line confirmed to CBS News on Tuesday.

A source familiar with the matter told CBS News more than 2,000 people were on board the ship.

MSC Cruises said the cancellation happened because of a "regulatory matter" that arose before departure. The cruise line said it was unable to resolve the issue in time to set sail.

"We have made the difficult decision to cancel the current sailing," MSC Cruises said in a statement. "We recognize how disappointing and frustrating this news is for our guests, and we sincerely apologize for the disruption to their holiday."

Guests will receive a full refund of their cruise fare, MSC Cruises said. The cruise line also said it was helping people get back home.

The Coast Guard "identified deficiencies with systems on board the vessel that we are addressing with MSC," Capt. Frank Florio, commander of the Miami sector, said Tuesday in a statement. The ship will remain detained until "the deficiencies are corrected and it is cleared for departure," the Coast Guard said.

The cruise ship MSC Poesia in the Baltic seaside resort of Warnemünde. Stefan Sauer/picture alliance via Getty Images

Before Tuesday's cancellation, the Coast Guard said in a statement to CBS News on Monday its teams "are verifying the cruise ship's compliance with international standards and U.S. regulations."

The Coast Guard's Miami sector detained the ship for inspection on Sunday.

"The Coast Guard is tasked with verifying safe and secure commerce. It is the Captain of the Port's priority to ensure the safety of passengers, crew, the vessel, and the environment," the Coast Guard said.

In an earlier statement, MSC Cruises said the company was fully cooperating with authorities.

MSC Cruises says the MSC Poesia has a capacity of more than 3,200 passengers and over 1,000 crew members.

World.title: How to watch live election results on CBS News
World.content:
Control of Congress and the future of President Trump's agenda are on the line in the 2026 midterm elections on Tuesday, as voters cast their ballots for all 435 House seats and 35 Senate races around the country. Candidates for governor are on the ballot in 36 states and three U.S. territories, along with some high-profile measures like California's proposed billionaire tax.

CBS News will have extensive live coverage throughout the day and all the latest results after the polls close.

How to watch election coverage with cable

CBS News' "America Decides: Election 2026" live coverage on TV and cable starts Tuesday at 7 p.m. ET. (Find your local CBS station here.)

Anchors Tony Dokoupil and Norah O'Donnell will be joined on the set by "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King, "Face the Nation" moderator and chief foreign affairs correspondent Margaret Brennan, and CBS News' team of political reporters, including Robert Costa, Major Garrett, Nancy Cordes and Ed O'Keefe.

There will be live updates throughout the evening from CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Anthony Salvanto and reporting from correspondents in Washington and around the country, including Weijia Jiang at the White House, Nikole Killion, Adriana Diaz, Matt Gutman, Skyler Henry, Lana Zak, Kris Van Cleave, Taurean Small, Jan Crawford and Nicole Sganga. Contributors will also include political analysts from both sides of the aisle and experts on election law and security.

How to watch election coverage without cable

Live coverage is streaming on CBS News 24/7 throughout the day Tuesday and all evening long, with election results expected to start coming in Tuesday night.

Watch on the free CBS News app on your connected TV or smartphone, on Paramount+, and all platforms where CBS News 24/7 is available, including CBSNews.com and YouTube.

Beginning at 5 p.m. ET, dive into the latest data on "Election 2026: The Nerd Show," hosted by CBS News executive director of elections and surveys Anthony Salvanto and CBS News congressional correspondent Caitlin Huey-Burns, joined by Democratic and Republican pollsters and other election data experts. Watch here until 2 a.m. ET.

Prime-time coverage anchored by Tony Dokoupil and Norah O'Donnell begins streaming live at 7 p.m. ET.

How to watch live streaming local election coverage from CBS Stations

CBS Stations are covering the election live across 15 owned markets. Local streaming channels plan sustained live coverage with a mix of local and network coverage.

World.title: See CBS News exit poll results for the 2026 midterm elections
World.content:
Note: Results will continue to update throughout the night.

Overview of CBS News 2026 exit polls for the midterm elections

President Trump is on track for the lowest approval rating for a president in a midterm election, according to early exit polls. Currently at 38%, it's lower than it was during Mr. Trump's first term, and lower than it was for George W. Bush in 2006 when his party lost both houses of Congress.

Midterm elections have often been a referendum on the sitting president, and this one is no exception. Roughly six in 10 say Mr. Trump is a factor in their vote for the House.

This is being driven largely by voters backing Democrats, who are overwhelmingly motivated by opposition to Mr. Trump.

But for those backing Republicans, it's less about the president. Back in 2018, most Republican voters said their vote was to support Mr. Trump. That figure is lower today.

The president has often told his supporters to pretend he is on the ballot, and for many in the MAGA base, they may be doing just that. Most MAGA Republicans say their vote is to support Mr. Trump, but most non-MAGA Reps say he is not a factor.

The mood of the electorate is a sour one

Voters are just plain not happy.

Current exit polls show roughly three-quarters of voters are at least dissatisfied with the direction of the country. More are angry now about how things are going than they were in 2024, as economic anxiety persists. Those voting for Democrats are particularly likely to be angry.

The issue of the economy and trust in Mr. Trump to fix it helped propel him to victory in 2024, but voters feel no better about the condition of the economy today.

In fact, more voters have negative views of the economy now than they did two years ago, and views of the economy are more in line with what we saw in the 2022 midterms, when the party in power lost seats.

Cost of living: Voters are feeling the pinch

Voters are feeling it in their pocketbooks. They are more than twice as likely to say their finances are worse rather than better, based on early exit polls.

Voters across parties express concern about affording everything from gas to groceries to utilities.

For two consecutive elections, most voters have said inflation caused hardship for their family, including about one in five who describe that hardship as severe.

All this adds up to the cost of living being a major factor for voters across parties, but it's more crucial for those backing Democrats. Immigration enforcement is more crucial for those backing Republicans.

When voters are asked to pick their most important issue from a list, the economy comes out on top, followed by the state of democracy. Those voting for Democrats prioritize the state of democracy — an issue that has long concerned them.

For those backing Republicans, the economy is their most important issue, followed by immigration.

Voters who pick the state of democracy as their top issue are particularly likely to say government corruption is a crucial factor in their vote.

Government corruption: It's a major factor for voters across party lines

Roughly nine in 10 voters nationally say government corruption is a major factor in their vote — about the same as cost of living — and it's crucial to those voting for Democrats.

About six in 10 voters think President Trump puts his own personal interests over the country.

The Iran War

While the war with Iran is less of a factor for voters than the cost of living, the conflict is not popular. Most think the U.S. made the wrong decision to take that military action, including about a quarter of Republicans.

Those most concerned about affording gas are the most likely to disagree with the decision to attack Iran.

Does all this dissatisfaction translate to satisfaction with the party out of power?

Neither political party is viewed favorably by a majority of voters.

About one in five backing Democrats for the House have an unfavorable view of the Democratic Party. Most Democrats are motivated by their opposition to Mr. Trump.

And the Democratic Party isn't overwhelmingly seen as the party better able to handle key issues.

Emerging issues

Data centers arose as an issue in this campaign. In all the Senate battlegrounds, majorities oppose the construction of a data center in their community.

More voters see artificial intelligence as doing more to harm society than to help it.

Voter confidence

Large majorities of voters are at least somewhat confident that their votes will be counted accurately both nationwide and in their own states, and that eligible voters will be allowed to vote. But while they are confident in their votes being counted, those voting Republican are far less confident that people who are not eligible to vote will be prevented from voting.

This national exit poll measures the general preference for voters nationwide in their choice for the House of Representatives. The House of Representatives, of course, is elected seat by seat.

A quick note on the states

Mr. Trump's job approval is currently underwater in nearly all the Senate battleground states, according to early exit polls, including in states that he won by double digits in 2024.

In all the Senate battlegrounds, more say their finances are worse, not better, compared to years ago.

And party control of the Senate was on the minds of voters. Majorities of those voting for Republican candidates and those voting for Democrats say which party controls the Senate was a major factor in their vote.

The CBS News exit poll interviewed thousands of voters across the country at polling locations on Election Day and in the weeks leading up to Election Day. This is how the voter polling was conducted.

World.title: Connecticut bakers are bringing joy back to election day, one cake at a time
World.content:
Connecticut bakers are bringing joy back to election day, one cake at a time

toggle caption i Barbara Glassman Dell

Election day can be described in many ways: stressful, overwhelming, anxiety-inducing — and the list goes on.

But in Hartford, Connecticut, it's a piece of cake — specifically a mutli-tiered red, white and blue patriotic cake decorated with an American flag, stars and a bald eagle made entirely of frosting.

This masterpiece won the annual Election Cake Bake-Off at Connecticut's Old State House in Harford, CT. Nicole Sousa, the events and outreach manager at the Old State House, told Morning Edition about the Bake Off and rich tradition behind it.

A slice of history

Election cake first appeared in Hartford, in 1771, when the northeast United States was still a collection of 13 original colonies. Connecticut was a pioneer in early self-government, and it was one of the only regions who could elect their own officials.

Sponsor Message

"It was definitely something that Connecticut, as a colony and then later as a state, celebrated and really felt attached to," Sousa said.

So, election day was joyous. It was marked with parties, parades and community-wide celebrations — often involving cake.

But election cakes looked nothing like they do now. At that time, the iconic cakes resembled a tough, fruit cake, often soaked in alcohol.

toggle caption i Barbara Glassman Dell

Plus, this cake definitely couldn't fit in your modern fridge. In the eighteenth century, Sousa said the cakes were made using 30 quarts of flour, ten pounds of butter, 14 pounds of sugar, 12 pounds of raisins, three dozen eggs and over a quart of wine or brandy. Sousa said the massive cakes were baked to feed huge crowds of celebrating voters.

Writer Amelia Simmons featured a scaled-down recipe for traditional election cake in American Cookery, which is widely recognized as the first American cookbook.

One sweet competition

More than 250 years later, Connecticut's Old State House hosted its fifth annual Election Cake Bake Off on Oct. 26. Professional pastry chefs and bakers were challenged to create a deliciously non-partisan, election-themed cake that inspires voters and celebrates American democracy.

"They're in it to win it for sure," Sousa said. "But they're also in it for the love of Election Day, the love of baking and the love of the idea of election cakes."

Sponsor Message

A panel of judges scored the cakes based on presentation, creativity and of course taste. The winning confection was crowned the official Connecticut Election Cake of 2026, and its baker received a commission to make Connecticut's Old State House birthday cake in 2027.

Taking the cake

This year's winner was a mother-daughter duo led by Sophia Grestini of Amy's Cakes LLC in Cheshire, CT.

Their cake had four layers, alternating between sweet lemon blueberry and traditional spiced sponge flavors. The exterior was covered in red, white, blue and gold accents and featured iconic election day symbols like an "I voted" pin, ballot box and American flag.

On the second tier, handcrafted fondant figures of a donkey and elephant represented the two major political parties. Perched atop the masterpiece was a bald eagle sculpted entirely from frosting — guarding the cake from danger, or at least wandering forks.

Sousa said the cake was delicious, but, most importantly, the bakers had fun making it. She called the event joyous.

"That's what we're trying to do with the election cake contest — we're trying to bring that joy back to Election Day," Sousa said. "It should be fun, it should be a way to show that you're contributing to your country and part of your community."
