There are a few hopeful signs, and at the moment the vaquita is benefiting from a considerable amount of attention and goodwill. The Mexican government has implemented a vaquita refuge, where commercial fishing is prohibited.

Cement blocks fitted with metal hooks have been fixed throughout the exclusion zone, which capture abandoned and illegal gillnets.

A combination of monitoring by conservation groups, most notably Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, and support from the Mexican Navy has brought a notable reduction in illegal fishing activity within the protected area.

Science of vaquita still being understood

One recent surprise concerns the animal’s reproduction cycle. It was previously believed that females only gave birth every two years, but that is now questioned.

The best evidence comes from observations of a female called Frida, who is easily recognized by a bent dorsal fin. She was spotted with a calf in 2023 and another newborn in 2024.

In 2025, she was seen with a calf that appeared to be a year old, but was showing physical signs that she may have been pregnant again. If the breeding pattern is changing, this could be linked to less competition between the porpoises for food and might offer a ray of hope for the animal’s long-term future.

Another positive discovery was made by genetic scientists who examined the historical library of DNA collected from porpoises caught in nets over the years. Their work revealed that the species has been isolated for so long that they seemingly adapted to the risks of inbreeding.

This phenomenon has been observed in other species on the verge of extinction, from Bengal tigers to right whales.

Had the current conservation measures been put in place 10 years ago, when vaquita numbers were still in the low hundreds, there might have been some optimism. Now there is a fear that all the good intentions might have come too late.

Helping the vaquita to recover will take years of protection and monitoring. Pushing them into extinction might only require a few months of neglect. There are also new problems looming on the horizon.

New problems emerge for vaquita

While the establishment of a protected area has been generally successful, it only covers a small percentage of the animal’s known range. Most alarmingly, it fails to cover a northwestern zone where vaquita might well be active.

In addition, fishermen continue to place gillnets on the outer edge of the exclusion zone where they might still pose a danger to the porpoises.

Fishing is big business with the ability to lobby the government.

A 225-square-kilometer Zero Tolerance Area established in 2020 is also under attack. The argument is that with their declining numbers, vaquita are no longer found in much of the protected area, so unrestricted fishing could resume there.

There are other dangers building up that might be beyond our ability — or at least our will — to halt. Ever since the great Hoover and Glen Canyon Dams were built, little fresh water has flowed into the gulf. This has changed the salinity of the water and places another pressure on the ecosystem.

Plans to build distillation plants will only exacerbate this problem. Then, there is the whole question of climate change. The porpoises survive here because, over many generations, they have adapted to water that would normally be too warm for them.

How are they and their food source going to adapt to a future in which weather patterns appear to be changing, and doing so far more rapidly than ever before?

The vaquita is still with us, but its survival hangs by a thread.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a master’s degree in history.

World.title: Mexico’s New Coach Faces Jamaica Nov. 14
World.content:
Estadio BBVA in Monterrey, where Mexico hosts the second leg. File photo.

Key Facts

Kick-off: Saturday, Nov. 14, 8 p.m. ET in Kingston; Tuesday, Nov. 17, 9:30 p.m. ET (8:30 p.m. Mexico City) in Monterrey.

Saturday, Nov. 14, 8 p.m. ET in Kingston; Tuesday, Nov. 17, 9:30 p.m. ET (8:30 p.m. Mexico City) in Monterrey. Stakes: The winner over two legs reaches the Final Four and the 2027 Gold Cup.

The winner over two legs reaches the Final Four and the 2027 Gold Cup. Who: Rafael Márquez coaches Mexico in his first official competition; the team is winless in four under him.

Rafael Márquez coaches Mexico in his first official competition; the team is winless in four under him. Not known: As of Nov. 3, no official squad list, US broadcaster or prediction-market price had been published.

Mexico’s new coach has a rough start to repair, and two matches against Jamaica will show whether he can. The tie is a two-leg quarter-final in the Concacaf Nations League, the regional tournament of North America, Central America and the Caribbean, and it is covered in our Mexico vs Jamaica live hub.

Concacaf, the confederation that runs the competition, has confirmed both kick-off times. The first leg is in Kingston, Jamaica, and the return is in Monterrey, northern Mexico.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

When and Where to Watch

The first leg is on Saturday, Nov. 14, at the National Stadium in Kingston, with kick-off at 8 p.m. ET, which is also 8 p.m. local time. It is 7 p.m. in Mexico City.

The return leg is on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at Estadio BBVA in Monterrey. Kick-off is 9:30 p.m. ET, or 8:30 p.m. Mexico City time, and Concacaf lists the venue as Estadio Monterrey.

What the Winner Gets

The team with the better combined score over the two matches advances to the Final Four, the semi-finals and final of the tournament. Those are played on March 25-28, 2027, at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles.

The four quarter-final winners also qualify for the 2027 Gold Cup, the main regional championship. The losers drop into a qualifying round for that tournament.

If the tie is level on aggregate, Concacaf’s rules go to away goals first. After that come extra time and a penalty shoot-out.

A Coach Under Pressure

Rafael Márquez, who took over this year, is coaching his first official competition. His team opened with 1-1 draws against Colombia and Peru, then lost 3-0 to the United States and 2-0 to Chile.

Mexico is still the defending Nations League champion, having beaten Panama 2-1 in the March 2025 final under his predecessor Javier Aguirre.

Several players are in doubt. Forward Raúl Jiménez had knee surgery and is expected to be out until about January 2027, which leaves a gap in attack.

Márquez had not published his squad list as of Nov. 3, and the date of the announcement is not known. Jamaica’s squad has not been named either.

What It Means for US Readers

The return leg falls on a weeknight evening on the East Coast, and the first leg is a Saturday-night kick-off. No US television channel or streaming service has been confirmed for either match.

The United States plays its own quarter-final against Haiti. That tie is on Nov. 14 at 4:30 p.m. ET in Miami and on Nov. 17 at 7 p.m. ET in Cincinnati, so US fans can follow both ties on the same days.

What Is Not Known

We do not know who Márquez will call up, or whether Jiménez’s absence changes his plan. We also do not know who will broadcast the games in the United States.

We found no active prediction market on this tie, so there is no market price to show. Our hub will carry the squad lists once they are official.

Sources

Concacaf, 2026/27 Nations League November schedule; Concacaf match report on Mexico’s 2025 Nations League final; The Rio Times Mexico vs Jamaica hub and match guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

When do Mexico and Jamaica play?

The first leg is on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 8 p.m. ET in Kingston. The second leg is on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at 9:30 p.m. ET in Monterrey.

What does the winner of Mexico vs Jamaica get?

The winner over two legs reaches the Concacaf Nations League Final Four in March 2027. It also qualifies for the 2027 Gold Cup.

World.title: Senegal Lawmakers Reportedly Reject Budget
World.content:
SENEGAL · BUDGET

Key Facts What is happening Parliament appears to have rejected the revised 2026 budget without debate on Tuesday 3 November.

Why it matters The budget fight puts a US$2.2 billion International Monetary Fund programme and Senegal’s debt plans in doubt.

The numbers Ousmane Sonko’s Pastef party holds 130 of the Assembly’s 165 seats; no official tally is public.

Who is who Ousmane Sonko, ex-prime minister, now leads parliament; President Bassirou Diomaye Faye dismissed him in May.

What to watch Whether the government resubmits a revised bill, invokes constitutional powers or governs on existing credits.

What it means for you Holders of Senegal’s dollar bonds face more uncertainty while the IMF board has yet to approve the programme.

Local reports say Senegal’s parliament threw out the amended 2026 budget on Tuesday 3 November without a debate. The official record is not yet public, and a US$2.2 billion IMF programme waits on the standoff.

Senegal’s National Assembly rejected the government’s revised 2026 budget on Tuesday 3 November without holding a general debate, local reports say. Deputies adopted a preliminary motion, so the amended finance law, called the LFR, gets no examination on its merits.

The vote deepens a clash between President Bassirou Diomaye Faye’s government and a parliament run by his former ally. For US readers it bears on a US$2.2 billion programme from the International Monetary Fund, the IMF, and on Senegal’s dollar bonds.

Ousmane Sonko, who leads the Pastef party and presides over the Assembly, was dismissed as prime minister by Faye in May. Pastef holds 130 of the 165 seats.

What Happened in the Chamber

Amadou Ba, a deputy, moved the preliminary motion, known in French as the question préalable. Under Article 83 of the Assembly’s rules, adopting it rejects the bill without general discussion.

Local reports give the vote as 109 for, 20 against and 3 abstentions, with 132 of 165 deputies taking part. The Assembly’s official record was not available when this was written.

Ba said the bill lacked budgetary sincerity and questioned its deficit of 7.6% of economic output. He also questioned FCFA 644 billion (about US$1.1 billion) of foreign-financed investment due by year end.

He added that he did not dispute the need for an agreement with the IMF. Conversions in this article use the exchange rate of 3 November 2026.

Finance Minister Cheikh Diba replied that the debate was about the government’s recovery plan, known by its French initials PRES, not sincerity. He accused deputies of wanting to avoid the debate.

How the Budget Got Here

The amended budget lifts the 2026 deficit forecast to 7.6% of economic output and tackles energy subsidies, which Sonko opposed. On Friday 23 October the Assembly’s finance committee rejected the bill amid disputes over fuel and power subsidies and presidential special funds.

On Tuesday 27 October Diba asked for the bill to go back to committee, hoping for a compromise. The committee rejected it again on Friday 30 October.

Prime Minister Ahmadou Al Aminou Lô heads a government that Pastef refused to join. He said on Monday 26 October that the opposition could not bring the country to a standstill.

Pastef says it accepts revising the budget but objects to the trade-offs, the financing and parliament’s guarantees. The prime minister has accused its deputies of obstruction.

What the IMF Deal Needs

On Tuesday 1 September 2026 the IMF announced a staff-level agreement, meaning officials agreed terms, for about US$2.2 billion over 36 months. The deal still needs IMF management and board approval, and Dakar must first take corrective action on past misreporting.

The IMF release does not mention the amended budget, but news accounts treat its passage as important for the deal. Public debt was estimated at 132% of economic output at the end of 2024.

An earlier IMF programme was suspended in 2024 after the government said its predecessor had hidden the true size of the deficit. That history lies behind the corrective steps the lender now requires.

Related Rio Times reports include Senegal Budget Cuts 15 Projects, Ba Claims. More is on the Senegal hub and in Senegal Chases an IMF Deal as Debt Tops 130% of GDP.

What It Means for US Readers

Holders of Senegal’s dollar bonds are watching because the IMF programme is the route to new financing and a debt plan. A long standoff would raise doubts about whether Dakar can meet its obligations.

A budget that parliament will not pass may force the government to rely on existing credits, which limits new spending. Companies that supply the state could face delayed payments.

What Is Not Known

The Assembly’s official record of the 3 November session was not available, so the vote tally rests on local reports. It is not known whether the government will resubmit the bill.

No decision from President Faye or the prime minister on the next step has been found. The IMF has not said how the vote affects its timetable.

What Comes Next

Watch for a government reply, a new bill or use of Article 86 of the constitution. That article lets the prime minister stake the government’s responsibility on a finance bill, though specialists are divided on it.

None of this means the budget is dead or that the IMF programme is cancelled. A statement from the IMF or the presidency would clarify the next steps.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the LFR?

The LFR is Senegal’s amended finance law for 2026, the government’s revision of the current budget. Parliament must authorise the changes before they take legal effect.

Why did parliament reject it without a debate?

Local reports say deputies adopted a preliminary motion moved by deputy Amadou Ba, who said the bill lacked budgetary sincerity. Under the Assembly’s rules, adopting that motion rejects the bill without general discussion.

Who controls Senegal’s parliament?

Pastef, the party of former prime minister Ousmane Sonko, holds 130 of 165 seats, and Sonko presides over the Assembly. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, his former ally, dismissed him as prime minister in May.

How does this affect the IMF programme?

The IMF reached a staff-level agreement on 1 September for about US$2.2 billion over 36 months, which still needs board approval. The IMF has not said how the vote affects its timetable.

What happens to the budget now?

The government has not announced its next step. It could resubmit a bill, use constitutional powers or run on existing credits, and lawyers disagree on some of those options.

Sources: IMF, Press Release 26/282, Senegal staff-level agreement, 1 September 2026; IMF, Senegal country page (all accessed 3 November 2026).

World.title: Congo Deal Would Reopen Deadly Mine Site
World.content:
DR CONGO · MINING

Key Facts What is happening A local report says a deal lets a miners’ cooperative return to part of Mulondo, where dozens died.

Why it matters Congo mines about 73% of the world’s cobalt, used in batteries; net imports cover 79% of US use.

The numbers The provincial interior minister said 32 died on 15 November 2025; the deal reportedly gives miners two squares.

Who is who Pajeclem runs the industrial quarry; COMIKAN is the miners’ cooperative; Louis Watum Kabamba is Congo’s mines minister.

What to watch Whether the squares are marked out, security is guaranteed and the 2025 inquiry concludes.

What it means for you Battery supply chains depend on Congolese cobalt; the US advises Americans to reconsider travel to Congo.

A local news site says artisanal miners may return to part of Mulondo in Congo’s Lualaba province. Dozens died there a year ago, and no official text confirms the deal.

A settlement lets a miners’ cooperative return to part of the Mulondo mine site in Lualaba province, a local news site says. Dozens of artisanal miners, who dig by hand, died there on Saturday 15 November 2025.

Lualaba is the heart of Congo’s copper and cobalt belt, and Congo mined about 73% of the world’s cobalt in 2025. The US Geological Survey says net imports covered 79% of US use, so these mines matter to American batteries.

The deal rests on one outlet’s account, with no published text, signing date or company statement. The facts of the 2025 accident come from officials and agencies named below.

What the Settlement Says

Pajeclem, the company officially operating the quarry, will hand two mining squares to the COMIKAN cooperative, the outlet says. The squares lie inside a marked perimeter, and the company keeps its rights over the rest of the site.

National mines minister Louis Watum Kabamba brought the sides together and oversaw the handover on Monday 2 November, the outlet says. A provincial mines minister and a commission charged with cleaning up the mining sector joined the site inspection.

The outlet says the sides disagreed over access, and miners were kept off the site for over a year. It adds that the cooperative’s director general welcomed the outcome.

What Happened at Mulondo in 2025

Dozens of miners died on 15 November 2025 at Kalando, a hand-dug site inside the Mulondo quarry near Kolwezi, Lualaba’s capital. Roy Kaumba Mayonde, the province’s interior minister, said on Sunday 16 November 2025 that 32 bodies had been recovered.

He said diggers had forced their way in despite an access ban linked to heavy rain and landslide risk. News accounts describe a crowd rushing across an improvised bridge over a flooded trench.

A report by SAEMAPE, a state service for small-scale miners, put the toll at about 40. It reportedly blamed soldiers for the panic, and a Congolese rights group, AFREWATCH, said survivors reported gunfire from soldiers.

Those accounts are unproven allegations, the army’s response has not been found and no official finding has been published. Counts differ by source, from 32 to about 40.

Why Artisanal and Industrial Mining Collide

Artisanal miners dig by hand and sell ore to traders, often on land that companies hold under licence. At Mulondo the dispute involved miners, a cooperative meant to supervise them and the operators.

Related Rio Times reports include Who Runs DR Congo’s Economy and UN Counts 464 Congo Rights Abuses in July. More is on the DR Congo hub and in DR Congo Politics, Who Holds Power in 2026.

What It Means for US Readers

Congo supplied 73% of mined cobalt in 2025, the US Geological Survey says, so mine disruption matters to battery makers. Net imports covered 79% of US cobalt use that year.

The US State Department, Washington’s foreign ministry, tells Americans to reconsider travel to Congo because of crime and civil unrest. It lists four regions as Do Not Travel, and Lualaba is not among them.

What Is Not Known

The settlement text, its signing date and its signatories have not been published, and no statement from Pajeclem has been found. The account of the 3 November deal rests on a single local outlet.

The death toll differs by source, and the cause of the panic is not officially established. No sanctions or findings from the 2025 inquiries have been published.

What Comes Next

Watch for the marking of the two squares, a published agreement and security arrangements for the cooperative’s members. A final report on the 2025 deaths would also show whether sanctions follow.

The deal does not mean the dispute is over, since success depends on respecting the perimeters. A statement from the mines ministry would confirm the terms.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Mulondo mine?

Mulondo is a copper and cobalt quarry, Lualaba province, in south-eastern Congo, near the city of Kolwezi. Dozens of artisanal miners died there on 15 November 2025.

How many people died at Mulondo?

Lualaba’s interior minister said 32 bodies were recovered. A state mining-service report reportedly put the toll at about 40.

What does the new deal change?

One local outlet says the operator Pajeclem will hand two mining squares to the COMIKAN cooperative so artisanal work can resume. The full terms have not been published.

Why does Congo’s cobalt matter to the United States?

Congo mined about 73% of the world’s cobalt in 2025, according to the US Geological Survey. Net imports covered 79% of US cobalt use.

Is it safe for Americans to travel to Lualaba?

The US State Department says to reconsider travel to Congo because of crime and civil unrest. Its Do Not Travel list covers four regions, and Lualaba is not named.

Sources: US Geological Survey, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, Cobalt; US State Department, Democratic Republic of the Congo travel advisory; AFREWATCH, press release 07/2025 on the Mulondo quarry, 15 November 2025 (all accessed 3 November 2026).

World.title: Central African Fuel Monopoly Faces Change
World.content:
CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC · FUEL

Key Facts What is happening Neptune Oil’s fuel import monopoly is said to have passed to Sopraf; no official confirmation yet.

Why it matters The IMF says costly, opaque imports keep pump prices high in this landlocked country.

The numbers Press summaries of an audit put the state’s loss at about US$1.7 million a month.

Who is who Neptune Oil, a Cameroonian importer, holds a ten-year licence from 2023; Sopraf is said to be state-owned.

What to watch Whether the government publishes the new hydrocarbons law and names which companies may import fuel.

What it means for you The US State Department advises Americans not to travel there; check its advice before any trip.

A Central African news site says the president has moved the country’s fuel import monopoly from one company to another. No official document confirms it, and the checkable facts point to a slower change.

A Central African news site says President Faustin-Archange Touadéra has stripped Neptune Oil of its fuel dominance. It says Sopraf, a company linked to the state, takes over, but it cites no decree or official statement.

The matter reaches beyond Bangui, the capital, because this landlocked country imports its fuel overland through neighbouring states. For US readers it bears on safety advice, aid logistics and a US$197 million programme from the International Monetary Fund, the IMF.

The claim appeared on Tuesday 3 November 2026 and no government text confirming it has been found. The checkable record shows a country trying to end a ten-year fuel monopoly, with the details still unclear.

What the Local Report Says

The outlet says Touadéra withdrew Neptune Oil’s dominant position and handed it to Sopraf, the Pan-African Petroleum and Refined Products Company. It says the state officially holds 51% of Sopraf, which was created in December 2022.

It says the new beneficiary lacks the money to supply the market regularly, which could worsen queues in Bangui. It gives no figures, and no official is quoted confirming the handover.

The outlet makes further claims about who benefits financially. Those claims rest on unnamed sources, no document has been shown, and they are not repeated here.

How One Company Won the Fuel Market

In 2023 the government gave Neptune Oil, a Cameroonian company, an exclusive ten-year licence to import fuel. A Geneva-based research group, the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, published a study on it on 6 November 2025.

The study says the licence sidelined other licensed fuel marketers and breaches existing law. It estimates excess revenue in 2024 of between US$17.5 million and US$30 million.

The IMF, the country’s reform lender, said in June 2025 that costly, opaque imports keep pump prices high. It called an overhaul of the fuel market pivotal to macroeconomic stabilisation and approved a US$58 million payment.

What the Audit Found

An independent audit requested by the IMF, written by the Canadian consultancy CPCS, is dated October 2025. Its findings emerged in December 2025, after delays in passing the report to the authorities.

It found no justification for a gap between the assumed fuel purchase price and market prices, which inflates pump prices. The state loses about 1 billion CFA francs (about US$1.7 million) a month as a result, press summaries say.

The auditors recommended opening the market to other importers for a steadier supply and lower costs. Conversions in this article use the exchange rate of 3 November 2026.

The Law Meant to End the Monopoly

On Monday 13 July 2026 the National Assembly, the country’s parliament, adopted a law reorganising the hydrocarbons sector. Local outlets say it is meant, in theory, to end the exclusivity of fuel imports.

As of late July the text had not been published, so it is unclear whether the law is in force. No list of approved importers has been found.

Local business press said in August 2025 that Sopraf would manage a fund fed by sales of donated Russian diesel. That shows the company is known to the authorities, but it does not show that it now holds import rights.

Related Rio Times reports include Bangui Truck Blockade Strands 100 Lorries and Central African Republic Defends 12% Diesel Price Rise. More is on the Central African Republic hub and in Central African Republic Neighbours, Borders and Trade.

What It Means for US Readers

The US State Department, Washington’s foreign ministry, advises Americans not to travel there because of crime, unrest and kidnapping. Its embassy in Bangui has limited ability to help citizens.

US sanctions on Wagner, a Russian private army active in the country, bar American firms from dealing with it. Any Russian-linked fuel deal would therefore need careful legal checks.

For investors, the IMF programme is the main link, with about US$197 million approved in total in April 2023. A change in who controls fuel imports could affect pump prices, tax revenue and the next IMF review.

What Is Not Known

No decree, ministerial order or company statement confirming a handover to Sopraf has been found, and Neptune Oil’s response is unknown. The ownership of Sopraf and its financial capacity rest on one outlet’s account.

It is not known whether the July 2026 law is in force or who will receive import approvals. The full audit has not been published, so its findings are known only from press summaries.

What Comes Next

Watch for publication of the hydrocarbons law, a list of approved importers and any statement from the presidency or the energy ministry. A future IMF review would also test the fuel reforms.

None of this means pump prices will fall soon, since supply still depends on long overland imports. A confirmed decree or a licence list would settle the open questions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Neptune Oil?

Neptune Oil is a Cameroonian company that received an exclusive ten-year licence to import fuel into the Central African Republic in 2023. A 2025 study by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime criticised the arrangement.

Has the Central African government ended the fuel monopoly?

A local news site says so, but no decree or official statement has been found. Parliament passed a hydrocarbons law in July 2026 that is meant, in theory, to end exclusivity.

What is Sopraf?

Sopraf is the Pan-African Petroleum and Refined Products Company, created in December 2022. A local outlet says the state officially holds 51% of it, which has not been independently confirmed.

Why is fuel so expensive in the Central African Republic?

The country is landlocked, so its fuel is imported overland through neighbouring states. The International Monetary Fund says costly and opaque imports keep pump prices high.

Is it safe for Americans to travel to the Central African Republic?

The US State Department advises Americans not to travel there because of crime, unrest and kidnapping. The US embassy in Bangui has limited ability to help citizens.

Sources: IMF, Press Release 25/179, Central African Republic, 4 June 2025; Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, Central African Republic fuel study, 6 November 2025; US State Department, Central African Republic travel advisory; US Treasury, Wagner designation, 26 January 2023 (all accessed 3 November 2026).

World.title: Pope Leo Youth Vigil Tickets Open 9 November
World.content:
Free tickets for Pope Leo XIV’s youth vigil in Lima go on sale on Monday 9 November 2026. The event takes place on Thursday 12 November at the Estadio Nacional, Peru’s National Stadium.

Leo is the first US-born pope, so many Americans will want a place in the crowd. Anyone aged 16 to 35 can apply, and a passport is accepted as identification.

The tickets cost nothing, but they are personal and cannot be passed on to anyone else. The Archdiocese of Lima, the Catholic Church’s governing body for the capital region, is organising the evening.

Who: Young people aged 16 to 35 meet Pope Leo XIV, the first US-born pope.

Young people aged 16 to 35 meet Pope Leo XIV, the first US-born pope. What: About 51,000 free tickets via Teleticket, Peru’s ticketing platform, from Monday 9 November.

About 51,000 free tickets via Teleticket, Peru’s ticketing platform, from Monday 9 November. Where: Estadio Nacional (National Stadium), Lima, Peru.

Estadio Nacional (National Stadium), Lima, Peru. When: Thursday 12 November 2026. Gates open 11:00 a.m., vigil starts 6:00 p.m. Lima time (UTC-5).

Thursday 12 November 2026. Gates open 11:00 a.m., vigil starts 6:00 p.m. Lima time (UTC-5). Status: As of 3 November 2026, 19:00 GMT

What We Know

The vigil is an evening prayer gathering where the pope meets young people, with his arrival set for 6:00 p.m. Lima time. Gates open at 11:00 a.m., and preparatory activities begin at 2:00 p.m.

Capacity is about 51,000 young people. Reports differ slightly, with one citing 52,000.

File photo: Lima’s Municipal Palace on the Plaza de Armas, the city’s main square.

The venue changed earlier, moving from the Estadio Monumental, a football stadium in Lima, to the Estadio Nacional, as we reported in our earlier article on the youth rally. Cardinal Carlos Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, has said the event will include choreography and questions from young people.

The Archdiocese of Lima says 99% of the stadium’s gates will be open for entry. That matters for a crowd of this size arriving across several hours.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How to Get a Free Ticket

Distribution runs through Teleticket, Peru’s ticketing platform, from noon Lima time on Monday 9 November. The tickets are free of charge.

You must be between 16 and 35 years old, and each person can hold only one ticket. Tickets are personal and non-transferable.

At the gate, you need valid identification that matches the name on the ticket. Accepted documents are the DNI (Documento Nacional de Identidad, Peru’s national ID card), a foreign ID card or a passport.

A digital or printed ticket is accepted at entry. Organisers stress that entry is strictly personal, so tickets cannot be given to others.

Young people aged 16 and 17 must be registered by an adult aged 18 or over through the adult’s Teleticket account. The adult automatically receives an accompanying ticket.

A signed sworn statement from a parent or guardian, known in Spanish as a declaración jurada, is also required. Both the minor and the adult must show ID and ticket at the gate.

Check that the name on your ticket matches your document exactly. Gates open seven hours before the pope arrives, so there is time to enter calmly.

What Is Not Known

It is unclear whether the tickets will run out quickly. Reports also differ on capacity, with figures of 51,000 and 52,000.

Arrangements for non-Peruvian visitors, beyond the acceptance of a foreign ID card or passport, have not been detailed. Readers should watch Teleticket and the Archdiocese of Lima’s announcements for changes.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

US citizens aged 16 to 35 can use a passport as identification for this event. The tickets are free, so the main cost is the trip itself, which this article does not cover.

The vigil falls inside Leo’s visit to Peru from 11 to 16 November 2026. Our guide to the Lima and Cusco trip sets out the wider schedule.

Lima uses UTC-5, the same offset as US Eastern Standard Time after clocks went back on 1 November. So 6:00 p.m. in Lima is 6:00 p.m. on the US East Coast.

Leo served as a bishop in Chiclayo, a city in northern Peru, and is a naturalised Peruvian, which gives the visit special weight in the country. Free tickets for the Lima Mass on 16 November are covered separately, and our Peru hub tracks the wider story.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is the youth vigil?

It is on Thursday 12 November 2026 at the Estadio Nacional in Lima. Gates open at 11:00 a.m. and the vigil starts at 6:00 p.m. local time.

Who can get a free ticket?

Anyone aged 16 to 35 can get one free ticket through Teleticket from noon Lima time on Monday 9 November. Tickets are personal and non-transferable.

Can US visitors use a passport?

A passport is accepted as valid ID, provided the name matches the ticket. Other arrangements for non-Peruvian visitors have not been detailed.

How do 16 and 17 year olds register?

An adult aged 18 or over must register them through the adult’s Teleticket account and receives an accompanying ticket. A signed sworn statement from a parent or guardian is required.

Sources: Archdiocese of Lima and Peru’s papal visit commission announcements, 3 November 2026; Teleticket ticketing terms.

World.title: Colombia Says Rio Tinto Will Invest US$5B
World.content:
COLOMBIA · MINING

Key Facts Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

What is happening Colombia’s trade minister says Rio Tinto, the Anglo-Australian miner, will invest US$5 billion in the western Chocó region over four years.

Why it matters Colombia is courting mining investors, and Rio Tinto is one of the world’s largest miners, with shares traded in New York, London and Sydney.

The numbers The sum is US$5 billion over four years. No metal, mine site, start date or company statement has been published.

Who is who Mauricio Gómez Amín is Colombia’s trade minister under President Abelardo de la Espriella. Rio Tinto mines iron ore, copper and aluminium.

What to watch Whether Rio Tinto confirms the amount, the metal and the site, and whether security improves in Chocó, which the minister tied to investment.

What it means for you Investors in Rio Tinto and US copper buyers should treat the figure as a government claim until the company confirms it.

Colombia’s trade minister says Rio Tinto plans to invest US$5 billion in Chocó, a Pacific-coast region, over four years. The company has not confirmed the sum, the metal or the site.

What the Minister Said

Trade Minister Mauricio Gómez Amín spoke on Wednesday, 28 October, at a regional planning meeting in Barranquilla. He said he met Rio Tinto the day before, and that it would invest US$5 billion in Chocó over four years.

He tied foreign investment to security, saying President Abelardo de la Espriella is committed to retaking territorial control. The minister named no metal, no mine site and no start date.

What Rio Tinto Has and Has Not Said

Rio Tinto is a mining group listed in London and Sydney, with shares also traded in New York. It produces iron ore, copper and aluminium, among other metals.

No Rio Tinto statement confirming a Chocó plan was found in public reports on 3 November. The company has not said how much it would spend, or on what.

Why the Figure Needs Care

Colombian news sites printed the sum differently, some in pesos and others in dollars. The reports that quote the minister directly give US dollars, so this article uses US$5 billion.

Read as pesos, 5 trillion pesos would be only about US$1.6 billion at 3,183 pesos per US$, the official rate. That gap is why a company confirmation matters.

The Wider Mining Push

The National Mining Agency announced nine new exploration contracts on Friday, 9 October. They cover copper, gold, polymetallic and phosphate areas in Cesar, La Guajira, Antioquia, Tolima and Huila.

Their projected investment is about 54,000 million pesos (about US$17 million), a small fraction of the Rio Tinto figure. Chocó was not among the departments named for those contracts.

What It Means for US Readers

Rio Tinto shares trade in New York, so a confirmed Colombian copper project could matter to US investors. Until then the plan is a government claim, and no output has been announced.

Colombia is also courting other foreign investors, as our reports on a PepsiCo plan and an aluminium zone in Sucre show. Trade talks with Washington are covered in our tariff report.

More is on the Colombia hub, with guides to who runs the economy and who holds power. The nearest city page is Medellín.

What Is Not Known

Rio Tinto has not said which metal it would target, where in Chocó or when work would start. No project list has been published with the minister’s statement.

No official has linked the plan to Rio Tinto’s past exploration in Colombia. Reports that it involves earlier projects rest on a single source and are left out.

The wording and date of the statement come from news reports, because no transcript was found. Whether the US$5 billion is a firm budget or a hope is also unclear.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Rio Tinto investing US$5 billion in Colombia?

Colombia’s trade minister says so, over four years in Chocó. Rio Tinto has not confirmed the amount.

Where is Chocó?

Chocó is a department on Colombia’s Pacific coast in the north-west, near Panama. Its capital is Quibdó.

Which metal would Rio Tinto mine in Chocó?

That has not been said. The minister named no metal, mine site or start date.

Has Rio Tinto confirmed the plan?

No confirming statement was found in public reports on 3 November. The company mines iron ore, copper and aluminium elsewhere.

What other mining deals has Colombia signed lately?

The National Mining Agency announced nine exploration contracts on 9 October for copper, gold, polymetallic and phosphate areas. Their projected investment is about 54,000 million pesos (about US$17 million).

World.title: Brazil Refines More, Yet Diesel Imports Rise
World.content:
BRAZIL · ENERGY

Key Facts Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

What is happening Brazil’s energy planner projects refining capacity up 10% by 2036, yet net diesel imports still rise to 51,000 cubic metres a day.

Why it matters Imports would cover about a quarter of Brazil’s diesel in 2036, tying its fuel costs to the same world market that sets US prices.

The numbers Capacity grows from 2.29 to 2.53 million barrels a day. Diesel imports reach about 320,000 barrels a day, 39% above 2026.

Who is who EPE is the state energy-planning company. The Mines and Energy Ministry, led by Alexandre Silveira, sets national energy policy.

What to watch Public comment on the draft ten-year plan closes on Friday, 6 November, and no date for the final plan has been published.

What it means for you Investors in Petrobras, the state-run oil major listed in New York, will watch the refinery projects. Brazilian fuel costs will keep following the world diesel market.

Brazil plans to refine about 10% more crude oil by 2036, but its own planner says it will still import more diesel. Diesel demand is simply growing faster than new refinery units.

Brazil’s government energy planner expects refining capacity to grow about 10% by 2036, yet the country will still import more diesel. The finding sits in a refining chapter of the draft ten-year energy plan, dated 3 November.

EPE, the state energy-planning company, wrote the chapter for the Mines and Energy Ministry. The ministry opened the full draft for public comment on 8 October, and comment closes on Friday, 6 November.

What the Plan Projects for Refining

Refining capacity rises from 2.29 million barrels a day in 2026 to 2.53 million in 2036, a gain of 10%. The number of working refineries goes from 16 to 19.

Much of the new capacity comes from projects of Petrobras, the state-run oil company, taken from its business plan. The biggest is a second line at the RNEST refinery in Ipojuca, Pernambuco, adding 130,000 barrels a day from June 2027.

Diesel-cleaning units are planned at RNEST, the Boaventura complex in Itaboraí and the Repar and Refap refineries. EPE gives start dates from 2029 to 2032.

Why Diesel Imports Still Grow

Diesel demand is projected to rise 19% between 2026 and 2036, from 173,000 to 206,000 cubic metres a day. Domestic diesel output grows only 13%, to about 155,000 cubic metres a day.

Net diesel imports therefore reach 51,000 cubic metres a day in 2036, about a quarter of demand. That is some 320,000 barrels a day and 39% above the 2026 estimate of 37,000 cubic metres.

It is also 27% above the 2025 record of 40,000 cubic metres a day. EPE says output peaks at 161,000 in 2031, then slips as refiners move from S500 to cleaner S10 diesel.

Oil Products and Crude Overall

Across all oil products, net imports reach 37,000 cubic metres a day in 2036, below the record of 79,000 set in 2017. Their share of domestic demand falls from above 15% in the past decade to 8%.

Brazil stays a net exporter of crude, with output expected near 4.9 million barrels a day in 2036. The planning studies, made from March to June 2026, assume a Brent price near US$80 a barrel.

What It Means for US Readers

Brazil will remain a buyer on the world diesel market, so its trucking and farm costs track prices US truckers also face. Investors in Petrobras, whose shares trade in New York, will watch whether the refinery dates hold.

Brazil’s government is also paying a diesel subsidy, as our report on the aid renewal explains. A separate analysis shows how global refining margins reach Brazilian pumps.

More is on the Brazil hub, with guides to who runs the economy and who holds power. The refining hub city is covered on the Rio de Janeiro page.

What Is Not Known

The plan is a draft, and the numbers may change after public comment. No date for the final version has been published.

The project dates come from EPE’s list of Petrobras plans and were not checked against a Petrobras filing. The chapter gives no cost for the refinery projects.

The plan is a ten-year projection, not a forecast for any single year. Actual imports will depend on prices, freight costs and how refineries run.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will Brazil import more diesel by 2036?

Yes, net diesel imports are projected at 51,000 cubic metres a day in 2036, about 320,000 barrels. That is roughly 25% of demand.

How much will Brazil expand its refining?

Capacity is projected to grow about 10%, from 2.29 million barrels a day in 2026 to 2.53 million in 2036. The number of refineries rises from 16 to 19.

Why does diesel need imports if refining grows?

Diesel demand is projected to grow 19% while domestic diesel output grows only 13%. New units cannot close the gap.

Who published the projections?

EPE, Brazil’s state energy-planning company, wrote them for the Mines and Energy Ministry. They sit in a draft plan open for public comment until 6 November.

Is Brazil still an oil exporter?

Yes, the plan keeps Brazil a net crude exporter, with output near 4.9 million barrels a day in 2036. It still imports diesel.

Sources: EPE, Ten-Year Energy Plan 2036, Refining and Supply Infrastructure chapter, version of 3 November 2026; EPE, Ten-Year Energy Plan 2036 page (public consultation 8 October to 6 November 2026); Brazil Ministry of Mines and Energy. Barrel conversions use 6.29 barrels per cubic metre.

World.title: Brazil’s Tariff Hit City Bets on EU Deal
World.content:
BRAZIL · TRADE

Key Facts Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

What is happening Piracicaba, a machinery-making city in São Paulo state, is courting new export markets, Europe among them, as US tariffs hit its factories.

Why it matters US duties of 25% plus 12.5% add up to 37.5% on Brazilian goods not excluded, and machinery has no sector exemption.

The numbers About 50 local firms with 10,000 direct workers are exposed, and a federal plan of 210 million reais (about US$38 million) can back 5,300 exporters.

Who is who Simespi is the metalworking employers’ union of Piracicaba. ApexBrasil is the federal agency that promotes Brazilian exports.

What to watch Whether the EU-Mercosur trade deal, applied provisionally since 1 May, lowers European duties on Piracicaba’s machinery, and whether Washington offers any tariff relief.

What it means for you US importers of Brazilian machines and parts pay the extra duty at the border, so their costs rise unless a product is excluded.

Piracicaba, a São Paulo state city that builds machinery for US factories, is turning to Europe and other markets. US duties of up to 37.5% have made it the face of Brazil’s tariff pain.

Why Piracicaba Is Exposed

Piracicaba and nearby towns export machinery and parts used in US industry. In August the local union Simespi said the duties touched about 50 firms that employ roughly 10,000 direct workers.

Simespi is the metalworking employers’ union of Piracicaba, Saltinho and Rio das Pedras, led by Paulo Estevam Camargo. Brazil’s Vice President Geraldo Alckmin called it to a meeting set for Friday, 7 August.

The US notice has no general machinery exemption, and its trade office declined to exempt farm, electrical, mining or construction machinery. Some lines, like civil aircraft parts, are excluded.

What Brazil Is Offering Exporters

ApexBrasil, the federal export-promotion agency, runs a plan worth 210 million reais (about US$38 million at 5.49 reais per US$, 3 November). It says it can support about 5,300 of the roughly 5,600 companies it counts as directly hit.
