Hit firms pay no ApexBrasil participation fees, and the agency reimburses certification costs up to 40,000 reais (about US$7,300) per company. That cap covers certification only, not the full cost of winning a new market.

The plan lists 36 priority markets, among them Canada, Mexico, Germany, Turkey, South Africa, Indonesia, India and China. Companies apply through ApexBrasil or its 29 partner sector associations and must give their product code.

Where the EU-Mercosur Deal Stands

The EU and Mercosur, the trade bloc of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, signed their agreements on 17 January 2026. The European Commission says the interim trade agreement has applied provisionally since 1 May 2026.

That trade-only text is to be replaced by the wider partnership agreement once all sides fully ratify it. The Commission’s page gives no tariff schedule, so the gain for Piracicaba’s machinery lines is not confirmed.

Our explainer on the EU-Mercosur interim agreement sets out what is in force and what is still pending. It covers the farm quotas too.

What It Means for US Readers

US importers of Brazilian machinery and parts pay these duties at the border, so landed costs rise unless a product is excluded. US machine makers could meet Brazilian rivals chasing the same buyers in Europe and Latin America.

Brazil’s trade minister has said the government expects a written US tariff proposal in November, as our earlier report explains. Washington has not confirmed a date or announced any cut.

More on the economy is on the Brazil hub, with guides to who runs the economy and who holds power. The nearest city page is São Paulo.

What Is Not Known

No official figure shows how many Piracicaba jobs have been lost since 22 July. The August estimate of 50 firms and 10,000 workers measures exposure, not layoffs.

A union study released on 3 November, ranking Piracicaba first, could not be checked against customs data. Its export totals are left out until a public source confirms them.

Whether the EU deal cuts duties on Piracicaba’s machinery, and how soon, is not shown on the Commission’s page. No company has said it has won a new European order.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Piracicaba called the hardest hit by US tariffs?

The city exports machinery and parts used in US industry, and the US duties reach goods of that kind. Its employers’ union says about 50 firms and 10,000 direct jobs are exposed.

How high are US tariffs on Brazilian goods?

A 25% duty applies from 22 July and a separate 12.5% duty from 24 July, making 37.5% on goods covered by both. Some products, such as civil aircraft parts, are excluded.

Is the EU-Mercosur trade deal in force?

Its interim trade agreement has applied provisionally since 1 May 2026, says the European Commission. The wider partnership agreement still has to be fully ratified.

What help does Brazil give exporters hit by US tariffs?

The plan, worth 210 million reais (about US$38 million), offers fee waivers, trade-fair slots and certification refunds. ApexBrasil, the federal export agency, runs it.

Does this matter to US buyers?

Yes, if they import Brazilian machines or parts. They pay the extra duty at the border unless the product is excluded.

Sources: Office of the US Trade Representative, Section 301 action on Brazil, Federal Register notice of 20 July 2026 and forced-labour Section 301 action, notice of 23 July 2026 (12.5% on Brazil from 24 July); European Commission, EU-Mercosur agreement page; ApexBrasil (export diversification plan of August 2026); Simespi (statements of 5 August 2026); Banco Central do Brasil (PTAX rate of 5.4935 reais per US$, 3 November 2026).

World.title: Forbes Picks Costa Rica’s Rancho Pacifico to Beat the Crowds
World.content:
A Forbes travel feature published Oct. 26 names Rancho Pacifico, an adults-only resort in the rainforest above Uvita on Costa Rica’s southern Pacific coast, as one of its picks for travelers who want to avoid the crowds by going in the shoulder season. The piece, by Forbes contributor Wendy Altschuler, argues that time is the real luxury on any trip and that the weeks between a destination’s busy and quiet periods often bring lower prices, more availability and shorter lines. Costa Rica shares the list with the English countryside, Montana, Lake Tahoe and Mexico’s Chichen Itza.

Altschuler pitches the property as a couples retreat built around slowing down rather than following a packed itinerary. She describes coffee on a private balcony surrounded by rainforest, with more birdsong than a visitor can identify. Early mornings, she writes, bring sightings of blue morpho butterflies, yellow-throated toucans and white-faced capuchin monkeys. Guests can also hike to a waterfall on the property with an onsite naturalist.

The feature praises the food, prepared by experienced chefs, and a warm, attentive staff. It also highlights shared spaces designed for time with other guests or quiet moments as a couple, along with the Pacific sunsets that are one of the resort’s main draws. The resort sits about 600 meters (2,000 feet) up a mountainside, reached by a steep 3-kilometer (2-mile) road from Uvita, on 101 hectares (250 acres) of private rainforest. It holds two Michelin Keys, and the Michelin Guide lists room for a maximum of 20 guests, all over 18.

According to the Michelin listing, the drive takes about 45 minutes from the Quepos airport or roughly three and a half hours from the international airport outside San José. Beyond the resort, Forbes points readers to three national parks. Marino Ballena, known for its whale-tail sandbar, sits on the coast just below Uvita, Manuel Antonio National Park lies to the north, and Corcovado is on the Osa Peninsula to the south, where visitors must enter with a certified guide. The feature also recommends a horseback ride on the beach.

Shoulder season works a little differently in Costa Rica. The high season runs roughly from December through Easter week, while the green season, from about May through November, brings thinner crowds and often lower rates. On the southern Pacific coast, the heaviest rain usually falls in September and October, though mornings are often dry. Altschuler notes that destinations with wet and dry seasons take more planning so the weather does not get in the way of activities.

The feature adds to a run of Forbes coverage of Costa Rica this year, including a September piece on La Fortuna’s turn toward Costa Rican fine dining and the country’s selection as Best Nature Destination at the Forbes Travel Awards in March.

World.title: Costa Rica Researchers Study Pollution Exposure in Ostional Sea Turtles
World.content:
Researchers are examining olive ridley sea turtles at Ostional for exposure to antibiotic-resistance genes as part of a broader investigation into marine pollution. Details released yesterday describe an initial sampling visit conducted in March. The team collected noninvasive samples to establish a starting point for future conservation decisions. No test results were released.

Ostional is known for its arribadas, mass nesting events when thousands of turtles come ashore to lay eggs. The protected area includes Ostional, Nosara, Pelada and Guiones beaches in Guanacaste, along with surrounding marine habitat. The investigation focuses on pollution associated with farming, livestock operations and pharmaceutical use that can reach the ocean through waterways and runoff. Its broader scope includes heavy metals and seabirds, with bird sampling planned for the Gulf of Nicoya.

Scientists from several disciplines are participating in the project, which aims to improve understanding of pollution exposure in marine wildlife and help guide conservation efforts. For people visiting Ostional, existing wildlife protections remain central to the experience. Visitors must enter with a local guide during arribadas, and nighttime flash photography is prohibited. Visitors should also ask their guide before using a flashlight because light can disrupt nesting turtles.

The refuge prohibits vehicles on the beach, horseback riding on the sand, bonfires and pets in protected areas. Those rules help protect the nesting habitat that makes Ostional one of Costa Rica’s best-known wildlife destinations.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Highway Cameras and Radar Every 1.5 Kilometers on San Ramón Route
World.content:
Drivers on the widened highway between San José and San Ramón would be watched by cameras and radar sensors at least every 1.5 kilometers (0.9 miles), according to documents for the long-delayed expansion of Route 1. The system would track vehicle speeds, traffic volume, congestion and crashes along the corridor around the clock, including at night and in fog or heavy rain. If built as specified, the route would be the first in Costa Rica covered end to end by video surveillance.

The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) has not said whether the equipment will be used to issue automated speeding tickets. The requirements are part of the tender MOPT published on Oct. 21 for widening roughly 55.6 kilometers (34.5 miles) of Route 1 between La Sabana in San José and San Ramón in Alajuela. The project is financed by a $770 million loan from the Central American Bank for Economic Integration and the OPEC Fund.

Under the tender, contractors must install dome-style cameras that pan, tilt and zoom, record in color and see at least 1.5 kilometers. The cameras also need infrared or thermal night vision and must keep working in fog, cloud cover and low light. Coverage has to reach the entire roadway with no blind spots. Contractors would have to prove that with a three-dimensional coverage map and add cameras wherever gaps appear.

The units would sit on 15-meter (49-foot) poles inside the highway right of way. Where grid power is not available, they would run on solar panels. The radar sensors would count vehicles, measure their speed and classify them by type. They would also record vehicle length, the average gap between cars, how much of the road is occupied and where traffic jams begin to form.

A separate set of cameras would send automatic alerts for crashes, stalled vehicles, wrong-way drivers, congestion and people on foot in restricted areas. Those alerts would go to a traffic control center planned at the Los Arcos toll plaza in Belén. Operators there would monitor the corridor and the new Río Segundo connector, coordinating with the Road Safety Council (Cosevi) and the Traffic Police. The tender requires a protocol to activate the response to a major crash within five minutes.

Drivers would see the information on LED message boards similar to those on Route 27. The boards would warn of crashes, breakdowns, lane closures, roadwork, rain and fog, and could show travel times or suggest alternate routes when traffic stops. The package also includes a weather station recording rain, wind, temperature and visibility. It adds emergency call posts linked to the control center and scales that weigh trucks while they are moving.

The same technology would make barrier-free tolls possible. The tender includes requirements for electronic vehicle identification and automatic license plate recognition, and contractors must leave conduits, foundations and equipment space for future toll gantries. Toll stations must also be designed so their islands and booths can later be removed to leave a continuous roadway. That switch depends on legislation that does not yet exist.

Public Works Minister Efraím Zeledón has said MOPT is preparing a bill to allow toll payment without barriers. One option would charge tolls through digital marchamo technology linked to the vehicle, similar to a Quickpass tag. A separate bill to the same effect, filed in March by lawmaker Alexander Barrantes Chacón remains in committee.

The highway is planned to have four main toll stations at Los Arcos, El Coyol, Grecia and the Río Segundo connector. Zeledón has put the full one-way trip for a light vehicle at about ₡1,523, roughly $3.34, while cautioning that the figure is approximate. Construction is expected to begin in the second half of 2027 in seven sections. Each section would open as it is completed, with the full project due within six years.

Automated speed enforcement has a troubled history in Costa Rica. A first attempt at camera-issued fines in 2011 stalled over notification problems, a lack of funding and a Constitutional Court ruling, and a separate private proposal to bring the cameras back on high-crash routes, submitted in 2023, is still under study.

Speeding remains the leading cause of road deaths and officers fined 2,254 drivers for speeding in the first half of 2026, a period in which 330 people died on Costa Rica’s roads. Whether the San Ramón cameras end up writing tickets will depend on decisions MOPT has yet to announce. For now, the tender presents them as a way to spot crashes and congestion faster on one of our busiest commuter corridors.

World.title: El Niño Is Already Cutting Costa Rica’s Coffee Harvest by Up to 15%
World.content:
Costa Rica’s coffee growers now expect a harvest 10% to 15% smaller than first estimated as El Niño’s irregular rains and rising heat reach farms across the country, according to the Coffee Institute of Costa Rica (Icafé). Rice, banana, melon and cattle producers are issuing similar warnings, and the Central Bank now projects that the farm sector will shrink next year.

Miguel Barquero, deputy director of Icafé, said irregular rainfall delayed fertilization by about 30 days and that harvest estimates have fallen across the country’s coffee regions. He added that the quality and weight of export-grade green coffee are also being affected, while the National Meteorological Institute (IMN) projects higher temperatures in December and January.

In its October Monetary Policy Report, the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) lowered its outlook for agriculture, which it now projects will grow 0.7% in 2026 and contract 0.5% in 2027. The bank cited a larger drop in coffee production, lower onion and sugarcane output, the effects of El Niño and higher international fertilizer prices. As recently as April, it had projected 0.8% farm-sector growth for 2027.

The BCCR said pineapple and coffee are especially exposed because much of their production sits in areas where rainfall is expected to be scarce, and higher temperatures could spread fungi and plant disease. For livestock, it expects less pasture and water to lower productivity and raise operating costs. In its July report, the bank had already warned that climate shocks could create a negative supply shock, mainly in agriculture, and add to inflationary pressure.

Citing IMN projections, the BCCR said El Niño is expected to remain in the very strong category from October 2026 through February 2027 before easing to strong in March and April, in line with global forecasts of an El Niño peak in December. Rainfall is forecast to drop about 60% in the North Pacific and about 40% elsewhere on the Pacific coast, in Upala, Los Chiles, Guatuso and the Central Valley. The Caribbean slope and the rest of the Northern Zone are expected to see 10% to 15% more rain than average.

That split is already visible in rice fields. Mainor Cruz, executive director of the National Rice Corporation (Conarroz), said the Brunca region and the Central Pacific have reported losses tied to rainfall deficits, while the Huetar Norte region has reported problems from excess rain. He said the losses cannot yet be quantified and that a technical assessment is underway, with November a key month for the North Pacific harvest.

On the Caribbean side, the National Banana Corporation (Corbana) said excess rain has affected nearly all banana-growing cantons, with some plantations flooded for 12 to 36 hours. A plantation needs about 200 millimeters (7.9 inches) of rain a month, but some Caribbean areas recorded 280 millimeters (11 inches) in two days in August, the same wet pattern that has threatened the region’s cacao harvest. Corbana said temperatures running 0.5 to 1 degree Celsius (0.9 to 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) above average favor black sigatoka, a fungal disease, and that El Niño effects could last until June 2027.

Sigurd Vargas, president of the melon and watermelon exporters’ chamber Caproexmes, said producers expect a strong rise in pests, mainly insects, during the November-to-May season. He also warned of possible flowering losses from heat and said planted area, hiring and exports are likely to fall because of the exchange rate, input costs and higher diesel prices, pressures that coffee growers have also blamed for job cuts on farms. Vargas said the Agriculture Ministry has not responded to a bio-input proposal the sector submitted on May 26.

Pineapple growers have not yet felt an impact, according to Abel Chaves, president of the pineapple producers’ chamber Canapep. He said losses could come from excess rain in the Atlantic zone, which blocks machinery access, and that because harvests are planned a year ahead, any drop in volume would likely appear in late 2026 or early 2027.

Cattle ranchers expect the hardest blow once the dry season sets in. Luis Diego Obando, executive director of the Livestock Corporation (Corfoga), said national production has not yet been affected, though rain has already caused problems in the northern zone. He said producers are building water reservoirs and pasture reserves and that Corfoga is coordinating with the National Emergency Commission (CNE). Costa Rica has already issued its first red alert at sea as drought hits Guanacaste.

Together, the warnings describe a dry season in which too little rain on one coast and too much on the other could shape what reaches the country’s markets. With the Central Bank flagging possible pressure on prices and officials already warning of risks to water supplies, the coming months will test farms, food budgets and public planning alike.

World.title: Your 2027 Marchamo Is Due and the New Sticker Can Only Go On Once
World.content:
You can now check and pay your 2027 marchamo, Costa Rica’s mandatory annual vehicle fee, and you have until Dec. 31 to do it without surcharges. This year the payment comes with something new for your windshield: a ¢1,200 electronic sticker designed to last up to 10 years, and one you can only stick on once.

The National Insurance Institute (INS) opened collection today. This year 2,090,602 vehicle owners have to pay, and INS expects to collect about ¢365 billion (roughly $800 million). By 10:30 a.m. on the first day, the system had logged 1.37 million queries and 1,256 payments.

Before you pay, look closely at the total. On Monday, the INS online calculator added Más Protección, an optional accident insurance policy costing ¢11,900 (about $26), to the amount it showed as the total to pay. The box was ticked by default, and you had to untick it on the next screen to avoid buying it.

After complaints from drivers and a call from the general superintendent of insurance, INS said it would stop pre-selecting the policy from midnight Monday. If you looked up your amount on the first day, the figure you saw may have been higher than what you owe. The optional policy is still available if you want it.

The new 10-year digital sticker covers cars, buses, trucks and other vehicles with a windshield. Motorcycles and special equipment keep the traditional sticker for now. A motorcycle sticker sits outside, exposed to sun, rain and mud, so INS will test the technology on motorcycles in a pilot first.

You receive the sticker when you pay at an INS branch or one of the 2,407 authorized collection points around the country. Its ¢1,200 cost is already included in your marchamo total. In later years you only pay the fee, and the same sticker stays on the glass.

Put it on carefully, because you get one try. Clean the glass, then place the sticker on the inside of the windshield, at the top and in the center. The chip inside is destroyed if you peel it off, a security feature meant to stop stickers from being stolen or moved to another vehicle. If you later replace the windshield or the sticker is damaged, you will have to request a new one through INS.

If you own more than one vehicle, check before you stick. INS President Gabriela Chacón said owners should confirm in the INS Móvil app that the code on each sticker matches the right plate. INS General Manager José Arévalo said the code is tied to your vehicle and should only be shared with someone you trust.

The paper receipt is gone, too. Your proof of payment, the derecho de circulación, arrives by email at the address you give when you pay. You can also download it as a PDF from grupoins.com or the INS Móvil app, or save it to your phone’s digital wallet. If you don’t use email, INS suggested giving a relative’s address and printing the document to keep in the car. Either way, keep a copy handy in case a traffic officer asks for it.

You don’t need to scrape off your 2026 sticker. The Public Works and Transport Ministry (MOPT) said leaving it in place will not get you fined. MOPT expects Traffic Police to switch to new devices in 2028 that can check whether a vehicle is up to date just by reading the sticker. The sticker is not a tracker. It uses passive UHF radio-frequency identification, and INS said it has no battery and no GPS, stores no record of where you drive and responds only when an authorized reader scans it at close range.

To see what you owe, go to marchamo.grupoins.com, choose your vehicle type and enter your plate number without spaces or dashes. You can also call 800-MARCHAMO (800-6272-4266), message INS on WhatsApp at 2287-6100 or use the INS Móvil app. You can pay on grupoins.com, in the app, by phone at 800-TeleINS (800-835-3467), at INS offices or at any authorized collection point.

Your total covers more than the fee itself. Any unpaid municipal parking-meter charges are added, with interest. Property tax makes up about 59% of the marchamo, and the mandatory vehicle insurance about 27%.

That insurance, known as SOA, rose ¢1,643 for private cars, ¢4,487 for motorcycles and ¢10,048 for buses compared with last year. It fell ¢1,672 for light cargo vehicles, ¢834 for heavy cargo and about ¢5,500 for taxis. Sidney Viales, who heads mandatory insurance at INS, said traffic accidents drove this year’s rates. INS said motorcycle riders account for 65% to 70% of the people injured in crashes.

The deadline is Dec. 31. From Jan. 1, unpaid vehicles face surcharges, and driving without a current marchamo can bring fines under the Traffic Law.

World.title: Costa Rica Now Has Its Own Wine Grape After a 50-Year Quest
World.content:
Costa Rica now has a wine grape of its own. Peppevidor, a hybrid bred to grow in tropical heat, was certified as a new plant variety by the National Seed Office (Oficina Nacional de Semillas), capping roughly half a century of work by Italian-born grape breeder Virgilio Vidor. Vidor, 78, says it is the first wine grape developed in Costa Rica to receive official registration. He crossed a wild grape native to Costa Rica with a European wine grape and named the result after his late brother, Giuseppe.

Peppe is the familiar Italian short form of that name. The official notice of his application, filed with the seed office in June 2024, lists the cross as Vitis tiliifolia, a wild grape that grows across Central America, with Vitis vinifera, the species behind nearly all of the world’s wine. That pairing matters because European grapes struggle here for two reasons. They need a cool season to rest and then bud evenly, which the tropics do not provide.

And in warm climates they are vulnerable to Xylella fastidiosa, a bacterium that clogs the vine’s water-carrying tissue and causes what growers call Pierce’s disease. Peppevidor grows without a cold season and resists the bacterium, according to Vidor. He said the grape is at home in Costa Rica because part of its ancestry comes from the local wild vine, describing it as functionally rather than perfectly tropical, since its Costa Rican and Italian genes are mixed.

Vidor said the certification confirms the plant is a new variety, distinct from all others. He added that he was delighted Costa Rica now has the grape, which he said belongs to Costa Ricans. Tasters who have tried wine made from Peppevidor describe it as light red in color, with notes of coffee that they say capture something of Costa Rica.

The Costa Rica Institute of Technology (TEC) carried out the technical examination needed to register Peppevidor as a new variety. Carlos Alvarado, director of the TEC’s Centro de Vinculación, said it was the first time the university had conducted an examination of this kind. He said the experience will allow it to take on more in the future and will be passed on to its students.

Vidor arrived from Italy in December 1972, at 24, with his parents and younger brother. His father’s family came from the Prosecco wine country near Treviso, and the Vidors settled on a farm near Playa Panamá, in the northwestern province of Guanacaste, where they began planting vines.

In the 1970s the farm became the base of a tropical viticulture project financed by the Costa Rican government and the U.S. Agency for International Development, with Vidor as its director. When disease began attacking the vines, he turned to hybridization rather than abandon the effort, searching for a grape that could withstand Guanacaste’s long dry season and tropical pests.

Breeding a grape is slow work. Vidor has said a new hybrid needs at least a decade of trials before its viability can be confirmed or ruled out. The grapes long grown in Costa Rica, such as Isabella, are hybrids developed elsewhere, and until now none bred in the country had been officially registered, according to Vidor.

His farm still works as an experimental vineyard, where he tests hundreds of hybrids. Italy has named him a Commendatore of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic, one of its highest honors, for his rural development work in Central America and his research on tropical viticulture.

Wine has always been a niche product in Costa Rica, and our few vineyards have relied on varieties bred for other climates. A grape bred here, from a native vine, gives that small scene something it has never had before, a variety that started in Costa Rica’s own forests.

World.title: Prosecutors Find No Costa Rican Victims in Epstein Files Investigation
World.content:
Costa Rican prosecutors have asked a court to dismiss their investigation into possible child sexual abuse linked to mentions of Costa Rica in the Jeffrey Epstein files, after finding no Costa Rican victims and no evidence that any crime took place here. The gender crimes unit of the Public Prosecutor’s Office filed the request with the Criminal Court of San José, which must now decide whether to close the case. The investigation was opened in February on the instructions of Attorney General Carlo Díaz.

Prosecutors worked on the case with the gender violence section of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) and with international agencies, including the FBI, according to the request. Investigators were unable to identify any Costa Rican minors among the victims of Epstein’s network. They also could not establish that the criminal conduct occurred in Costa Rica,or link any specific person to an offense under Costa Rican jurisdiction.

The police report found multiple references to Costa Rica in the files released by the US Department of Justice, but no specific information or objective evidence to support the theory that prompted the case. Prosecutors described the investigation as having started from a generic suspicion based on press reports that could not be corroborated with material evidence.

The case was filed against unknown persons and no suspect was ever named. When it opened, the attorney general said media reports had placed Costa Rica among the possible countries where such crimes were committed. He also noted that a 2019 legal reform could keep older cases from expiring, since victims can now file complaints up to 25 years after reaching adulthood.

Costa Rica appears hundreds of times in the Epstein files, across emails, phone records and court documents. Many of those references involve child sex tourism, including records from an FBI undercover operation that used a fake travel agency called Costa Rica Taboo Vacations.

Other references concern trips to Costa Rica by people in Epstein’s circle, including his former partner Ghislaine Maxwell. The court has not yet ruled on the request to dismiss the case.

World.title: Gota a Gota Extortion Cases Keep Climbing in Costa Rica, OIJ Data Show
World.content:
Extortion complaints linked to informal gota a gota loans in Costa Rica reached a record 935 in 2025, more than double the 427 filed in 2022, according to data from the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ). The trend has not eased this year. The OIJ’s criminal analysis unit recorded 840 complaints from January through Oct. 15, 2026, leaving 95 cases short of last year’s total with two and a half months still to go.

Michael Soto, the OIJ’s interim director, described gota a gota lending as a well-established criminal phenomenon. He also said that people file few complaints, which means the official figures likely understate the scale of the problem. The loans are typically offered without paperwork, guarantors or credit checks, often to people who need cash quickly for medical costs, utility bills or food. Lenders collect payments every day and charge interest that borrowers frequently cannot pay down, turning a small loan into a debt with no clear end.

When payments fall short, collectors turn to intimidation, according to the OIJ. Victims have reported threats at their homes, harassing phone calls and, in some cases, physical attacks. Authorities say the groups also pursue relatives when a borrower cannot pay. Investigators link the organized groups behind the loans to drug trafficking and money laundering. In October, a national team defender was among four people detained in a gota a gota extortion investigation, a case that remains at the investigative stage.

Authorities have also identified a newer variant known as chorro a chorro. It involves loans of millions of colones to borrowers with higher incomes, rather than to people facing an emergency. The yearly figures show the sharpest jump between 2022 and 2023, when complaints rose from 427 to 864. They dipped slightly to 857 in 2024 before reaching the 2025 high.

Across the five years, complaints have been highest in August, September and October, and lowest in December and February. Authorities urge anyone being pressured by an informal lender not to give in to threats and to report the case to the OIJ as soon as possible. Knowing the warning signs of a gota a gota loan can help people avoid the trap before it starts.

World.title: Belize City Mayor engages CARICOM and Commonwealth leaders at CHOGM 2026
World.content:
Belize City Mayor engages CARICOM and Commonwealth leaders at CHOGM 2026

By Zoila Palma: Today, Bernard Wagner, Mayor of Belize City and Chair of the Commonwealth Local Government Forum (CLGF), continued his high-level engagements at CHOGM 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda, connecting with distinguished leaders from across CARICOM and the wider Commonwealth.

Among the notable engagements were Prime Minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley, and Commonwealth Secretary-General, Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey, highlighting the importance of strengthening regional and international partnerships.

Mayor Wagner also participated in the Commonwealth Secretary-General’s Lunch Reception, which brought together representatives of Commonwealth organisations and key partners to deepen collaboration and advance shared priorities.

As Chair of CLGF, Mayor Wagner continues to champion the interests of local governments across the Commonwealth’s 56 member states, advocating for stronger local democracy, sustainable urban development, and greater recognition of cities as essential partners in national and global progress.

World.title: Celebrating Janal Pixano’ob in Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Celebrating Janal Pixano’ob in Orange Walk Town

By Zoila Palma: On October 31, 2026, Orange Walk Central Park featured vibrant altar displays celebrating Janal Pixano’ob, a cherished Yucatec Maya tradition of remembering and honoring loved ones who have passed.

Rooted in Yucatec Maya cultural heritage, Janal Pixano’ob is a tradition where families honor their departed loved ones and maintain the enduring bonds between the living and those who came before us. Through these traditions, ancestral memory, cultural identity, and knowledge continue to be shared across generations.

The Institute of Social and Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) extended heartfelt appreciation to the Northern Maya Association of Belize for organizing this event and to their many partners including the Orange Walk Town Council and the Bishop Martin High School, and the Belize Tourism Board.

The Ministry of Culture through NICH-ISCR and the Banquitas House of Culture says that it remain committed to safeguarding and promoting Belize’s living heritage and ensuring that these traditions are passed on to future generations.

World.title: Belize and Taiwan explore academic collaboration in Smart Agriculture and Agro-Processing
World.content:
Belize and Taiwan explore academic collaboration in Smart Agriculture and Agro-Processing

By Zoila Palma: A delegation from Taiwan visited the University of Belize’s Central Farm Campus on October 27, 2026, as part of efforts to strengthen academic partnerships and promote collaboration in agriculture, innovation and education.

The delegation was welcomed by Egbert Irving, Director at the University of Belize, along with university staff, for a guided tour of the campus.

The visiting delegation included representatives from TaiwanICDF, the Taiwan Technical Mission and partner institutions National Dong Hwa University, Ming Chuan University, Kun Shan University and Meiho University.

During the visit, the group toured campus facilities and learned about the University of Belize’s key areas of focus, particularly Smart Agriculture and Agro-Processing.

The visit provided an opportunity for both sides to exchange knowledge, explore areas of mutual interest and strengthen ties between Belizean and Taiwanese academic institutions.

World.title: United Nations Development Programme and NEMO host workshop to strengthen disaster recovery efforts
World.content:
United Nations Development Programme and NEMO host workshop to strengthen disaster recovery efforts

By Zoila Palma: The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), in partnership with the National Emergency Management Organization (NEMO), is working to strengthen Belize’s disaster recovery arrangements through a two-day workshop that began on November 3, 2026, at Dream Valley Resort in Teakettle, Cayo.

The workshop brings together representatives from various government ministries and departments to review existing recovery arrangements and identify ways to improve coordination among agencies.

Discussions are focusing on ensuring that government institutions are better prepared to work together when supporting communities and restoring essential services following a major disaster.

Participants are also reviewing the roles and responsibilities of different agencies and the procedures required to guide recovery efforts.

The workshop, which concludes on November 4, forms part of broader national efforts to strengthen Belize’s disaster preparedness, response and recovery systems.

World.title: Dad remanded to prison after woman he brought home from a night of drinking allegedly stole his daughter’s clothes
World.content:
Dad remanded to prison after woman he brought home from a night of drinking allegedly stole his daughter’s clothes

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 50-year-old Belize City man was remanded to prison on Monday after being unable to post bail on a theft charge involving his daughter’s clothing, despite claiming that a woman he met while drinking was responsible for the missing items.

Kirk Errol Pitts, a resident of Antelope Street Extension, appeared unrepresented before a Magistrate in Belize City, where he was accused of stealing clothing belonging to his daughter on October 30, 2026.

The missing items reportedly included two pairs of blue jeans and a white blouse.

Pitts initially pleaded not guilty but attempted to explain that the charge resulted from a misunderstanding between him and his daughter.

According to Pitts, he met a woman while drinking at a Chinese shop and eventually invited her to his home. He claimed that while he was using the bathroom, the woman stole some of his daughter’s clothing without his knowledge.

Pitts told the court that he had no one to assist him with bail because his mother and brother had died. He also expressed concern that going to prison would cause him to lose his job.

At one point, Pitts indicated that he wanted to plead guilty, apparently believing it would help him avoid being remanded. However, the Magistrate refused to accept a guilty plea because his explanation continued to deny responsibility for the alleged theft.

With no objection from the prosecution, Pitts was offered bail of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount. However, he was also required to settle an outstanding court fine of $55 before securing his release.

Pitts requested bail on his own recognizance, but that request was denied.

Unable to pay the outstanding fine or secure a surety, Pitts was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until he can meet the conditions for his release.

His next court appearance is scheduled for January 2027.

World.title: Mayor of Belize City leads Commonwealth Local Government delegation at CARICOM Heads of Government meeting 2026
World.content:
Mayor of Belize City leads Commonwealth Local Government delegation at CARICOM Heads of Government meeting 2026

By Zoila Palma: Today, Mayor Bernard Wagner, in his capacity as Chair of the Commonwealth Local Government Forum (CLGF), is leading a delegation at CHOGM 2026 in Antigua and Barbuda, championing the interests of local governments across the Commonwealth’s 56 member states.

Building on his recent participation in the Wilton Park Dialogue on Sustainable Urbanisation in Guyana, Mayor Wagner continues to advocate for stronger local governance, sustainable urban development and greater investment in resilient infrastructure.

At the business forum held on November 2, Mayor Wagner contributed to a high-level roundtable discussion on building resilient, smart and sustainable cities, highlighting the importance of integrating emerging technologies, innovative financing and inclusive urban planning into the future of Commonwealth cities.

Mayor Wagner also highlighted practical initiatives, including the Yabra Flood Pumping Station, the eRide electric mobility programme and the Floating Pavilion, demonstrating how local innovation can strengthen climate resilience, modernise urban infrastructure and improve quality of life.

“His intervention reinforced a central message; Commonwealth cities must be empowered with the resources, partnerships and autonomy to transform ambitious development goals into practical solutions for their communities,” the Belize City council said.

As Chair of the CLGF, Mayor Wagner continues to position Belize City at the forefront of Commonwealth discussions, ensuring that the voices and priorities of local governments are represented at the highest levels

World.title: Police seek information on burglary at Quality Poultry Belmopan
World.content:
Police seek information on burglary at Quality Poultry Belmopan

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Police Department is seeking any information leading to the culprits who reportedly burglarized Quality Poultry Products in Belmopan on October 31 at around 9pm.

Reports indicate that 4 armed masked men entered the establishment and stole cash, cell phones, jewelry and a black in color 9mm pistol Smith & Wesson Brand SN: HPU3190.

Anyone with information is urged to call Crime Stoppers at 922, use the P3 APP, or contact the nearest police station.

World.title: Belize to lead CARICOM negotiations on Climate Finance and markets at COP31
World.content:
Belize to lead CARICOM negotiations on Climate Finance and markets at COP31

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s Minister of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, Orlando Habet, has been selected by the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) to lead negotiations on climate finance and markets ahead of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for November 9 to 20, 2026.

Habet is among ministers from nine CARICOM member states appointed to lead the region’s engagement across critical climate negotiating areas.

He will represent the region in discussions on finance, alongside Barbados’ Minister of Economic Affairs and Investment, Marsha Caddle, and Antigua and Barbuda’s Minister Michael Joseph.

Habet will also lead negotiations on climate markets alongside Suriname’s Minister of Oil, Gas and Environment, Patrick Loys Brunings.

Other ministers will lead negotiations on adaptation, the cover decision, global stocktake and just transition, loss and damage, and science.

The appointments are intended to coordinate CARICOM’s position and strengthen the region’s voice on issues that directly affect Caribbean countries, particularly their vulnerability to climate change and limited resources to respond to its impacts.

Ahead of COP31, CARICOM ministers are calling for a balanced, ambitious and implementation-focused outcome that protects the goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius.

World.title: Terrelonge extends condolences amid ‘agonising’ loss of two brothers in house fire
World.content:
State minister in the Ministry of Education, Youth and Information, Alando Terrelonge.

ST CATHERINE, Jamaica — Member of Parliament (MP) for St Catherine East Central, Alando Terrelonge, has expressed profound sorrow over the deaths of 10-year-old Dion Bell and his five-year-old brother, Jausha Bell, who perished in a house fire on Monday, pledging support for their grieving family.

In a statement on Tuesday, Terrelonge said the incident has plunged the Gregory Park community into mourning.

“No family should ever have to endure the agonising pain of losing children under such catastrophic and unfortunate circumstances. The loss of these two young souls, one of whom is believed to have been autistic, has cast a dark shadow of sorrow over the entire community and our nation,” he said.

The MP said the Government’s thoughts and prayers are with the boys’ mother, who remains hospitalised as she battles to recover, as well as their father and surviving sibling, who are grappling with the devastating loss.

According to Terrelonge, reports indicate that the fire spread at a “terrifying speed”, overwhelming the desperate efforts of residents who attempted to extinguish the blaze.

Having visited the scene alongside Divisional Councillor Joy Brown, Terrelonge said he witnessed first-hand the destruction left in the fire’s wake.

READ: Brothers, aged 5 and 10, die in Portmore house fire

“We are actively mobilising emergency support, grief counselling and relief services for the surviving family members. Furthermore, I will be speaking with the Minister of Local Government and Community Development, Desmond McKenzie, to secure urgent social and housing assistance for the family,” he said.

Terrelonge also commended the firefighters and other first responders who attended the scene, as investigations continue into the cause of the blaze.

“We express our deep gratitude to the first responders from the Waterford Fire Station and the Jamaica Fire Brigade who are currently working to investigate and determine the root cause of this fire,” he said.

He further appealed to residents of Gregory Park and the wider constituency to rally around the bereaved family.

“I urge everyone in Gregory Park and across the constituency to wrap this family in comfort, love, and community support in the difficult days ahead,” Terrelonge added.

World.title: UTech to confer honorary degrees on Oliver Samuels, Richard Pandohie and Vivian Crawford
World.content:
This Combo Photo shows from left Oliver Samuels, Richard Pandohie and Vivian Crawford. All three men are to be awarded with honorary degrees from the University of Technology UTech

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Vivian Crawford, Oliver Samuels and Richard Pandohie will receive honorary degrees from the University of Technology (UTech) for their significant service to the nation during its 2026 graduation ceremonies.

Samuels, a Jamaican cultural icon, actor and comedian; Pandohie, chief executive officer and managing director of Seprod Jamaica Limited; and Crawford, the retired/former executive director of the Institute of Jamaica and educator, financier and heritage historian were described as nation builders by the institution.

UTech said Samuels will be conferred on Saturday, November 14, at 10:00 am with the Honorary Doctor of Letters (Honoris Causa) in recognition of his significant contributions to Jamaican culture, theatre and comedy through a distinguished career spanning more than 55 years in theatrical performance, television and film.

Pandohie will receive the Honorary Doctor of Technology (Honoris Causa) on Saturday, November 14, at 4:00 pm in recognition of his three decades of leadership and contributions spanning engineering, business and Jamaica’s economic development.

On Sunday, November 15, at 10:00 am, Crawford will be conferred with the Doctor of Laws (Honoris Causa) in recognition of his distinguished career bridging education, finance, culture and public service, and his significant role in advancing the preservation and international recognition of Jamaica’s cultural heritage.

The university will also confer the Chancellor’s Medal on Hilory Pamela Kelly, retired university public orator and accomplished Jamaican educator, language specialist and curriculum developer during the first ceremony. The Chancellor’s Medal award, of equal status to an honorary doctorate, is bestowed by the chancellor to recognise the contributions of individuals or institutions of national or international significance.

“Their achievements span industry, cultural heritage, the creative arts and education, reflecting the diverse talents and commitment that drive national progress. As we honour their legacies, we also celebrate the example they set for our graduates, inspiring them to use their knowledge, skills and talents to serve their communities, contribute to national development and make a meaningful impact on the world,” said UTech President Dr Kevin Brown.

During the three ceremonies slated for the Alfred Sangster Auditorium at the university, the institution will present degrees and other academic distinctions to over 1,800 graduates.

World.title: Molynes United sack coach Thomas
World.content:
Jermaine Thomas, Molynes United coach (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Observer Online has learnt that Jermaine Thomas has been sacked by Molynes United following a 1-2 loss to Mount Pleasant on Monday.

It was Molynes’ sixth defeat from eight games this season which saw them lurking just above the relegation zone in 12th spot on six points.

With only two wins, the management team has seen enough, according to Observer sources.

Thomas took charge of Molynes during the 2023–24 season after Alex Thomas was removed. He subsequently guided the club through difficult periods, including relegation battles, but sources said the management has lost confidence in him this season.

Thomas has made a name for himself leading McGrath High to prominence in schoolboy football in recemt times. McGrath reached the daCosta Cup semi-finals in 2019 and finals in 2024, losing to Garvey Maceo on penalties.

He also led McGrath to the 2023 Ben Francis title, his best achievement to date.

Previously he coached at Rivoli United, Federal United, Mico Colllege University and was a member of the Reggae Girlz coaching staff in 2023 for two games.

– Howard Walker

World.title: Hit job foiled
World.content:
A dog sits beside this Toyota Voxy in which a man, who police say engaged them in a firefight, was fatally shot in Knockpatrick, Manchester, on Monday. The dog had been in the motor vehicle.Photo: Kasey Williams

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — A man who police say was on his way to commit a contract murder was fatally shot after being intercepted and engaging cops in a firefight in Knockpatrick, Manchester, on Monday.

Up to press time police had not released the identity of the man, who was travelling with a lap dog. The pet was not harmed in the shoot-out.

Head of the Manchester police, Deputy Superintendent Odean Dennis, said about 12:10 pm cops were acting on information of a “threat to life” when they intercepted a Toyota Voxy motor vehicle.

“…Police received information that someone was about to be killed. They went in search of a black Toyota Voxy motor vehicle with DC plates affixed. They came upon a vehicle fitting the description and signalled it to stop. The occupant opened fire at the police, who defended themselves,” Dennis told the Jamaica Observer.

He said an Armscor .38 special revolver along with rounds of ammunition was found inside the vehicle.

“A police service vehicle was also damaged by bullets. The man was taken to hospital where he was pronounced dead,” Superintendent Dennis said.

Detectives said that the dead man was a person of interest in the February 1 double murder of Raheem Ward, otherwise called Richie Rich, and Adrian Reid in Old England, Manchester.

“I want to take this opportunity to highlight that it is increasingly coming to our knowledge that the issue of contract killing is real in this parish, but I want to assure the public that the Manchester police are prepared to deal decisively with this issue,” Dennis said.

“We want to encourage the public to keep sharing information, as this is how we will continue to fit the pieces of the puzzle of organised crime together in this parish. I want to implore young men to go and find a skill, get yourselves gainfully and legally employed, because engaging in these kinds of illegal activities for monetary gains can lead to incidents such as these, and we really don’t want that for our young men,” Dennis added.

He also commended police personnel and their Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) counterparts for maintaining order in Manchester, pointing out that the division recorded no murders for the month of October.

“We attribute this to a number of things. Firstly, the skilful and well-thought-out planning, coordinating, and directing of our management

— the expert execution of plans by our boots on the ground and better coordination between our key elements within the division, and the unwavering support of our partners within the JCF (Jamaica Constabulary Force). Our external partners such as the JDF and the business community also come in for mention when it comes to the achievement and, most importantly, the support of the public, which was tremendous,” said Dennis.

World.title: Mammogram woes worsen in western Jamaica
World.content:
A radiologist examines a mammogram scan for breast cancer detection.Photo: Adobe Stock

MONTEGO BAY, St James — The National Health Fund (NHF) is developing an initiative to have a mobile mammography unit travel across the island, providing critical screening service to the public.

While the programme is still in its early stages, it comes as western Jamaica faces a severe shortage of mammography equipment used to screen for and diagnose breast cancer.

“We’re working on a mobile solution, but are not at the point to say it’s fully sorted, but early in the new year we can update you,” NHF CEO Everton Anderson told the Jamaica Observer in an interview last Friday.

The limited availability of mammogram machines in the region has left patients with few options. One resident told the Observer that she will have to travel to Kingston for her annual examination.

A private medical facility in St James that typically offers the service is reportedly operating without a functional machine. Efforts to reach a representative of the institution by phone were unsuccessful.

Clinical coordinator for the Western Regional Health Authority (WRHA) Dr Delroy Fray outlined the gravity of the situation in western Jamaica.

“Unfortunately, none of the private places in Montego Bay do mammograms. However, Radiology West does CT [computed tomography] of the breast, and CT of the breast can give you the information that you need to know, but it costs more than a mammogram,” explained Dr Fray.

Dedicated breast CT is a modern imaging technology designed to examine breast tissue directly, without painful plate compression. Public institutions offer little relief.

Dr Fray noted that across the four parishes managed by the WRHA ­­— St James, Hanover, Westmoreland, and Trelawny — Cornwall Regional Hospital (CRH) in St James is the only facility with a functioning unit, and access is strictly prioritised.

“It’s hard to provide that for the private patient because it will take up a lot of our time, so we use it for our public cancer patients, and sometimes we have to be on a waiting list,” said Dr Fray.

The WRHA clinical coordinator estimated the backlog at approximately three months.

In the meantime, the resident who spoke with the Sunday Observer said she underwent alternative screening last year, but her doctors remain firm that a mammogram is the standard.

Dr Fray emphasised that mammograms remain the safest and most cost-effective diagnostic tool for women aged 40 and older, or for those aged 35 and above with a strong family history of breast cancer. For women under 35, a breast ultrasound is typically recommended.

“Mammography is very sensitive to pick up breast lesions. We like to use that, and it’s cheap for the patient,” stated Fray, adding, “I would be in favour of having mammograms available in the private sector in the west, and I’m hoping that somebody will come along and do it,” added the senior medical doctor.

With the planned implementation of a mobile service and at least one private entity showing an interest in offering the service in the future, Dr Fray is now hopeful. For now, the public can access the mammogram service in St Ann, Manchester, and Kingston.

Addressing common patient concerns regarding discomfort and radiation, Dr Fray offered reassurance, noting that radiation exposure during a mammogram is comparable to passing through an airport security scanner.

“Just to put their heart at rest about the radiation, and squeezing the breast is not going to spread anything. It’s a very safe thing. And now they have a digital mammogram, which is the modern one, in which the pressing is not as hard as before,” assured Dr Fray.

He also dispelled reports of lengthy delays for men seeking colonoscopy appointments in the region, clarifying that at least three private facilities currently offer the procedure.

A colonoscopy uses a thin, flexible tube equipped with a light and a camera to examine the inside of the large intestine and rectum.

“That’s optical, where you put an instrument up. You can do what’s called virtual colonoscopy, which is a CT scan, and they are indicated to have your colon screened from that aspect,” stated Dr Fray.

He added that once the ongoing rehabilitation of CRH is complete, public access will expand significantly.

“We are going to have a dedicated endoscopy suite that will perform both upper GI [gastrointestinal] endoscopy and lower GI endoscopy, which includes colonoscopies. That will come on stream soon for public patients,” stated the clinical coordinator.

World.title: New Miss Jamaica World crowned
World.content:
Matea Mahal Smith, Miss Jamaica World 2026, is flanked by Celine Walters (left), Miss Earth Jamaica, and Daniella Bullock, Miss Jamaica International (Photo: Samuel Edie)

On Sunday night, inside the Karl Hendrickson Auditorium at Jamaica College, Matea Mahal Smith was crowned Miss Jamaica World 2026.

The 24-year-old whose initiative, Love Always, Matea, supports children with disabilities, said she saw the Miss Jamaica World pageant as an opportunity to enhance the work that she started.

“What drew me to the Miss Jamaica World contest was its Beauty with a Purpose initiative. I have always believed that beauty should extend beyond what people see,” Smith told the

Jamaica Observer moments after she was announced as the winner from a field of 23 competitors.

Last year, Smith — whose father is Jamaican and mother Filipino — finished in third place in the 2025 Miss Universe Jamaica pageant. She also represented Jamaica at Miss Grand International last year.

Even though she has had previous pageant experience, Smith didn’t feel that competing for the Miss Jamaica World title would be a walk in the park.

“I think it’s difficult to describe this journey in just one word. I’ve learned so much, not only about the world around me, but about myself, the strength I carry, and the impact I can make. It’s also shown me just how blessed I am to have such an incredible support system. Their belief in me, especially on the challenging days, is what helped me keep going,” she said.

A resident of Kingston, Smith shared what she felt were highlights along the journey.

“Honestly, it was all the laughs and memories I’ve shared with my sisters throughout this journey. The friendships we’ve built and the moments we’ve shared are things I’ll cherish long after the competition is over,” she said.

Looking beyond the stage of the pageant she said she hoped to use this platform to create meaningful opportunities for others, particularly children with disabilities.

“I want to expand the reach of Love Always, Matea, and most importantly, create opportunities for children and families who may not otherwise have access to them. But to also inspire young girls who may feel uncertain about what their future holds. I want them to understand that sometimes life takes us in directions we never expected, and if we remain open to those possibilities we may discover that an even greater destiny was waiting for us all along,” Smith shared.

Sponsored by Aveeno, she won the fast-track Fitness Challenge a few weeks ago. She also made the top 3 in Beach Beauty, Top Model, and the Head-to-Head Challenge.

Daniella Bullock, who finished in second place in the regional Miss Jamaica World Eastern pageant, was named first runner-up to Smith and secured the Miss International Jamaica title.

“I’m feeling so elated, I can’t believe it,” she told the Observer. “I already felt like I won before my name was even called, because, for me, it was about improving from where I am coming from. So just going out there on the stage and not messing up my responses, I felt I already won,” said Bullock, who wore the sash Haven Beauty House.

Celine Walters, who wore the sash Frazsiers Whip Football, is the new Miss Earth Jamaica, having finished as second runner-up. She said she was shocked when her name was announced.

“I’m feeling amazing, and to be surrounded by all these amazing ladies and then to be selected as Miss Earth Jamaica, it was not easy. I was shocked when my name was called, but I am excited and I’m really just soaking it up,” Walters explained.

The coronation show got under way almost half hour after its advertised 8:00 pm start time, featuring the 23 finalists in a choreographed routine.

After the ladies introduced themselves to the audience, they appeared in evening wear and then the dreaded elimination round.

Making the Top 12 were Bullock, Smith, Walters, Seana’kaye Wright (winner of the Beach Beauty fast track), Deidre Wadsworth (winner of the Head-to-Head Challenge), Talent winner Shade’ Ashley-Ann Barrett, multi-media challenge winner Realla Benguche, winner of Top Model Dr Samantha McLeod, Regina Heron, Fiona Bartlett, Tyler Rae Rerrie, and Rasheeda Murphy.

Sectional prize winners were Seana’kaye Wright, Best Personality and Best Smile; Most Congenial and Most Photogenic – Rasheeda Murphy; Most Poised – Samantha McLeod; and Most Improved – Tyler Rae Rerrie.

Making the Top 6 were People’s Choice winner Jessie Freeman, Rerrie, Bullock, Wright, Smith, and Walters.

After the final interview segment, the winners were announced.

Among the highlights for the evening was the recognition given Cindy Breakspeare on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of being crowned Miss World 1976.

Jamaica Cultural Development Commission Festival song winner D Burnz serenaded the ladies during the evening wear segment, while Geo Sax thrilled the audience with his interpretations of popular R&B songs.

Everton Pesso was also a crowd-pleaser reeling out songs like When Somebody Loves You Back and Just Don’t Want to Be Lonely.

World.title: LASCO Financial Services throws support behind Soccer Saints
World.content:
Melville Lumley, Soccer Saints manager, receives a donation of medical supplies from Samantha Fuller-Maragh, brand manager for card services at LASCO Financial Services, at the organisation’s headquarters on October 30, 2026.

LASCO Financial Services Limited (LFSL) has reaffirmed its commitment to community development and the advancement of grass roots sports through a donation of medical supplies to St Catherine-based corner league team, Soccer Saints Football Club. The supplies are aimed at strengthening the club’s ability to provide care for players and manage minor injuries sustained on the field.

The donation forms part of LASCO Financial’s continued efforts to support organisations that positively impact the communities they serve. The medical supplies, which include gauze, band-aids, wipes, pain relief gel, knee and wrist supports, and other essential first aid items, will assist the club in responding to minor injuries and ensuring that players have access to basic medical care during training and matches.

For Soccer Saints, the contribution represents meaningful support for a club that has spent the past decade building its presence in local football competitions while fostering a strong sense of camaraderie among its members.

Melville Lumley, manager of Soccer Saints Football Club, expressed gratitude for the partnership, noting that the club’s initial outreach to LASCO Financial Services came amid financial challenges and a need for sponsorship to support its operations.

“Soccer Saints is a corner league football team based in St Catherine. We’ve been here for 10 years. We have always been playing in different leagues in St Catherine and a corporate league, winning most of them. We, unfortunately, encountered some financial challenges and so we started the conversation about sponsorship. LASCO Financial was open to it, and they have been very kind in doing their best to equip us with medical supplies,” Lumley said.

The donation also holds particular significance for the club’s management team, which places considerable emphasis on unity, discipline and the familial bond shared among its players. Gabrielle Thompson, assistant manager of Soccer Saints, described the team as a close-knit group whose passion for football extends beyond the pitch.

“The team is full of vibrant players. They’re very much dedicated to their game, and they look forward to every time they get to participate in all of the corner leagues. So, it’s always a joy to see them out on the field having fun, and off the field as well, because they are a family,” Thompson said.

Samantha Fuller Maragh, brand manager for card services at LASCO Financial Services Limited, said the company was pleased to respond to the club’s request.

“When the Soccer Saints Football Club reached out to us, we were elated to collaborate with them. We’re sponsoring the nursing department by donating medical supplies to help the players if they get injured — whether it’s any minor cuts or sprains that they might have,” Fuller-Maragh explained.

She expressed optimism about the continued partnership, noting that LASCO Financial Services looks forward to supporting the team as they continue their football journey and represent themselves on the field.

Through initiatives such as this, LASCO Financial Services Limited continues to demonstrate the importance of partnerships in strengthening community organisations and supporting initiatives that promote teamwork, camaraderie and positive engagement.

World.title: ‘Purely financial’
World.content:
West Indies players celebrate the dismissal of Mitchell Marsh of Australia during the first Twenty20 match at Sabina Park, Kingston, Jamaica, on July 20, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

WITH cricket in the Caribbean at a financial crossroads, Jamaica Cricket Association (JCA) President Dr Donovan Bennett says the association’s interest in hosting India and England next year is driven purely by the need to boost its limited revenues.

The West Indies will host the two international cricket powerhouses in 2027 in what could be the region’s only major international series next year.

Although not announced by the respective cricket boards or the ICC, it’s been reported that reigning Twenty20 (T20) World Cup champions India will visit the Caribbean next summer for two Tests, three One-Day Internationals (ODIs) and five T20s. England are scheduled to arrive next December to play the Windies in five T20s in preparation for the 2028 T20 World Cup.

Despite revealing significant financial challenges in September, Cricket West Indies (CWI) stands to earn substantial revenue from hosting India and England, with both tours expected to be more lucrative than recent series involving other Test-playing nations.

The Jamaica Observer first reported the JCA’s interest to host matches from the two tours back in June. The

Observer has learnt that Cricket West Indies is looking to finalise the host territories for the India series before the end of the year.

Sabina Park has been a primary venue for the West Indies over the past few years, hosting South Africa and Bangladesh in 2024, Australia in 2025 and Sri Lanka last summer.

Bennett told the Observer that the JCA formally expressed their interest and revealed that it’s eyeing the T20 encounters with the highly ranked Indians and England.

“When they [CWI] start negotiations for the legal part of the arrangement, they just want to know who they’re to deal with and who aren’t interested,” he said. “So Jamaica has sent off communication to the West Indies board, saying that they are interested in hosting three T20s against the Indians and two T20s against the English team. And I want to stress the words interested in hosting because that is where it is right now.”

“CWI will now have to send out a document explaining what the commitments will be to host those games and then the territory will then have to decide whether they are receptive to that type of financial arrangement, or they are not interested.”

When elected as JCA president in April 2024, Bennett said he wanted to bring more international cricket to the island in a bid to revive local interest in the sport. However, he says the desire to host the India and England tours next year is strictly financial with boths teams capable of generating millions of US dollars.

Bennett is hoping the Government will help secure the tours, although the ultimate decision will be out of the JCA’s hands.

“This is purely a financial decision that we have right now facing us and it is dependent on the government to decide whether they think it’s an investment that will be for the benefit of the tourism product in the country,” he said. “All the other benefits are given. Of course, it will help cricket in Jamaica. Of course, it will generate interest in the game in Jamaica but the main one is a financial consideration that is beyond us. At the end of the day, it is a governmental decision and it has to do with whether the Government thinks it’s a good business to invest that money or they don’t think so.”

“There are serious implications regarding tourism because the English team, when they are travelling, they come with 4,000 or 5,000 spectators who come into the country. There’s a tremendous amount of Indians that are living in the USA, especially on the Eastern Seaboard, which is a very short trip down to Jamaica and I have been told that the Ministry of Tourism has an interest in penetrating that market.”

Jamaica is expected to receive strong competition as Trinidad and Tobago, Guyana, Barbados, Antigua and Barbuda and St Lucia are among the other Caribbean countries who are said to have an interest in hosting games.

World.title: Spain’s transport minister resigns after deadly train crash
World.content:
Puente has been cornered by allies and foes alike, who called for him to step down after last week’s train crash, in which 69 people died. It was the second deadly rail disaster in Spain this year after January’s accident in Adamuz, which killed 46 people. Puente had held the post since 2023.

After a cabinet meeting on Tuesday morning, Puente brushed off calls for his resignation from some of the government’s allies, including members of Sumar, the coalition's junior partner.

Sánchez has backed Puente after the Toledo crash raised questions about how Spain manages its rail infrastructure and dealt a blow to his re-election hopes.

This breaking story is being updated.

World.title: Clash intensifies between Tusk and Nawrocki over Poland’s top court
World.content:
Tusk’s government and the European Commission have insisted the court must be overhauled to conform with EU norms on impartiality, and on Friday suspended the court’s president and his deputy.

On Tuesday, eight judges elected by the current ruling majority led by Tusk convened the court and declared they had sufficient numbers to resume its long-stalled work.

Hitting back, Nawrocki used the televised opening of a National Security Council meeting, attended by Tusk and other political leaders, to attack the prime minister. Tusk was not given a chance to respond while the cameras were on.

“Full responsibility for every police officer outside the tribunal, for all the illegal actions, including suspending judges and issuing unlawful orders, lies with one man who is present in this room — Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” Nawrocki said, referring to Friday’s confrontations in front of the tribunal.

“I expect [the prime minister] to rein in his government’s ambitions and put an end to the illegal actions of his representatives inside the Constitutional Tribunal,” Nawrocki added.

Earlier, Tusk had accused Nawrocki of escalating the conflict and called on him to end his opposition to the judges elected by parliament.

World.title: Trump says Europe gave Greenland to US as ‘greatest gift’ ever
World.content:
Donald Trump looks on during the signing of a security pact between the U.S., Greenland and Denmark in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Earlier this year, the U.S. president refused to rule out using military force to gain control of the mineral-rich island.

U.S. President Donald Trump called Greenland the greatest gift the United States had ever received in a call to Fox News on Tuesday.

“Remember, [Europe] just gave the United States the greatest gift we were ever given. Do you know what it was? Greenland. We just got Greenland, you know that, right?” he said during a broadcast about Tuesday’s midterm elections, which was reshared on X by the U.S. State Department. Someone else on the call quickly clarified that Trump was referring to “a military deal.”

Until September, Trump had repeatedly pushed for the U.S. to take control of the large, mineral-rich island, which is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, citing national security reasons.

World.title: Germany’s Merz warns Europe needs seat at the table as Trump renews Ukraine talks
World.content:
“The U.S. and Russia — with all due respect to the U.S. — cannot decide whether Ukraine will become a member state of the European Union,” Zelenskyy said. “For that we need the support of other countries, and all of those countries are in Europe.”

Merz’s meeting with Zelenskyy in Berlin comes as the Trump administration renews efforts to reach a negotiated end to the full-scale war in Ukraine and before U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia are set to resume in Abu Dhabi next week.

The meeting in Berlin also comes a day before talks hosted by the European Commission with representatives from the U.S., Ukraine and key European allies on Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic future.

Merz also sharply criticized the U.S. decision to invite Russian President Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit in Miami, saying the move is shutting Ukraine out of talks about its own fate.

“If President Trump were to decide to invite the Russian president, then Ukraine must be the first topic of discussion,” Merz said. “And if Ukraine is discussed, then the president of Ukraine must be seated at the table. In any case, from my perspective, it is completely unacceptable for third countries to discuss Ukraine’s fate without involving Ukraine itself.”

European leaders, including Merz, have long feared the U.S. may pursue a Ukraine peace deal on terms that sideline Europe and disadvantage Ukraine.

World.title: The 5 most brutal political moggings of 2026
World.content:
According to Collins, the term originated in the bodybuilding community as a shortening of AMOG (“alpha male of the group”) and penetrated into the so-called manosphere, a collection of typically online male communities united by their beliefs about masculinity.

“Fast forward to 2026 and it’s everywhere,” Quin added. And, crucially for POLITICO’s purposes, it can be applied to literally any situation.

With that in mind, we looked back at five top political moggings in 2026 — the more brutal, the better.

Andy Burnham job mogged Keir Starmer

One minute, Keir Starmer was British prime minister with a thumping Labour majority cheering his every move. The next, he was humiliated and ousted by a northern rival who had done little to hide his own leadership ambitions.

Starmer, of course, tried to block the Downing Street takeover by Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham.

But once Burnham loyalists and grumpy ministers had quit Starmer’s government in droves, the prime minister bowed out this summer after just two years in office and Burnham — having manufactured, at the second attempt, an opportunity to enter parliament — waltzed into the top job unopposed.

World.title: Moscow in talks to arrange Trump, Xi and Putin meeting, Kremlin says
World.content:
Trump told reporters last month he would meet Putin and Xi, initially “on denuclearization,” but also to discuss Ukraine. “I would meet in order — anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody is there or not, whatever I can do to end the war.”

Kyiv met the prospect of a trilateral meeting with concern, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy stressing that it should take place after a meeting that includes Ukraine. “I really don’t want this to be a ‘Yalta – 2, 3, 4,’ when there is a redistribution of influence,” Zelenskyy told reporters in late October — referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the U.S., British and Soviet leaders agreed on aspects of the postwar settlement in Europe, including the occupation of Germany.

China has not commented on the possibility of a trilateral meeting. But German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who met Xi last week, told ARD the Chinese leader looked “surprised” when asked about potential Ukraine talks and rejected the idea that China, Russia and the U.S. would discuss Ukraine in a trilateral meeting.

The Chinese foreign ministry told the Financial Times it was “in communication with relevant parties regarding the meeting between the Chinese and Russian heads of state,” without mentioning Trump.

World.title: Poll: Brits want the Democrats to win the midterms
World.content:
Brits see a Republican hold as a riskier result for the world, with a third expecting global affairs to get more chaotic if the U.S. president’s party controls Congress, compared to 17% who believe it will be less chaotic.

Trump has long been unpopular with the British public, and 55% say his presidency has been bad for the U.K. compared to 17% who think it’s been good. His administration is slightly more popular with Reform supporters — but 38% of that cohort still view it negatively, compared to 27% who regard it positively.

EU is a more ‘reliable ally’

Brits see a raft of other nations and blocs as more reliable partners than the U.S., the PF Global survey suggests. Only 35% trust the U.S. to act as a reliable ally to the U.K. — a far lower figure than for Australia (66%), Canada (65%), Germany (54%), the European Union (53%) and France (50%). Of the seven options given, those surveyed only saw China as a less trusted partner than the U.S.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s push for a closer relationship with the EU appears to also have public support.

The survey suggests more than half the British public (54%) back prioritizing strengthening relations with the EU over Commonwealth countries (46%) and the U.S. (29%).

Burnham traveled to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in the Caribbean on Monday as he seeks to build greater economic cooperation with the 56-strong association of countries — most of which are former territories of the British Empire.

World.title: Cristina Fernández Cubas wins 2026 Cervantes Prize for Spanish literature
World.content:
The Catalan writer Cristina Fernández Cubas was on Tuesday named the winner of the Cervantes Prize 2026, the highest distinction in Spanish-language literature, worth 125,000 euros.

 

The Minister of Culture, Ernest Urtasun, announced the jury's decision, which acknowledges her contribution to renewing the contemporary short story.

The jury highlighted "the originality, excellence and coherence" of a body of work that has transformed Spanish-language fantasy fiction. It also praised her ability to explore human experience through stories marked by mystery and ambiguity.

Born in Arenys de Mar (Barcelona) in 1945, Fernández Cubas is one of the leading figures in Spanish short fiction. Among her works are 'Mi hermana Elba', 'El ángulo del horror' and 'La habitación de Nona'.

Over the course of her career she has also received the National Narrative Prize and the National Prize for Spanish Literature.

With this recognition, Fernández Cubas becomes the seventh woman to receive the Cervantes, following in the footsteps of writers such as María Zambrano, Ana María Matute and Elena Poniatowska. The prize consolidates her career and her influence on new generations of writers.

World.title: Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente resigns over Urda train crash that killed 69
World.content:
Spain’s Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on Tuesday over last week’s train crash near Urda, in the central province of Toledo, which killed 69 people.

 

He announced the decision during an appearance before the Permanent Deputation of the Congress of Deputies, the standing committee that represents Spain’s lower house when it is not in full session.
