Puente, a member of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party, said stepping down was “good for the country and for democracy”. He presented it as an act of political responsibility, adding: “It is not true that all politicians are the same.”

He also said he would not stand as a candidate at the next election, saying he wanted “to live up to my party”.

During the session, Puente defended the safety of the Madrid-Seville high-speed line, where the crash happened. As well as the 69 dead, around 200 people were injured.

“It is neither an abandoned nor a forgotten piece of infrastructure,” he said, pointing to a €780 million renewal plan launched by the government.

He ended his speech with a farewell: “I trust my country will live up to the occasion. I have tried to live up to it. Farewell.”

Second disaster on the same line

The Urda crash came nine months after a derailment near Adamuz, in the southern province of Córdoba, killed 46 people in January. That accident also happened on the Madrid-Seville line.

Puente told MPs that the control centre run by Adif, Spain’s state-owned rail infrastructure manager, had allowed the AVE high-speed train involved to continue its journey even though its LZB automatic safety system had failed. A train operated by the private company Iryo had stopped further along the track.

The AVE then travelled about 25 kilometres at more than 160 km/h before the collision.

Puente defended the reliability of the LZB system and announced new technology to strengthen rail safety.

Opposition attacks

Ester Muñoz, spokesperson for the conservative People’s Party (PP), said the minister’s job “is not to explain fatal accidents, it is to prevent them”.

Pepa Millán, spokesperson for the far-right Vox party, accused Puente of “shirking his responsibilities” and criticised how he had behaved after the crash. “He has neither dignity nor shame,” she said.

The PP and Vox had demanded his resignation, as had two parties whose votes the Sánchez government has relied on: the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts.

Meanwhile, the works council at Adif has agreed to push for a strike on 17 November to demand better rail safety, although the strike has not yet been formally called.

The planned protest reflects growing concern about the safety of Spain’s high-speed network after two deadly crashes in less than a year.

World.title: Italy holds emergency talks as supermarket fridge attacks spread across Europe
World.content:
Italy’s government held emergency talks with intelligence chiefs on Tuesday after cyberattacks on supermarket freezer systems hit at least 11 European countries in recent days.

 

Supermarkets in at least 10 EU countries, including Germany, Italy and the Netherlands, have been forced to throw away food after temperatures rose in their fridges and freezers. The UK has also been affected.

Nobody has claimed responsibility and the motive remains unknown.

The Italian government said the impact so far was “highly limited”, and that only outlets with outdated security systems had been affected. Around 20 stores were reported hit nationwide.

Ministers nevertheless met intelligence chiefs and Italy’s National Cyber Security Agency, which issued technical advice to retailers on protecting their systems.

Giuseppe Spadaro, director of a group that runs Coop supermarkets in Sicily, said four of its 300 stores had been hit. “We had to throw away everything. The shelves are empty,” he told the Corriere della Sera newspaper.

EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said EU agencies were working with national authorities on a collective response. “These are not isolated incidents, and of course, we have to be collectively resilient and prepared for such cyber incidents,” he said.

On Monday, EU food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen called the attacks a “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain”.

Romania’s cybersecurity chief took a different view. Six Romanian outlets were affected, but Dan Cimpean, director of the country’s National Cyber Security Directorate, said: “It seems semi-amateurish. We do not suspect, under any circumstances, that it is a state actor.”

In the UK, National Cyber Security Centre chief Richard Horne told the BBC the issue affected “the whole food supply chain”, and that there had been a couple of instances where “vulnerable technology had been exploited”.

Four stores were hit in Germany. In Sweden, the Coop chain said its seven affected shops were back to normal, and that the equipment involved had been connected over old 4G mobile networks.

Belgium was among the hardest-hit countries, and federal prosecutors there have opened an investigation. Hundreds of French supermarkets were hit by a similar attack last month.

Supermarket refrigeration systems are often connected to the internet so that contractors can monitor and repair them remotely. Recent research by the security firm Forescout found nearly 13,000 refrigeration control services openly reachable online in 99 countries

World.title: French government launches fertility awareness campaign targeting 29-year-olds
World.content:
A report from the monitoring committee for the fertility plan was submitted on Tuesday 3 November to the health minister, Stéphanie Rist. Immediately afterwards, she announced the launch of a major information campaign to support all couples who are planning to have children.

 

By the end of November, women and men in France aged 29 will receive an awareness letter from Assurance Maladie in order to "give every adult the means to understand and preserve their fertility", the minister said.

The letter will invite people who wish to have children to consult a health professional for "a preconception consultation", to review their health, lifestyle habits and any concerns "so as to prepare a future pregnancy as well as possible".

For couples who are trying to have a child but are not succeeding, the letter recommends consulting a specialised health professional, where there is no particular problem, after "one year of trying before the age of 35" and after "six months of trying after the age of 35".

While age is a decisive factor, fertility also depends on many medical, environmental and behavioural factors, including diet, sleep, physical activity and the consumption of tobacco and alcohol.

At the same time, the government says it is rolling out the "Ma fertilité" portal, which brings together a set of dedicated information on the Santé.fr website, as well as audio messages and posters in doctors' waiting rooms.

Towards an increase in the number of centres able to provide egg freezing

The novelty of this information campaign is relative, since it corresponds to one of the 16 measures in the plan against infertility presented last February by Stéphanie Rist, following the call for "demographic rearmament" launched by President Emmanuel Macron in 2024.

"In France, 15 to 25% of couples who wish to conceive a child encounter difficulties, that is more than three million people", the health minister recalled. She wants to increase the number of centres able to provide egg self-preservation for non-medical reasons.

The information letter that is about to be sent out recalls that in France, "it is possible to self-preserve one's gametes" (male or female reproductive cells) in view of a possible parenthood project.

Oocytes (female reproductive cells) can be collected and stored for women "between 29 and 37, for possible use up to the age of 45". For men, sperm can be stored "between 29 and 45, for possible use up to the age of 59".

Last year, more than 20,000 women asked to store their oocytes with a view to a future child. That is an increase of 30% in one year. But waiting times vary from 14 to 24 months depending on the region.

"Fertility is a major public health issue that concerns both women and men. Too often, difficulties are discovered late, whereas we can act earlier to better inform, prevent and support", the health minister wrote in her statement.

World.title: Progress and pitfalls on the path to a bigger EU: Five takeaways from the Euronews Enlargement Summit
World.content:
From the Western Balkans to the Southern Caucasus and Europe’s eastern flank, the Euronews Enlargement Summit revealed a European Union closer to expansion than at any point in the past decade – but also the political obstacles that could still derail it.

 

Leaders gathered in Brussels to discuss candidate countries’ ambitions to join the EU, and whether the bloc is ready to admit them as the prospect of expansion looks more real than it has in years.

From Ukraine and Georgia to Montenegro and Armenia, each country faces its own mix of political sensitivities, painstaking reforms and diplomatic hurdles. Progress can be swift, but setbacks can be equally dramatic.

“The ambition to join the European Union must help overcome historical grievances, reject nationalist rhetoric, and encourage countries to move towards genuine cooperation. Europe’s experience demonstrates that enlargement benefits us all,” European Council President António Costa told Euronews in a written address.

Armenia and Georgia head in opposite directions

In the Southern Caucasus, Armenia and Georgia are moving in opposite directions. Yerevan is preparing to apply for EU membership, while Tbilisi’s accession bid remains frozen, with little prospect of an imminent breakthrough.

Georgia’s candidacy has been stalled since 2024 over controversial laws on foreign influence and family values. At the summit, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze insisted he remained “very committed” to joining the bloc.

Pressed on how he intends to restart negotiations, however, he had no clear plan. He said Tbilisi did not intend to repeal the controversial laws, and accused the European Commission of double standards and of politically blackmailing Georgia.

“The Parliament of Georgia, with dignity, passed the legislation, which is fully in line with international standards,” he said, arguing that the request to repeal the laws interfered with the principle of sovereignty and likening it to Soviet methods.

Asked why Georgia still wanted to join the EU, Kobakhidze said he was “optimistic” that the bloc itself would change, both in its attitude towards Georgia and more broadly.

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, meanwhile, said formally applying for EU membership in 2027 or 2028 was “realistic”, calling the EU the main path to protect the country’s democracy since the 2018 revolution.

“Our first intention is to create an alternative for the people of Armenia and for the Republic of Armenia, because, traditionally, the perception of our society and maybe our neighbourhood was that Armenia has no alternative,” he added.

Pashinyan said he was aware of the trade-off between joining the EU and remaining in Russia’s Eurasian Economic Union, and that the choice would be for the Armenian people.

Montenegro enters the final stretch

Montenegro is leading the accession race, aiming to become the EU’s 28th member state by 2028. But European Affairs Minister Maida Gorčević warned that her country would not accept second-class membership.

Last month, the Commission proposed an institutional safeguard for newcomers: a 15-year probation period that, in the most serious cases, could lead to the suspension of voting rights.

“We don’t want second-grade membership inside the European Union, because that wouldn’t be fair and that wouldn’t be full membership as well,” Gorčević said, adding that her government was not against additional safeguards.

She also said Podgorica was working to resolve outstanding bilateral issues with Croatia, though the border dispute could be settled after Montenegro joins the EU.

Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, for his part, warned that the upcoming French election could derail enlargement, as Eurosceptic candidates lead in the polls.

“The political events may affect the enlargement more substantially than anybody can imagine today,” Plenković said. “Some of the electors and parties are clearly opposing the process.”

He also questioned the timeline, saying that setting up a deadline was “not very smart”, warning that “something always unpredictable happens and things get postponed.”

Western Balkans moving at different speeds

Albania, the second-closest candidate, is also the second-fastest. Prime Minister Edi Rama reiterated his commitment to conclude negotiations by the end of 2027.

Defending enlargement as a merit-based process and acknowledging that his country still faces challenges, he called for a “Helmut Kohl moment” for the EU, a reference to the chancellor who unified Germany.

He also warned that Serbia’s new leadership was unlikely to soften Belgrade’s opposition to recognising Kosovo, a major obstacle to its own EU membership ambitions.

Asked how the prospect of EU membership would affect Albania’s controversial deal with Italy to transfer irregular migrants to deportation camps, Rama said “the deal will stay for as long as need be”, promising to keep it in force as long as Giorgia Meloni remains in power.

While Albania and Montenegro make significant progress, North Macedonia has been stalling for years over a dispute with Bulgaria about the treatment of the Bulgarian minority.

North Macedonia’s President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova said her country’s EU hopes are being held hostage by Bulgaria, which is demanding constitutional changes to recognise the minority.

Ukraine pushes back against farm restrictions

Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi rejected the proposed exclusion of certain agricultural products, such as wheat and grain, from the EU market even after Kyiv becomes a full member.

The Commission pitched the measure last month after pressure from several member states that feared the scale of Ukraine’s agricultural output could threaten their farmers.

“Transitional measures can be part of enlargement, but they must address specific risks. And be appropriate, and have clear review and exit conditions. They cannot become a permanent restriction or a subset of the single market,” Koretskyi said.

He said EU accession was at the heart of his government’s policy and that Kyiv aims to start closing negotiation chapters in the first half of 2027.

“I realised that these are ambitious objectives. We are not asking for shortcuts. We are asking for credible, merit-based paths with clear milestones and timely decisions when those milestones are met,” he said.

Moldova, the rising star

Moldova has rapidly joined the leading group of accession candidates, pursuing reforms at a pace the European Commission has struggled to match.

Chișinău could even find itself ready to close negotiating chapters before all the clusters have formally opened.

Asked whether his country should be “decoupled” from Ukraine, with which it has moved forward since Russia’s 2022 invasion, Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said it was not helpful to frame the discussion as a “racing game”.

“I fundamentally believe that Ukraine’s advancement on the EU integration path makes Moldova stronger, and vice versa, works the same way. So, the faster we go on our EU integration path, the better for Ukraine,” he said.

Tofan could not attend the summit in person, as he had to oversee the government’s response to a massive cyberattack that compromised the data of about 750,000 people.

“We suspect a state actor is behind it, and seeing what’s happening in Europe,” he added. “You can probably only guess. But I don’t think the list of suspects is very long.”

Asked whether Moldova would favour joining NATO, he said his government would “firmly support it”, but that there is no parliamentary majority to change the constitution, which enshrines neutrality.

World.title: Trump says US will end military aid to Israel as Americans vote in midterms
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Washington would stop giving Israel around $4 billion a year in military aid from 2027. He made the announcement as polls opened across the United States for the midterm elections.

 

Speaking by phone to Fox News, Trump said Israel no longer needed the money, but that the US would keep selling arms to its closest Middle East ally. He said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had come to him with the idea, and that they had been discussing it for a couple of years.

“Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it,” Trump said.

He also tied the decision to the campaign. He said the aid had become too easy a target for critics such as Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat and outspoken critic of Israel who is running for the Senate in Michigan.

Unlike France, Spain, Italy and many other European countries, the US has no electoral silence period banning campaigning or political comment on polling day. The main restrictions are state laws on campaigning near polling stations, so politicians, the president included, are free to give interviews while voting is under way.

Netanyahu’s office did not immediately comment. Gadi Eisenkot, his main rival, said it was dangerous that Israel’s defence establishment had learned of the change through the media, and called for the prime minister to be replaced.

The current 10-year, $38 billion agreement was signed in 2016 under Barack Obama and runs until 2028.

The announcement came as tensions rose again in the Gulf. A US official said American forces had carried out defensive strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz that were using surface-to-air missiles. Iranian state television reported explosions on Qeshm Island.

Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, said Tehran had delivered a “firm and rational response” to Washington and that it was now up to the US to prevent renewed war. He told parliament Iran remained ready “with its finger on the trigger”, but did not say what the response was.

World.title: La bola negra becomes Spain's third highest-grossing film ever
World.content:
'La bola negra', directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, has become the third most successful Spanish film of all time, with 36,7 million euros taken and 5,4 million cinema-goers up to 1 November.

 

The production, starring Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close and inspired by Federico García Lorca, is only behind 'Ocho apellidos vascos' and 'Lo imposible'.

The film’s success comes as Spanish box office revenues recover, with a 40% increase in takings during the first 41 weeks of 2026, reaching 489,4 million euros. This figure is 8% higher than the average for the same period before the pandemic.

The film has also managed to attract a younger audience than usual for the drama genre. According to data from Rentrak, almost 40% of those surveyed were under 35, while women accounted for more than 62%. Its success has also strengthened the role of independent distributors in the Spanish market.

In addition, 'La bola negra' has been preselected to represent Spain at the 2027 Oscars, a recognition that could further boost its box office run.

Despite the improvement in revenues, cinema attendance has still not returned to pre-pandemic levels. Between January and September, the number of cinema-goers rose by 29% compared with 2025, but remained 13% below the average recorded between 2017 and 2019.

World.title: Portugal signs TAP sale contract with Lufthansa, pledging to keep airline Portuguese
World.content:
The Government on Tuesday signed the share sale contract for TAP with Lufthansa, formalising the conditions of the deal that was confirmed in October.

 

In a speech to those present, Luís Montenegro congratulated everyone involved in the deal, stressing that it makes it possible "to anchor the country’s strategic interests and preserve TAP’s identity and brand". "If that were not the case, we would not have taken the decision we ultimately took," he said.

The Portuguese prime minister said that the Lufthansa group, which is now formalising the acquisition of part of TAP’s capital, has always been keen to preserve the airline’s uniqueness, keeping its "positioning in terms of making the most of the potential of our community, regions and economy".

"Making full use of the potential of the connection we have with our Autonomous Regions and with our communities spread around the world and with the countries with which we share a common language, is an asset for TAP and not a burden, contrary to what some might think," said the prime minister, insisting that this uniqueness "has been safeguarded", as well as "social peace within the company and the commitment we have to TAP’s workers".

"Today the country is taking an extremely important step to ensure it will continue to have a Portuguese airline, with a Portuguese brand and identity," the prime minister said.

The contract signing ceremony took place at the TAP Campus next to Lisbon airport and was attended by the prime minister, Luís Montenegro, the finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, and Lufthansa’s chief executive, Carsten Spohr, who said: "TAP will continue to be a Portuguese airline".

The chief executive of the German group described it as "an important milestone for TAP, for Portugal, but also for the Lufthansa group", and stressed that the company still intends "to develop Lisbon as one of Lufthansa’s hubs, while preserving its uniqueness", but recalled that the company’s perspective "is not limited to the capital". Porto, Funchal, Madeira and the Algarve are also important parts of the group’s strategy.

"For us, this is a unique opportunity," the CEO said, adding that the deal gives access to new markets, not only in Portugal but also on the African continent and in Latin America, particularly Brazil.

On 14 October, the Government announced the choice of Lufthansa for the partial privatisation of TAP. The offer included 1.201 billion euros for up to 49.9% of the airline’s capital, of which 5% would preferably be allocated to workers. The Portuguese government expects the transaction to be completed by early 2028.

For now, the state will retain 51% of the capital and a majority on the board of directors.

With the formalisation of the contract between the entities involved, completion of the sale and TAP’s future integration into the Lufthansa group now depend on an assessment by Brussels.

The Government expects European approval to come in the first half of 2028. Until then, the airline will continue to be managed independently, with oversight from the German group.

World.title: Spain transport minister offers resignation in wake of train accident
World.content:
After two deadly train crashes this year, Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente has said he will step down.

Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente offered his resignation on Tuesday in the wake of one of Europe's worst rail disasters in recent memory last week that killed 69 people.

The tragedy, Spain's second fatal rail collision in less than a year, has intensified scrutiny of railway safety and added political pressure on Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez ahead of parliamentary elections on November 29.

In January, a train crash in the southern Andalusia region killed 46 people.

"A transport ​minister ‌in a country like Spain cannot continue in ‌office with two accidents ‌of ​this severity in less than a year," he told lawmakers while announcing his intention to resign.

Puente, member of Sanchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party, also said he would withdraw his name from the list of parliamentary electioncandidates. He did not specify when he would leave ​his post.

Puente's political opponents had demanded he step down, while train unions had been unhappy with him for appearing to pin blame for the disaster on one rail control center operator.

Second rail accident in a year kills dozens in central Spain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Government unveils new rail safety measures

Just hours before addressing lawmakers, Puente had presented improved rail network safety measures and told a press conference the government would "work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public's trust in high-speed rail."

This included plans for control center software that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot traffic anomalies, and an AI agent for system oversight to "minimize the possibility of human error."

Another measure Puente mentioned was requiring a second operator confirm decisions made in scenarios involving a faulty automatic safety system.

The accident happened during the failure of an automated safety system that had stopped all trains along a 63-kilometer stretch of track between Madrid and Seville on Wednesday morning.

Despite the stoppage on the line, a control center allowed a high-speed train operated by state-owned rail company Renfe to continue its journey.

The Renfe train collided with stopped train owned by private Spanish company Iryo outside the village of Urda in Toledo province.

World.title: Greenland's parliament ratifies Trump's US security agreement
World.content:
The US is set to expand its military footprint on the Arctic island, part of the Kingdom of Denmark. It follows pressure from Donald Trump earlier in the year which opened a major rift in the transatlantic alliance.

Greenland's parliament on Tuesday signed off on a trilateral security and military-access agreement with the United States and Denmark that paves the way for an expanded US' military presence on the strategically located and mineral-rich island.

The deal has alleviated pressure coming from US President Donald Trump, who earlier this year had repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory, citing US security interests.

After months of negotiation the agreement was signed in September by Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.

The agreement allows for two new US military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system. It also keeps Greenland under Danish control, while reaffirming Greenlanders' right to self determination.

Greenland cannot take 'stability for granted'

On Tuesday, shortly before the vote in the capital, Nuuk, Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede welcomed the agreement's ratification.

"We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted," Egede said.

In a first debate last month, a majority of Greenlandic lawmakers had already signalled support for the agreement.

Pele Broberg, chair of the pro-independence Naleraq party, questioned the deal's value for Greenland.

"We are looking for a better agreement that we can benefit from when we become an independent state. But no economic benefit has been gained from the agreement," Broberg said.

The agreement will come into effect after ratification by the Danish parliament, which is due to read the bill over two sessions in November. A vote is scheduled for November 19 in Copenhagen.

What's really in the Greenland deal? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump pressures Greenland

In January 2026, Trump began calling for the US to control Greenland, and threatened the use of military force and tariffs against US European allies if he did not get his way.

Trump had claimed that Denmark was not doing enough to defend its autonomous arctic territory from unspecified threats from China and Russia.

Trump's repeated threats damaged US ties with Denmark and rattled the US' European NATO allies.

On January 21, after Trump met with NATO chief Mark Rutte on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos, tensions cooled after Rutte and Trump announced a "concept of a deal" allowing for expanded US defense access to Greenland, which would later evolve into the agreement signed in September.

Denmark had repeatedly said it was willing to discuss expanding the US military footprint in Greenland, while rejecting Trump's more extreme demand that Greenland become US territory.

Critics have pointed out the same deal could have been made without the extreme disruption caused by Trump's territorial and tariff threats.

Under a 1951 agreement, the US already has considerable military freedom of action in Greenland.

After years of voluntarily drawing down its military presence, the US only maintains the Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which is used for missile defense and radar surveillance.

World.title: UK's King Charles III decries 'monstrous injustice' of slave trade
World.content:
King Charles has told leaders at a Commonwealth summit that the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade "fills my heart with horror." He did not address calls for apologies and reparations.

The United Kingdom's King Charles III on Tuesday opened this week's Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, a summit of 56 Commonwealth member-state leaders, by speaking of the tragic legacy of the transatlantic slave trade.

Charles told those gathered that he had furthered his "own understanding of the issues through listening, learning and looking."

"The ​transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with ⁠horror ​and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

The monarch stopped short of apologizing for Britain's role in the dark trade, as well as refraining from any talk of reparations. Instead, he spoke of the need to look forward when addressing the "monstrous injustice" of the past to insure that "evil need not have the last word."

Ghana revives slave trade history through theater To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Will the UK apologize for slavery, offer reparations?

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is also in attendance, has previously said that he could be open to an apology, and the run up to the summit has been dominated by talk of apologies and potential financial reparations.

Both the king and the prime minister have spoken of using the summit as an opportunity to address future partnerships by devising approaches to tackle healthcare, education and climate protection needs among those "who struggle against ⁠hardship and disadvantage" rather than dwelling on the past.

"We cannot change the actions of those who came before us," said the monarch as he opened Tuesday's session, "We can, however, learn from the past."

Burnham has said he would like to discuss debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations as well as announcing ⁠a €48.2 million ($54 million) investment into ​critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

Despite calls for reparations, King Charles has emphasized building strong future partnerships within the Commonwealth rather than dwelling on the past Image: Matias Delacroix/AP Photo/picture alliance

What was the British Empire's role in the transatlantic slave trade?

The British joined the institutionalized slave trade in the seventeenth century, and quickly eclipsed other European powers before involvement in the trade was outlawed for British subjects in the Slave Trade Act of 1807 and then done away with in the wider British Empire in the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833.

During that time, Britain outfitted almost one-third of all transatlantic slave voyages, facilitating the forced transport of over 3.2 million Africans, mainly to British colonies in the Caribbean and North America.

The Commonwealth of Nations consists largely of former British colonies whose combined GDP of roughly $14.5 trillion accounts for about 15% of the global economy.

World.title: Why South Africa's local elections matter
World.content:
South Africans head to the polls on Wednesday amid water shortages, frustration with local services and questions over whether the ANC's support will keep falling.

"We've decided not to vote. At all," Vatiswa Zoya said two days before voters in South Africa cast their ballots for new municipal government leaders. "What is the point? We will still sleep hungry."

These very same frustrations are what will lead 22-year-old Lindokuhle Mbandazayo to the polls, although she has yet to decide where to place her cross.

"When we vote for councilors, we ask them to fix the area," Mbandazayo told DW. "The electricity goes off regularly here. There is also sewage in the streets, and we have to jump over this. There are a lot of things that need to be fixed here."

Both women live in Tembisa, a township in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city. Both express an "embedded frustration" over their living conditions.

Many voters will be asking whether they'll have water to shower on election day, as shortages persist Image: Siphiwe Sibeko/REUTERS

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, said it was this "embedded frustration" that prompts people to vote.

"Your vote actually puts some of these political parties' feet to the fire, but I think that frustration is also inherently coming from the fact that it's not going to happen overnight," Naidu said.

On Wednesday, South Africans will vote in municipal elections that will determine control of the country's largest cities and test whether the African National Congress (ANC), the leading party in the national government coalition, continues its electoral decline.

Here are five things to know about Wednesday's election.

1. Water is a key voter issue

Many voters will be motivated by whether they can shower or not on election day, as many parts of South Africa experience water supply issues.

In Johannesburg, several neighborhoods have faced water cuts and rationing for weeks as old infrastructure struggles to keep up with supply.

"Every province has an issue. So if we take for example drinking water quality, half of the drinking water systems in South Africa are not fit for drinking," Ferrial Adam, executive director of water rights NGO WaterCAN, told DW at a protest over water cuts in Johannesburg.

"Almost 70% of our wastewater treatment works are in a critical state and spewing sewage into rivers and streams across the country," Adam said. "It is a definite water crisis across South Africa," she added.

In Tshwane, a metropolitan area that includes South Africa's administrative capital, Pretoria, a recent water treatment failure left more than 400 residents sick.

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, said that, despite widespread worries about water quality and supply, many candidates have not provided adequate details on their solutions.

"I think their promises have been very transactional," Naidu said. "Their promises are always, you know: 'We're going to bring water to your community. We're going to make sure the taps are flowing. We're going to ensure that we're going to deal with the old infrastructure around water, etc.' But I don't think they've dug deeper in terms of understanding what the budgets say about water access."

2. ANC in decline

Many voters place blame for the state of municipalities on the African National Congress, which has historically held an outright majority in most municipalities.

In 2016 the ANC secured 53.91% of the overall vote and had an outright majority in 161 of 213 councils. In 2021, that decreased to 45.59% of the overall vote with a majority in 122 of 213 municipalities.

The global marketing research firm Ipsos predicts that the party's support could fall as low as 30% in this election, resulting in an increase in coalition-run municipalities.

South Africa sees nationwide protests over migrants To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Naidu said the party had struggled to keep up with the expectations of evolving voters, particularly the Millennial and Gen Zdemographics, who now make up the bulk of voters.

"You have an electorate that wants to see who are these people that you're putting out there to say you're going to make things work for us," Naidu said.

Mbandazayo is one such voter. She is casting a ballot in her second election and said she was looking for a new voice in politics.

"We need change," Mbandazayo said. "I am considering voting for another party because the current party is not doing well for us because we've been voting for them for a long time."

3. Migration a big talking point

South Africa has seen a wave of protests around migration for several months, ramping up in October with opposition to the country's asylum process.

According to Murmur Intelligence, a digital analysis firm, parties such as Action SA, the MK Party and the Patriotic Alliance have used immigration as a campaign issue.

"The party that might claim the most benefit from that sentiment … is Action SA," Murmur Intelligence co-founder Aldu Cornelissen said.

"They would make a clear argument that we need to get rid of illegal immigrants. We need to improve immigration. We need to protect our borders, which are all legitimate concerns, right? So, if any of the parties could capitalize on this sentiment, it would be them."

"But for what percentage?" Cornelissen said. "I would wager between 6% and 8%, roughly."

Those margins may seem low, but, in an increasingly fractured political landscape, parties are fighting for every vote.

According to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC), 136,760 candidates are contesting across the country, with 75 parties contesting in Johannesburg, 70 in Tshwane and 69 in eThekwini (Durban and surrounding areas).

4. Election misinformation

Fake news and false AI-generated content have become a feature in this election, with the IEC investigating more than 700 complaints of disinformation. One of the prominent claims has been an accusation that the ANC plans to mobilize asylum seekers to vote for them.

Asylum-seekers, refugees and permanent residents can't legally vote in South African elections regardless of how long they've been in the country.

South Africa election hit by disinformation surge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

William Bird, director of media monitoring agency Moxii Africa, said misinformation and disinformation "are now kind of part and parcel of your standard buildup to any electoral environment, wherever you are in the world."

"What we see with disinformation is that it always picks up on whatever the hot-button news issues are, as well as the standard kind of tropes about elections," he said. He added that there will always be "some bunch of clowns" saying the elections are rigged.

"And, in South Africa's case, there's no evidence to support that at all. The IEC is one of the best electoral-management bodies in the world. So of course, you then see people that are either wanting to destabilize, or they're wanting to just shake things up and make people scared or angry, and so they use those kinds of narratives. And that, unfortunately, is becoming an increasingly common trait," Bird told DW.

Bird said social media platforms often "incentivize and deliberately encourage people" to attack others online.

5. Will people make it to the polls?

Municipal election turnout has historically been lower than turnout in national elections. In 2016, turnout was at 57.95% and dropped to 45.87%. In 2024, in the most recent national elections, turnout was at 58.64%.

Naidu said the election would ultimately depend less on online discussions or campaign slogans and more on how many people make it to the polls.

Voters will mark two ballots — one for a direct local representative and a second for a political party under a proportional representation (PR) system.

Seats allocated through the PR vote account for half of all council seats, making them as important as the direct votes for councilors and this is where voter turnout becomes a key element.

"That is why political parties are saying to people, go out and vote, go out and vote, because if you don't go out and vote, it has an impact on the calculation of what you win as a PR vote in the council and the seats that you get," she said. In turn, this affects the makeup of each municipality and whether new coalition governments will form.

Could you still afford to live in Cape Town today? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Additional reporting by Ahmed Kajee and Sofia Christensen

World.title: Ukraine war: Merz doubts Russia is serious about a truce
World.content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin. Both leaders said the EU needs to be included in peace talks with Russia. Merz also expressed doubts that Russia is serious about seeking a truce.

Speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he had seen no sign that Russia is serious about negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine.

Zelenskyy and Merz both said the European Union must help shape any lasting peace.

Germany expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi for next week's US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the table.

"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," Merz said when asked about the Abu Dhabi talks. "I do not see that happening so far."

Zelenskyy said he hopes the Abu Dhabi talks, the first trilateral sit down since February, could pave the way for a direct meeting between the Ukrainian president and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who has thus far refused several offers from Zelenskyy for face-to-face talks.

"We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders," he told reporters.

Europe must have a say on postwar security

Merz said Europe must have a say on sanctions and postwar security.

He said the local ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a model for a wider truce, but warned that Russian attacks in the Black Sea risked further escalation. "Russia is precipitating a global food crisis, to the detriment of the poorest nations and countries in the world," he said.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain shipments through the Black Sea and further prisoner exchanges.

Lavrov sets conditions for talks with Zelenskyy at G20 meeting To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire alone would not secure a lasting peace. Ukraine would need security guarantees backed by Europe and the US. He insisted Europe must be involved in the negotiations.

"There cannot be a sustainable peace if Europe is not at the negotiating table," Zelenskyy said.

He said Ukraine would join the US, European partners and NATO for talks on security guarantees and reconstruction in Brussels on Wednesday.

Russia increases attacks on Ukrainian civilians

The talks in Berlin come as Russia continues to increase airstrikes on Ukrainian civilians.

Zelenskyy said at least 33 people were killed, and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble, after multiple Russian strikes on a school building used as an aid distribution center in the frontline southeastern village of on Monday.

Ukrainian officials said Russian forces launched an initial strike on residents waiting to receive aid, and then hit the same location again after waiting for rescue personnel to arrive on the scene, killing several of them and destroying emergency vehicles.

Speaking in Berlin, Zelenskyy described the strike as "one of the largest Russian killings of this war."

On Tuesday, at least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, and 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals, regional prosecutors said.

Russian forces struck the aid center twice after waiting for rescue workers to arrive Image: REUTERS

Germany pledges aid ahead of winter

"Ahead of the next winter, air defense and the energy sector are our priorities," Merz said. He said Germany would soon deliver new aid in both areas and provide further winter assistance this year.

Zelenskyy thanked Germany for helping protect Ukraine's skies and supporting its energy infrastructure.

"Without Germany, we would not be as strong as we are," he said.

He said Ukraine urgently needed more air defense equipment, including Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.

How has Berlin stepped up security?

The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.

Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.

Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.

World.title: China and India achieved diplomatic thaw. Now the border is flaring up
World.content:
Indian authorities have confirmed a new border "face-off" between Indian and Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh, raising questions about the still fragile thaw in relations between New Delhi and Beijing.

Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur sounded alarm bells across India by confirming that Indian and Chinese troops had confronted each other at several locations along the de facto border in Arunachal Pradesh state, in India's northeast.

"In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened (with Chinese troops) at various locations in Arunachal and it still continues," he told reporters last month.

"It may be difficult to counter China by conventional means because their PLA and BDR (Border Defense Regiment) have gone way ahead with investment and modernization," he said.

The disputed China-India border runs through a remote mountainous region.

Throughout the decades, clashes along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border, have repeatedly triggered security crises between the world's two most populous nations.

Ties between Beijing and New Delhi are still affected by the deadly violence in 2020, when both countries accused each other of trying to seize territory.

In June that year, a clash in the Galwan River valley in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops, according to Indian sources. China later confirmed four of its soldiers died.

Arunachal Pradesh leader Pema Khandu says situation normal

Kapur's remarks have brought renewed attention to the Himalayan frontier. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has acknowledged but also downplayed the border transgressions, saying such incidents were not new and the situation along the border was normal.

Khandu acknowledged that the border was not properly demarcated and that China did not recognize the McMahon Line, drawn by the British Empire in 1914, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet.

It was also not clear if the latest confrontations between the Chinese and Indian troops involved physical violence.

Tracking the tense relationship between India and China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China rejects wrongdoing

The opposition Congress party criticized Khandu's remarks, and accused the ruling BJP, led by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, of "rationalizing" Chinese actions instead of asserting India's position.

"On this there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X, referring to the face-offs confirmed by the border police chief.

Meanwhile, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal attributed the incidents to Chinese forces changing up their patrol routes.

"As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," he said.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations, saying Chinese troops were conducting "normal patrols" and strictly abiding by bilateral agreements.

Why do face-offs keep happening?

The LAC largely separates Indian- and Chinese-controlled territory. However, as forces from both nations patrol territory they regard as their own, they sometimes venture into disputed areas.

"There is a very simple reason — because there is no agreed line between the two," Gautam Bambawale, a former Indian ambassador to China, told DW.

The de-facto border stretches for 3,488 kilometres (2,167 miles) according to India, but China claims it is shorter. The two countries have held 25 rounds of talks between their Special Representatives since 2003, but have yet to reach a boundary settlement.

The dispute is particularly sensitive in Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as part of southern Tibet.

Finding home in exile: Tibetans in India resist China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China building a hydropower dam in Tibet

Aravind Yelery, a China expert at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the region has become more strategically important to Beijing.

"Both sides patrol a contested LAC, so friction is built into the arrangement," Yelery told DW.

"What is new is China's intensified focus on the eastern sector. Since announcing the 60,000-megawatt Medog hydropower project in Tibet, Beijing has poured infrastructure, troops, engineers and machinery into the area."

South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He described the LAC as "not a thin line but a deep zone of overlapping claims where patrols inevitably meet." Face-offs will continue, he argued, until diplomacy produces concrete arrangements on the ground.

According to Yelery, the diplomatic pledges made by Indian and Chinese leaders will take time to implement.

"A wide gap separates the leaders' promises from the measures that would prevent a repeat of 2020, namely disengagement and mutual restraint," he added.

What is different about the latest developments?

For India, the immediate concern is whether the recent encounters reflect familiar patrol disputes or a more significant change in Chinese activity along the frontier.

Ashok Kantha, another former Indian ambassador to China, said Chinese transgressions in the eastern sector were not new, but that their location and extent mattered.

"If the Chinese have now made deeper intrusions on our side of the LAC, or established a presence in new areas, or expanded their existing presence, that would be a serious development," he added.

He also pointed to agreements signed by the two countries to maintain peace along the border.

"Any such transgression would be in complete violation of several border-related agreements India and China have signed (1993, 1996, 2005, 2012 and 2013). In these, both sides committed to respect and strictly observe the LAC, and not to alter the status quo."

The Indian government has not publicly provided details of the locations or circumstances of the latest face-offs, making it unclear whether they have changed the situation on the ground.

A fragile diplomatic thaw

The renewed encounters come as India and China try to stabilize relations and move past the 2020 clashes. Both Beijing and New Delhi made reconciliatory moves, including restoring some direct flights and easing restrictions on travel and economic exchanges.

The diplomatic reset gathered pace after Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping met at the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024. They met again at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi this year.

The boundary dispute, however, remains unresolved.

India builds tunnel in Himalayas to counter China threat To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Alka Acharya, director of the Institute of Chinese Studies in New Delhi, cautioned against drawing conclusions about the latest encounters without more information.

The government has described the incidents as face-offs, she said, but has not indicated that Chinese troops have taken control of Indian territory.

"The question is what is the nature of the so-called 'clashes' … not why the clashes are happening again? Any opinion on this latest kerfuffle would at best be conjecture without any definitive evidence," Acharya told DW.

Border incidents have occurred regularly over the past decade and a half, despite political and diplomatic negotiations. The unresolved dispute, she added, will continue to sustain distrust and constrain the broader relationship.

Whether the latest encounters signal a more serious escalation will depend on details that New Delhi has yet to make public.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community
World.content:
As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

"Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.

Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival , which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.

Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.

Inspired by 'imperfect' divas

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person."

The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.

Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens.

"And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

Hassandra out of drag: They are also a DJ and cultural organizer Image: Gönna Ketels/DW

Building community through drag

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.

In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.

Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.

Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.

As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.

That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.

What does the Berlin Pride attack mean for city's identity? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."

Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."



"There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.

The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

World.title: Cyprus: From ties with Russia to a strategic alignment with the US
World.content:
The Republic of Cyprus long balanced ties between Russia and the West. Now, it is phasing out Russian weapons, expanding defense cooperation with the United States and redefining its place in the Eastern Mediterranean.

In an interview with the Cyprus News Agency on October 4, the new US ambassador to Cyprus, John Breslow, outlined plans to upgrade the Andreas Papandreou Air Base in Paphos to accommodate large US military transport aircraft.

He also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports and an expansion of joint military activities.

But one statement carried particular political weight: his assurance that "the United States will protect Cyprus in the future."

Although the remark does not constitute a formal US security guarantee, it reflects the growing cooperation between the two countries.

For a country that for decades maintained close ties with Moscow, viewed US foreign policy with suspicion and is not a member of NATO, the prospect of an expanded American military presence marks a significant geopolitical shift.

The ambassador also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports. Pictured here: US amphibious assault ship USS Wasp docked at the port in Limassol in 2024 Image: Iakovos Hatzistavrou/AFP

It is perhaps the clearest indication yet of Cyprus's gradual loosening of ties with Russia and its increasingly close strategic alignment with the United States.

The nonalignment years

The shift is particularly striking given Cyprus's political history.

In the years after it gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1960, the Republic of Cyprus sought to balance its relations between East and West.

Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III, the first president of independent Cyprus, the country became a founding member in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement, a forum of nations that did not align with either of the two superpowers of the day: the United States and the Soviet Union.

Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III (left), Cyprus became a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961 Image: Nicholas Tsikourias/ZUMA/picture alliance

This approach allowed Nicosia to maintain close ties with the Soviet Union without severing its connections to the West.

EU membership

Even after joining the European Union in 2004, Cyprus maintained strong political, economic and military ties with Moscow.

Relations with the United States, by contrast, remained overshadowed by the Turkish invasion of the island in 1974 and the US's failure to take decisive action against Ankara.

The United States prioritized maintaining its strategic relationship with Turkey, a key NATO ally, over taking a tougher stance against the invasion.

The US position fueled widespread anti-American sentiment in Cyprus, culminating in a violent demonstration outside the embassy in Nicosia on August 19, 1974, during which US Ambassador Roger Davies was shot dead.

Mistrust deepened further in 1987, when the United States imposed an arms embargo on the Republic of Cyprus, officially intended to prevent an arms race on the island and avoid undermining efforts to resolve the Cyprus conflict.

Close relations with Moscow

The US arms embargo contributed to the reliance of the Cypriot National Guard (the armed forces of the Republic of Cyprus) on Russia-made weapons systems, strengthening the Kremlin's position as a major military partner.

The response by Cyprus to Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 illustrated the strength of these ties.

The Cypriot government expressed serious reservations about imposing tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Then-Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides warned that such measures could have devastating consequences for the Cypriot economy.

Even after joining the EU in 2004, Cyprus maintained close ties with Moscow. Pictured here: Nicos Anastasiades (left), president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Russian President Vladimir Putin after signing agreements in Russia in 2015 Image: Nikita Shvetsov/Anadolu/IMAGO

Relations with Moscow deepened further in February 2015, when President Nicos Anastasiades visited the Russian capital and signed a series of agreements with President Vladimir Putin.

These included a naval cooperation memorandum facilitating visits by Russian warships to Cypriot ports. Moscow also agreed to more favorable repayment terms for its €2.5 billion loan to Cyprus in 2011.

Cooperation remained close as recently as October 2021, when then Foreign Minister and current President Nikos Christodoulides signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework for 2022–2024 in Moscow alongside his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.

Turning point in 2022

The decisive turning point came just four months later, in February 2022, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Konstantinos Adamides, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nicosia, told DW that the invasion accelerated a geopolitical shift toward the West that had already begun.

"For the first time, the Republic of Cyprus openly and unequivocally chose to side with the West, despite the economic and political costs of breaking with Moscow," Adamides said.

Nicosia aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia, despite the Cypriot economy's strong links to Moscow, particularly in services, investment and tourism.

The decision marked a significant departure from Cyprus's traditional foreign policy approach of maintaining a balance between Russia and the West.

Adamides said the government's position on Russia paved the way for closer relations with the United States, particularly in the field of security.

Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian military equipment. Pictured here: Russian-made T-80 tanks in a 2021 military parade in Nicosia Image: Philippos Christou/AP Photo/picture alliance

Cyprus, he said, succeeded in convincing Washington that it could serve as a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean.

What form does the rapprochement take?

The rapprochement had already gained an institutional foundation before the war, with a bilateral statement of intent on security cooperation signed in 2018.

Further initiatives followed, including the Cyprus Center for Land, Open-seas and Port Security (CYCLOPS), a US-funded training facility inaugurated in Larnaca in April 2022. The center provides training for security personnel from Cyprus and other countries in the region in areas such as port security, counterterrorism and preventing the trafficking of hazardous materials.

An even more significant development for the Cypriot National Guard came in September 2022, when Washington announced the full suspension of the arms embargo imposed in 1987.

The decision allowed for the export of lethal military equipment to Cyprus, subject to the necessary US approvals. The suspension, which was not permanent and remains subject to periodic renewal, has been renewed until September 30, 2027.

Cyprus and NATO

The strategic security reorientation is also significant because Cyprus is not a member of NATO.

The crash landing of an Iranian done on the British military base at Akrotiri in March reignited a debate in Cyprus about whether the country should join NATO.

Earlier this year President Nikos Christodoulides said that Cyprus would apply to join NATO 'even tomorrow if it were possible' Image: Nicolas Tucat/AFP

At the time, Christodoulides said Cyprus was preparing for potential membership at the military, operational and administrative level and would apply to join NATO "even tomorrow if it were possible."

Christodoulides said, however, that joining the alliance was not possible because "the political conditions are not there, taking into account the well-known position of Turkey."

Phasing out Russian weapons

The country's changing strategic orientation is also reflected in the modernization of its armed forces.

After decades of relying heavily on Russian military equipment, Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian-made T-80 tanks and Tor-M1 and Buk air defense systems.

The process accelerated following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, as sanctions against Moscow made it increasingly difficult to secure spare parts and ammunition for Russian weapons systems.

Another important step came in January 2025, when then President Joe Biden authorized Cyprus to participate in US defense procurement programs, including Foreign Military Sales (FMS) and Excess Defense Articles (EDA).

The decision gave Nicosia access to additional mechanisms for acquiring US military equipment, further strengthening defense cooperation between Cyprus and the United States.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: Última hora del accidente de trenes de Urda, en Toledo, en directo | Óscar Puente dimite: “Un ministro no puede continuar en su puesto con un accidente de este tipo”
World.content:
Sánchez elogia a Puente: “Ha dado la cara y, después, un paso al lado” | El ministro ha comunicado su decisión al presidente minutos antes de hacerla pública | Tampoco irá en las listas del PSOE al 29-N | El PP achaca la dimisión al cálculo político

El ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, ha anunciado su dimisión tras la tragedia ferroviaria que ha causado 69 víctimas mortales en Urda: “Un ministro de Transportes de un país como España no puede continuar en su cargo tras dos accidentes en menos de un año”, ha lanzado el ministro al final de una comparecencia de cuatro horas en el Congreso para dar cuenta del accidente. El ministro ha comunicado su decisión al presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, apenas minutos antes de hacerla pública, y el presidente ha elogiado luego su gesto: “Ha dado la cara, soluciones y, después, un paso al lado”. Durante un tenso y bronco debate, Puente ha recordado que su Gobierno puso en marcha un plan de renovación de 780 millones de euros y ha reiterado las dudas sobre la decisión del centro de control de Adif de autorizar al AVE implicado en el accidente de Urda (Toledo) a reanudar la circulación en marcha normal, pese a la caída del sistema de seguridad LZB y a que había un tren de Iryo detenido más adelante. Tras el anuncio del ministro, el PP ha achacado su decisión a un cálculo político: “No se va por las víctimas ni por dignidad, sino por la encuestas”, han señalado fuentes de Génova. Minutos antes, durante el debate, la portavoz del PP, Ester Muñoz, había replicado al ministro que su responsabilidad “no es explicar accidentes mortales”, sino evitarlos. Sumar también había pedido su dimisión, aunque aclaraba que no le atribuía la culpa del accidente. Por su parte, el portavoz de ERC, Gabriel Rufián, había insistido en que un error humano refleja “un sistema de seguridad fallido”. El accidente ha dejado 69 muertos y alrededor de 200 heridos, 40 de ellos aún hospitalizados.

Renfe ha puesto a disposición el número 900 10 10 20. Iryo ha habilitado el 900 001 403.

EL PAÍS ofrece de forma gratuita la última hora de la actualidad política y el accidente de Urda. Si quieres apoyar nuestro periodismo, suscríbete.

World.title: Óscar Puente dimite “por dignidad”: “Quiero estar a la altura de mi país”
World.content:
Óscar Puente dice que decidió dimitir como ministro de Transportes solo unos minutos después de que tuvo noticia del trágico accidente ferroviario de Urda. Lo acordó, según ha relatado, la misma mañana de ese miércoles 28 de octubre de camino al centro de control de la estación de Atocha y así se lo comunicó a su familia. Y lo mantuvo en silencio hasta pasadas las 21.00 de este martes, cuando lo anunció por sorpresa ante el Congreso de los Diputados. Ha sido una escena desconocida en la democracia española: ver a un ministro presentar su dimisión ante los grupos políticos que se la acababan de pedir casi unánimemente en la Diputación Permanente del Parlamento.

Puente reveló ante los diputados que la decisión estaba tomada desde hace seis días. Pero en todo este tiempo, mientras afrontaba las consecuencias del accidente, lo había negado de forma reiterada. Lo volvió a hacer la mañana de este mismo martes, tras el Consejo de Ministros en el que se aprobaron las primeras ayudas a las víctimas. Y en su comparecencia en la Diputación Permanente, en la que todos los grupos, salvo EH Bildu, le reclamaron, en distinto tono, que se fuera, se guardó el anuncio para el final.

Fue en su intervención de cierre, después de cuatro horas de debates, cuando admitió, muy tranquilo y sin dejar traslucir excesiva emoción, que un ministro de Transportes no puede seguir en el cargo cuando, bajo su mandato, y “aunque no sea responsable directo”, se han producido dos trágicos siniestros con 116 víctimas mortales en apenas nueve meses. Confesó entonces que siempre tuvo claro que ya no podía seguir en el cargo, aunque hasta ahora lo negase en público. Ya en los pasillos, abordado por los periodistas, comentó que tampoco el presidente del Gobierno lo sabía y que se lo acababa de comunicar él mismo. Momentos antes de su último discurso, se le había visto enfrascado en su teléfono móvil enviando mensajes.

Afirmó que se va por “dignidad”, que su marcha es “necesaria y positiva” para “la democracia, para el país” y para su partido. Y que renuncia a presentarse a las elecciones. “Quiero estar a la altura de mi país y de los que me precedieron”, comentó en tono muy sereno. Y en referencia a su partido, agregó: “Nadie es más grande que las siglas a las que pertenece”. Agradeció a Pedro Sánchez su “confianza sin límites” e hizo un llamamiento: “Animo a todos los progresistas de este país para que sigan ayudándolo”. Tampoco evitó referirse a la proximidad electoral con la advertencia de que un Gobierno del PP con Vox acarrearía el “recorte de los servicios públicos”. Él ya no estará en esa batalla: también anunció que renuncia a encabezar la candidatura socialista por su provincia, Valladolid.

Las peticiones de dimisión se habían sucedido desde el comienzo del debate. En tono muy crudo, como era de esperar por parte de PP y Vox, que no solo se dedicaron al reproche político, sino que dirigieron, sobre todo la formación ultra, descalificaciones de carácter moral al ministro. La izquierda y los demás socios, salvo Podemos, lo hicieron en un tono mucho más comedido, incluso mostrando su respeto a Puente y subrayando que no lo estaban culpabilizando de los accidentes, sino que la suya era una exigencia de meras responsabilidades políticas. “Demuestre que usted no es como los del PP”, lo emplazó la portavoz de Sumar, su socio de Gobierno, Verónica Barbero. “Usted es un buen político y da la cara, pero alguien tiene que hacerse cargo de esto”, le insistió Gabriel Rufián, de ERC.

Puente asentía mientras iba escuchando esas peticiones en las que, a pesar del tono constructivo, los portavoces iban dejando constancia de que el sistema ferroviario español ha fallado. El ministro no quiso contestarles directamente y anunció que lo dejaba para su discurso de cierre. Y fue ahí, ya sin lugar a réplica de los grupos, cuando asumió los argumentos favorables a su renuncia. Dijo que quiere demostrar que “no todos los políticos son iguales” y que tampoco es cierta la consigna populista de que “solo el pueblo salva al pueblo”. Insistió en que no se considera responsable de los accidentes, pero que la sucesión de dos siniestros de semejante magnitud y con tal coste en vidas humanas lo abocaba a la dimisión. Un gesto, dijo, “propio de un Estado moderno, y no de un Estado fallido como algunos andan diciendo por ahí”.

La dimisión cogió por sorpresa a los diputados, que, tras cuatro horas de debate en las que el ministro defendió con uñas y dientes su gestión, no esperaban ya ese gesto final. Poco antes, la portavoz del PP, Ester Muñoz, en un último intento, había apelado incluso a las intervenciones de los socios del Gobierno. “¿Pero no ve lo que ha ocurrido aquí? ¿No ha visto que le han pedido todos los grupos la dimisión menos el PSOE y Bildu, que cada vez son más indistinguibles? La única verdad que no ha podido explicar es que ha habido 116 muertos". Tanta fue la sorpresa que el portavoz socialista, Patxi López, se había afanado en desmontar los argumentos favorables a la salida del ministro comparando su actitud con la de responsables del PP ante otras catástrofes: “¿Por qué tiene que dimitir? ¿Por dar la cara? ¿Por estar en el centro de control en lugar de en un restaurante?”.

De entre los grupos que han apoyado al Gobierno en la pasada legislatura, solo Ione Belarra se mostró particularmente agresiva con Puente, más incluso que Miriam Nogueras, de Junts. Los demás grupos —Sumar, ERC, PNV y BNG— lo invitaron a irse sin culparlo directamente, pero con críticas al funcionamiento del sistema ferroviario. No lo hizo Mertxe Aizpurua, de EH Bildu, la única que centró su intervención en formular preguntas. Antes que ellos, había llegado la andanada de PP y Vox. Muñoz lo trató de “todavía ministro” y lo acusó de “ser incapaz de empatizar con el dolor ajeno”. Vox se retiró sin escuchar la respuesta de Puente después de que su portavoz, Pepa Millán, dejase un torrente de afirmaciones tremebundas, entre ellas que para los socialistas “la vida humana no vale absolutamente nada”.

Puente se había extendido en ofrecer datos para rebatir las críticas de los últimos días y sostener que con este Gobierno ha crecido el gasto en mantenimiento de la red y la plantilla de Renfe y Adif se ha incrementado en más de 3.600 empleados. Eso sí, reconoció que los accidentes han mostrado la “imperiosa necesidad de mejorar el sistema y los protocolos”. Frente a los reproches de algunos grupos, que le acusaron de descargar la culpa en un trabajador del centro de control de Atocha, alegó: “¿Qué hubieran hecho ustedes en mi lugar? ¿Cuál era la alternativa, ocultarlo, disfrazarlo, inventarlo? ¿hay alguna versión alternativa de los hechos?“. Durante más de dos horas, Puente defendió su gestión con toda clase de datos y digresiones técnicas. Su declaración final antes de reconocer que, a pesar de todo, dos tragedias consecutivas no le dejaban más opción que la renuncia.

World.title: El PP apunta ahora a Sánchez tras la renuncia de Puente: “Le dimitiremos en las urnas”
World.content:
La izquierda también ha celebrado la dimisión del ministro de Transportes, aunque en un tono más conciliador. El presidente del Gobierno ha elogiado su actuación: “Ha dado la cara, ha dado soluciones y, después, ha dado un paso al lado”

El Partido Popular echa por tierra la dimisión del ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, atribuyéndola al mero cálculo político, y apunta ahora al presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez. “No ha dimitido él, le ha dimitido Tezanos. No se va por las víctimas ni por dignidad, sino por las encuestas”, ha reaccionado el PP a la renuncia de Puente en un breve comunicado, en el que reclama ahora responsabilidades al líder socialista. “No va a colar. El principal problema está en quién puso las infraestructuras en manos de Ábalos, primero, y de Puente después. La responsabilidad no se delega y Pedro Sánchez no puede esconderse detrás de Óscar Puente. Su responsabilidad todavía no ha sido depurada, pero le dimitiremos en las urnas. 116 fallecidos exigen verdad, explicaciones y responsabilidades al más alto nivel”, subrayan en la dirección del Partido Popular, donde ya habían anticipado que con la dimisión de Puente no sería suficiente.

Los populares venían advirtiendo en privado, como publicó EL PAÍS, que apuntarían a Sánchez directamente como responsable del accidente de Urda, y que la posible dimisión del ministro de Transportes, cuya renuncia, en todo caso, ha sorprendido al PP, no bastaría para colmar sus peticiones de asunción de responsabilidades políticas. Poco después de que Puente anunciara que daba un paso atrás, el partido ha enviado un comunicado en el que señala al presidente del Gobierno y los principales dirigentes del PP han insistido en ese mensaje. “La dimisión de Puente era imprescindible, pero no suficiente”, ha afirmado el secretario general del PP, Miguel Tellado. “Sánchez es el responsable de haber nombrado como ministros de Transportes a Ábalos, hoy en la cárcel, y a Puente, un tuitero pendenciero al que mantuvo después de la tragedia de Adamuz”, ha escrito el número dos de Feijóo en X.
