We cannot do what we do without your support. A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country. Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”. Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u — Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026 Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry. The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection. However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years. Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7 — Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026 Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”. Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”. At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha. In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream. Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively. However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians. OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024 Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”. Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”. “One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case. Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? World.title: Polish ambassador to UN becomes third envoy to resign amid crisis over constitutional court

Poland’s ambassador to the United Nations, Krzysztof Szczerski, has resigned, becoming the third Polish ambassador to do so since a government-backed move by a group of judges to take control of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw. All three of the departing ambassadors were previously aides or advisers to former President Andrzej Duda, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. They have criticised the attempt to oust the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed to the court under PiS. Following the resignations of Poland’s Ambassadors to China and Romania, Prof. Krzysztof Szczerski, Poland’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, has also submitted his resignation. All three are senior state officials and experienced diplomats who have served at the… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 2, 2026 On Monday afternoon, foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór announced that Szczerski had “submitted a request to shorten his diplomatic mission at the UN”, where he has served as ambassador since 2021. Szczerski’s resignation followed those of Jakub Kumoch, Poland’s ambassador to China, and Paweł Soloch, the Polish envoy to Romania, who quit their posts on Friday and Saturday, respectively. While Szczerski has not yet commented on the reasons for his departure, Kumoch and Soloch made clear that their decisions were motivated by Friday’s move to suspend Święczkowski from the TK. Soloch wrote that the “attempt to unlawfully take over the Constitutional Tribunal” left him with “no possibility of continuing to serve as ambassador”. Kumoch said his decision was a “matter of conscience”, as “there are certain things I cannot explain abroad without losing face, and I have no intention of speaking ill of Poland”. There is chaos at Poland's constitutional court tonight as a group of government-backed judges moved to take control from the opposition-aligned chief justice. Riot police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing the chief justice from entering https://t.co/xpkp3sjPFn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2026 Szczerski previously served as a member of the European Parliament for PIS. In 2015, he joined the chancellery of PiS-aligned President Duda, later becoming the head of his cabinet and then head of his International Policy Bureau. Kumoch was a member of Duda’s National Development Council, an advisory body to the president, before serving as ambassador to Switzerland, Turkey, and then China. Soloch was the head of Duda’s National Security Bureau from 2015 to 2022. On Monday, after Szczerski’s resignation, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski suggested that the three ambassadors had quit at the urging of the current president, Karol Nawrocki, who is also aligned with PiS. Sikorski sardonically suggested that, in contrast to Polish ambassadors who quit in 1981 over the imposition of martial law despite “risking vengeance from the communist regime”, the newly resigned trio “will surely be handsomely rewarded for their heroic deeds”. The developments are part of a much broader fallout from the crisis around the TK, which began on Friday evening when large numbers of riot police appeared outside the court. It soon transpired that a group of eight judges appointed by parliament to the TK this year – but five of whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in – had entered the court and declared that Święczkowski had been suspended from his position for failing to fulfil his duties. Święczkowski, who before becoming a TK judge previously served as a member of the former PiS government, declared their actions unlawful and an attempted “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the six other justices appointed when PiS was in government. Święczkowski has also been supported by Nawrocki, who dramatically entered the court in the early hours of Saturday morning, clashing physically and verbally with the self-proclaimed acting head of the court, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 The developments have created an unprecedented situation at the TK. However, the court has been in crisis since 2015, when Duda and the then-PiS government – which came to power that year – unlawfully rejected three judges appointed by the former parliament and replaced them with three of their own. The current government, a broad coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, does not recognise the TK due to those illegitimate judges and has ignored its rulings since replacing PiS in power in December 2023. This year, Tusk’s coalition began appointing judges to fill vacancies on the court. It has condemned Nawrocki and Święczkowski for refusing to accept those judges, saying that their actions are unlawful. Given those circumstances, Tusk and his government have argued that tough action is necessary to restore the legitimacy of the TK. On Saturday evening, Tusk gave an address to the nation declaring that there can be “no compromise” over the rule of law. "On some issues, there can be no compromise," declared Prime Minister @donaldtusk in an address to the nation on the crisis around the constitutional court. He condemned the actions of President Karol Nawrocki, accusing him of "intimidating judges" https://t.co/RPyt87mcFO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 However, a number of legal experts – including many who were highly critical of PiS’s policies towards the TK and other courts – have expressed doubts over the manner in which Korwin-Piotrowska and her colleagues have sought to take control of the tribunal. Further developments are expected on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska has called a general assembly of the tribunal. However, it is uncertain that she will obtain the necessary quorum of 10 judges normally required for the assembly to be valid. While the eight judges appointed by the ruling coalition this year are all expected to attend, those appointed under the PiS government appear likely not to. Polish police have launched a special operation to secure the area along the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad after receiving information that acts of sabotage may take place there in the coming days. The operation – which has involved sending additional officers, including counter-terrorism forces, to the northeastern Podlasie and Warmia-Masuria provinces – was first reported by broadcaster RMF and confirmed by the national police chief, Marek Boroń. “Police are putting security measures in place around the Kaliningrad region in anticipation of possible incidents that could lead to acts of sabotage,” he told RMF. “This is based on information we also have from external security services.” “We are responsible for ensuring the safety of the citizens living there, as well as for facilities and any situations that may pose a threat to society,” he added, noting that the police were coordinating their operation with the army, border guard and security services. RMF reports, based on unnamed sources, that Poland’s Military Intelligence Service (SWW) and agencies from unnamed allied countries last week issued a warning that sabotage activities could take place on the Polish-Russian border, potentially including border violations by armed groups. In a separate statement, the national police headquarters told RMF that the ongoing operation is “directly related to the situation taking place in our country today, that is, acts of sabotage…and the actions of eastern services”. That was a reference to the activities of Russia and its ally Belarus, which have in recent years carried out a series of acts of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” against Poland and other countries in the region. A spokeswoman for the police headquarters, Katarzyna Nowak, told broadcaster TVN that they were unable to provide any further information on the nature of the operation as the details are confidential. W Komendzie Głównej Policji powstał sztab operacji specjalnej prowadzonej w Warmińsko-Mazurskiem i na Podlasiu przez policję przy współpracy wojska, straży granicznej i służb specjalnych – mówi dziennikarzowi RMF FM Krzysztofowi Zasadzie szef KGP Marek Boroń. Chodzi o działania… — Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) November 2, 2026 On Thursday last week, the deputy police commander, Tomasz Michułka, issued an order for officers to be on “full readiness” between 2 and 8 November due to the “operational situation across the country”. Some had interpreted that order as related to the situation around the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) in Warsaw, where riot police were called in on Friday to secure the court amid protests against an attempt by a group of government-backed judges to take control of the TK. However, on Friday night, the police issued a statement “emphatically denying” that the order had anything to do with the situation at the TK. They said that it was, in fact, “related to the current threats regarding acts of sabotage and subversion”. The following day, Boroń himself wrote to police officers confirming that Thursday’s order had been issued in response to “attempts to destabilise our country by foreign intelligence services from the east”. List Komendanta Głównego Policji do funkcjonariuszy pic.twitter.com/3jTMdme1bz — Polska Policja 🇵🇱 (@PolskaPolicja) November 1, 2026 Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism identified Poland as the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Those operations have included an arson attack that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and an attempt to derail a train. In September this year, a Russian military helicopter crossed the border from Kaliningrad and remained in Polish airspace for around 42 seconds before returning. In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile carrying a significant explosive payload entered Polish airspace from Ukraine before landing in a field in eastern Poland. The Polish government has regularly warned in recent months that Moscow is planning further provocations against eastern NATO member states, including potential border violations. World.title: First Asian hornet nest in Poland eliminated but experts warn more to appear next year
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year. Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries. The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology. The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males. The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added. “I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.” Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas. With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps. The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees. “Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.” The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers. Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022 The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out. The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites. World.title: Polish president in physical confrontation with judges amid power struggle at constitutional court

We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis. However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters. On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw. At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors. The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her. Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”. Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”. Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”. ⚠️Mamy kolejne nagranie z TK. Tym razem prezydent krzyczy do sędziów, że „nie są sędziami” i w otoczeniu funkcjonariuszy SOP wchodzi po schodach na górę. pic.twitter.com/rkhoQLIv94 — Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) October 31, 2026 The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 On Friday evening, the judges appointed by parliament this year entered the TK and Korwin-Piotrowska announced that she had suspended Święczkowski for failing to properly exercise his duties. She said that, as the judge with the longest experience, she had assumed the position of acting head of the tribunal. Outside the court, riot police held back protesters, including opposition politicians, who called the events a “coup d’état”. Święczkowski himself was prevented by police from entering the grounds after some of his supporters had used a power tool to cut through the fence. At around 5 a.m., Nawrocki was seen leaving the TK. “There has been a violation of the constitutional order of Poland and a forceful takeover of a constitutional body,” said the president in a statement read by the head of his cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker. The president announced that he would hold urgent consultations with parliamentary groups in an attempt to “restore the legal order”. Those meetings are scheduled to take place on Saturday afternoon. Hołownia said that his party had “watched last night’s events with concern” and that they “bring shame on Poland”. While he criticised Święczkowski and other PiS-nominated judges, he said that trying to fix the TK “by force” would only “exacerbate its downfall”. Sytuacja w… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 31, 2026 Tusk’s only comment so far has been a social media post saying that restoring the rule of law “requires decisive action”. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki. One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool. Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’état” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw. Prezes Świeczkowski wraz z grupą posłów przeciął łańcuchy i próbuje dostać się do trybunału konstytucyjnego. Policja nie chce go przepuścić! Przecież to bezprawie! pic.twitter.com/XbIXigwIi3 — Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026 The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis surrounding the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy. That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench. That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court. However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications. Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court. In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling. The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026 Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening. On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered. The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence. However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’s judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK. “I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.” Ze szczątkowych informacji, na jakiej podstawie zawieszono B. Święczkowskiego, wynika, że ma to być art. 19 ustawy o statusie sędziów TK, który mówi, że do spraw nieuregulowanych w tej ustawie stosuje się „przepisy dotyczące praw i obowiązków sędziów SN” i art. 130 ustawy o SN,… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) October 30, 2026 Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański. He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”. That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties. She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio. Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995. 🗣️ “Bogdan Święczkowski narusza zasady funkcjonowania TK. Według jej relacji siedem osób wybranych na sędziów weszło do budynku w asyście funkcjonariuszy SOP, natomiast wiceprezes Bartłomiej Sochański nie został wpuszczony na teren Trybunału. pic.twitter.com/VwxU4UrYuz — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) October 30, 2026 The developments at the court prompted outrage from the opposition. World.title: “The Art of James Cameron” to Open at Prague’s Municipal House in April 2027
World.content:
An exhibition dedicated to filmmaker James Cameron will open at Prague’s Municipal House (Obecní dům) on April 29, 2027, bringing more than 300 items from the director’s archive to the Czech capital.

Titled The Art of James Cameron, the exhibition will run until October 3, presenting original drawings, paintings, film props, costumes and photographs connected to the Canadian director’s career.



Visitors will also see examples of 3D technologies developed or adapted for his films, alongside multimedia installations and audio commentary in which Cameron discusses his artistic development.

The collection will cover several decades of his work, from early sketches and storyboards to the technical innovations behind some of Hollywood’s biggest productions, including The Terminator, Aliens, Titanic and the Avatar films.

Although Cameron is widely recognised for pushing the technical boundaries of cinema, the exhibition will focus on his work as an artist and illustrator.

His creative process often began with pencil and paper, with early sketchbooks filled with imaginary creatures, futuristic machines and visions of distant worlds.

The exhibition will also explore recurring themes in his films, including the threat of nuclear catastrophe and the risks posed by rapid advances in artificial intelligence.

Cameron made his feature-film debut in 1981 with the action horror film Piranha II. His breakthrough came three years later with The Terminator, followed by Aliens in 1986. He continued to explore science fiction with The Abyss (1989), which follows a team investigating an underwater encounter with an unknown form of life.

His biggest success at the time came with Titanic (1997). The film won 11 Academy Awards and became one of the highest-grossing productions in cinema history, earning approximately $1.85 billion worldwide.

World.title: Prague Music Week Brings Czech and International Music Names to Prague
World.content:
From November 4 to 6, Výstaviště Praha will become a hub for musicians, industry professionals, and fans interested in everything happening both on and off the stage.

The fourth edition of Prague Music Week—themed “Women Shaping the Industry”—will feature keynote interviews with Aneta Langerová and Jana Kirschner, as well as discussions with local artists such as Lenny, Jiří Burian, Eva Saija Burešová, Klára Vytisková, and Ventolin.



A newly confirmed guest is singer Ben Cristovao, who will join a panel addressing the surge of AI-generated music.

International guests include renowned PR expert Fiona Bloom, Sziget Festival Operations Director Ádám Kiss, diversity, equity, and inclusion specialist Brechje Merckx, and representatives from Spotify.

Will also join: Finnish music industry professional Maija Talvisto; Christine Osazuwa—founder of Measure of Music and an expert in music data and analytics; Vasja Veber, co-founder of the leading analytics platform Viberate; Kristina Janušauskaitė, Executive Director of the IFPI European Office.

The event will offer practical workshops, speed-meeting sessions, opportunities to receive feedback on one’s own work, a technology expo, industry awards, informal gatherings, and space for forging new collaborations.

Tickets for the festival portion of the program are available for purchase via the GoOut and NFCtron networks.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Prague Music Week (@praguemusicweek)

Conference tickets can be obtained via a voluntary contribution through the NFCtron platform. More information is available at www.praguemusicweek.cz.

Prague Music Week will feature an Expo spanning 2,000 m², showcasing companies and products that are driving the music industry forward.

Throughout the day, attendees can combine conference sessions with exploring new innovations, participating in hands-on activities, and connecting with exhibitors.

The Expo will also include an “Experience Lab,” where visitors can try out new skills and discover the technologies used in producing music events.

World.title: German Rock Legends Scorpions to Play Prague’s O2 Arena in 2027
World.content:
One of the most successful hard rock bands of all time will perform on June 9, 2027, at Prague’s O2 arena.

Fans can look forward to an evening filled with unforgettable hits, iconic guitar riffs, and the electrifying energy that has defined the Scorpions for over six decades.

Led by charismatic frontman Klaus Meine, the band will revisit tracks that have left an indelible mark on the history of rock music, including “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” “Still Loving You,” and the timeless ballad “Wind of Change.”



In 2027, the Scorpions will embark on another extensive world tour titled “Love, Peace & Rock’n’Roll,” following up on their successful “60th Anniversary – Coming Home” anniversary concerts.

The schedule includes approximately thirty performances across three continents—ranging from European festivals and arena shows (including stops in their native Germany) to dates in North and Latin America.

The Scorpions rank among the most significant and influential rock bands in music history. Formed in 1965 in Hanover, Germany, the group has built a global reputation over the course of an extraordinary career, thanks to their unmistakable sound, high-energy live shows, and an ability to connect with audiences across generations. They have sold over 100 million records and performed countless times on the world’s biggest stages.

Their major breakthrough arrived in the 1980s with the albums Blackout and Love at First Sting, which catapulted the band into the global rock elite. It was during this period that hits such as “No One Like You,” “Rock You Like a Hurricane,” and “Big City Nights” emerged—songs that remain an essential part of their live repertoire to this day.

The Scorpions also gained fame for their emotive ballads, most notably “Still Loving You” and “Send Me an Angel.”

A truly special place in their discography is held by the song “Wind of Change,” which became a symbol of the political and social changes at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s.

Inspired by the atmosphere at the end of the Cold War, the song remains one of the most famous rock ballads of all time.

World.title: Sherlock Holmes Exhibition Lets Visitors Play Detective in Prague
World.content:
Visitors can test historical investigative techniques, examine crime scenes and follow clues at a new interactive Sherlock Holmes exhibition in central Prague.

The exhibition, located on the third floor of the Bílá labuť department store, covers more than 2,000 square metres and features over 200 exhibits.

Rather than simply moving between display cases, visitors take on the role of an investigator and work through a series of tasks inspired by the methods used by detectives more than a century ago.



Each visitor receives a detective’s notebook to record observations and clues. The notebook guides them through the exhibition as they investigate evidence, solve puzzles and gradually build their own picture of the case.

One section focuses on the history of criminal investigation around the turn of the 20th century. It includes authentic objects loaned by the Police Museum, ranging from historical fingerprinting equipment and tools used by safecrackers to more disturbing evidence connected with violent crimes.

The exhibition also explores the development of forensic science. Visitors can make footprint impressions, examine insects found at a crime scene, send messages by telegraph and learn how investigators studied bullets and other evidence. Several interactive stations test whether visitors can identify clues and apply the techniques used by detectives of the period.

The literary side of the exhibition looks at the life and work of Arthur Conan Doyle. Visitors can see early editions of the Sherlock Holmes stories and learn more about the author behind one of literature’s most enduring fictional detectives.

A reconstruction of Holmes’s famous Baker Street apartment is among the main attractions. The exhibition then moves into a series of crime scenes where visitors search for evidence and attempt to connect the clues. Some puzzles draw on well-known Sherlock Holmes stories, while others require close attention to details hidden throughout the exhibition.

Period newspapers are also part of the investigation, and visitors are encouraged to look carefully: a coded message may be concealed within the reports.

The final section examines Sherlock Holmes’s lasting influence on popular culture, including books, comics, films and television adaptations. Vintage Sherlock Holmes comic books are also on display.

A scavenger hunt for younger visitors has been added for the current school year, with children asked to find objects hidden throughout the exhibition. The format also works well for school groups, which can divide into smaller teams and compare their discoveries.

Visitors are allowed to take photographs without flash. A full visit typically takes between 90 minutes and two hours, and booking a timed entry is recommended.

Opening hours: Daily from 9 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.

Duration: The exhibition is scheduled to run at least until January 10, 2027.

Admission: Adult tickets start at 380 CZK, while family tickets start at 980 CZK.

World.title: Czech Billionaire Strnad Offers €30 Billion for Ray-Ban Family’s Firm
World.content:
Czech billionaire Michal Strnad has offered €30 billion to acquire Delfin, the investment vehicle of Italy’s Del ​Vecchio family and the key shareholder in eyewear giant EssilorLuxottica.

News of the offer, which was first reported by Italian newspaper Il Domani, comes amid growing tensions within Delfin, whose investment portfolio includes also large holdings in Italy’s ​financial sector.

Il Domani published a copy of a letter dated October 20 ​outlining the offer.



“I am looking for long-term investment opportunities in companies ⁠operating in, or investing in, businesses positioned at the top of their value chain,” ​Strnad said in the letter said, according to the newspaper.

Delfin “perfectly fits my investment approach and ​strategy,” the letter added.

Jan Osuch, a spokesperson for AKIPIA, which oversees some of Strnad’s investment activities outside the defence sector, said the group did not comment “on market speculation or potential business negotiations.”

Strnad earlier ​this year bought a 14% stake in Italian tyre maker Pirelli, opens new tab from China’s ​Sinochem.

Strnad, 34, heads the family’s defence company Czechoslovak Group (CSG) which listed in Amsterdam earlier this year.

Delfin shareholder Leonardo ‌Maria ⁠Del Vecchio, one of the six children of the late Ray-Ban billionaire Leonardo Del Vecchio, confirmed he had been recently informed of an offer for the company received from a foreign investor.

“The work of a lifetime by my father must remain part of ​Italy’s heritage”, he said in a ​statement.

The late Luxottica ⁠founder built his business empire from scratch having grown up in a Milan orphanage.

Delfin’s ownership is divided equally among Del Vecchio’s ​eight heirs: his six children, his widow Nicoletta Zampillo and her ​son from ⁠a previous marriage.

A sale would require a virtually unanimous decision from the heirs, who have become increasingly at odds with one another.

In addition to its stake in EssilorLuxottica, Luxembourg-based Delfin holds stakes in ⁠Italian ​insurer Generali and lenders Monte dei Paschi di Siena (MPS) and ​UniCredit, for a combined current market value of €43 billion.

Delfin declined to comment. A representative for Strnad was not ​immediately available for comment.

World.title: Prague’s Only Christmas MINT Market to Take Place on November 28–29
World.content:
Don’t leave your Christmas shopping until the last minute this year.

On the weekend of 28–29 November, head to Hall 13 at Holešovice Market and discover original gifts directly from the people who made them.

MINT Market will bring together more than a hundred carefully selected brands from across the Czech Republic, offering a relaxed alternative to the pre-Christmas rush in shopping centres.



On Saturday from 10 am to 6 pm and Sunday from 10 am to 4 pm, visitors can look forward to independent fashion, designer jewellery, ceramics, natural cosmetics, illustrations, original accessories and plenty of Christmas gift inspiration.

And, of course, there will be the relaxed and friendly atmosphere that has become an essential part of MINT Market. The event is suitable for all generations and admission is free.

The youngest MINT Market visitors and their families can enjoy the beautiful NOOK Family Lounge, featuring high-quality wooden toys, a creative play area, a quiet zone with books and space to relax, as well as facilities for babies and parents, including a changing table and a peaceful place for breastfeeding.

There will also be Christmas-themed creative workshops.

MINT Market has been active for sixteen years. During that time, it has become an important platform for small and emerging creators, often directly from Prague, who are given the opportunity to present their products to a wide audience.

Residents of Prague and the surrounding area thus have several opportunities each year to purchase quality products that are literally made by their neighbors – locally, sustainably, and with an emphasis on honest craftsmanship.

MINT Market is not just about shopping. Since 2010, the project has been run by a team of people who systematically support small and local brands and are the only ones bringing high-quality Czech design to more than twenty cities across the country.

What started as a small project has gradually grown into a community of more than 1,500 creatives and a platform that has hosted over 450 events and welcomed more than 1.3 million visitors.

World.title: Czech Government Proposes Voluntary TV and Radio Fees Without State Budget
World.content:
People in the Czech Republic could soon be allowed to decide whether they want to pay television and radio licence fees under a new funding model being prepared by the government.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said the Finance Ministry is working on a system that would make contributions to Czech Television (ČT) and Czech Radio (ČRo) voluntary while ensuring the two public broadcasters receive a guaranteed level of funding.

The proposal is expected to be discussed by the coalition council on Monday.



For now, however, the existing system will remain in place. Although the government had initially hoped to introduce changes at the beginning of 2027, Babiš said the legislative timetable makes that unlikely.

Under parliamentary rules, the bill requires a 60-day review period before moving forward. That means its second reading would fall during the Christmas period, delaying further debate until at least January 2027.

The proposed changes have already sparked political and public opposition.

On October 24, the Chamber of Deputies approved in its first reading a proposal to abolish television and radio licence fees. The governing coalition, made up of ANO, SPD and the Motorists party, added the measure to its priority legislative agenda. The vote took place early in the morning after a lengthy parliamentary debate.

Opposition parties have warned that changing the funding system could expose public broadcasters to greater political pressure. Government representatives have rejected those concerns, saying the planned reform does not threaten democratic standards.

Babiš has said the final model must comply with European requirements concerning the independence of public media and predictable funding.

The issue has also prompted demonstrations. On October 25, thousands of people gathered in Prague’s Old Town Square for a protest organised by the Million Moments for Democracy movement.

Participants expressed concern that changes to the financing of Czech Television and Czech Radio could increase political influence over the broadcasters.

World.title: Prague Welcomes a Week of Polish Films and Culture
World.content:
Prague will host a week of Polish cinema and culture from November 9 to 15, as the 3Kino – Polish Film Festival Prague returns for its 13th edition.

The festival will screen 13 feature films representing contemporary Polish cinema, with a program that also includes theater, stand-up comedy, exhibitions, music and events for children.



This year’s festival opens with The Doll (Lalka), directed by Maciej Kawalski. Based on the classic novel by Bolesław Prus, the film is among the most expensive Polish productions ever made and takes audiences to 19th-century Warsaw.

The story explores love, ambition and social divisions, with Marcin Dorociński, one of Poland’s best-known contemporary actors, in a leading role.

Freedom will be the central theme of this year’s edition. The festival will explore the idea through historical events as well as everyday life, personal relationships and decisions that can alter a person’s future.

The program extends beyond the cinema. Visitors can attend theatrical performances, stand-up shows and exhibitions, while this year’s edition will also put a special focus on Poland’s Lower Silesia region.

Among the accompanying events is the opening of photographer Rafał Pawłowski’s exhibition Shadows of Sounds. Another exhibition will mark the 100th anniversary of the birth of Polish filmmaker Andrzej Wajda, featuring a selection of Polish film posters.

The festival aims to bring Polish culture to audiences across Prague, with screenings and accompanying events taking place at several venues throughout the city.

Ticket sales are now open, and the full program is available on the festival’s official website.

World.title: “Enemies and fools”: Leaked recording reveals alleged Fidesz election campaign instructions in Vojvodina
World.content:
A leaked audio recording reportedly captures a Hungarian consul and the head of the Hungarian National Council in Serbia discussing voter data, the distribution of postal ballots and political preferences ahead of Hungary’s 12 April parliamentary election. The council’s president has described the report as an attempt to discredit him but has neither confirmed nor denied the recording’s authenticity.

The Serbian-based news outlet Szabad Magyar Szó published excerpts from what it says is a recording of a briefing for activists involved in organising postal voting among ethnic Hungarians in Vojvodina before the election. The exact location and date of the meeting are unknown, although the outlet believes it took place before 23 March, probably in Novi Sad.

According to the report, the voices of Ervin Simon, a consul at Hungary’s consulate in Subotica, and Árpád Fremond, president of the Hungarian National Council (MNT), can be recognised on the recording. Its sound quality is reportedly poor, and the outlet believes it may have been made secretly using a mobile phone.

If you missed it: Was Viktor Orbán a communist agent? Former PM shared documents of communist recruitment and surveillance

Personal data and instructions on political support

At the beginning of the briefing, Simon reportedly told activists that, acting on instructions from the Hungarian government, they would be given the personal data of people holding both Serbian and Hungarian citizenship.

Fremond allegedly instructed participants to work exclusively as activists of the Concordia Minoritatis Hungaricae (CMH), the civil organisation involved in coordinating postal voting in Vojvodina, rather than displaying signs associated with the Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians (VMSZ).

The recording also reportedly includes remarks about political preferences. Fremond is heard saying that more than 90% of Serbian and Croatian voters would support the Fidesz-KDNP alliance, and that activists did not need to persuade them extensively.

In another excerpt, he allegedly tells activists not to engage with people they considered enemies or fools, but simply to leave their voting envelopes in their letterboxes.

The report also describes an operation involving around 800 activists. According to the recording, anyone delivering 100 letters would receive EUR 100. Fremond reportedly referred to the total cost of paying the 800 participants as a considerable sum.

Fremond calls the report an attempt to discredit him

Szabad Magyar Szó contacted Fremond for a response. He described the publication as an attempt to damage his reputation, pointing to its timing during the final days of the campaign for Serbia’s national council elections.

He did not confirm or deny the recording’s authenticity, saying that establishing its origin and verifying its contents would take time. He said he intended to deal with the matter after the election.

The CMH had previously announced that it signed an agreement with the Serbian Post in 2022 to forward postal ballots. It also said it could help voters complete the identification declaration and return sealed ballot envelopes.

The Hungarian National Election Office states that registered Hungarian citizens without a residential address in Hungary can vote by post. Another person may deliver a sealed reply envelope to an election office, but the identification declaration must be signed by the voter personally.

World.title: One of Hungary’s most beautiful castles could close as funding runs out
World.content:
One of Hungary’s most remarkable historic buildings could shut its doors early next year, putting 18 jobs at risk. The future of the L’Huillier–Coburg Castle in Edelény now depends on whether the necessary state funding can be secured for 2027.

The Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Assembly voted on 30 October to terminate its asset management agreement for the castle complex with the Hungarian National Asset Management Inc. The decision came after it became clear that funding for the site’s operation next year had not yet been guaranteed.

The county council has managed the castle since 15 June 2023, receiving state support for its operation each year. A total of HUF 260 million (approximately EUR 713,000) was allocated for 2026, but this only covers expenses until 31 December.

There is currently no confirmed funding for 2027. According to Boglárka Bánné Gál, president of the county assembly, the responsible ministry has asked for time until the end of November to find the money. However, the local authority could not postpone its decision any longer because of contractual deadlines.

If no solution is found, the castle could close on 2 January 2027, and all 18 employees could lose their jobs. Bánné Gál said the county assembly had initiated talks with the ministry four times over the past two months. If the necessary funding is secured in the coming weeks, the local authority is willing to negotiate the continuation of its management responsibilities.

If you missed it: Budapest’s Castle District votes on Airbnb ban: majority back a complete shutdown

A Baroque treasure visited by more than 89,000 people

Located on an island in the River Bódva, the L’Huillier–Coburg Castle was built between 1716 and 1730 at the request of Jean-François L’Huillier. One of its most distinctive features is a series of Rococo wall paintings by Ferenc Lieb, created in 1769–1770. The works decorate six interconnected rooms in the eastern wing and depict mythological and allegorical scenes, the seasons and aristocratic life.

The building’s history was not always so impressive. During the 20th century, it was used as both housing and public offices. A major restoration project began in 2009, with approximately HUF 2.4 billion spent on its first phase. The renovated castle, including its restored wall paintings and renewed park, opened to visitors in spring 2014.

Since the county council took over its operation in 2023, more than 89,000 people have visited the historic complex, according to local government figures.

The L’Huillier–Coburg Castle in Edelény at night. Photo: Edelényi kastélysziget

Closure could affect the wider region

The possible shutdown would not only affect the castle’s employees. Local restaurants, accommodation providers and other tourism businesses could also lose an important source of visitors.

Several development projects are linked to the site, including an Interreg programme worth EUR 500,000 and an active tourism project valued at nearly HUF 96.5 million. However, these investments do not automatically cover the castle’s day-to-day running costs.

You can check out some photos of the castle on this website.

World.title: Christmas markets in Hungary 2026: Opening dates, locations, programmes and everything you need to know
World.content:
Hungary is getting ready for the festive season, with Christmas markets, sparkling lights, ice rinks and seasonal programmes set to take over Budapest and several other cities from November. Whether you are planning a festive weekend in the capital or looking for a Christmas getaway elsewhere in the country, here is everything you need to know about Hungary’s Christmas markets in 2026, including opening dates, locations and confirmed attractions.

The country’s two best-known Christmas markets, Advent Basilica and Vörösmarty Classic Xmas, will open in Budapest on 13 November. Several regional cities, including Debrecen, Szeged, Eger, Győr and Sopron, will follow later in the month. We have collected the most important information published by the organisers and local tourism offices so far.

Budapest Christmas Markets

Advent Basilica: Budapest’s award-winning Christmas market

Dates: 13 November 2026 – 1 January 2027

Location: Szent István Square, in front of St Stephen’s Basilica

Advent Basilica is one of Hungary’s best-known festive attractions and a must-visit for anyone spending Christmas in Budapest. The market will once again welcome visitors to Szent István Square, with nearly 100 Hungarian craft exhibitors, food stalls, a giant Christmas tree and spectacular festive light displays.

The event has been voted Europe’s Most Beautiful Christmas Market for the fourth time. Visitors can also expect daily programmes and a festive atmosphere in the heart of the Hungarian capital.

Opening hours:

Monday–Thursday: 11 am–10 pm

Friday–Saturday: 11 am–11 pm

Sunday: 11 am–10 pm

Special opening hours apply during the holidays:

24 December: 11 am–3 pm

25–26 December: 11 am–8 pm

31 December: 11 am–3 am

1 January: 11 am–6 pm

Official website: Advent Basilica

Vörösmarty Classic Xmas: A festive atmosphere in the city centre

Dates: 13 November 2026 – the early hours of 1 January 2027

Location: Vörösmarty Square

Another major attraction is Vörösmarty Classic Xmas, held in one of Budapest’s most popular central squares. The market offers Hungarian handicrafts, festive food and drinks, Christmas decorations and a miniature railway, making it a popular stop for families and international visitors alike.

The organisers have also announced special New Year’s Eve celebrations. Craft exhibitors and the miniature railway will be available until 28 December, before preparations for the New Year’s Eve event take over the square.

Opening hours:

Monday–Thursday: 11 am–9 pm

Friday–Saturday: 11 am–10 pm

Sunday: 11 am–9 pm

Special opening hours:

24 December: 10 am–2 pm

25–26 December: noon–6 pm

29–30 December: 11 am–9 pm

31 December: 11 am–3 am

The miniature railway operates from 2 pm to 8 pm on weekdays and from 11 am to 8 pm at weekends.

Official website: Vörösmarty Classic Xmas

Christmas Markets Outside Budapest

Budapest is not the only place worth visiting during the festive season. Several Hungarian cities organise their own Christmas markets, often combining traditional stalls with concerts, family activities and winter attractions.

Debrecen Advent

Dates: 20 November – 23 December 2026

Location: Debrecen city centre, including Kossuth Square

Debrecen’s Advent celebrations are among the most extensive outside the capital. The programme includes a Christmas market, an outdoor ice rink, a Baroque carousel, a miniature railway and several family-friendly attractions.

One of the highlights is the Jégvirágkarnevál, or Ice Flower Carnival, a winter version of the city’s famous Flower Carnival. The event is scheduled for 21 November, with illuminated floats and performers bringing a festive spectacle to the streets.

The outdoor ice rink will remain open until 10 January 2027, giving visitors the chance to enjoy some winter activities even after Christmas.

Christmas market opening hours:

Monday–Thursday: 11 am–8 pm

Friday–Saturday: 11 am–9 pm

Sunday: 11 am–8 pm

23 December: 11 am–7 pm

The ice rink has separate opening hours, so visitors should check the organiser’s website before planning their visit.

Official website: Debreceni Advent

Szeged Christmas Weeks

Dates: 27 November – 24 December 2026

Location: Dóm Square and other central locations

Szeged’s Christmas Weeks will once again bring festive activities to the city’s historic centre. The main venue is Dóm Square, where visitors can expect a Christmas market, seasonal food and drinks, and a range of family programmes.

Among the announced attractions are a straw maze, a story corner for children, craft workshops and film screenings. Fire-juggling performances are planned for Fridays, while spectacular light painting will take place during the final two weekends.

The city’s 50-metre-high Ferris wheel will also remain open into early January, offering panoramic views of Szeged’s festive decorations. Advent celebrations will extend to Klauzál Square and Dugonics Square as well.

Official information: Szeged Tourinform

Eger Advent

Dates: 27 November – 24 December 2026

Location: Dobó Square and the city centre

Eger will welcome visitors with its own Christmas market in the picturesque historic centre. The programme includes nearly 80 festive events, with concerts, children’s performances, craft activities and traditional Advent candle-lighting ceremonies.

The opening ceremony and the switching on of the Christmas lights are scheduled for 27 November at 5 pm. The first evening will feature performances by Mátyás Svéd and Elemér Báder, followed by a concert by the Balázs Elemér Group.

Other announced performers include the Hot Jazz Band, Gájer Bálint and several children’s groups. The main stage programme runs until 20 December, although the Christmas market itself will remain open until Christmas Eve.

The organisers have also confirmed that admission to the Eger Advent programmes is free.

Official website: Eger Advent

Győr Advent

Dates: 27 November – 23 December 2026

Location: Győr city centre, including Széchenyi Square and Dunakapu Square

Győr’s historic centre will also turn into a festive destination from late November. The Advent celebrations will feature Christmas stalls, seasonal food and drinks, festive decorations and cultural programmes.

Visitors can also look forward to an ice rink and a Ferris wheel, with attractions spread across the city’s central squares. The organisers have announced the dates, while further programme details are expected to follow.

Official information: Hello Győr

Sopron Advent

Dates: 25 November – 20 December 2026

Location: Várkerület and Fő Square

Sopron’s Advent celebrations offer another opportunity to enjoy the festive season outside Budapest. The city’s historic centre will host Christmas activities, with the main locations including Várkerület and Fő Square.

Visitors can expect seasonal stalls, handicrafts, festive food and drinks, as well as cultural and family programmes. The detailed schedule is still being announced, so it is worth checking the city’s tourism website closer to the event.

Official information: Visit Sopron

What to eat at Hungarian Christmas markets

No visit to a Hungarian Christmas market would be complete without trying some traditional seasonal food and drinks. Popular choices include kürtőskalács, also known as chimney cake, a sweet pastry baked over an open flame and coated with sugar, cinnamon or other toppings.

Visitors can also find lángos, a deep-fried dough traditionally served with garlic, sour cream and cheese, as well as grilled sausages, hearty hot meals and a variety of sweet treats.

For drinks, mulled wine (forralt bor) is a festive favourite, while hot chocolate and other warm beverages are popular among families and visitors who prefer non-alcoholic options.

Planning your visit: What should you know?

Most of Hungary’s major Christmas markets are free to enter, although some attractions and activities may require separate tickets. Opening hours can also vary on public holidays, particularly on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day.

If you are visiting Budapest, the two main markets are within walking distance of each other, making it easy to explore both in one evening. Public transport is generally the most convenient way to reach the city centre, especially during the busy festive period.

For trips outside the capital, it is worth checking the local organisers’ websites before travelling, as additional performances and programme details may be announced closer to the opening dates.

With Budapest’s major markets opening on 13 November and several regional cities following later in the month, Hungary’s 2026 Christmas market season is just around the corner.

World.title: FM Anita Orbán shares the deadline set for Hungary to stop importing Russian gas
World.content:
Hungary’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Anita Orbán, has shared the deadline for phasing out Russian natural gas. The statement comes as Budapest explores alternative energy supplies and seeks to strengthen its role as a regional oil and gas hub.

FM Anita Orbán shared her views on Russian energy

In an interview with Telex, the foreign minister was asked whether Hungary could continue accessing Russian gas in the future. Citing the European Union’s timetable, she claimed “the EU has set a clear deadline for phasing out Russian natural gas, which is autumn 2027,” she said.

The minister also discussed efforts to diversify the country’s oil supply. Hungarian energy company MOL is working to prepare its refineries for the potential import of non-Russian crude through Croatia’s JANAF pipeline, which could provide an alternative route from the south.

The United States has granted Hungary a temporary exemption from certain sanctions affecting Russian oil imports, with a deadline of 21 November. Orbán said the exemption concerns oil purchased from Russian companies Lukoil and Rosneft, and that MOL is working on the necessary technological adjustments to enable sourcing from other suppliers.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán in the parliament. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Anita

MOL’s potential acquisition of Serbian oil company

Another key issue concerns MOL’s potential purchase of Gazprom’s stake in Serbia’s NIS oil company, which owns the country’s only oil refinery. The US Office of Foreign Assets Control has granted an exemption allowing negotiations with Gazprom to continue until 11 December.

Foreign minister Anita Orbán she could not comment on ongoing business negotiations, but indicated that Serbian, Russian and Hungarian parties all appeared strongly committed to completing the transaction by the deadline. She added that the acquisition could strengthen Hungary’s position in regional energy infrastructure discussions, including those involving the JANAF pipeline.

Anita Orbán described Hungary as a potential major transit and distribution centre for both natural gas and crude oil. She pointed to the country’s extensive storage capacity, connections with six neighbouring countries and MOL’s influential regional position as factors that could support energy supplies to other states.

Stay up-to-date: Leading Czech magazine portrays Viktor Orbán in handcuffs

Strategic interests stay unchanged

The foreign minister also addressed Hungary’s recent diplomatic engagement with the United States. During her visit to Washington, Orbán and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed two declarations of intent, one on energy cooperation and another on joint efforts against terrorism.

Anita Orbán described the visit as the result of a broader confidence-building process and said its swift organisation demonstrated that Washington regarded Hungary’s new government as a partner and ally. Asked whether the Tisza-led government was continuing certain policies pursued by its predecessor, she emphasised that some national priorities transcend changes in government.

“There are strategic interests that do not change with a change of government, such as the security of the country,” she said. The comments underline the challenges facing Hungary as it navigates EU energy policy, sanctions and regional supply arrangements while seeking to maintain energy security.

World.title: Hungary elects new chief public prosecutor after years of controversy – who is Péter Fejes?
World.content:
Hungary has a new chief public prosecutor. Parliament elected Péter Fejes to the nine-year post on Tuesday, with the experienced prosecutor promising to restore public trust in an institution that has faced serious criticism over its independence and handling of politically sensitive cases.

Fejes received 139 votes in favour and six against in a secret ballot. Following his election, he acknowledged that some decisions made by the prosecution service in recent years had rightly damaged public confidence, and issued an apology on behalf of the organisation.

Speaking at a press conference, he said:

“On behalf of the prosecution service, I apologise to society for certain decisions – and failures to act – which have rightly and justifiably offended the public’s sense of justice.”

He also apologised to former colleagues who had devoted their lives to the institution but had felt compelled to leave.

Péter Fejes and Hungarian President András Baka. Photo: MTI

Nearly 40 years in the prosecution service

Fejes, who describes himself as a native of Szombathely in western Hungary, graduated in law from the University of Pécs and was appointed as a prosecutor in 1988.

He began his career at the local prosecutor’s office before moving to the Vas County Chief Prosecutor’s Office. There, he became a group leader and later served as the organisation’s spokesperson, becoming one of its best-known public faces.

In 2008, he was appointed chief prosecutor of Veszprém County. However, his career took an unexpected turn in 2012, when then-chief public prosecutor Péter Polt dismissed him with immediate effect and without giving a reason, Telex reports.

Fejes subsequently continued working as a subordinate prosecutor at the Győr Appellate Chief Prosecutor’s Office. His final position was deputy chief prosecutor for criminal law at the Vas County Chief Prosecutor’s Office. He retired in 2025 after almost four decades of service.

Péter Fejes and András Baka. Photo: MTI

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

High-profile criminal cases and academic work

Over the years, Fejes has been involved in several major criminal cases that attracted nationwide attention.

His first nationally known case was the 1998 child murder in Körmend. He also supervised the investigation into the murder of Romanian handball player Marian Cozma in 2009. However, he considers the proceedings against those responsible for the 2010 red mud disaster one of the most important cases of his career.

Beyond his prosecutorial work, Fejes remains active in academia. He teaches criminal law and sports law at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE) and Pázmány Péter Catholic University. He is also a devoted supporter of Szombathely’s Falco basketball team and holds a senior position in the European Wine Knights organisation.

If you missed it: Hungary makes 24 December a public holiday starting this year

Plans for a major overhaul

Before his election, Fejes told Válasz Online that the prosecution service needed immediate and far-reaching personnel and organisational changes.

His proposals include reducing the size of the Office of the Prosecutor General, reviewing the role of the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office of Investigation, addressing significant salary differences and making a prosecutorial career more attractive.

He described the organisation as morally shaken and professionally stalled, pointing to a lack of trust and prolonged vacancies in senior positions.

Fejes also suggested that cases should be reopened where new evidence emerges, saying that some files may need to be “dusted off”. He believes senior prosecutors should be more visible in public, with important decisions explained by the people responsible for them rather than communicated solely through official statements.

A difficult task ahead

The new chief public prosecutor inherits an institution whose reputation has been seriously damaged. Under Péter Polt, who led the service for years, critics repeatedly accused the prosecution of failing to pursue corruption allegations involving government politicians and business figures close to the former administration.

The leadership crisis deepened in 2026. Former chief public prosecutor Gábor Bálint Nagy resigned in July, while the former head of the Central Chief Prosecutor’s Office of Investigation, Pál Fürcht, had already stepped down in June. Fürcht subsequently alleged that investigations into politically sensitive cases had been influenced by the Office of the Prosecutor General.

Fejes now faces the challenge of restoring confidence in the institution and demonstrating that prosecutors can operate independently, regardless of political interests.

World.title: Hungary’s Foreign Ministry abruptly sacks foreign policy institute chief over links to previous government
World.content:
Hungary’s Foreign Ministry has dismissed Botond Feledy as head of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs (MKI) with immediate effect, citing a loss of trust over his previous working relationship with the former government. The unexpected decision comes less than three months after his appointment, when he was tasked with rebuilding the institute’s professional reputation after years of political controversy.

The dismissal was announced on Monday evening by György Velkey, the ministry’s parliamentary state secretary. According to the statement, the ministry had only learned a few days earlier about Feledy’s professional relationship with the previous government, which had lasted for years and continued into the spring of 2026.

“Based on the information received by the ministry, we are terminating Botond Feledy’s managerial appointment with immediate effect due to a loss of trust,” Velkey said.

HUF 84 million in contracts with Lázár’s ministry

The controversy centres on contracts between Feledy’s company and the Ministry of Construction and Transport, led at the time by János Lázár. Documents obtained by Telex show that the ministry paid Feledy’s company a total of HUF 84.2 million (EUR 230,000) for foreign policy analyses over several years. According to the report, the working relationship continued until after the 2026 parliamentary election, with a further HUF 19 million paid after the vote.

Feledy responded to his dismissal in a Facebook post, explaining that his company had provided independent analytical work rather than traditional consultancy or political advice.

He said the ministry had approached his three-person company in 2023 because it wanted an independent perspective on international affairs. He argued that this allowed him to provide critical assessments of countries such as Russia and China, which government-aligned think tanks might have been reluctant to publish.

Feledy insisted that his clients had never influenced his professional opinions and said he intended to continue working towards political change in Hungary.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar commented on the post, saying that anyone accepting a senior government appointment should disclose potentially controversial previous contracts.

He specifically criticised Feledy for failing to mention that his company had received HUF 84 million in public money from the previous government, including HUF 19 million after the election.
