A key figure in the institute’s attempted renewal

Feledy was appointed director of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs in August, alongside Russia expert András Rácz, who became his deputy. The new leadership was expected to move the institution away from its previous political orientation, which had been associated with Balázs Orbán and the American MAGA movement.

Their priorities included developing a new Hungarian foreign policy strategy, strengthening the professional foundations of foreign policy decisions and rebuilding expertise on European Union affairs.

Feledy had spent around 20 years working in foreign policy as a journalist, analyst, media entrepreneur and university lecturer. He had previously lived in Brussels but moved back to Budapest with his family to take up the position.

At the time of his appointment, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said the new leadership would promote thorough, independent and forward-looking research.

If you missed it: Was Viktor Orbán a communist agent? Former PM shared documents of communist recruitment and surveillance

Ministry refuses to provide further details

The Foreign Ministry has offered little additional explanation for the sudden dismissal. Responding to questions from Telex, it said senior appointments require proof of professional qualifications and language skills, as well as a criminal record certificate, a competency test and national security screening.

Velkey later told Telex that Feledy had been asked during the appointment process whether there was anything in his professional background that could make him vulnerable to criticism. According to the state secretary, the new institute chief did not disclose his previous contracts with Lázár’s ministry. Velkey also stressed that the Foreign Ministry had learned about the agreements from another government department, rather than from Telex’s reporting.

The ministry also confirmed that the institute is a separate legal entity owned by the Foreign Ministry, adding that similar employment suitability criteria apply there as within the ministry itself.

However, it declined to provide further details about Feledy’s dismissal or his successor. It also did not clarify whether his deputy, András Rácz, could temporarily or permanently take over the leadership.

World.title: Was Viktor Orbán a communist agent? Former PM shared documents of communist recruitment and surveillance
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has revealed that Hungary’s communist-era state security services attempted to recruit him as an informant during his compulsory military service, a claim that has reignited debate over his past and the country’s unreleased intelligence files.

Viktor Orbán talked about recruitment and surveillance

In a statement published on Tuesday, the former prime minister said he had rejected the recruitment attempt during the early period of his military service. He also claimed that, following the failed effort, he, his wife and fellow opposition figures were subjected to continuous surveillance by the communist authorities. The former prime minister wrote that

“During the first period of my compulsory military service, they tried to recruit me, but I refused, so the attempt ended unsuccessfully.”

According to Orbán, secret surveillance operations against him and his associates included monitoring, the use of informants and the installation of listening devices at their workplaces and homes – allegedly even in their bedrooms. A formerly classified report issued by the Szolnok County Police Headquarters reportedly records that the former prime minister was examined for potential recruitment in 1982, but the authorities ultimately abandoned the effort.

Rumours started spreading very quickly about Orbán’s past

The latest statements have emerged amid renewed media speculation about whether Orbán ever worked for the communist-era state security apparatus. Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi recently said in a podcast that former Hungarian Prime Minister Miklós Németh claimed to have seen three handwritten and signed intelligence reports allegedly authored by Orbán.

According to the account, Németh was shown the documents in 1990 by then Defence Minister Ferenc Kárpáti. The reports reportedly contained observations about the conduct and personal characteristics of conscripts serving in Zalaegerszeg. Németh allegedly recognised Orbán’s handwriting and signature, although he could not independently verify their authenticity, as per Telex.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Historian urges caution over agent allegations

Historian Krisztián Ungváry, who is involved in a committee reviewing classified documents, cautioned against drawing conclusions based on the allegations. He stressed that the presumption of innocence applies to everyone and that the claims require evidence. Ungváry said that after Orbán’s military service, he was himself a target of state surveillance. While he acknowledged that it was possible the politician had carried out intelligence tasks before his discharge, he argued that this had not been proven.

The historian also pointed to references in another person’s file suggesting that authorities attempted to recruit Orbán again in 1988 under the codename “Kurázsi” (Courage). Ungváry said the available indications suggested this attempt had also failed, as Orbán continued to be listed as a surveillance target. In his 2017 book A szembenézés hiánya (The Absence of Confrontation), Ungváry devoted a chapter to the allegations and concluded that there was no evidence of closer cooperation between Orbán and the state security services.

Stay up-to-date: Viktor Orbán reported to police over controversial speech about ‘handing out appropriate tools’

Fidesz rejects the allegations

Orbán’s Fidesz party also responded to the claims, insisting that the available facts, data and documents demonstrate that the politician was not an agent but a person monitored by the communist state. The renewed discussion comes amid broader calls for greater transparency regarding Hungary’s communist-era intelligence archives and the identities of those who collaborated with the secret services.

World.title: Hungarian prison ordered to apologise after father was denied chance to say goodbye to dying son
World.content:
A Hungarian prison has been ordered to apologise and pay compensation to a father who was not informed in time that his son had suffered life-threatening injuries in custody and was denied the chance to speak to him while he was still conscious. The Győr Court of Appeal issued the final ruling on 15 October, finding that the prison had violated the man’s right to private and family life.

His son was brutally beaten in his cell

József Ruckel’s son, René, was seriously injured at Szombathely Prison on 25 January 2023, following a fight with a cellmate. The young man emerged from his cell with a bloodied head before collapsing in the corridor. He suffered a spinal injury that left him paralysed from the neck down and was transferred to hospital, where he later died. One of his cellmates was convicted over the assault that led to his death.

René’s father was not notified directly by the prison. Instead, he learned that his son had been hospitalised through a friend of the young man. When he contacted the prison service, he was told that René had become dizzy, fallen and hit a door. The fight that had preceded his injuries was not disclosed.

Father’s request to visit delayed for three days

József immediately went to the hospital, hoping to see his son while he was still conscious. However, he was not allowed to visit him. According to the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, René even called out to his father, saying, “Dad, I’m here”, but the meeting was not permitted. The father spent several days making phone calls and attempting to secure an extraordinary hospital visit.

His request was only assessed three days later, as the application had been filed during working hours shortly before the weekend. By the time he was finally allowed to enter, René was in a deep medically induced coma and never regained consciousness. József was able to hold his son’s hand for an hour, but they could no longer speak to each other.

The father initially did not want to take legal action, saying he would have accepted an apology and an admission of wrongdoing. The prison commander expressed condolences but repeatedly refused to apologise or reach an out-of-court settlement, reports 444.hu.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Appeal court finds prison responsible

The Szombathely Court of First Instance had rejected the father’s claim. However, the Győr Court of Appeal overturned that decision, establishing that René had already been in a life-threatening condition on the day he was admitted to hospital.

The appeal court noted that medical records showed René required circulatory support from 12.45 PM on 25 January. It ruled that prison authorities should have obtained adequate information about his condition and that a request for an urgent visit could not be delayed for days simply because of weekend working arrangements.

The prison has now been ordered to issue a formal apology and pay HUF 500,000 (approximately EUR 1,370) in compensation. József intends to donate the compensation to charity. The father said the ruling offered some satisfaction because he felt he had fought for justice. He added that its real value would depend on whether the prison learned from the case and prevented similar tragedies from happening again.

World.title: Seven Arrested in International Investment Fraud Crackdown in Balkans
World.content:
Kosovo police and Europol during the raids against an international investment fraud scheme, November 3, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Police

The European Union Agency for Criminal Justice Cooperation, Eurojust, announced on Tuesday that seven persons were arrested in an international action against investment fraud in an action conducted with the EU police agency Europol that also involved Germany, Cyprus, Finland, Albania, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Israel.

“Authorities, supported by Eurojust and Europol, have taken action against a criminal network running an investment fraud scheme, leading to the shutdown of over 100 servers and seven arrests,” Eurojust announced. According to Europol, extradition to Germany is being considered for the arrested.

The operation started in 2022 after a German couple reported that they had been victims of a fraud scheme after they invested savings but could not withdraw their profits from the online platform they had used.

Europol explained that, “led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor’s Office (Staatsanwaltschaft Itzehoe), the operation targeted a company suspected of supplying fraudulent trading websites to criminal groups. The entity is connected to call centre operators who allegedly persuaded victims to hand over their savings. Investigators estimate losses exceeding EUR 4 million.”

Kosovo police announced on Facebook that after raiding five locations, three suspects were arrested in Kosovo. “M.P., I.H., and F.Z., [were arrested] on suspicion of committing the criminal offences of participating in or organising an organised criminal group, fraud, unauthorised computer access and computer fraud”. Police announced that “cars, mobile phones, computers and other electronic devices that may serve as evidence in criminal proceedings” were seized.

This is not the first time the international operation has made arrests in this case.

In May 2025, Eurojust announced that one suspect had been arrested in Cyprus after “an organised criminal group (OCG) operating globally defrauded more than 100 victims of over EUR 3 million through a fake online investment platform”.

In September 2022, Eurojust announced that two suspects had been arrested after raids in 12 locations. “With the support of Eurojust, authorities in Finland, Germany, Belgium and Latvia have succeeded in striking a blow against the operators of various fraudulent online investment platforms that have defrauded victims from 11 different countries out of several million euros,” it said.

World.title: Serbia Detains Police Officials Over Abuse of Position, Torture, Allegations
World.content:
The Higher Court in Belgrade on Tuesday ordered 30 days of detention for the head of the Criminal Police Directorate, Marko Kricak, and the head of the Crime Suppression Service, Bosko Sekulovic.

They are charged with abuse of official position, while Kricak is also charged with mistreatment and torture, both linked to a murder in a Belgrade restaurant in May.

Detention was ordered to prevent them influencing witnesses. However, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said it would complain about the court’s decision and demand that detention be ordered both due to the potential to influence witnesses and to prevent any repeat of the criminal offence within a short period of time, as earlier proposed by the prosecution.

Kricak and Sekulovic were arrested on Sunday, a week after parliamentary elections in which the long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party lost power after 14 years.

Belgrade’s chief prosecutor, Nenad Stefanovic, insisted on Monday that the arrests “have nothing to do with electoral processes or the results of the parliamentary elections”.

Kricak and Sekulovic are suspected of abusing their official positions and of “failing to perform their official duty” during their handling of the case of the murder of A.N. in “27” Belgrade’s restaurant on May 12, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade said on Tuesday.

Their actions between May 12 and June 3 allegedly caused damage and also violated the rights of the former head of the Belgrade Police Department, Veselin Milic.

Milic was arrested on May 15 under suspicion that he had assisted an offender in the murder and had failed to report the crime. In June, the Higher Prosecutor’s Office dropped part of the complaint relating to assisting an offender after the commission of a crime.

The prosecution said on Tuesday that Sekulovic had drafted a criminal complaint that also named Milic, even though he knew that Milic had left the restaurant before the murder took place. Kricak allegedly gave verbal approval to Sekulovic to submit the criminal complaint, despite being aware of its contents.

On May 21, police found a dead body in a metal drum buried near the town of Indjija. Five days later, it was confirmed that it belonged to A.N. Media have reported that the victim was a gangland figure.

Kricak was also suspected of having used force against those suspected of being involved in the murder.

“Additionally, there are grounds for suspicion that Marko K. on May 16, 2026 … abused the victim N.L. while performing his official duties, in such a way that he, together with unidentified police officers, first struck him with open hands and closed fists in the head area, and placed a hood over his head, suffocating him,” the prosecution’s press release said.

Furthermore, Kricak is suspected of removing the victim’s socks and of beating him on the soles of his feet and back with a belt.

During the massive anti-government protests in Serbia in the last two years, some protesters have claimed that Kricak used force against them. One female detainee, Nikolina Sindjelic, said in August 2025 that Kricak had threatened her with rape. He has not been prosecuted over these allegations.

World.title: Bosnian Serb Army Ex-Members Jailed for 83 Years for Sokolac Crimes
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Six former Second Romanija Brigade members have been sentenced by Bosnia’s state court to 83 years in jail in total for crimes against humanity committed near Sokolac in eastern Bosnia in 1992.

Momcilo Pajic was sentenced to 20 years, Miladin Gasevic to 15 and Branislav Kezunovic, Zeljko Gasevic, Jadranko Suka and Nikola Koprivica to 12 years each.

The first-instance verdict acquitted Dragomir Obradovic and Aleksa Gordic.

By the state court’s decision, Pajic, Kezunovic, Gasevic and Suka were ordered to be detained. Miladin Gasevic and Suka did not appear at the hearing at which the verdict was pronounced.

According to the verdict, the six defendants knew about a widespread and systematic attack on the Bosniak civilian population in the Sokolac area lasting from May to September 1992, when disarmament, arrests, transportation and military operations took place.

“All this could not have gone unnoticed by the defendants,” said presiding judge, Enida Hadziomerovic in the verdict explanation.

The chamber concluded that the aim of the action in Novoseoci village was the ethnic cleansing of the population who had previously surrendered their weapons and were loyal to the Bosnian Serb authorities in Sokolac.

Members of the Second Romanija Brigade reportedly deployed themselves around the village on the night of September 21,22, 1992. “The assignment and deployment were managed by Momcilo Pajic and Miladin Gasevic,” Judge Hadziomerovic stated.

Pajic was found guilty as commander of the Military Police, and Gasevic as deputy commander of the Reconnaissance Company.

According to the verdict, the villagers were ordered to leave their homes in the morning and gather at the Metaljka site. Pajic was summoned to the nearby Buljukovina site by the commander of the Second Romanija Brigade, Radislav Krstic, who ordered him to return to Novoseoci and implement the agreed plan to kill the men and deport the women and children.

Meanwhile, in Novoseoci, an elderly woman, Devla Karic, who had been told to look for her husband, was killed by Reconnaissance Company member Slavisa Cvijetic.

Upon Pajic’s return to the village, the women and children were separated and taken to Sarajevo by bus. “The men were detained with Pajic’s announcement that they would be designated for exchange,” the verdict statede.

Pajic, as noted, selected a group to liquidate the village men, which included former members of the Reconnaissance Company, Miladin and Zeljko Gasevic, Momir and Branislav Kezunovic, Jadranko Suka, and former military policeman Nikola Koprivica, as well as other members who have since died.

“They got into the vehicles, knowing that they were being taken to kill [people],” the chamber stated.

As stated, the men were taken in two trucks to the Ivan Polje location, where the group was led by Miladin Gasevic. There, at the sinkhole, they first brought men from one truck and then from another and killed all 44 of them.

“178 shots were fired from automatic weapons … The remains were found in 2000, covered in garbage and the ruins of the mosque in Novoseoci,” Hadziomerovic stated.

She added that, for the killing at Ivan Polje, the Chamber was primarily guided by the statements from the investigation from protected witnesses N-2 and N-3, as well as other witnesses. According to her, later denials by N-2 and N-3, that they were not at Ivan Polje, were unconvincing.

The chamber said the sentences imposed were in accordance with the actions committed by the accused. “The court did not establish special mitigating circumstances,” Hadziomerovic noted.

The chamber concluded that the prosecution had not proven a joint criminal enterprise. On this basis, the former commander of the Sokolac Police Station, Dragomir Obradovic, was acquitted. Hadziomerovic said it was not proven that Obradovic took any other actions or knowingly assisted them.

The chamber also did not establish that Gordic, indicted as deputy commander of the Military Police, took any specific actions.

The trial began in May 2021. Proceedings against Milan Tupajic and Momir Kezunovic were suspended by their deaths. The former commander of the Second Romanija Motorized Brigade of the Bosnian Serb Army, Radislav Krstic, who is serving a sentence in Estonia imposed by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, ICTY, for aiding and abetting genocide, was later indicted.

An appeal against this verdict is allowed.

World.title: Jailed Albanian Mayor Accuses PM of Sending Threats Via Minister
World.content:
Jailed Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj being accompanied to the Constitutional Court in October 2025. Photo: LSA

Relations between Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama and jailed Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj further deteriorated on Monday after the Mayor claimed that Rama used a minister to pressure him to resign and to admit he stands behind the violent protests that have rocked Tirana in recent weeks.

Veliaj’s lawyer, Plarent Ndreca, disclosed that last Friday, the Minister of Justice, Toni Gogu, visited the prison where Veliaj was transferred last week with a list of demands from Rama.

Later, Gogu accepted holding the meeting but denied sending any such messages from Rama to Veliaj.

“I met with Erion Veliaj on Friday. In the exercise of my responsibilities as Minister of Justice, I went to assess the conditions of his treatment and to hear the complaints that had been publicly voiced by his lawyer,” Gogu wrote on Monday.

He added: “Those who know me are aware there is no chance, in this world or the next, that I would ever utter the ‘messages’ attributed to me. I am truly taken aback.”

Hours later, Veliaj himself posted two handwritten notes allegedly taken from the meeting, with Rama’s demands.

“I may indeed have less freedom than the Prime Minister but I possess far more dignity than he does … I challenge the Prime Minister to produce even a single piece of evidence to support his insinuations about the protests,” Veliaj said.

The allegations about threats being made against Veliaj emerged just days after his transfer from the pre-trial detention centre in Durres to one in Fier, a move carried out via a contested procedure. In the absence of a written order, Veliaj denounced the transfer as politically motivated and a “police abduction”.

The General Directorate of Prisons said the transfer was a “standard procedure” but that the transfer order had been classified as a “state secret”.

Veliaj’s claims prompted the Albanian Helsinki Committee to conduct monitoring at Fier prison, which revealed serious issues regarding Veliaj’s rights and legal guarantees, specifically about a lack of transparency over the reasons for his transfer, the classification of the transfer order as restricted information and obstacles to exercising the right to an effective appeal.

“Pre-trial detention does not entail the loss of rights that have not been restricted by law or a judicial decision, and security cannot be used as a blanket justification to circumvent transparency, proportionality, and judicial oversight,” it stated.

Veliaj’s prison transfer and his claims have become a hot topic, as Veliaj was once a close ally of PM and Socialist leader Edi Rama.

Political analyst Lutfi Dervishi said that, “for the first time, Veliaj is publicly challenging Rama using language that leaves little room for misunderstanding.”

“If Socialists begin to question whether they should support the party or defend every decision made by its leader, the debate ceases to be merely personal, and for Rama, a new problem emerges,” Dervishi said.

“Until now, the Prime Minister has had to contend with managing government scandals, street protests and the opposition in parliament; now he also faces public accusations from one of his most prominent associates,” he added.

Former Socialist minister Ermelinda Meksi commented that, “if Veliaj’s claims are substantiated, we are dealing with a highly concerning precedent: the use of state authority and instruments to exert political pressure on an individual in pre-trial detention”.

On a local show, “Opinion”, Veliaj’s lawyer, Plarent Ndreca, said that it all arose “from a message issued by Mr Veliaj regarding the Belgrade issue; ever since that message was sent, there has been a shift in institutional behavior.”

Ndreca referred to a congratulatory message that Veliaj issued about the recent elections in Serbia that toppled the regime of Aleksandar Vucic.

“Congratulations to the students for toppling the Machiavellian and populist from Belgrade! Student movements and protests do not signify the ‘end of the world’ but rather the end of ‘a world’. The sooner we as citizens and policymakers grasp this, the better equipped we will be to respond to the needs and expectations of this generation,” Veliaj wrote on October 26.

Albanians have been similarly protesting for almost five months against the government, with students in October joining the anti-government protests, demanding Rama’s resignation.

Veliaj has been in a jail since February 10, 2025, when he was arrested by the Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, on charges of corruption and money laundering, allegedly carried out through a scheme that also involves his wife, Ajola Xoxa. He has denied the accusations.

World.title: Albanian Journalists Complain of Police Violence, Abuse During Anti-Govt Protests
World.content:
Glidona Daci was reporting live from anti-government protests in Albania when she was pepper-sprayed by police.

In her report for Klan News, Daci is seen telling police officers: “The camera is live, don’t touch the operator, and don’t spray me with pepper spray.”

Pushed by police, Daci said police ignored her protestations.

World.title: Post-Vucic Serbia Will Reengage with Europe, But It Will Not Be a Honeymoon
World.content:
On October 25, 2025, Serbian students and the coalition they formed, the Student List, shocked the world by defeating the ruling Serbian Progressive Party in a landslide electoral victory. This ended 14-years of rule by the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and its leader Aleksandar Vucic, a period in which the SNS dominated public institutions, the media and national security services.

After the elections, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos declared that “a new chapter can begin for Serbia. The door to the EU is open, and we are ready to move forward together.” Not so fast. The end of the old regime does not mean the EU-Serbia honeymoon can begin, nor does it mean EU membership for Serbia is a slam dunk.

What is realistic to expect in the post-election period? The new government will make goodwill gestures towards Brussels and European capitals. Ilija Srdanovic, first on the Student List, said Serbia remains committed to European integration and that the new government will continue normalisation talks between Belgrade and Pristina, mediated by Brussels.

World.title: Waste Crisis Blights Kosovo’s Capital and its Mayor’s Political Ambitions
World.content:
Earlier this month, in a video made by an influencer in New York, Pristina mayor Perparim Rama unveiled his latest ambition - to become prime minister of Kosovo.

The response from many residents of Kosovo’s capital was tongue-in-cheek, to say the least.

They flooded social media with photos and videos depicting the waste crisis afflicting Pristina for the past couple of years, questioning Rama’s readiness to lead the country if he can’t even fix its biggest city.

Uncollected garbage regularly blights Pristina’s streets, as the result of a lack of resources and a row between local authorities and the state government.

Last week, Rama, who is not a member of any party but ran for mayor on behalf of the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, said the crisis was the fault of the central government, and accused Finance Minister Hekuran Murati of failing to sign off on the money needed to pay for new waste trucks and dumpsters.

Rama said the government was blocking municipal efforts to open a new city waste company, while preventing trucks from unloading waste at the landfill overnight.

“The city then gets filled with waste,” he told TV Dukagjini. “Then they photograph it and tell me ‘look how you have filled the city with garbage.’”

World.title: Serbia Bank Owner Arrested Following Licence Revocation
World.content:
Alta Bank HQ in Belgrade. Photo: Wikimedia/Andrei Romanenko

The owner of Serbia’s Alta Bank, Davor Macura, was arrested on Monday, three days after the National Bank revoked the bank’s licence.

Macura was arrested on suspicion of abuse of office for withdrawing money from Alta Bank’s treasury and obtaining a financial gain of 45 billion dinars (nearly 385 million euros).

In addition to Macura, G.M., director of the Bank’s Treasury and Cash Management Department, and I.P., an employee responsible for treasury operations, were also arrested on the orders of the Public Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime. They are suspected of assisting Macura in committing the alleged criminal offence.

The prosecution suspects that Macura exceeded the limits of his authority up until October 31. G.M. and I.P., who were responsible for the direct handling of assets held in Alta Bank’s treasury, allegedly provided Macura with “access cards or used their own cards and were physically present to enable unauthorised entry into the bank’s treasury”.

“During these unauthorised entries, D.M. [Macura] allegedly removed money from the vault, thereby obtaining an illicit financial gain amounting to approximately 45 billion dinars,” the prosecution said.

The National Bank of Serbia, NBS, revoked Alta Bank’s operating licence on October 31 citing a significant deterioration in its finances and concerns over its liquidity.

“The Executive Board noted that the revocation of the licence was preceded by supervisory measures aimed at ensuring that the bank increased its liquidity levels,” the NBS said, adding that the interests of the bank’s depositors had been put at risk.

Alta Bank expanded its operations during the Serbian Progressive Party’s time in power under former President Aleksandar Vucic. In 2025, for example, Serbia’s state-owned electricity company, Elektroprivreda Srbije, EPS, changed its payment arrangements, directing Belgrade residents to pay their electricity bills into Alta Bank accounts.

Shortly before calling parliamentary elections, former President Vucic launched a podcast on his YouTube channel with Alta Bank among its main sponsors, featuring s for it displayed in the studio.

Vucic’s list in the October 25 parliamentary elections lost power after 14 years of rule to the Student List, which has won an absolute majority.

North Macedonia Bank takes control of Alta subsidiary

Meanwhile, in neighbouring North Macedonia, the central bank has placed Alta Bank AD Bitola under temporary administration, taking control of its assets following the collapse of its majority shareholder, Alta Bank AD Belgrade, in Serbia.

The measure on Sunday was intended to protect the bank’s assets and depositors amid a sharp withdrawal of funds, North Macedonia’s Central Bank governor, Trajko Slaveski, told a press conference.

Slaveski said around 2 million euros had been withdrawn from the Bitola-based bank within days, prompting the intervention. He stressed that the North Macedonian bank remained liquid and had a sound loan portfolio. The Serbian bank’s exposure to its North Macedonia counterpart was relatively small, he added, at around 1 million euros, and did not threaten its liquidity.

Under the temporary administration, which can last up to three months, central bank-appointed administrators will assume management responsibilities, while the Serbian-majority shareholder will lose its voting rights. Customers will be meanwhile allowed to withdraw no more than 10,000 denars [around 160 euros] per week through payment cards issued by the bank.

The bank said its branches will temporarily stop serving customers from Monday until further notice. Slaveski also said potential buyers may acquire the Serbian shareholder’s stake in the bank as a potential long-term solution.

World.title: Dubrovnik Airport Scandal – Wrong Pipes Used, €22 Million Must be Returned
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – The Dubrovnik Airport scandal is being hailed as among the worst ever involving EU cash and an airport, with the wrong piping installed and a massive €22 million now needing to be returned.

Dubrovnik Airport must return €22 euros received of European Union funds after the uncovering of a scandal like few could have imagined. Index reports that the decision was made due to established irregularities in public procurement procedures during the airport reconstruction project, which began a whole thirteen years ago and was one of the largest infrastructure projects co-financed with EU funds.

problematic procurement processes and unusable system…

The total value of the reconstruction amounted to an enormous €230 million, of which almost €160 million was non-refundable The total amount that must now be returned represents around 14 percent of those funds. “It’s an amount of approximately €22 million that must be returned. That’s about 14 percent of the non-refundable funds provided by the European Union. The problem related to public procurement procedures and the signing of the main contracts, mostly in the period from 2013 to 2017,” explained Viktor Šober, director of Dubrovnik Airport.

Among the disputed public procurement procedures, the one for the aircraft fuel supply system stands out in particular. The problem arose because the wrong pipes were installed during construction. “We engaged a serious international company specialised in underground hydrant systems for fuel delivery to the apron. They are not optimistic,” Šober added. Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković confirmed the scale of the problem. “The fact is that ten public procurements were penalised, and instead of adequate pipes for aviation fuel, sewage pipes were installed, which is why the entire system is not operational,” Franković said.

information was received about the case in 2022…

The European Public Prosecutor’s Office also commented on the genuinely somewhat shocking Dubrovnik Airport scandal case. They explained that they received information from national authorities back in 2022, but decided not to take over the case because the reported facts were outside their temporal jurisdiction.

Former airport director Roko Tolić, now executive director of Airports of Montenegro, also reacted to the scandal. He claims that the fuel system was not constructed during his term. “The building permit for that facility was issued on the 3rd of September 2018, seven whole months after my departure, and the works were carried out from September 2018 and completed during 2019. Whether the installed pipes are in accordance with the permit and the project is determined by a technical inspection before the competent authority. I cannot speak about the pipes and the as-built condition from my own knowledge because I did not participate in those works,” Tolić said. The management of Dubrovnik Airport emphasises that this is a serious issue for them, given that they invested significant funds in a system that they ultimately cannot use at all.

World.title: First Snow of Winter Arrives – 20 cm Falls in Highest Croatian Settlement!
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – The very first snow of the winter has arrived, with around 20 cm falling and settling in the highest Croatian settlement.

In the highest parts of Croatia, the very first snow of the winter season has fallen. Approximately 12 centimetres were measured on Zavižan, and a snow cover also formed on Platak near Rijeka and in mountainous Gorski Kotar. Index reports that the highest amount of snow, currently measuring at around 20 centimetres, has been measured in Begovo Razdolje, the highest inhabited settlement in all of Croatia.

Because of the fresh snowfall, the residents of Begovo Razdolje had to take up their shovels a little later than usual and clear the approaches to their houses and driveways. “I’m 82 years old, so this comes as recreation for me. A bit of physical activity and fresh air does me good,” local resident Franjo Štritof told Nova TV. For the twenty or so permanent residents of the settlement, snow at the beginning of November at 1,078 metres above sea level is no surprise. “Everyone chooses whether this is for them or not, but life here is good,” says farm owner Bojan Francišković.

During the day, the air temperature hovered around three degrees Celsius, meaning that eventually, the snow turned into rain. “Now, it’s raining a little and snowing a little, and at night, pure snow falls,” Franjo Štritof explained. According to current forecasts, the first snow of the season won’t stay until the weekend. “This is nothing new. Usually it turns white like this in the middle of October, lasts for about a day or two, and after that the weather improves again and autumn is still alright for a while,” concluded Bojan Francišković.

World.title: HDZ Candidate and Hospital Commission Member Arrested in Corruption Probe
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – Vladimir Ovčarić, HDZ local candidate and head of the Technical and Service Activities Department of the Zabok General Hospital and Croatian Veterans’ Hospital, has been arrested in a wider corruption probe.

Ovčarić is also particularly active in local politics and holds positions in the Krapina Hunting Society. Index reports that as was shown by the official election results for Krapina, HDZ’s Ovčarić was the lead candidate of the joint HDZ and Zagorje Party list for the Podgora Local Committee in the elections for local committee councils back in May 2025.

politics, hunting and hospital fire brigade president

His list won 291 votes, or 42.61 percent, and three seats on the seven-member local committee council. Alongside Ovčarić, Slavko Vincelj and Marijo Družinec were elected. At the constitutive session held on 9 June 2025, Ovčarić was elected deputy president of the Podgora Local Committee Council, while Tomislav Pernjek from the SDP list was elected president.

Ovčarić is also active in the Krapina Hunting Society. According to publicly available data, he is listed as the society’s secretary and as one of the persons authorised to represent it. On the society’s official website he also appears among the members of the executive board and is listed on the register of full members of the society. Ovčarić was previously president of the Volunteer Fire Brigade of the Zabok General Hospital. His name appears in the data of the Firefighting Association of Krapina-Zagorje County, while publicly available data show that this function ended on the 11th of March 2020. He has worked at the hospital for very many years. Back in 2012, he was mentioned as head of the technical and service department when he took part with the police in a project to place anti-burglary warnings for cars in the hospital car park.

he was on the commission for the hospital kiosk tender

Particularly interesting are also the official minutes of the hospital’s Governing Board. From the minutes of the session held on the 10th of October 2024 it emerges that Ovčarić was appointed to a three-member commission for the implementation of a public tender for the lease of hospital premises and land. The tender concerned space for the installation of machines for hot and cold drinks and land for the installation of a fast-food facility. According to the decision of the Governing Board, the commission was responsible for preparing the tender, opening and reviewing bids, and proposing the selection of the most favourable bidder. Ovčarić was, according to the minutes from March 2025, also appointed to the commission for the implementation of the tender for the lease of parking spaces in the hospital garage. These documents confirm that Ovčarić had a role in conducting hospital tenders. For the time being, however, it has not been officially confirmed whether precisely these procedures are the subject of the current investigation.

what sort of corruption is he suspected of?

As was previously reported, Ovčarić is suspected of having accepted several hundred euros in bribes from convicts in order to enable them to avoid the community service work they were required to perform at the hospital. Investigators also suspect that he favoured companies in obtaining jobs. In one case a company allegedly received a new job with the explanation that it had leftover unused stone from previous works, which enabled it to offer a lower price.

According to information obtained by Index, the award of the contract for the hospital kiosk to the owner of a service craft business with whom Ovčarić was close is also being investigated. It is suspected that Ovčarić himself actually ran the kiosk and earned income from its turnover. Allegations that hospital employees performed work on his private properties are also being checked. According to unofficial information, the USKOK action has involved eight persons. Police are carrying out arrests and urgent investigative measures in the area of Krapina-Zagorje County, Zagreb and Osijek. The Zabok General Hospital and Croatian Veterans’ Hospital confirmed that the police had requested documentation relating to one employee. They said they are cooperating with investigators but that, due to the ongoing investigation, they currently cannot comment on media reports.

World.title: 56,000 People in Croatia Diagnosed With a Disability in One Year
World.content:
November the 3rd, 2026 – There has been a staggering increase of 56,000 people across Croatia diagnosed with some kind of disability in just one year. As things currently stand, every fifth person in Croatia is disabled.

In just one single year, the number of recorded persons with disabilities in Croatia rose by as many as 56,000, according to a new report by the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ). Ivana Krnic reports for Jutarnji that according to the report, on 28 September this year there were 730,987 persons with disabilities living in Croatia, compared with 675,213 one year earlier. In other words, almost every fifth resident of Croatia is now officially recorded as a person with a disability.

Such a worrying and high increase is primarily, according to those familiar with the matter, a consequence of the introduction of the inclusive allowance. Namely, the Register of Persons with Disabilities is actually a database of persons who exercise some right on the basis of disability: persons who have not been assessed or do not exercise any right cannot be in that database, regardless of their actual disability.

Since the criteria for obtaining the inclusive allowance are incomparably milder than the criteria for the personal disability benefit or the allowance for another person’s assistance and care — rights that preceded the inclusive allowance — the number of persons receiving the inclusive allowance is significantly higher than the number of persons who previously received cash assistance. Specifically speaking, before the introduction of the inclusive allowance, around 150,000 persons received the personal disability benefit and the allowance for another person’s assistance and care, while the inclusive allowance is now received by around 240,000 persons, with around another hundred thousand applications still pending. The majority of persons receiving the inclusive allowance had the same or very similar difficulties earlier, but did not meet the strict criteria for receiving cash assistance and were therefore not registered as persons with disabilities.

The HZJZ response also confirms that the new rights have significantly increased interest in assessments.

new rights prompted an assessment increase

“It covers a wide range of rights and that has attracted a large number of persons who hadn’t previously been assessed to undergo assessment and try in this way to exercise some of the mentioned rights,” doc. dr. sc. Tomislav Benjak, assistant director of the HZJZ for the quality of healthcare and author of the Report on Persons with Disabilities, told Jutarnji list.

In addition to the inclusive allowance, he also mentions other rights, such as priority in employment, transport privileges, scholarships and tax reliefs, which can be exercised on the basis of an established disability. The method of collecting data also influenced the increase. Today almost all findings and decisions arrive digitally, practically immediately after the assessment, whereas previously they were partly delivered by post. Such a system did not guarantee that all of the data was indeed recorded in the Register. The largest part of the increase relates to persons over the age of 65. Their number rose in one year from 317,164 to 358,806, i.e. by 41,642 persons. That is almost three quarters of the total annual increase.

Today almost half of all persons recorded in the Register are over 65 years old, and disability has been established in approximately 40 percent of the population of that age. Benjak says that the ageing of the population is one of the main reasons for the long-term increase in the number of persons with disabilities. In older age, difficulties with mobility, impairments of sight and hearing, and the consequences of chronic diseases occur more frequently. However, part of the increase also stems from the fact that persons who were already recorded eventually move into the older age group.

“The natural transition from the age group up to 65 years into the age group of 65 years and over affects this distribution by approximately 30 percent,” he explains. Croatia is also not helped by the health habits of the population. Benjak warns of the high frequency of cardiovascular and malignant diseases, smoking, obesity and insufficient physical activity.

how much does croatia actually deviate from global trends?

Despite this, he emphasises that Croatia does not deviate significantly from international trends. When the first Register data was published back in 2007, the share of persons with disabilities was 10.7 percent, and today it is 18.9 percent. According to the data he cites, the World Health Organisation estimates that persons with disabilities make up around 16 percent of the world’s population, while Eurostat for the European Union cites 23.9 percent. These data, however, are not necessarily completely comparable because they are based on different methods of establishing disability. The new HZJZ report for the first time also brings a division according to the severity of disability. According to that classification, 106,724 persons have severe disability and 142,722 persons have more severe disability. Together that is almost 250,000 people. However, for as many as 206,902 persons, or 28.3 percent of all those recorded, the severity of disability has not been classified.

Benjak explains that these are mostly persons who were assessed many years ago, when the findings from the then social welfare centres did not contain the data needed for today’s classification.

Interestingly, a large part of these persons, despite the possibility of exercising these new rights, have not undergone a new assessment. It is also possible that they are not sufficiently informed. “What somehow surprises us as well is that around 200,000 persons assessed at that time with rights from social welfare and elements for entry into the Register have not requested new assessments in order to exercise the right to, for example, the inclusive allowance or rights in transport,” Benjak is also surprised.

He emphasises that this is not a matter of double entries or of deceased persons. Every person is tracked by personal identification number (OIB), and the HZJZ also has data on deaths. He confirms that all 206,902 persons are alive and that there is a legal basis for their entry into the Register. The new division according to the severity of disability serves exclusively for statistical purposes and does not affect the exercise of rights. Nevertheless, the fact that data needed for classification are missing for more than a quarter of the recorded persons shows how difficult it is to obtain a complete picture of the structure of disability in Croatia.

huge differences on a county by county basis

There are also large differences among counties. In Šibenik-Knin County disability is recorded in 24.4 percent of the population, almost twice as much as in Istria County, where that share is 12.3 percent. The range is even greater among those over 65 years of age. In Šibenik-Knin County 49.6 percent of the population of that age have a disability, in Požega-Slavonia County 49.5 percent, and in Istria County 25.1 percent.

Data for children and young people in Sisak-Moslavina County are particularly worrying. There the prevalence of disability in the age group up to 19 years rose from 17.9 to 20.5 percent, while the Croatian average is 12.3 percent. This means that disability is recorded in approximately every fifth child or young person in that county. Asked why the differences are so large, Benjak says that a special study would need to be conducted. Nevertheless, he warns that Sisak-Moslavina is one of the most deprived Croatian counties, with lower wages, weaker employment, higher unemployment and unfavourable demographic trends.

“All of the above certainly also has as a consequence the occurrence of disability and developmental difficulties in children,” Benjak believes. Without additional analysis it is not possible to determine how much health and social conditions, and how much the availability of diagnostics, assessments and the method of recording, influence such a high prevalence.

the case with children across croatia

Another seemingly unusual piece of data appears in the report. Although the total number of children and young people with disabilities is rising, the number of persons for whom decisions on an appropriate form of schooling arrived in the Register has decreased from 57,703 to 49,847. Nevertheless, it seems that the reason is not necessarily a smaller number of children with difficulties, but a change in the records.

According to Benjak’s explanation, the Ministry of Education requested the deactivation of records of persons up to the age of 21 whose only basis for entry into the Register was a decision on an appropriate form of schooling, and who after 2015 weren’t ever reassessed. Among them are persons who during childhood had developmental difficulties such as dyslexia, dysgraphia, behavioural disorders or learning difficulties, which over time may have decreased or disappeared. Changes in the records also explain the decrease in the number of Croatian war military invalids. Their number fell from 54,640 to 46,132, i.e. by 8,508 persons.

According to instructions from the Ministry of Croatian Veterans, only persons who are in its official database remain in the HRVI category. Some previously recorded persons no longer appear in that database, so their HRVI status in the Register has been deactivated. Despite such changes, Benjak claims that the annual reports have been prepared using the same methodology and that it is possible to track trends. In fact, the only novelty in the 2026 report is the additional statistical division according to the severity of disability. However, precisely the changes in the records of children and veterans show how much administrative decisions can influence the statistics.

World.title: New Rules are Coming for Road Users in Croatia
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – New rules are coming into force for road users across Croatia, with higher penalties and significant amendments to the Road Traffic Act.

The Ministry of the Interior has now released for public consultation a draft of amendments to the Road Traffic Safety Act. Index reports that it will introduce significantly stricter penalties for dangerous behaviour in traffic, new parking rules and easier removal of vehicles by tow truck, as well as special registration plates for taxis and electric cars.

higher fines for those filming and posting dangerous driving

One of the key novelties concerns drivers who film their own dangerous driving in order to post it on social media, which the legislator now treats as a significantly more serious offence. While such behaviour was previously punished as ordinary mobile phone use while driving with a fixed fine of 130 euros, the new proposal introduces fines of 800 to as much as 2,000 euros for anyone who uses a mobile phone or other device while driving to record their own unlawful behaviour and then makes it publicly available. The explanatory notes state that such posts have additional social harm because they encourage others to imitate them and normalise dangerous driving patterns.

police no longer need to attend minor collisions

For the first time ever, the law defines the concept of a “minor traffic accident,” which means an accident involving only material damage that does not impair the technical soundness of essential parts of the car and allows it to be easily removed from the road. Under the new Article 182, police officers are no longer obliged to go to the scene of such an accident if the participants are able to exchange details with each other or complete the European Accident Statement. Drivers who nevertheless refuse to immediately move their cars off the carriageway and continue to block traffic while waiting for the police will be fined 200 euros, whereas the fine until now was 60 euros.

a total ban on parking on squares

The draft also introduces the concept of a restricted traffic zone into the law, together with significantly stricter rules for stopping and parking in city centres. The previous practice whereby drivers, especially delivery vehicles, parked in city squares and pedestrian zones while invoking the rule about leaving a 1.60-metre passage for pedestrians will no longer apply. Article 82 introduces an absolute ban on stopping and parking in squares, in cultural-historical complexes and on surfaces that local authorities have designated exclusively for pedestrians, regardless of how much free space remains. At the same time, the rules for the operation of the tow-truck service are also changing. A tow truck will be legally able to lift an improperly parked vehicle from the pavement if the free passage between the car and any obstacle is less than one metre. An obstacle is no longer considered only a building, but also bollards, waste bins, outdoor café terraces or any other physical obstacle on the sidewalk.

special registration plates for taxis and electric cars

The law also introduces the obligation to issue special registration plates for two categories of vehicles — taxis and electric-powered cars. While in the case of taxis this is about easier control and alignment with market rules, for electric cars the reason is directly linked to the safety of emergency services. Lithium-ion batteries in electric and hybrid vehicles, in the event of a collision and fire, generate extremely high temperatures, release toxic gases and require completely different firefighting tactics from classic petrol and diesel engines. Special plates will enable firefighters, already upon arrival at the scene of a traffic accident, to recognise electric propulsion and immediately apply the appropriate extinguishing and rescue procedure.

World.title: 135 Years of the Zagreb Tram – From Horses to Modernity
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – 135 years is the time period during which the now iconic blue Zagreb tram has snaked through the capital city. From being pulled by horses to new vehicles, let’s look back at the history of what we now know as ZET.

Dubravko Grakalic reports for Index that frequent trams have been circulating Zagreb’s streets for 135 years now. They have become the blue symbol of the city, living history on the rails, and transport without which Zagreb can hardly function, something Zagreb residents felt most clearly during the recent multi-day ZET workers’ strike, which caused days of traffic problems until a court declared it illegal and banned it.

horse-drawn trams named after vineyard pests…

The first tram circled Zagreb back in 1891. It was pulled by horses and was far from the technical modernity we know today. Zagreb’s trams were once yellow and ran on only a few lines through the very city centre. People affectionately called them “konjka” (horse-tram), but also mockingly “filoksera”, after the notorious wine louse (phylloxera) that was ravaging vineyards in those years, because the workers laying the tracks had dug up and torn apart half the city. Before the trams, passengers were transported around Zagreb by omnibuses that resembled stagecoaches from Western films. They ran from the city centre to the bathing spots on the Sava and from the railway station to a few hotels. As ZET explains, “the city fathers in Zagreb began discussing the need to introduce a horse-drawn tram as a means of transport” in 1885.

French engineer Raoul Pierre Alexandre Gautier proposed a contract for the introduction of tram traffic to the Zagreb City Magistrate on the 20th of June 1887. The city municipality accepted his offer and on the 26th of March 1889 issued him a permit to build a tram line on the ground of the city streets. The Association of Engineers and Technicians allowed the construction of a 76-centimetre-wide track, and the Tramway Company, a special private enterprise, began work. The first tram depot was built on the site of today’s Nikola Tesla Technical Museum.

ilica, zagreb’s modern main artery, was dug up

zagreb.hr

The first lines were built from the corner of Ilica and Mandaličina Street to Maksimir, from the corner of Ilica and Frankopanska Street to the Sava Bridge, and from the corner of Ilica and today’s Republic of Austria Street to the Western Railway Station. Construction began in May 1891, and the trams started running a few months later. Historian Lelja Dobronić, in the article “Old Notes on the Zagreb Tram” published in the magazine Kaj, cites a document from the 17th of August 1891: “Since the long-awaited rails from England and the carriages from Graz (in Austria) have finally arrived, Upper Ilica has been being dug up since last Thursday, and from today Frankopanska Street as well, so that the rails can be laid. Certainly by this Sunday the rails will be laid through the whole of Ilica and Jelačić Square. Up to 500 workers are working a day.”

At the time when Zagreb’s trams were pulled by horses, there were ten closed and six open vehicles available, manufactured at the Weitzer factory in Graz. The average speed of the horse-drawn tram cars was 7.5 km/h. Zagreb’s horse-drawn tram also carried passengers in Velika Gorica, where the joint-stock company Horse Railway was founded back in 1907. They had a seven-kilometre line from the railway station, through the centre of Velika Gorica, to Novo Čiče. It was called “konjača.” After 1945 the horses were replaced by a small diesel locomotive.

electrification and expansion

The electric tram started in August 1910, but horse-drawn trams continued to operate for the following year. Zagreb’s trams changed colour in 1923. They became blue instead of yellow, while the vehicles were reconstructed. A new model, the M-24, manufactured in Zagreb and running on the right-hand track, also appeared on the streets. Summer open-air trams soon became available as well. During the time of the Independent State of Croatia (NDH), Zagreb’s trams ran with increasing difficulty because of bombing, and services were suspended in 1944. Traffic resumed after liberation, and in the autumn of 1945 tracks were built through Vodnikova and Mihanovićeva streets. From then on, the tram lines had numbers. In the following years lines were built towards Žitnjak as well as the Mihaljevac–Dolje line. A building for ZET workers was constructed in Puljska Street.

bull, czech and katica…

At the beginning of the 1950s, Zagreb’s residents also received the first domestically produced tram, built in the ZET workshop. It was prototype 101 with 95 passenger seats. This was followed by cooperation with the “Đuro Đaković” wagon factory from Slavonski Brod and the purchase of M-201 vehicles.

The last example of the M-201 tram, nicknamed “Đuro” or “Bik” (Bull), ran until June 2024 on line 9. Its predecessor, the M-24, ran from 1924 to 1977. Today it is used as the Christmas tram. In 1977 Czechoslovak trams from the ČKD-Tatra factory in Prague were purchased. The Czech T4 model trams, known as “Čeh” (Czech), ran for years on lines 4, 6 and 14. Years later the Tatra KT4YU trams, better known as “Katice,” also arrived. An important date in the history of the Zagreb tram was the 25th of November 1979, when the line along Držićeva Street, across the Bridge of Youth, to New Zagreb was opened. That was when the tram crossed the Sava. In 1980 a tram-bus terminal was built at Črnomerec on the site of a former brickworks. In November 1985 the tram also started running across the Adriatic Bridge towards New Zagreb. Further development of ZET includes the abolition of the conductor’s job in 1996 (conductors had been cancelling and selling tickets in the vehicles for 105 years) and the extension of tram routes to Dubec and Prečko.

and then came končar…

Over the last thirty years or so the old trams, Bulls, Czechs and Katicas, have been replaced by trams manufactured at Končar, Zagreb’s technological giant.

“In more than 30 years of operation on Zagreb’s tram network, Končar trams have covered more than 140 million kilometres, confirming their quality, reliability and indispensable role in the lives of Zagreb residents,” Končar told Index. The company had already begun manufacturing electric rectifier stations for ZET back in 1954. “After almost three decades of cooperation on energy infrastructure, ZET and Končar began joint development of tram vehicles. Production of the TMK 2100 series trams began in 1993, and the prototype was presented on the 5th of September 1994 and immediately put into regular service,” the company notes, also recalling the TMK 2200 trams. “From June 2010 a total of 140 TMK 2200 series trams and two shorter TMK 2200-K trams (which carry the designation TMK 2300 in ZET’s fleet) have been produced for Zagreb,” Končar says. The company later also manufactured shorter trams for the Latvian city of Liepāja.

zagreb’s blue trams

In order to fill gaps in the timetable until the delivery of new vehicles, ZET bought 11 used GT6M trams from Augsburg, Germany, at the end of 2023 and during 2024. This sparked lively public debate because of their age and the fact that the passenger areas are not air-conditioned. The newest Zagreb trams, the TMK 2300, have been in service since February 2025, and there will be forty of them. Through their rich history Zagreb’s trams have become the city’s blue symbol, a mark of the development of domestic technology, and an indicator of Zagreb’s expansion ever further from its historic centre. Zagreb is, along with Osijek, the only Croatian city with tram traffic. Trams once also ran in Pula (from 1904 to 1934), Dubrovnik (from 1910 to 1970), and Rijeka and Opatija.

World.title: Zoran Milanović Accuses EU of Wanting to be a Superstate
World.content:
November the 2nd, 2026 – Croatian President Zoran Milanović has accused the EU of wanting to become a superstate, adding that Montenegro, with which Croatia has multiple open issues, is otherwise welcome to join.

President Zoran Milanović stated that Montenegro is welcome to become a full member of the European Union, while at the same time criticising the direction in which the EU is developing. Index reports that the president believes the EU is increasingly trying to become a superstate, whereas it should focus on free trade, freedom of movement and the harmonisation of rules among member states.

Milanović spoke at the 27th Lučindan Gatherings in Zagreb, a traditional meeting of the Montenegrin community in Croatia. The event was also attended by Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović, who is on a working visit to Croatia. The two presidents discussed relations between the two countries and Montenegro’s European future.

“montenegro is welcome to join”

“Montenegro is a candidate for membership of the European Union, it is moving towards the EU and let it come. As far as I am concerned, it is welcome,” Milanović said. Nevertheless, he repeated his criticisms of the European Union, which he believes is exceeding the powers and possibilities on which it was originally founded. In his view, the EU should stick to economic cooperation, free movement and the alignment of rules, rather than striving to create a superstate.

Milanović told Montenegrins that the greatest value they have is their state. He emphasised that Montenegro has realised its statehood and that its future success does not depend exclusively on membership of the European Union. “The greatest thing you have is your state. Montenegro has realised itself, and everything else consists of greater or lesser advances that do not stand in the way of Montenegro being successful, well-governed and relatively prosperous,” Milanović said. He wished Montenegro to continue on its own path and develop as a successful and well-governed state. He concluded his address with verses by the Montenegrin ruler and poet Petar II Petrović Njegoš.

trust between croatia and montenegro must be strengthened

Montenegrin President Jakov Milatović assessed that Croatia and Montenegro are friendly countries and that Montenegro’s membership of the European Union is in the interest of both countries. He stressed that improving relations requires continuing political dialogue and resolving existing open issues.

“It is our shared responsibility to build good-neighbourly relations, foster open dialogue, overcome current challenges and strengthen mutual trust,” Milatović said. He emphasised that a common European future implies political and economic cooperation, mutual respect and a willingness to resolve disagreements. He thanked the Montenegrin community in Croatia for preserving national identity, culture and ties with the home country.

The Lučindan Gatherings are a traditional event dedicated to preserving Montenegrin cultural identity, tradition and ties with Montenegro. They bring together members of the Montenegrin national minority in Croatia as well as representatives of the cultural and public life of the two countries. According to the 2021 census, 3,127 members of the Montenegrin national minority live in Croatia, or 0.08 percent of the total population.

World.title: Before You Apply: The Legal Deadline Blocking Croatian Descendants
World.content:
November the 1st, 2026 – There is a somewhat unknown legal deadline blocking Croatian descendants from obtaining their Croatian and as such EU passport.

That issue relates to the exact reason your family left the former Yugoslavia, and why exactly this could throw a spanner in the works of your EU future. Let’s turn the clock back to October the 8th, 1991… If you’re exploring your eligibility for Croatian citizenship by descent, you have likely come across a specific date repeatedly, and that date is October the 8th, 1991. In the (often confusing) world of Croatian citizenship law, this is the ultimate historical line in the sand. Under the descent and emigrant pathways of the Croatian Citizenship Act, your ancestor must have left the territory of what is now the recognised territory of Croatia before this exact date to grant you a pathway to a Croatian and therefore EU passport of your own.

For many second- and third-generation descendants of those who left what was then Yugoslavia, this seems straightforward at first glance. They look at their family history, note that their parents or grandparents moved to the United States 1960s, 1970s, or 1980s, and check the box. However, many “DIY applicants” face rejections from the Croatian side of the fence because they fail to realise that the Ministry of the Interior (MUP) enforces strict, hidden caveats regarding why and how your ancestor left when they did. Simply proving your family departed before the clock struck 1991 is not quite enough. To secure your Croatian citizenship, you must prove the exact legal nature of their exit. That is where, quite understandably, many people become unstuck and their citizenship applications get shoved to the back of a shelf somewhere to gather dust.

what exactly does croatia deem to be an emigrant?

The Croatian side evaluates citizenship applications based on a highly specific legal definition of what they deem an emigrant to actually be. Under the law as it stands, an emigrant is someone who left the territory of Croatia with the clear, permanent intention of abandoning their domestic residence and resettling somewhere abroad. Because of this ultra-narrow definition that leaves very little wiggle room, there are two major legal traps that routinely catch DIY applicants by surprise.

the so-called internal migration problem

If your ancestor was born in Croatia but moved to another republic within former Yugoslavia, such as Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or Slovenia, and then moved across the pond to North America, Croatia’s authorities may not view them as a legal emigrant from Croatia because of that, regardless of the fact that they still ended up in the USA. If that person’s initial move was treated as an internal migration within the same federal state, the chain of continuity for Croatian descent can be heavily compromised or, as is often the case, simply rejected outright.

the curse of the Croatian gastarbajteri…

A Monument to Croatian Emigrants – Anglogermantranslations

During the 1970s and 1980s, hundreds of thousands of people left the former Yugoslavia to work abroad as temporary economic migrants, often referred to as gastarbajteri (guest workers). Many of these individuals retained their active residency rights, property registrations, and legal ties to Croatia and as such to Yugoslavia, fully intending to return after a few years. If MUP reviews your ancestor’s file and determines that their departure was legally categorised as a “temporary economic migration” rather than a permanent severance of domestic ties, your application under the emigrant track can be denied.

verifying permanence…

Commons/Bain News Service

When you submit your application to a Croatian consulate, the reviewing officers will thoroughly inspect your paperwork to determine the legal permanence of your ancestor’s departure. A simple plane ticket or family story will not suffice. To build an airtight case, you must present a synchronised paper trail that cross-references multiple things.

The first is what’s known as a foreign naturalisation timeline. This works to document precisely when your Croatian ancestor applied for and received citizenship in their new country, showing a definitive shift in legal allegiance. Then come the international arrival records. These are official historical maritime or flight manifests matching the timeline of their permanent resettlement. Last but not least comes the so-called letter of motivation. This might seem odd, but there should always be an explicit structure built up of your family’s narrative, framing their historical departure to meet the rigid legal thresholds expected by Croatia.

for croatia, the year 1991 represents a minefield in several ways…

Proving the legal nuances of a person’s departure that took place forty or fifty years ago is a massive bureaucratic challenge. It requires a deep understanding of historical (and of course needlessly complicated) Yugoslav exit laws, international naturalisation records, and precise legal phrasing in the Croatian language. This is exactly why the structured service provided by Croatian By Descent is an essential safeguard for diaspora families.

croatian by descent‘s experts understand the complexities of the former state

Rather than treating your citizenship application like a roll of the dice, their team conducts an exhaustive upfront document review. They analyse your family’s specific migration timeline, identify potential vulnerabilities in how your ancestors left Yugoslavia, and help you with your application package. By coordinating the procurement of records and managing the precise drafting of your legal motivation letter, they ensure that the Ministry views your family’s departure as a definitive, permanent emigration. They handle the heavy administrative legal lifting, protecting your application from common 1991 cutoff traps and turning your family history into a submission package. Outsource the endless guesswork and verify your eligibility with the expert team at Croatian By Descent.

World.title: Expert warns against 'Christmas' wish list in Estonia's defense plans
World.content:
Defense expert Meelis Oidsalu warns that Estonia's new defense plans risk becoming a wish list of costly military capabilities the country can't afford to maintain.

In a recent blog post, Oidsalu cautioned that pre-election pressure could lead to costly purchases without enough consideration of the associated long-term maintenance.

Speaking to ERR, he said his biggest concern is Estonia's National Defense Development Plan becoming a patchwork document as it is continually expanded.

"Each branch of the military walks away with some shiny new gift," Oidsalu said, bringing up 90-meter ships for the Navy, missile defense or aircraft for the Air Force and more firepower for the Army. "I've gotten the impression this year that it's Christmas in the defense sector."

The expert warned that adding capabilities Estonia cannot afford to maintain could divert funds from more immediate needs, including ammunition stocks.

"If we start building 'trophy' capabilities that we'll never be able to manage to develop at a meaningful scale, we're wasting resources that could instead go toward increasing the number of days we could sustain combat."

Martin Herem. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

Minister of Defense Martin Herem said Tuesday that the threat posed by Russia could grow if the war in Ukraine ends, making it necessary to develop certain capabilities quickly even if they prove difficult to maintain.

He later clarified that he did not expect Estonia to actually acquire capabilities beyond what it could sustain.

'Take a step back'

Oidsalu emphasized that Estonia has little experience estimating the long-term costs of major naval vessels and missile defense systems, which international experience suggests often exceed initial estimates.

"We should take a step back and calculate over the long term whether we can afford to deploy all these capabilities," he added.

While acknowledging that the military's assessment of its needs has changed this year, Oidsalu said planning cannot remain in flux. He warned against adding impressive-sounding capabilities in the run-up to an election without ensuring Estonia can actually afford to put them into service and maintain them.
