World.title: Drone imagery reveals likely sites of future Pakri cliff collapses
World.content:
Years of drone surveys by University of Tartu geologists have shown that the Pakri Cliffs often erode from below, with seawater washing away soft sandstone until overlying limestone collapses into the sea. The resulting 3D models can identify dangerous areas before a collapse occurs.

Two winters ago, in mid-January, an observation platform at the Pakri Cliffs collapsed into the sea. A 30-meter section of the cliff edge broke away, and the cliff retreated 12 meters in a single event. About 2,800 cubic meters of rock, equivalent to roughly 160 dump truck loads, fell into the water. Although the collapse appeared sudden from above, it could have been anticipated from the side, writes University of Tartu junior research fellow in geology Tiia-Linda Purge.

Not everything is visible from the top

Near Paldiski, the Baltic Klint rises directly from the sea to heights of up to 25 meters. A historic lighthouse dating to the era of Russian czar Peter I stands at the edge, alongside well-worn visitor trails. Geologists have studied this section of the cliff for more than two centuries, focusing mainly on its rock layers and composition. Until now, however, cliff retreat has largely been measured from above by comparing historical maps and aerial imagery.

The cliff edge tells only part of the story. The Pakri Cliffs resemble a layer cake. The upper seven meters consist of limestone, with harder, fractured rock near the top and more clay-rich, sandy, and fragile layers below. Beneath that lies green glauconitic sandstone, once studied as a source material for potassium fertilizer, followed by black shale, also known as graptolite argillite, and softer sandstones at the base. These rocks were deposited on the floor of an ancient sea nearly 500 million years ago.

If scientists evaluate cliff retreat solely by studying the edge, they miss what is happening beneath it. A significant part of the process occurs midway down the vertical cliff face, an area inaccessible to people without ropes and difficult to observe from conventional aerial surveys. That is why researchers set out to map the cliff from the side and in three dimensions.

Potential zones of cliff failure based on the study authors' expert opinion. Source: Tiia-Linda Purge et al. / Estonian Journal of Earth Sciences

Using drones to reach inaccessible areas

Researchers photographed the cliff using drones in 2015, 2022, and 2024. Software then combined the images into a three-dimensional model, allowing every layer, fracture, and cave to be measured and analyzed on a computer. The team also traced the cliff edge using six aerial photographs covering the period from 1959 to 2024.

The work was far from simple. Drones had to be flown just a few meters from the cliff face and the water's surface while avoiding fallen rock debris and ensuring all key features were captured. Waves and boulder fields prevented researchers from surveying the base of the cliff as closely as they would have liked, and the ceilings of deeper caves remained hidden from view.

The method, known as photogrammetry, more specifically structure-from-motion photogrammetry, involves photographing the same location from multiple angles. Computer vision algorithms identify common points across images and create a three-dimensional model from ordinary photographs. The more sharp, overlapping images available, the more accurate and detailed the result.

To detect change over time, researchers aligned models from different years. Precise drone positioning helped with newer surveys, while older datasets required the use of stable reference points that had remained unchanged.

The secret of cliff collapses lies below

Aerial photographs show the Pakri Cliffs have lost more than a football field's worth of land over the past 65 years. The cliff edge retreated by an average of 18 centimeters per year, and by as much as 30 centimeters annually near the historic lighthouse and the collapsed observation deck.

Those rates are similar to coastal cliffs in northern Germany and northwestern Poland, which retreat at rates of 19 and 14 centimeters per year, respectively. Unlike those cliffs, however, Pakri is capped by hard limestone. The cliffs of Osmussaar, which consist entirely of limestone, retreat on average by only seven centimeters per year.

Average figures can be misleading. The cliff does not retreat at a steady pace. Years may pass with little change before a large section suddenly collapses, as happened in January 2024 when the observation deck fell and the cliff retreated 12 meters. Smaller collapses often go unnoticed by the public, but drone models can detect them.

The underlying cause is the interaction between geology and rock layers. Rainwater seeps through fractured limestone and emerges along weaker sandstone layers beneath it. The water gradually washes away the sandstone grain by grain, leaving limestone suspended overhead. Repeated freeze-thaw cycles widen fractures until a rock block finally breaks away. Both the observation deck collapse and a collapse near the lighthouse in 2021 were preceded by significant sandstone erosion beneath the limestone.

The cliff also breaks along existing joint systems (natural rock fractures). Researchers mapped more than 400 joint surfaces from drone models. Two dominant fracture systems, running northwest-southeast and northeast-southwest, create the Pakri coastline's distinctive zigzag shape. The cliff retreats most rapidly where fractures intersect and where underlying sandstone has already been eroded away.

The sea also plays a key role. Waves carve coastal notches (wave-cut undercuts) into the sandstone at the cliff base. Geologists mapped 18 such notches and 19 shallow indentations representing proto-notches in the early stages of formation. These features develop where the rock is naturally weaker. Poorly cemented sandstone yields to wave action, while the black shale layers above it resist erosion longer. As a result, the cliff erodes unevenly, with each layer wearing away at its own pace.

The cliff also has a natural defense mechanism. Fallen limestone blocks accumulate at the base, forming a rubble slope that absorbs wave energy. After the observation platform collapse, a rock barrier nearly five meters high formed in front of the cliff. The protection lasts only until waves carry the debris away and regain access to the base of the cliff.

Pakri peninsula coastline. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Mapping hazardous areas

The 3D models help scientists identify locations where sandstone has already eroded from beneath limestone, leaving dangerous overhangs. Based on those findings, researchers mapped potential collapse zones along the Pakri Cliffs. Such maps can help redirect hiking trails away from hazardous areas and warn visitors of potential risks.

Researchers caution that not everything can be predicted. The hazard zones are based on expert assessment rather than precise forecasts because the behavior of such a complex system cannot be predicted with complete accuracy. The visible fractures on the rock surface may represent only part of a much denser network hidden within the cliff. Scientists also lack a full understanding of how the underwater cliff base modifies wave energy.

The team plans to produce a new model at least once a year. The longer the dataset becomes, the better researchers will understand the cliff's natural rhythm and identify areas preparing for future collapses or responding to changing environmental conditions.

While coastal scientists around the world already make extensive use of drones and related surveying technologies, the approach remains relatively new in Estonia. Compared with satellites and aircraft, drones offer a flexible and cost-effective tool that can be deployed exactly where and when it is needed. The Pakri Cliffs demonstrate how this new perspective can advance coastal research in Estonia.

The study was published in the journal Estonian Journal of Earth Sciences.

World.title: Estonian-American producer umru to headline Tallinn club on Saturday
World.content:
New York-based producer and DJ umru has worked with the likes of Tommy Cash and Charli XCX. This Saturday, the Estonian-American artist takes the stage at Tallinn's club MOD.

Brooklyn native Umru Rothenberg began producing music as a teenager, uploading his early tracks to SoundCloud. His work caught the attention of A.G. Cook, founder of the influential label PC Music, who invited him to contribute to Charli XCX's 2017 song "I Got It" when he was just 18.

The collaboration helped launch umru's international career, leading to projects with a range of experimental pop artists, including Laura Les of 100 Gecs, Dorian Electra, Empress of and Caroline Polachek, as well as Estonia's own Tommy Cash.

Having made his name in the hyperpop scene, umru has increasingly moved toward club music. Last year, he released the EP "Matter of Time" on Scottish label LuckyMe, featuring producers Jacques Greene and Nikki Nair.

He also released the single "Poplife" together with American musician Underscores.

This Saturday, umru will headline at Tallinn's club MOD, joined by DJs Vaatab Jooksvalt and White Gloss.

Close Estonian ties

In an appearance on the No Tags podcast last year, umru shared that he spent a year living and attending school in Estonia at age seven, but has otherwise lived his entire life in New York.

His mother is Estonian-born artist Jaanika Peerna.

World.title: KOOS party may be allowed to pay 2027 Riigikogu election deposit in cash
World.content:
An exception may be granted for a political party to pay its deposit ahead of the March 2027 Riigikogu election in cash.

The KOOS party has been unable to open up a bank account in Estonia, which would be the normal means of making payment according to the rule-book.

However the requirement may more be a case of the spirit of the law rather than the letter of the law.

Justice Ministry Deputy Secretary General Heddi Lutterus said the requirement is not enshrined in law however, and an exception may be granted in this case.

"The Political Parties Act, which regulates the establishment of political parties, their activities and the supervision of their financing, does not require a registered political party to have or open an account with a credit institution," Lutterus said in a written response to a request for clarification from party representative Igor Hopp.

"If a party duly fulfills its obligations under the Accounting Act and the Political Parties Act and maintains financial discipline without having an account, then, while this is not standard practice, the mere fact of not having an account cannot in itself be held against the party," Lutterus added in her response.

Lutterus pointed out that the financing reports available on the website of the Political Parties Financing Surveillance Committee (ERJK) show that KOOS has submitted income and expenditure reports, Lutterus noted, though added that in establishing the rules for paying election deposits under another act, the Riigikogu Election Act, the Riigikogu likely had the payment of deposits in cash in mind.

Consequently, a party must submit a copy of the payment order confirming payment of the deposit along with its other candidacy documents.

Another aspect of the law is the fact that a party's deposit need not be made from that party's own account, Lutterus went on, with the most important parameter being payment is made on time – if a credit institution or other financial services company provided cash payment, for instance, this could be a feasible avenue of payment, Lutterus continued, noting that "the service may involve fees or transaction limits."

Polling day is March 7, 2027.

World.title: Raimond Kaljulaid leaving politics, will not run at Riigikogu election
World.content:
Social Democratic Party (SDE) MP Raimond Kaljulaid has announced he will not be running in next spring's Riigikogu election, and is leaving politics.

Kaljulaid, who is a member of the Riigikogu National Defense Committee, said he made his decision in August, and is going back to work in the private sector.

"Returning to the private sector, I can also draw on the knowledge and experience in management and business development that I had before entering politics, when I worked as an entrepreneur in marketing and communications," Kaljulaid said.

"For the past eight years, I have been involved in foreign and security policy. I have worked on the principle that maintaining very good relations with all our allies and partners is vitally important for Estonia. I cannot count how many meetings I have had during this time with politicians, diplomats and entrepreneurs from Europe, the U.S., the Gulf states and Asian countries," he went on.

Kaljulaid added he has not yet made a final decision on exactly what he will do next. "I am considering various options and thinking things through carefully. I will make a decision in the coming months."

While he said he does not rule out ever returning to politics, he is certain that he will not consider doing so in the immediate next years, nor likely beyond that either, adding he is "serious" about working in the private sector again.

Kaljulaid also stated former Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov's decision to join SDE did not play a role in his move either.

"Jonatan Vseviov's decision to join obviously could not have influenced my decision in any way, as it happened long after I had made my decision. However, I welcome this step. Jonatan Vseviov brings very strong knowledge of foreign and security policy to the party. Alongside that, I would also consider it very important that he is coming from the position of secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Kaljulaid on this.

He expressed a hope that the party's current upward trend in the polls will continue and that it will play a highly significant role both in the next Riigikogu composition and in the next administration.

He noted that the example of where " neoliberal right-wing economic policies lead" from some of the Western European countries, adding "what happens to society when inequality grows rapidly and people feel that the state does not need them and that they do not need the state either has had a "destabilixing" effect in those lands, and one which Estonia and its political parties could pay heed to.

He said he would continue to vote for SDE and encouraged all voters to do so too.

Kaljulaid 44, had been a Center Party member for the best part of 20 years before joining SDE in 2019. He won a Riigikogu seat in his own right with Center at the 2019 elections, but quit in protest of the party's coalition talks which involved the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE). He was re-elected at the 2023 elections with SDE. In the current Riigikogu he sat on the Security Authorities Surveillance Select Committee, as well as the defense committee, and chaired the Estonian delegation to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly. His 20,643 votes attained at the 2019 European Parliament elections was the seventh best result.

Riigikogu election polling day is March 7, 2027.

World.title: Consumer inspection finds violations in all e-scooters checked
World.content:
Estonia's consumer watchdog found issues with all e-scooters on sale in a sample taken this year, with several models banned from sale as a result.

The Consumer Protection and Technical Regulatory Authority (TTJA) investigated 18 e-scooter models on sale across 10 different retailers, between April and September this year.

The TTJA found violations in all products, with the most common shortcomings relating to product documentation: 11 e-scooters lacked a declaration of conformity, or information that was provided in it was incomplete.

Nine sales listings for high-powered or high-speed electric scooters lacked information stating that the product must not be used in traffic. Several products also lacked an Estonian-language user manual.

During the supervisory proceedings, businesses submitted missing manuals or conformity documents for nine products and, where necessary, clarified the information provided in sales listings, the TTJA said.

As a result of the proceedings, five product models have been withdrawn from sale and sales of two product models have been temporarily suspended. Sales were suspended or products withdrawn from sale in cases where the company was unable to provide the required conformity documents or remedy shortcomings, for example by failing to provide the product with a user manual.

The seller is responsible for the information provided in sales listings: if the technical specifications of a personal mobility device exceed the limits established for its use, consumers must be clearly informed of this and, where necessary, told that the device is not intended for use in traffic.

Misleading consumers is not permitted, the TTJA noted. When purchasing an e-scooter, consumers should in any case check not only the price and technical specifications but also that the product meets the requirements and that the necessary information and documents are available.

World.title: Funding shortfall forces museum of communist crimes to cut Holocaust section and other exhibits
World.content:
A planned museum of communist crimes at Tallinn's Patarei Prison has cut roughly one-third of its exhibition because of budget constraints, raising doubts about whether it will have the funding needed to open and operate in 2027.

In 2018, the government decided to establish an international Museum of Communist Crimes and Research Center in the former Patarei Prison in Tallinn. The plans were ambitious: the 5,000-square-meter museum was intended to become the first large-scale exhibition in the Baltic Sea region dedicated to the crimes and operating mechanisms of communist regimes.

Now, historian Martin Andreller, a board member of the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory, which is curating the museum, said the funding allocated by the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs is insufficient to complete the exhibition as originally planned.

"When the exhibition procurement was launched, about 35 percent of the content had already been cut," Andreller said.

Martin Andreller Autor/allikas: Kirke Ert/ERR

The cuts included the audio guide, the entire Holocaust section, as well as other content blocks and technical solutions needed to stay within the available budget, he explained.

"We are heading toward the opening with a heavily reduced exhibition that does not represent the complete vision developed during the planning process," Andreller said. "At the same time, it remains unclear whether and how next year's budget will be resolved, even though that funding is needed to open the museum, keep it running, and provide services to visitors."

Andreller said an additional €500,000 is needed to complete the exhibition, not including personnel costs.

"The reduced exhibition will be completed by June 14, but we still have no certainty about next year's budget. That makes it impossible to plan pre-opening activities such as marketing, communications, educational programs, staffing, and the museum's day-to-day operations," he added.

2027 budget mostly unclear

"In the worst-case scenario, no funding will be provided, and there will be no way to open the museum on June 14."

"We have never operated a museum before. The doors will somehow open in June, but we do not know how many visitors will come because we also need to market and promote the museum, and for that we need additional staff," he added.

"The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs has not told us we will receive nothing, but we have not received any confirmation about next year's budget, even though we informed them how much funding is needed to open the museum. We requested €2.4 million to complete the exhibition in full," Andreller said.

According to Andreller, the ministry has also not indicated when information about next year's budget will become available or how much funding the museum could expect to receive.

"The relevant regulation has not yet begun moving through the ministry," he said.

In an effort to raise additional funds, the museum has begun collecting donations through its website.

The construction site of the Patarei Museum for the Victims of Communism in Tallinn. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

No extra funding made available

The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs acknowledged that it has no funding available for the museum's operating support and plans to provide resources on a project-by-project basis. The amount available will be determined after the state budget is approved.

"Next year's state budget cuts affect all ministries and government agencies. Unfortunately, foundations that receive sectoral support from the Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs are not exempt," said Rein Oidekivi, the ministry's head of strategic communications.

Oidekivi noted that the museum's budget for next year will become clear after the Riigikogu adopts the state budget.

"Under amendments to the State Budget Act that took effect on December 29, 2025, the Estonian Institute of Historical Memory Foundation must apply for project-based funding instead of receiving its previous operating grant," he added.

Patarei Sea Fortress is being rehauled and repurposed into a museum. March 2025. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Oidekivi said it has been clear for some time that the exhibition, originally planned years ago, could not be completed in full by opening day.

"Prices for services and other direct and indirect costs have risen significantly in recent years, and the ministry cannot find additional funding. Parts of the planned exhibition and necessary technical solutions will be completed in the coming years as financial resources become available," he said.

The international design competition for the museum, held in spring 2018, was won by Japanese architect Shuhei Endo with the proposal "Red Erosion." Before the extensive renovation began, the east wing of Patarei opened in 2019 with the popular temporary exhibition "Communism Is Prison."

In September 2024, the future museum's cornerstone was ceremonially laid. The opening was originally planned for June 14 this year, the 85th anniversary of the June deportations, but was postponed by one year.

World.title: Expert on US midterms: Trump's low approval rating hard to recover from
World.content:
Speaking to "Välisilm;" Arras, an election and political communication expert, noted the Democrats' chances of securing a majority in the House of Representatives at least are high.

President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen into negative territory, making his political future difficult, but much depends on voter turnout, she wen ton.

How likely is it that the Democrats will get a majority in both chambers?

Various prediction models and analysts have put this possibility at rather high. If we are talking about both chambers, that estimate is perhaps a little lower, but when it comes to the House of Representatives, estimates range between 80 and 90 percent that it is achievable. Whether it will also happen in the Senate – there the probability is 50–60 percent, and in some assessments a little higher. But it seems that change is coming.

But couldn't these opinion polls also be wrong in some way? If, for example, the Democrats for some reason do not turn out to vote, the result could still be that the Republicans retain their majority.

Predictions are always just that, predictions, while actual voter behavior will only become clear on election day, as has always been the case. I would say that the main thing to watch out for is which will prevail: money or voter turnout, since the Republicans have considerably more money invested in the campaign – that figure has already exceeded the $1 billion-mark. At the same time, studies indicate that Democrats have much greater motivation to go out there and vote. Dissatisfaction with Trump is running very high, and dissatisfaction, as we know, is a very strong motivating factor for voter mobilization.

We know how Donald Trump reacted when he didn't get the Nobel Peace Prize, or when he doesn't get all the medals and trophies. So how will he take it if he loses this?

He has already been asked that question, and I think he said, with his usual arrogance, that 'I can still veto', meaning that he can continue to veto everything that is decided against him. He certainly won't simply accept defeat.

Another thing worth watching for is whether, and to what extent, Republicans will begin challenging the election results. The first situation of this kind is already unfolding in some states, and there will certainly be more. I believe we may see this kind of deep-state narrative and questioning of the legitimacy of the elections, though of course only if he does not get a result favorable to him.

Are the Democrats prepared for the possible outcome that they might win? Do they have any outstanding leaders in sight, are they ready to start torpedoing everything the Republicans do? We could say that this might lead American life down a path of turmoil, but on the other hand, at least we would see some change.

The Democrats have been part of U.S. politics for just as long as the Republicans, so there is surely some readiness among them, and at the moment there is certainly also a greater desire to do something. At the same time, we cannot really state that there is one clearly established leader today. The Democrats are still in a period of testing the waters to understand who could potentially become their next presidential candidate, and the next elections are in 2028. I believe the results of these midterm elections will also reveal quite a lot about how the balance of power within the Democratic Party will develop.

How can it be that in a country like America, where so many people live, where democracy prevails, where it is basically possible to scramble your way into any position, they cannot find a single outstanding candidate everyone can agree on?

I think the key word is interests. Interests exist both between parties and within parties, and there are surely quite a few people within the Democratic Party who want to be number one themselves. That is why they are testing the waters. It has also been said of Kamala Harris that she could potentially give it another try. But within certain groups in the Democratic Party, there is considerable strong sentiment among those who, after she failed once already, no longer believe in her. On that basis, one would not expect her to run again, although there is talk about her doing so.

So what, ultimately, is it about Donald Trump that has disappointed the voters, including Republican voters, the most? Here we imagine it is the Strait of Hormuz crisis, perhaps we also think about Ukraine, but what is it that has now disappointed Americans?

The biggest concerns are actually domestic ones, but these domestic concerns largely stem from those same issues. Inflation is one of the main concerns. On the subject of inflation, I looked at a recent survey – nearly 75 percent of people say they are highly dissatisfied with how Trump has handled this issue.

The same applies to immigration, where he has made rather abrupt decisions that have affected certain voter groups. In light of this, it is certainly worth watching constituencies with Latin American backgrounds and Latino voters. That is another major source of dissatisfaction, and certainly the war in Iran and everything related to it in the energy sector are under very strong criticism. This may also be one of the reasons why – although there was talk at one point that he might take some more active steps toward Iran again before the elections – I do not believe that will happen. But at the same time, there can always be surprises. Simply looking at the dissatisfaction in this area, it is very unlikely that they would do anything immediately before people go to the polls.

Donald Trump is in his second term, and essentially the president no longer has to worry about anything. He can do whatever he wants as he doesn't have to think about not being elected next time. Is losing even a substantial issue for him?

Looking at how he has operated so far, we cannot be certain that he himself believes this is his final term in office. I say this half-ironically, but given his conviction that he can still accomplish great things, and that he is also pursuing the Nobel Prize, in light of all this... I believe he may still see that he has something to lose, so he certainly does not regard this fight as an easy one.

Even if things now turn out such that the majority in the Senate or the House of Representatives shifts to the Democrats, things will not be easy for them. Even if you have a small majority, in the Senate, for example, they would need at least enough additional votes to be able to end obstruction in the first place. They need at least 60 seats.

If we look at these election results now, it is said that they need only five or six votes to achieve a majority, but those five or six votes or seats will not actually change the bigger picture much for the Democrats. So what is more likely to happen is that Trump will continue operating as he has so far. There will be an even greater deadlock and trench warfare, but no results will actually be achieved, which in turn will probably lead to the American people being even more dissatisfied than they already are today.

How might Donald Trump, if he loses, take it out on the rest of the world? We know he has a habit of doing that.

He has made various attempts regarding Ukraine, as we have seen. That is certainly one area where he can continue along that path. Another is something he has been somewhat threatening to do, where he has become friendlier with various autocratic countries than the democratic world considers reasonable or thinks he should be at all – that is certainly another direction.

Iran also cannot be overlooked in any way, because energy is one of his strategic objectives. If we look, for example, at the decision he signed a year ago launching a major artificial intelligence development program, one of its cornerstones, alongside technological dominance, was also securing energy and its supply.

Where might we now expect the biggest surprises in this spectacle?

Certain states should be watched: Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Michigan and Maine. These are said to be the six main states where the numbers currently indicate that the Democrats are very likely to be able to achieve some kind of breakthrough. These will become decisive, but it is certainly also worth watching voters in large cities and suburbs, who are usually unpredictable in their behavior. Whether and how actively will they turn out at all? They are also among those most strongly affected by inflation, and the same applies to rural areas. There could be surprises in turnout there – specifically, which side sees an increase in turnout.

A Democratic victory in Texas... He will certainly comment on that somehow, he will have something to say to the people of Texas about it.

If that should happen, then that is certainly one state where I would predict that the election results will be called into question. Presumably someone will have had their fingers in the till there.

If there is a defeat, could we also expect something similar to the Capitol riot?

I would like to hope not. So far, I have not really seen analyses from American analysts suggesting that this is considered likely. But Trump has surprised me before as well. At present, I would not really expect it to happen again.

It has also been said that there are fears he will start weakening NATO as well.

NATO is certainly one of the critical issues to watch. If he really takes offense to the depths of his soul, then Ukraine, NATO and liberal democratic principles are also things that will certainly come under attack.

If the election results turn out so that the Republicans win in both chambers, will we, along with the rest of the world, view it as though the elections were rigged?

I do not believe we will, because certain processes in that country are still functioning, and I think going along with the same kind of dubious theory does democracy no good whatsoever.

But we will certainly be seeing a very confident Trump, who will thump his chest and say that everything he has done so far has been right and that he must continue in the same way. However, he still has a problem, because according to the latest surveys, his rating today is minus 20, minus 30, meaning that the net figure is negative. When politicians' approval ratings fall into negative territory, it is generally very difficult to recover from that. Regardless of Trump, the Republicans would still like the next president to come from their own party, so what may happen instead is that a problem eventually emerges within the Republican Party itself.

Background:

The midterms are today, November 3. All 435 members of the House - the lower chamber of Congress - will be elected. Meanwhile, 35 of 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber, will also be up for grabs, prompting speculation of Trump and the Republicans losing their majorities in both the house and the senate.

World.title: Iraq and Chevron agree on West Qurna 2 terms, aim year-end signing
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Ministry of Oil stated on Tuesday that it has achieved an agreement with US energy giant Chevron on major points related to the West Qurna 2 oil field development contract, opening the way for a formal signature by the end of 2026.

The statement came during a meeting on November 3 between Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair and Chevron’s Vice President of Business Development, Joe Cook, to discuss the big oilfield.

The two sides also agreed to continue conversations for developing the Nasiriyah oil field and four more exploration blocks, which may increase Chevron’s role in Iraq’s energy sector.

The move comes at a crucial moment for Iraq, as the nation strives to deepen connections with Western oil corporations despite rising pressure on its energy industry due to interruptions in oil shipments caused by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Over the last six months, Iraq has increased collaboration with American and other foreign energy corporations in order to attract investment, modernize production facilities, and solve issues in the oil sector.

Khudair emphasized the government’s commitment to assisting Chevron and other American corporations working in Iraq, including reducing investment barriers and increasing engagement in the country’s oil and gas industries.

The Iraqi Oil Minister also emphasized the significance of American experience in oil field development, technological transfer, and training Iraqi experts.

Meanwhile, Chevron showed interest in forming a long-term collaboration with Iraq, namely via the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects.

While agreement has been achieved on many sections of the West Qurna 2 contract, the actual development contract has yet to be finalized, with both parties aiming for completion by the end of 2026.

The development signals a key step toward increasing American engagement in Iraq’s oil industry as the government seeks to rebuild its energy sector and deal with lingering export issues.

World.title: De Miguel death ‘shocking’: Real Madrid’s Mourinho
World.content:
Athens – Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho said on Tuesday the tragic death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel following a heavy on-pitch collision was “shocking”.

Tenerife’s De Miguel died on earlier on Tuesday after being put in intensive care on Monday.

The 30-year-old was clattered by FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono in a Spanish second division match, which was subsequently abandoned.

Spanish media said De Miguel suffered cardiac arrest and was resuscitated, before his death the next day in hospital.

Madrid held a minute’s silence before training on Tuesday in honour of De Miguel.

“I think it’s something very shocking for the world in general, so imagine for the world of football, for people like us who are on the pitch competing every day,” Mourinho told reporters.

“It’s hard, it’s sad. Obviously, all our words and feelings go out to the family and friends of the player who passed away, and I also think this has to be a very, very, very difficult moment for the other player (Owono) involved in the situation.

“It’s sad for everyone.”

Equatorial Guinea goalkeeper Owono had raced into the middle of the pitch to try and clear the ball, colliding with De Miguel. The Andorra stopper was sent off.

Mourinho’s Real Madrid face AEK Athens in the Champions League on Wednesday. Los Blancos have three wins from three so far in the league phase.

The veteran Portuguese coach said winger Vinicius Junior would start, amid a four-match domestic suspension.

Yan Diomande has excelled in Vinicius’s absence, while Brahim Diaz, Arda Guler and Endrick are also competing for minutes in Madrid’s star-studded attack, which also features France superstar Kylian Mbappe and England’s Jude Bellingham.

Mourinho insisted having so many talented players was no issue.

“We have a lot of quality players — having many players is never a problem for me, the problem is having few,” said Mourinho.

“The problem is not having options. Having many is good. Diomande is a player who can play on both wings, Brahim is a player who can play on both wings, Endrick more on the right but also on the left.

“Vini, of all of them, is the one who is best suited to play on the wing, on the left wing. We know that.”

World.title: BMW issues second profit warning in a year
World.content:
Frankfurt – Premium German carmaker BMW issued its second profit warning for the financial year on Tuesday, citing costs related to job cuts as well as a production ramp-up.

The core profit margin at the cars business was now seen at between minus 0.5 percent to plus 0.5 percent in 2026, BMW said, meaning it could make an operating loss in its key activity.

That compares to a core profit margin of between one and three percent which the Munich-based manufacturer expected back in June, itself a cut on expectations at the start of the year.

Like its peers, BMW has struggled with cutthroat competition and falling demand in China, the world’s largest car market.

Competitors Mercedes-Benz and Volkswagen have both also issued profit warnings this year and, like BMW, plan job cuts to bring costs down.

In its latest warning, BMW said its redundancy program was moving faster than expected, resulting in bigger-than-anticipated severance payments for the final quarter of the year.

“The company intends to leverage the momentum generated by its workforce restructuring program to expand its organizational and process realignment more quickly,” it said.

“The reduction in management functions will be implemented faster than announced,” it added.

Strong demand for new models based on the firm’s Neue Klasse platform meanwhile meant the company would incur charges to bring in extra shifts, it said.

Car and motorbike deliveries for the year are nevertheless expected to fall more steeply than expected, BMW said.

Across its brands — which apart from the namesake include Mini and Rolls-Royce — BMW last year delivered a total 2.46 million vehicles.

BMW reports its results for the third quarter on Wednesday.

World.title: Bomb threats disrupt Europe flights
World.content:
London – About 10 European flights were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday, forcing the brief closure of a Warsaw airport and the scrambling of air force planes in Rome, authorities said.

No explosives were found, despite extensive searches on the ground after the planes all took off and landed safely in different European cities just several hours apart.

Irish budget carrier Ryanair appeared to be the worst hit, with four of its flights to different destinations being targeted.

London’s Metropolitan police confirmed it “was made aware of threats… against four aircraft due to depart from or arrive at Heathrow Airport” Tuesday, one of Europe’s busiest air hubs.

It gave no further details, but also said there was a further warning about a flight at Manchester Airport.

Following checks “no security issues were identified”, the Met police added.

Two bomb warnings targeted planes heading to the Polish capital Warsaw, including an SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and one from Heathrow operated by Polish airline LOT, Polish airport authorities said.

Aena, the Spanish airport operator, confirmed an emergency protocol was activated “due to a bomb alert” on a Ryanair flight which landed at 10:30 am (0930 GMT) from Manchester at Murcia in southeastern Spain. The plane arrived without problems.

Other Ryanair flights from Lisbon to Rome, Dublin to Rome, and Dublin to the Bulgarian capital of Sofia also received warnings.

Italian air force jets were scrambled to escort Ryanair flight FR9611 from Dublin as it landed at Rome-Fiumicino at 10:45 am (0945 GMT), Rome Airport said in a statement.

Anti-bomb procedures were also put in place when an earlier Ryanair flight arrived at 9:40 am (0840 GMT) at the airport. “Checks on passengers, luggage and the plane were all negative and the alert was lifted,” the statement added.

A Wizz Air flight from Bergamo, Italy, was inspected after landing at 0910 GMT in the Bulgarian capital Sofia following an alert, a Bulgarian interior ministry spokesperson told AFP.

The incidents all come after fighter jets were scrambled on Monday when a Wizz Air flight from London’s Luton airport to Sofia was diverted following a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

– Airport briefly shut –

Scandinavian Airlines said it could “confirm that a threat has been made against flight SK751 between Copenhagen and Warsaw” but the plane landed Tuesday without any problem.

It arrived at Warsaw’s Chopin airport, which closed one runway as the plane underwent a security inspection, but no explosives were found.

The LOT flight, which had also been scheduled to arrive at Chopin, was diverted to the Polish capital’s other airport, Warsaw Modlin.

Authorities closed that airport following the alert, but the Boeing 737 MAX also landed safely. “Nothing was found,” Modlin airport spokesman Adam Szablowski told AFP.

Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said on Facebook that on Monday NATO’s air defence alert service had issued an alert for a Wizz Air flight from London’s Luton.

“The Hungarian Defence Forces’ Gripen fighter jets took to the air within minutes and ensured the safe landing of the passenger aircraft in Budapest,” he said.

World.title: Baghdad revives Iraqi Jewish heritage with historic museum opening
World.content:
Baghdad – Dozens of visitors have begun flocking to a new museum opened by Iraq’s Jewish community, the first of its kind, amid ongoing efforts by the minority to preserve its heritage.

Last month, the Shamash Jewish Museum opened inside a former Jewish school that was founded in 1928 on Baghdad’s al-Rashid street, in the heart of the capital.

“It’s the only museum in Iraq belonging to the Jewish community,” Ammar al-Tamimi, lawyer for the committee of Iraqi Jews that manages the community’s properties, told AFP.

The Jewish community in Iraq was once one of the largest in the Middle East, numbering more than 130,000 people in the 1940s, and traces its history back 2,600 years.

But today there are only a few dozen Jewish residents remaining, most of them in the Kurdistan region.

The museum, with its large wooden entrance topped by menorahs and stained-glass geometric patterns, consists of a hall displaying antique documents and photographs of Iraqi Jews, along with old school certificates, and has begun to attract local and foreign visitors.

Its walls are adorned with photos of prominent Jewish figures, including Iraq’s first finance minister Sassoon Eskell (1860–1932) and physician Dhafer Fouad Eliyahu (1960–2021), who was well known in Iraq for providing free services.

The Shamash Jewish School, started by Yaqub Shlomo Shamash nearly a century ago, offered an English-language curriculum to students from various communities, and in particular Jews.

The government confiscated the property in the 1970s and converted it into a public school, until a court ruling returned it to the community in 1992, according to Tamimi.

Efforts to revive the school faced successive setbacks: sanctions in the 1990s, the US invasion of 2003, sectarian clashes in 2006 and 2007, and the rise of the Islamic State group between 2014 and 2017.

But as Iraq finally begins to experience relative stability, accompanied by a growing thirst for culture and entertainment, Jewish community leaders led by Khalida Fouad Eliyahu, 63, have started bringing their sites back to life.

– Restoration efforts –

Visiting the museum, which he described as “important for remembering Jewish history and civilisation”, 74-year-old Ramzi al-Saadi recalled his Jewish neighbours as a child on Baghdad’s al-Kifah Street.

“They were kind, simple people who never harmed anyone,” he told AFP.

Today, fewer than 50 synagogues and Jewish sites remain in Iraq, most of them in Baghdad and Hilla, the capital of Babylon Province, to which large numbers of Jews were forcibly taken in what became known as the Babylonian Captivity in the sixth century BC.

Tens of thousands of Jews left the country following a deadly 1941 massacre known as the Farhud, when mobs killed over 100 Iraqi Jews, and after the establishment of the state of Israel in 1948.

For years the Iraqi Jewish community has been working to restore its shrines and synagogues, which have suffered from severe neglect, and many of which were turned into warehouses or destroyed during the wars that have plagued Iraq.

World.title: US midterms: the races to watch
World.content:
Washington – Americans voted Tuesday in midterm elections to decide whether President Donald Trump’s Republicans retain control of Congress or spend the final two years of his term confronting Democratic majorities.

High living costs, the war with Iran and Trump’s poor approval ratings have helped Democrats expand the electoral map, with unusually tight contests even in Republican strongholds.

But polling errors, redrawn districts and record campaign spending make the outcome uncertain.

– The arithmetic –

Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the upper chamber of Congress, as a 50-50 tie would leave Republicans in charge through Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives are contested. It is currently made up of 218 Republicans and one Republican-aligned independent, 214 Democrats, and two vacancies.

Democrats need at least 218 seats in the lower chamber to clinch a majority in the new session.

– Senate: eight battlegrounds –

North Carolina: The state’s Democratic ex-governor Roy Cooper faces Republican operative Michael Whatley in a bid to flip the seat being vacated by retiring Senator Thom Tillis, a vocal Republican Trump critic.

Strong polling for Cooper prompted both parties to shift some spending elsewhere, but the outcome is key for Democrats.

Texas: Democrat James Talarico, a Christian progressive, faces Trump-backed state Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose controversies have helped turn a longtime Republican stronghold into a closely watched contest. Paxton retains a loyal conservative following and enormous outside financial support.

Ohio: Former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown seeks a comeback against Republican Jon Husted, who was appointed to replace Vance when he became vice president. Among the country’s most expensive races, it’s also a test of whether economic discontent can shift a state that has moved sharply rightward.

Maine: Republican Susan Collins faces former state Senate leader Troy Jackson. She has repeatedly survived difficult elections in a state that votes Democratic for president.

Alaska: Former Democratic congresswoman Mary Peltola challenges Republican Daniel Sullivan. Her strong standing among voters has made another Trump-voting state unexpectedly competitive.

Iowa: Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek compete for retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst’s seat, while soaring agricultural and energy costs are prominent issues.

Kansas: Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton is challenging Republican Roger Marshall in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932. Tight polling has prompted Trump to campaign for Marshall.

Michigan: An important Republican pickup opportunity pits former congressman Mike Rogers against progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to fill the seat of retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters.

– House: watch the suburbs –

New York’s 17th district: Republican Mike Lawler faces Democrat Cait Conley in a Hudson Valley seat won by Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

Nebraska’s 2nd: Republican Don Bacon’s retirement leaves a competitive Omaha-area seat contested by Republican Brinker Harding and Democrat Denise Powell.

Pennsylvania: Republican incumbents Ryan Mackenzie, Rob Bresnahan and Scott Perry face closely watched Democratic challenges. Nearby New Jersey’s 7th district, where Rebecca Bennett challenges Republican Tom Kean Jr, is also in play.

Virginia’s 2nd: Democrat Elaine Luria seeks to reclaim the coastal seat she lost to Republican Jennifer Kiggans in 2022.

Iowa: Three Republican-held districts in the state’s east and center could provide an early indication of whether Democrats are making broad gains.

– Signs of a wave? –

For an indication of the scale of any Democratic advance, watch two Republican-held House districts in Virginia: the 1st, where Shannon Taylor challenges Robert Wittman, and the 5th, where former congressman Tom Perriello wants to unseat John McGuire.

A Democratic gain in Kentucky’s Republican-leaning 6th district, or unexpected defeats for Republicans in Florida’s 13th and Wisconsin’s 1st, would likewise signal a particularly broad electoral swing.

Conversely, Democrats face dangers of their own in redrawn districts, including Alabama’s 2nd, where Shomari Figures is defending his seat, and Texas’s 34th, where Vicente Gonzalez faces Republican Eric Flores.

World.title: Seen and heard at the US midterm elections
World.content:
Washington – AFP has deployed reporters, photographers and video journalists across the United States as American voters head to the polls for crucial midterm elections.

Here is a round-up of interviews on Tuesday at polling stations where voters agreed to share their thoughts about what was on their minds and motivating their choices.

– Hopeful Democrats –

With polling data suggesting the Democratic Party is on track to capture a majority in the House of Representatives and perhaps even in the Senate, many left-leaning voters said they were hopeful about the results.

“Two years ago was a really devastating outcome for me,” Emma Mondadori, a 39-year-old who works in philanthropy, told AFP in Brooklyn, New York, referring to President Donald Trump’s election.

“I’ve been really looking forward to this day where we get to have a say again in the future of our country… I’m cautiously hopeful, optimistic.”

– The cost of living –

With gasoline prices up by a third since last year and diesel prices nearly double — not to mention sharp food price inflation — everyday prices were on many people’s minds.

“It’s about the cost of living, gas prices, those kind of things. It needs to change for the everyday person, and I’m an everyday person,” Donta Comer, a 38-year-old project manager in Atlanta, Georgia, told AFP.

Tom, a 27-year-old businessman at the same polling station who declined to give his surname, agreed.

“Everyone, at least in my generation, is a little frustrated with the affordability crisis and gas prices and what’s going on abroad,” added the non-partisan voter.

– Leadership referendum –

Mid-term elections are typically seen as a form of referendum on the sitting president.

And few leaders have polarized public opinion as strongly as Donald Trump.

“I’m independent but I voted Democrat, I just wanted to go back into the culture of decency, integrity, honesty, and the rest follows,” Yan Cardineau, 59, told AFP in Austin, Texas. “If we lose that, it doesn’t matter how much money you make.”

– Immigration –

In his final pitch to voters, Trump has stressed his success in reducing immigration and stopping crossings along the southern border with Mexico.

While his tough stance plays well with his core supporters, others have been put off by the brutal tactics used by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.

“I am very concerned about climate change, school violence and the situation with people who still don’t have immigration status in this country,” Diana Alvarez, a 38-year-old Cuban-born attorney said in Doral, Florida.

“It’s tough for any presidency, but this one in particular has been a little violent and aggressive (with migrants) and I don’t think that was necessary.”

– Iran –

Trump’s most consequential foreign policy decision of his second term — the February 28 attack on Iran along with Israel — was referenced by several voters.

“It’s discouraging. Again, promises made, promises not kept. ‘No new wars’ was the mantra,” Wes Pyron, a 37-year-old who works at an environmental health nonprofit in Washington, said.

“I don’t understand what we’re doing there, objectives aren’t clear, priorities aren’t clear.”

– Fears of socialism –

Many Republican candidates and Trump have sought to portray their Democratic rivals as dangerous tax-and-spend Socialists intent on destroying American capitalism.

“A lot of today’s younger people think socialism is the way to go,” Daryl Ruley, an 84-year-old in Austin, Texas, told AFP. “They don’t understand history if they believe that’s the case.”

- Michigan –

In one of the most widely watched races for the Senate — in Michigan — Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed has made free universal healthcare and ending US support for Israel key planks of his platform.

The Muslim former medical administrator has been called a jihadist by Trump and has been smeared with accusations of sympathizing with Islamist groups such as the Muslim Brotherhood or Hamas.

“We just got to get it done because we all need help. I need help,” said Makeyla Borndes, a 51-year-old former teacher who was forced to retire after falling down a staircase.

She wore several El-Sayed pins on her green apron and neon pink socks.

World.title: Djokovic battles through Paris Masters opener
World.content:
Paris – Novak Djokovic battled from behind to beat Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5/7), 7-5, 6-1 in the first round of the Paris Masters on Tuesday.

For the 24-time Grand Slam winner, it marked a return to winning ways at ATP 1000-level tournaments for the first time since his run to the fourth round at Indian Wells back in March.

Djokovic also enacted his own bit of revenge on Vacherot in just the second meeting between the pair — the Monegasque downed the 39-year-old on his way to a sensational Shanghai Masters title last season.

More important for the veteran, however, were the further points he can gain in the French capital as he bids to earn his spot in the season-ending ATP Finals later November.

Djokovic is currently 11th in the race to the eight-man tournament in Turin.

His last appearance at the Paris Masters came three years ago, when he won his seventh title against Grigor Dimitrov.

“I’m very happy,” Djokovic said. “This is the year where I’ve got a lot of support (in Paris).

“I found a good groove in the end. I’m pleased about that, and I think it’s the energy created in the stadium — that’s what this year’s victory is all about.”

In an even opening frame, Vacherot got his nose in front at the end of an error-strewn first-set tie-break as he put together a run of four points to take the lead.

The 27-year-old kept up the momentum at the start of the second set, instantly breaking Djokovic to 30.

After getting on the scoreboard at 2-1, Djokovic called for a medical timeout during which he received a massage on his right shoulder.

The short stoppage seemed to break Vacherot’s concentration as he dropped his serve straight away.

On Djokovic’s second break point, Vacherot completely misjudged a routine return from his opponent and could only watch in disbelief as the ball bounced on the line right in front of him.

Vacherot then received treatment for a foot issue and soon found himself pegged back to one set-apiece as Djokovic displayed his trademark killer instinct to seize his first break opportunity in the 12th game of the set and send the match to a decider.

The 10th seed ground down Vacherot in his first service game to get his nose in front 2-0.

A second break of serve put Djokovic firmly in control and he sealed the victory with a backhand winner down the line.

He will next meet Rinky Hijikata in the second round.

– Rune out –

Holger Rune, who defeated Djokovic in the 2022 final, exited at the first hurdle in this edition as he continues his return from injury.

The Dane lost 7-5, 6-4 to Tommy Paul.

Former world number five Andrey Rublev went down in a third-set tie-break to Tomas Martin Etcheverry, while 15th seed Learner Tien battled past lucky loser Adolfo Daniel Vallejo in a three-setter.

Rising French star Moise Kouame was unable to recreate his Roland Garros heroics as the 17-year-old went down 6-3, 6-1 to lucky loser Nuno Borges, the Portuguese taking full advantage of his late call-up in place of Shanghai Masters champion Alejandro Davidovich Fokina.

But it was better news for 46th-ranked home player Quentin Halys, who eliminated Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery in straight sets.

French world number 68 Arthur Rinderknech — Vacherot’s cousin — also progressed through to the next stage, after Argentine 16th seed Francisco Cerundolo retired early in the third set of their encounter.

Later, the second round gets underway as US Open finalist and third seed Ben Shelton opens his campaign in Paris against Cameron Norrie, before 20-year-old Spaniard Rafael Jodar tests his mettle against former world number two Casper Ruud.

World.title: Judge needn't face strictures for typos in judgement: SC
World.content:
SC sets aside Rajasthan HCâs strictures against a trial judge over inadvertent errors in a judgment, ruling that the remarks were unwarranted as the errors did not affect the case outcome

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Some factual errors in a judgement delivered by her, allegedly due to a 'cut, copy and paste' job, had cost a trial judge dear, resulting in Rajasthan HC castigating her and sending her to a judicial academy for training. But Supreme Court has come to the judge's rescue and struck off the adverse observations against her, holding that criticising a judicial officer for inadvertent typographical errors in a judgement, which did not affect the outcome of the case, was unwarranted.A bench of Justices Sandeep Mehta and Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya allowed the plea of the judge and expunged the strictures and adverse remarks against her."Ex facie, we feel that the adverse observations and the strictures recorded by HC against the judicial officer were uncalled for and avoidable. These disparaging remarks and the strictures were recorded on the judicial side without affording an opportunity to the judicial officer to show-cause or to place her explanation on record before such observations and strictures were made, and hence, suffer from the vice of nonadherence to the principles of natural justice," it said.HC observed the judicial officer "had used the methodology of 'cut, copy and paste' and in all probability, the judgement had been scripted by the stenographer/clerk concerned and was signed without being read and corrected by the presiding officer as she failed to strike out the irrelevant paragraphs which related to the trial of the adult accused".The trial judge had passed two judgements arising out of the same case as one of the accused was a minor. After appreciating the evidence in both trials, the judicial officer pronounced separate judgements convicting both the accused of the charges against them and sentencing each to 20 years' RI.SC said it seemed that during the course of rendering judgements in the two cases, some extracts of evidence/numerical details from one trial were inadvertently incorporated into the judgement for the other.

World.title: Encouraged by response to defence of SIR, BJP plans next political push
World.content:
NEW DELHI: As the first phase of BJP's 'save democracy, remove anarchy' campaign winds down, its functionaries are encouraged by what they believe to be substantial support to their defence of SIR and appeared to be moving to seek to convert what appeared to be a challenge into an opportunity.

Simply carrying around a copy of the Constitution does not amount to supporting it. One's conduct must be constitutional," he added.



Targeting Rahul Gandhi, the face of opposition's campaign against EC and govt, Shah alleged Congress once supported 'Janatana Sarkar' run by Maoists and he has now himself made a mockery of Parliament by staging 'fake' parliament proceedings.

World.title: SC to define right to privacy of protesters in public places
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Tuesday agreed to examine the contours of right to privacy of people when they are part of a public protest as lawyers appearing for recent protesters in the capital claimed breach of privacy because of the deployment of CCTV cameras and facial recognition tools by Delhi Police.

Appearing for a petitioner, political activist and advocate Prashant Bhushan told a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana that deployment of facial recognition tools as well as CCTV cameras, and the use of data generated by them required scrutiny so that they were not put in the public domain or used for harassing young protesters.

Solicitor-general Tushar Mehta said CCTV cameras were installed for the safety of protesters.



He added that fears of anti-social and criminal elements mingling with protesters to cause damage to public property and resort to violence came true during CJP's "illegal" July 20 march to Parliament call. "It was primarily to ensure the safety of women," he said.

Justice Bagchi said CCTV surveillance may not per se violate the right to privacy but if that data was fed into a machine for facial identification and tracing history of an individual, then it may amount to breach of privacy.





"It has to be examined whether this action infracts privacy," he added.

Senior advocate Mahesh Jethmalani interjected and said the court was only determining the constitutional rights of protesters. What about the rights of innocent citizens whose daily lives and livelihoods got derailed by these protests, he asked and suggested that the court devise an SOP for protests to fasten liability on the organisers for loss and damage to public property and loss of livelihood.

The SC said the Identification of Prisoners Act, replaced by the Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022, empowers the state to identify people by using iris data and those provisions need to be kept in mind. The SG said though the case did not involve prisoners, the law does empower govt to collect data for interests of the state.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Justice Bagchi said, "When a person stands in a public place, what is his reasonable expectation?" The SG replied, "One cannot choose to protest in a public place and seek protection of privacy."

When Justice Bagchi said it was a competing right - right to privacy and legitimate state interest - Mehta said it was strange that protesters had no problem with scores of live TV channels broadcasting them or swarms of influencers making reels and uploading them on social media but had a problem with govt's CCTVs.

Mehta said no iris verification of protesters was ever done by police. The bench said police had said they had matched the IDs of people with NCRB database of criminals. "Does that amount to a legitimate state interest?" it asked. Mehta said after facial recognition, the person concerned with a criminal track record was investigated and called for inquiry.

The bench issued a notice on Bhushan's petition and tagged it with petitions questioning deployment of facial recognition tools .

World.title: Right to protest can't justify endless occupation of a site: SC
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

on Tuesday said no group, political party, NGO or civil society outfit could occupy a protest site indefinitely.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said there were competing fundamental rights right to carry on trade and business and right to free speech and expression when senior advocate Mukul Rohatgi, appearing for traders, said the court must restrain all parties, NGO and civil society groups from holding protests in Delhi for the next two months to enable businesses to resume and to ensure that workers got their due.

The court asked a tradersâ association, which has sought Rs 1,000 crore in damages due to protests by CJP and opposition INDIA bloc during the festive season, to implead the protest organisers in the case for determination of compensation and how it is apportioned if it is awarded.

Solicitor general Tushar Mehta said those who call for bandhs and agitations must bear responsibility towards compensating the loss caused to others.



The bench asked Rohatgi to make the individuals, organisations and political parties responsible for protests and the resultant closure of shops parties in the petition.

When senior advocates Menaka Guruswamy, Arundhati Katju, N Hariharan and others simultaneously argued that protests were part of the right to free speech and right of dissent in a democracy, the bench said, âThe right to protest and right to trade and business are both constitutionally recognised fundamental rights.





We are not talking about trade in the commercial sense.â

CJI Kant said, âWe are talking in terms of the source of livelihood of daily wagers, hawkers, rediwalas, sabziwalas â where will they go? Hence, a protest site must be identified which allows people to protest without hampering the livelihood of daily wagers.â The CJI emphasised that the right to protest was not an absolute right. âOne set of protesters cannot occupy a designated protest site for all times to come...

Everyone has a right to protest and they should be given a definite time period to protest...,â he added.

Mehta said, âCalling for a protest without permission and asking people to march to Parliament cannot be permitted.â On denotification of Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, Delhi Police commissioner Anurag Kumar said the decision was taken based on the recommendations of a committee constituted following the SCâs July 2018 order for regulating protests at Jantar Mantar.

World.title: EC: Okay to use Form 6 for re-inclusion in rolls
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Election Commission Tuesday clarified that no action will be taken against a previous elector, whose name is deleted from draft rolls published during Special Intensive Revision (SIR), who seeks re-inclusion by filling Form 6.

The declaration that the voter's name is being included in the electoral roll for the first time will not be liable for prosecution under election laws for making a false statement, EC said in a communication to chief electoral officers (CEOs) of states and UTs.

Recalling a Delhi HC order dated Oct 14 that held as "misplaced" the apprehension of an applicant, who argued that submitting Form 6 would amount to making a false declaration, EC directed that "no action shall be initiated under Section 31 of the R P Act by an ERO against an elector merely on the ground that the elector had been included in a previous electoral roll and has submitted Form 6 during the SIR process or afterwards, provided the elector is not already enrolled in any other parliamentary or assembly constituency and the declaration made is otherwise in accordance with law".



EC clarifies deleted voters can seek re-inclusion through Form 6 during SIR without facing prosecution for false declaration

Declaration prescribed under Form 6 has been in force since Aug 1, 2022: EC

Stating that submission of Form 6 for inclusion afresh under SIR or afterwards is not, by itself, false merely because the elector was previously enrolled, EC on Tuesday instructed chief electoral officers of states and UTs that no action should be initiated by electoral registration officers (ERO) against such electors under Section 31 of the Representation of the People (RP) Act, 1950. Section 31 of the RP Act provides for imprisonment up to a year or fine or both, for anyone making a false declaration during preparation or updation of electoral roll.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines





Certain previous electors, whose names did not figure in the draft electoral roll published during SIR, have been hesitant to submit Form 6 as they are also required to furnish a declaration prescribed in Form 6 that their name is being included for the first time in the electoral roll.

They believe that this would amount to falsehood in view of their previous enrolment, attracting Section 31. Stressing that the declaration prescribed under Form 6 has been in force since Aug 1, 2022, the poll body clarified that an elector whose name does not appear in the draft electoral roll may submit Form 6 to seek inclusion in the final electoral roll, âin accordance with the prescribed procedure,â both under SIR and afterwards, irrespective of whether such elector was enrolled previously.

World.title: A first, Bangaluru company tests expandable space habitat tech in near-space mission
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: An experimental inflatable structure designed as a precursor to future orbital factories and expandable space habitats has completed its first high-altitude flight test, taking Bengaluru-based Akashalabdhi Space a step closer to demonstrating technologies for building infrastructure in space.The company flew âa 250-litre rigidizable inflatable structureâ aboard a high-altitude balloon to approximately 30km, in a 25kg experimental mission conducted through the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research's (TIFR) National Balloon Facility in Hyderabad early on Tuesday (Nov 3).The flight carried two research payloads. The first, the Microbial Regolith Experiment (MRX), developed by Prof Aloke Kumarâs lab at IISc. It investigates microbial processes that could help consolidate regolith, the loose soil and rocky material covering the surfaces of the Moon and Mars, into construction materials.Biological methods of binding such material could eventually reduce the amount of building materials that future lunar and planetary missions would need to transport from Earth. The high-altitude flight provided an opportunity to expose the experiment to near-space conditions, with scientific assessment to follow after recovery.The balloon mission did not simulate sustained microgravity.Kumar said Tuesdayâs test flight will give them enough data and confidence to prepare for an orbital test. TOI was the first to report about Kumarâs lab building bricks for Moon and Mars using Lunar and Martial soil simulants.The second was an experimental perovskite solar-cell payload from Switzerland-based Perovskia Solar. The experiment was intended to assess how photovoltaic technology responds to low atmospheric pressure, low temperatures and changing solar illumination.During the test, one outcome surprised Akashlabdhi. Its CEO Siddarth Jena told TOI: âThe module, which was expected to sustain some damage during landing, absorbed the impact without the anticipated damage. The ability of the structure and its protective systems to withstand landing loads is important for future missions involving the recovery of experimental hardware and materials from space.âThe mission was designed to test how an expandable structure behaves when deployed from a compactly packaged configuration, inflated and subsequently rigidised to retain its shape without depending continuously on internal pressure. Such structures could eventually provide larger working volumes for orbital manufacturing, commercial space stations, microgravity laboratories and habitation modules without requiring equally large launch-vehicle payload volumes.At the time of writing this copy, the company was still awaiting confirmation of two parameters before declaring all mission objectives achieved. These concern the performance of the solar-cell experiment and whether the parachute deployment achieved the targeted terminal velocity of 5 m/second.The balloon flight also offered an opportunity to assess the behaviour of onboard electronics, power systems, sensors, autonomous controls and telemetry under conditions of low atmospheric pressure and extreme cold.At approximately 30km, atmospheric pressure is only 1-2% of that at sea level, while temperatures can fall to around minus 45-50Â° Celsius. These conditions provide an intermediate testing environment between lab experiments and spaceflight, although they donât replicate orbital vacuum, sustained microgravity or full radiation environment of space.The flight is part of its ANTARIKSHAB programme â TOI was the first to report about the programme â which aims to develop expandable infrastructure for future orbital manufacturing and habitation. The company is already looking beyond the balloon demonstration.Jena said the next major milestone is an orbital mission planned for March, using Skyrootâs Vikram-2 rocket. The proposed mission will carry a larger with the overall payload mass expected to be around 70kg. It will include two of the companyâs material-development experiments to be conducted in microgravity and a data-centre payload.Tuesdayâs flight provides the engineering data needed to refine the technology before it moves towards orbital qualification. It is an important intermediate step, rather than a demonstration of an operational space factory or an orbital re-entry system.

World.title: 'Deeply touched': PM Modi thanks Bhutan King for dedicating sacred stupa in his honour

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Tuesday expressed gratitude to Bhutan's King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck after a sacred Buddhist stupa was dedicated to him in Gelephu Mindfulness City, Bhutan.In a social media post, PM Modi said he was "deeply touched" by the special gesture of warmth and generosity shown by the King and the people of Bhutan, adding that he accepted the honour with gratitude on behalf of the people of India.He described the Jangchub Chorten as an enduring symbol of the shared spiritual and civilisational heritage and friendship between the two countries.In a separate social media post, the Bhutanese King said the 76th Stupa was dedicated to Prime Minister Modi on November 1, after 108 stupas were raised in Gelephu Mindfulness City.King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, along with India's Union minister for parliamentary affairs Kiren Rijiju, unveiled a plaque dedicating the stupa to Modi.The King said the dedication was an enduring symbol of his "profound appreciation" for PM Modi's unwavering commitment and India's steadfast support for the realisation of his vision for Gelephu Mindfulness City.The 108 Jangchub Chortens form part of Bhutan's effort to highlight its Buddhist heritage and spiritual identity through the Gelephu Mindfulness City project.The dedication of the 76th stupa to PM Modi adds a diplomatic dimension to the initiative, reflecting the close relationship between the two neighbouring countries. World.title: One move, two gains: NHAI to desilt Bihar rivers and build roads with excavated material
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In a move aimed at tackling

âs perennial flooding problem while creating assets for road construction, road transport ministry and NHAI will undertake desilting of rivers and water bodies across the state at their own cost and use the excavated silt and sand for road construction.

Under âNadi Sanjivaniâ (river rejuvenation) framework, which was signed between road transport ministry and Bihar govt on Tuesday, the first-of-its-kind initiative, will serve two purposes -- highway agencies will carry out dredging and will get construction material for free, and it will improve water flow of rivers to reduce the risk of floods. Under this agreement, 243 lakh cubic metres of silt will be utilised in 16 ongoing national highway projects and another 835 lakh cubic metres is proposed for 27 future projects.



Muddy water from Himalayas in Nepal flows into rivers passing through Bihar during rains, resulting in silt getting deposited in riverbeds, which causes floods every year. If the plan goes well, this problem would be addressed to a larger extent. âThe silt that was the cause of floods until yesterday will now become the foundation for development,â Union road transport minister

said after signing of the agreement.





He said this can be a template for other states to get construction materials from dredging of rivers and other water bodies. At present, highway builders get soil and other construction materials from far off places, which causes delay and pushes up construction cost.

In his address, Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary highlighted the stateâs vulnerability to recurring floods that cause losses to farmers, agricultural land, livelihoods and infrastructure.

âBihar doesnât face destruction because of its water but because of water from neighbouring nations and other states. Seven prominent rivers from Nepal pass through Bihar and if it rains in Nepal, Bihar faces destruction... There was more than 32% less rain this year, but the highest flood level (HFL) changed in three major rivers.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

HFL of Ganga was maximum in the past 200 years,â he said.

Choudhary said these were clear signs of deposit of silts in rivers and state govt quickly accepted the offer Gadkari made for desilting of rivers.
