It asks the Court to compel them to resolve the motion for reconsideration pending since 11 April 2024 and to docket the complaint, filed under Republic Act No. 9851 (the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity), and conduct a preliminary investigation,” said the petitioners.

On October 25, 2023, the Myanmar natives filed a complaint with the DOJ over the torching of their houses and the killing of their families in the besieged Chin state, located in western Myanmar. The Chin state pushed back against junta forces when the military coup ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.

But in retaliation, the soldiers went to their place and burned down the town. According to the Chin people, when their natives tried to put out the fire, they were shot and killed.

As of writing, the Philippine DOJ has yet to docket or formally act on the complaint.

It does not make sense at first to file a complaint in Manila for crimes that allegedly happened in Myanmar. But the petitioners invoked universal jurisdiction, a legal concept under which countries are obliged to prosecute grave crimes in the world due to the belief that all nations have equal duties to mankind.

The complaint is lodged under RA No. 9851, the local law that transformed international criminal law into a domestic law.

The law’s Section 17 states that Philippine “authorities may surrender or extradite suspected or accused persons in the Philippines to the appropriate international court, if any, or to another State pursuant to the applicable extradition laws and treaties.” (READ: PH may surrender suspects to international court, says DOJ)

According to the petitioners, the DOJ refused to act on the complaint because it read this section as requiring the accused to be present in the country.

“Mandatory universal jurisdiction means that when crimes of international concern, such as war crimes, are brought before Philippine prosecutors, the State has a legal duty, not a mere option, to investigate and, where the evidence warrants, prosecute them, whatever the perpetrators’ nationality and wherever they are. The petition traces this duty to the peremptory (jus cogens) prohibition of war crimes, which the Constitution makes part of Philippine law, and to Section 2(e) of the Act,” said the petitioners.

“Section 17(b) speaks of an ‘accused,’ a status acquired only when charges are filed in court; at the preliminary investigation stage, persons are merely respondents. The opening clause of Section 17 covers persons ‘suspected or accused.’ On the DOJ’s reading, the ban on double jeopardy would also protect only foreigners found in the Philippines, an absurd result,” they added.

The petitioners also raised concerns about the delay in resolving their complaint. They also invoked the constitutional right to the speedy disposition of cases and the guarantee of due process.

“The right to the speedy disposition of cases is not a courtesy. It is a guarantee written into Article III, Section 16 of our Constitution. Three years of silence is not neutrality. For a displaced population whose witnesses are aging, every month of delay is prejudice,” said Romel Bagares, co-counsel for the petitioners.

“If Section 17 is robust enough for the State to wield in other cases, it cannot be too weak for these Chin victims to invoke in theirs,” Gilbert Teruel Andres, co-counsel, added. – Rappler.com

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy at Crossroads After 5 Years of Failure
World.content:
China’s Myanmar policy rests on a central assumption: that the military remains the country’s decisive political and military force. That assumption may have been valid in previous eras, but Myanmar’s post-coup reality demonstrates Beijing has overestimated the military while underestimating the revolutionary movement that has emerged since 2021.

The revolutionary forces factor

Throughout Myanmar’s civil war since 1948, and again after the 1988 pro-democracy uprising, successive revolutionary movements have failed to establish dominance, leaving most of the country in control of the military. Beijing has shaped its Myanmar policy accordingly, viewing the military as the guarantor of stability in an otherwise fractured nation.

Yet Myanmar after the 2021 coup bears little resemblance to either of those earlier periods.

The political and military balance has shifted dramatically. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA), Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Arakan Army (AA), Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), and Chin and Karenni resistance forces have emerged as formidable military actors capable of seizing and controlling large swaths of territory.

Even the Karen National Union (KNU), weakened by decades of internal splits and defections since the 1990s, has regained momentum, recapturing numerous military bases and inflicting significant losses on regime forces.

Meanwhile, armed resistance has spread into the Bamar-majority heartland, posing an unprecedented challenge to central rule.

The National Unity Government (NUG) and its People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) have emerged as a major parallel authority, reinforced by cooperation with ethnic armed organizations.

China’s Special Envoy for Asian Affairs Deng Xijun has reportedly warned the United Wa State Army (UWSA) that the NUG will never be a genuine rival to Myanmar’s military. That judgement has historical precedent. Revolutionary movements that emerged after 1948 ultimately failed because of military and political mistakes coupled with weapons and funding shortages. Likewise, the National Coalition Government of the Union of Burma (NCGUB) and the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), which emerged after the 1988 uprising, never threatened military dominance.

Beijing has calculated that the NUG and PDFs will follow suit and collapse.

But today’s realities point in the opposite direction. Plagued by systemic corruption, declining battlefield effectiveness and shrinking troop numbers, the military has lost support among the Bamar majority amid growing public revulsion over its war crimes against civilians.

Resistance movement: Past and present

The post-1988 NCGUB enjoyed political leadership but little organizational structure on the ground. By contrast, NUG networks extend deep into local communities.

Meanwhile, the ABSDF lacked the strength to operate effectively in Myanmar’s heartland and depended on ethnic armed organizations for refuge. Today’s PDFs and Spring Revolution forces operate independently across Sagaing, Mandalay, Magwe, Bago and Tanintharyi regions, also pushing into Ayeyarwady Region and conducting urban guerrilla warfare in Yangon.

Their military expansion has been matched by broad support among rural Bamar communities. Ethnic armed organizations, meanwhile, increasingly credit PDFs and other Spring Revolution groups with contributing to their own battlefield successes. That combat strength is supported by a centralized command chain and disciplined organization. Battlefield setbacks and defections in 2025 barely dented the movement’s momentum and never matched the mass desertions seen within the Myanmar military in recent years.

While resistance forces still face constraints in weaponry and logistics, by historical standards they remain well equipped.

Also, while the NCGUB and ABSDF were bound by ideology, the link between the NUG and PDF is institutional and operational.

While the NCGUB and ABSDF subsided into political opposition groups within five years, the NUG and PDF remain a formidable military force — arguably the strongest and most expansive resistance movement in modern Myanmar history.

As such, China’s assessment that the NUG and its armed wing are not a serious rival to the military no longer reflects realities on the ground. In today’s Myanmar, it is impossible to understand the conflict without including the NUG and PDF in the equation.

Democracy and China’s concerns

If Beijing has underestimated the military significance of revolutionary forces, it also remains wary of their political agenda — particularly their commitment to democracy.

Yet democracy is hardly an alien concept in China. During its own revolutionary era, the Chinese Communist Party described its struggle as a “people’s democratic revolution” and promoted Mao Zedong’s concept of a “New Democracy.”

The fight against military dictatorship naturally carries democratic aspirations. But that does not mean importing a Western political model wholesale, nor would such a model be easily transplanted.

Myanmar’s revolutionary forces recognize the critical importance of relations with neighboring China. After all, long-term economic engagement with Beijing was also a cornerstone of National League for Democracy (NLD) government’s foreign policy.

New alliances

Chinese pressure has sidelined two major ethnic political and military alliances, namely the Federal Political Negotiation and Consultative Committee led by the UWSA and the tripartite Brotherhood Alliance. Yet new revolutionary coalitions have emerged.

One is the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), which brings together the NUG and major armed organizations including Kachin, Chin, Karen and Karenni forces. Another is the Spring Revolution Alliance (SRA), which unites anti-regime forces that emerged after the coup. Both alliances pursue political and military objectives, and coordination between them appears to be steadily improving.

The Arakan Army — which controls most of Rakhine State and remains the biggest thorn in the regime’s side — is forging deepening ties with both groupings.

The trajectory of once-isolated resistance organizations is thus becoming increasingly interconnected, gradually evolving into a broader political and military bloc. These organizations are indispensable not only to achieving peace and nationwide stability, but also to safeguard long-term China-Myanmar relations and Chinese interests in the country.

Weaknesses of revolutionary forces

The resistance continues to suffer gaps in institutionalization, chain of command, logistics and weapons supply, and unification. Yet these are offset by substantial public support, a reputation largely unstained by atrocities, and high internal morale.

Most revolutionary groups also refrain from the systemic corruption that characterizes regime rule. Those who do profit from drug trafficking or online scam operations remain exceptions rather than the norm.

Close public scrutiny and critical supporters generally ensures that revolutionary misrule is generally harder to conceal and easier to correct. Myanmar’s military, by contrast, exhibits many of the opposite traits and has also repeatedly failed to unite the country’s ethnic communities or deliver lasting stability.

China’s Myanmar policy vs Myanmar’s reality

Taken together, these developments expose two fundamental errors in China’s reading of post-coup Myanmar.

While Beijing justifiably views the military as a key actor in Myanmar’s future, it overestimates its ability to achieve stability in the face of an increasingly entrenched and unified armed resistance. A military-centric policy no longer reflects a landscape transformed since the 2021 coup.

The second error lies in the timing of Beijing’s intervention. China moved to shore up the regime as Min Aung Hlaing faced mounting pressure from battlefield defeats, economic crisis and growing dissent within the military.

Had Beijing waited for his removal before backing the regime, more pragmatic figures may have taken the military helm.

Instead, China’s hasty support strengthened hardliners around Min Aung Hlaing while sidelining moderates and internal critics. In effect, Beijing’s scramble to preserve the military prolonged the rule of a failing strongman. Desperate to salvage his diminished authority and prestige, Min Aung Hlaing has vowed to reclaim all territory lost to revolutionary forces. As such, the civil war looks set to escalate rather than ease.

China’s policy has yielded gains for the regime, most notably by pressing ASEAN countries to reengage with Naypyitaw. But it has come at the cost of entrenching Naypyitaw’s hardliners, the root cause of instability.

The generals’ flawed policies and spiraling military spending have opened the door to economic collapse and poverty, while systematic corruption has fueled narcotics trafficking and online scam networks.

Despite China’s support, they have failed to achieve the military, political, and economic stability that Beijing craves.

Time for a policy shift?

Recent developments suggest Beijing may already be reassessing its Myanmar strategy. While China remains Myanmar’s largest foreign investor, new investment in fiscal 2025-26 fell to just US$ 158.2 million. Large-scale Chinese investment and lending failed to materialize even after the junta rebranded as a pseudo-civilian government in April.

Meanwhile, China’s Special Envoy Deng Xijun has broken off from frequent visits to Myanmar, where he has not been seen since March. Likewise, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia, who regularly met Min Aung Hlaing and senior regime officials after taking up her post in August 2024, last met the junta chief in Naypyitaw on April 6, 2026.

The Chinese Communist Party regularly evaluates its policy outcomes. As pragmatists, Chinese leaders place considerable emphasis on results.

In Myanmar’s case, Beijing’s objective remains unchanged: stability. Yet stability remains elusive even as China’s core interests — including Belt and Road development and multibillion-dollar border trade — continue to face severe disruption. Under such circumstances, Beijing cannot afford to proceed with the status quo. While China’s core aim in Myanmar is unlikely to change, its strategic assumptions and methods must adapt.

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: Thai Military Chief Summons Myanmar Attaché Over Border Fighting
World.content:
Thailand’s Chief of Defense Forces General Ukrit Buntanont summoned Myanmar military attaché Brigadier General Win Thu Lin on Monday over fighting along the Thai-Myanmar border, warning the regime to exercise caution in its military operations.

The action was driven by rising concerns among Thai residents near the border, some of whom have staged protests calling for greater security after clashes and Myanmar regime airstrikes in Karen State injured a Thai person and damaged property on the Thai side.

During Monday’s meeting, the Thai defense chief emphasized the need to consider potential impacts on the safety of Thai citizens and their property, according to a statement from the Royal Thai Armed Forces Headquarters.

It stated that the discussion reflected a “shared commitment” to maintaining communication channels and promoting positive relations between the two militaries.

Thai officials also sent formal protest letters to Naypyitaw to prevent further escalation, Thai PBS reported on Tuesday, citing the chief of Thailand’s National Security Council.

Ongoing clashes between the Myanmar regime and the Karen National Union’s armed wings and its allies in Myawaddy, Karen State, have sent stray rounds into Thailand, while explosions have been felt across the border.

On October 22, a 40-mm mortar shell landed in Thailand and damaged two houses. On October 26, the Thai military deployed troops to reinforce security along the border and warned that it was ready to respond.

As fighting intensified in Min Let Pan Village in Myawaddy, spillover rounds injured a Thai citizen, prompting Thai forces to fire two warning smoke rounds back toward the Myanmar side on October 29.

Despite Thailand’s warning, Myanmar regime aircraft dropped two bombs on the KNU-controlled border checkpoint at Thaw Le Hta, opposite Mae Sam Laep pier in Mae Hong Son, Thailand, on October 31. The shockwaves shattered windows of buildings in Thailand, prompting the Thai Air Force to deploy two F-16 fighter jets to patrol the border.

Following the incident, a letter was leaked in which the Myanmar regime warned Thai businessmen to end contact with the KNU and to stop trading through Thaw Le Hta, which it described as a violation of Myanmar law.

Neither the Myanmar regime nor the KNU has yet released an official statement about the leaked letter.

World.title: America’s New Myanmar Strategy Puts a Price Tag on Peace
World.content:
For more than three decades, Washington’s Myanmar policy began with one question: how does the country get back to democracy? Under President Trump, that has changed.

The new “Integrated Country Strategy for Burma,” approved Aug. 31 and published recently, asks instead: what can Myanmar do for America? Its four goals are to stop scams and visa overstays, sell more American goods, broker peace by 2030, and push back against China.

That does not mean Washington has abandoned sanctions or opposition contacts. It means the embassy’s metrics of success have changed.

At times, the 11-page document reads like a scorecard: three commercial deals, triple Myanmar’s imports from the U.S., three peace forums, zero visa overstays. The embassy’s 2022 strategy prioritized restoring inclusive democracy. In the new one the word “democracy” does not even appear, nor do “political prisoners” or “airstrikes.” Human rights feature mostly as a benefit of stability.

Its most revealing line, on Page 9, says talks on “fiscal federalism and territorial demarcation…will create opportunities to access Burma’s bountiful rare earth resources and combat scam centers.”

There is nothing wrong with Washington pursuing its interests. But a country at war is not a market where one government can sign away the obstacles. In Myanmar, authority to sign agreements, control of territory and public consent rarely rest in the same hands, and this strategy confuses the first with the other two.

Assistant Secretary of State Michael Vance met Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Sept. 15-16, ostensibly to seek the release of American businessman Adam Castillo and discuss scam operations. Talks also took place in Tokyo in June and again in October. Some Myanmar-linked individuals have come off U.S. sanctions lists, though Min Aung Hlaing remains blacklisted. The generals have also made their case through a $3 million-a-year lobbying contract with DCI Group, later involving Trump ally Roger Stone.

No mineral deal can bypass China

Myanmar is a major source of heavy rare earths used in powerful magnets. In 2024, however, the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) took Pangwa and Chipwi, the heart of the border mining belt, from a military-aligned militia. Stimson Center researchers have documented mining expanding into other ethnic armed territories, including the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)’s.

Even if they wanted to forge a new deal with the U.S., the generals cannot hand over land they do not hold, nor would getting ore out of Myanmar by itself create an American alternative to China. The trade depends on Chinese buyers, routes, chemicals and processing. Almost all of Myanmar’s heavy rare earths are transported overland to China. No deal signed in Naypyitaw can replace a whole supply chain.

Asking the arsonist to fight the fire

On scams, Washington has a strong national-security case: Americans have lost billions to Southeast Asian fraud operations, some staffed by trafficked people forced to commit crimes.

But look at who protects the compounds. The most notorious epicenters of scam operations, such as Shwe Kokko and KK Park, grew up along the Thai border under the protection of Naypyitaw-allied armed militias. In May 2025, the U.S. Treasury sanctioned the Karen National Army, formerly the Karen Border Guard Force, and commander Saw Chit Thu for enabling scams and trafficking. Treasury knew that the militia had profited from its military ties.

In an Oct. 30 assessment, the Financial Action Task Force kept Myanmar on its high-risk list, citing scam centers. A law-enforcement deal with Naypyitaw might help individual cases but will not dismantle networks whose protectors profit from them. Washington cannot suddenly expect verifiable action against their finances and operators from the generals.

The human reality behind overstay numbers

The repatriation goal carries another danger. It seeks to eliminate visa overstays, a popular policy objective for Trump, by fostering closer cooperation with “Burmese authorities.” Yet Washington’s own travel advisory warns of arbitrary detention, punishment for criticism and military conscription in Myanmar, and the strategy offers no specific safeguards for dissidents, journalists, defectors or draft-age people facing return. Are overstay statistics to replace individual assessments of protection claims against these dangers that the U.S. itself has flagged? People fleeing persecution must not become bargaining chips.

Selling soybeans in a warzone

The State Department wants three deals worth more than US$5 million each and a tripling of goods and agricultural exports to Myanmar by 2030. In 2025, U.S. exports to Myanmar totaled $78.7 million, compared with $762.3 million in imports. The strategy blames import licensing and currency controls, again proposing talks with “decision-makers in Naypyitaw.” But these are not merely paperwork problems. They come from a regime that is short of dollars, prints money to pay for a war, and runs a banking system on the global watchdog’s blacklist. This is no emerging market waiting for American soybeans. It is an economy ravaged by the war these decision-makers in Naypyitaw unleashed.

Peace is not a box to check

Most troubling is how peace fits into this commercial plan. Ethnic and religious minorities, displaced communities and residents of mining areas need a say, not a place as beneficiaries of someone else’s deal. Without a federal government, there is no one in Myanmar who can govern, collect revenue, protect minorities and answer when armed men abuse civilians. Any peace forum is only as credible as the voices it allows in.

The strategy’s goal of reaching 3 million vulnerable people with humanitarian assistance is welcome. But access also depends on local authorities and civil groups whose futures cannot be negotiated in Naypyitaw.

None of this means Washington should stop pursuing its interests or categorically reject engagement with the military. Some channels can still free detainees, fight crime, and deliver aid. But the U.S. should maintain targeted pressure on military finances, arms procurement and jet-fuel supplies while continuing to engage seriously with the National Unity Government (NUG), Myanmar’s parallel pro-democracy government formed after the 2021 coup, ethnic armed organizations and local administrations, recognizing their different roles and political interests. Treating the generals as the principal brokers of Myanmar’s future would be a fundamental mistake.

America need not choose between its strategic interests and Myanmar’s democratic future. An “America First” policy could serve both: durable trade, credible law enforcement and secure mineral supplies depend on accountable power. The Trump administration needs to recognize that America’s long-term interests would be better served by a democratic, federal Myanmar than by continued military rule.

Nyein Chan Aye is a Burmese journalist based in Washington, D.C., who previously worked for the BBC and Voice of America. He writes on Myanmar, U.S. policy, China and regional affairs.

World.title: China’s BRI Plans Take Shape in Myanmar’s Rebel-Held Borderlands
World.content:
China’s long-standing plans to expand border trade and infrastructure links with Myanmar have stalled amid border instability and shifting power dynamics. But even as Beijing struggles to reassert control, two ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) in northern Shan State are taking steps that could advance its economic ambitions.

Chinese business interests and mineral extraction have drawn attention in territories controlled by the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) in northern Shan State. But drawing less attention is the strategic importance of these areas to Beijing’s China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) — part of its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

In early October, the MNDAA opened a new border-trade gate in Chinshwehaw. Further east, the TNLA is upgrading the border crossing in Namkham Township. Both developments effectively connect EAO-controlled territories to China’s broader cross-border economic plans.

Chinshwehaw: A strategic gateway

The new Chinshwehaw gate plugs into China’s long-standing plan for the Chinshwehaw–Lincang Border Economic Cooperation Zone (CBECZ) under the CMEC. The proposed zone would connect Myanmar’s Laukkai in the Kokang Self-Administered Zone with Lincang in Yunnan Province.

The CMEC route runs west from Kunming through Kokang to Kyaukpyu Port on the Bay of Bengal and is designed to grant China access to the Indian Ocean and markets in South Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. The CBECZ envisages a 200-square-kilometer cross-border development zone, with a new gate —now opened by the MNDAA — serving container and truck traffic and the existing gate reserved for passenger buses and cars. The plan includes export and import zones in Laukkai and Kunlong townships, factories in Kunlong, a bridge over the Salween River, upgraded highways, and interconnected economic zones, including the 125 Economic Zone near Laukkai.

The wider plan features railway and highway links from Kunming through Chinshwehaw, Kunlong, and Lashio. On the Chinese side, Lincang’s development strategy centers on Mengding’s Qingshuihe river port, with industrial parks also earmarked for border towns Nansan and Yonghe under a “One Zone with Multiple Parks” model. The master plan sets ambitious targets for cross-border trade and regional economic growth, but implementation was stalled by security and bureaucratic barriers during the Thein Sein and National League for Democracy governments. After the 2021 coup, the military regime revived the plan through reconstituted border economic cooperation committees and inspections of the 125 Economic Zone.

The MNDAA’s new gate marks a significant shift: infrastructure originally negotiated between the two governments is now emerging in territory controlled by an ethnic armed group. Although no formal agreement between the MNDAA and Beijing has been confirmed, the development suggests that control of crucial nodes in China’s cross-border economic plan has shifted from the central military government to ethnic rebel groups.

Mong Ko and Namkham: More border infrastructure

The MNDAA’s infrastructure initiatives extend beyond Chinshwehaw to other border territory it controls. In Mong Ko, the group plans a six-month, 2.3-million-yuan project to build an international bridge linking to the Chinese border town of Manhai. Since capturing Mong Ko in November 2023, the MNDAA has overseen improvements to local roads and infrastructure. However, residents complain that an influx of Chinese businesses has deprived local communities of economic benefits.

Similar developments are taking shape in Namkham Township, a strategic border town under TNLA control. The group is set to replace the existing Nongdao boat crossing to China’s Yunnan Province with a two-lane bridge for vehicles up to 100 tonnes. Construction of the bridge and border gate is scheduled to begin in December.

Nongdao — part of the CMEC’s Muse (Hosan)–Ruili (Jiegao) Border Economic Cooperation Zone — is envisaged as an international port and bonded agricultural-livestock manufacturing hub. Additional trade crossings are planned for Kyukok–Wanding, Kyin San Kyawt–Maimeng, and Manhero–Jiexiang, supported by road upgrades and new routes.

The Muse–Ruili CBECZ aims to establish an industrial, logistics, and import-export processing hub serving China’s trade with Southeast and South Asia. The plan targets regional GDP of US$6–8 billion and annual trade of $35–45 billion by 2030, with added service-sector value of $1–1.5 billion.

The long-term plan is to link five pairs of China–Myanmar border towns to establish a cross-border free trade zone covering Mangshi, Ruili, and Longchuan by 2040.

However, infrastructure development planned since 2018 has been stymied by border disputes and local opposition. Now, with the TNLA controlling Namkham and upgrading the Nongdao crossing, another component of China’s proposed strategic corridor looks set to proceed under an ethnic armed group rather than Naypyitaw.

Trade restrictions and changing border dynamics

While pressing its infrastructure initiatives, China has also eased import restrictions in some areas of northern Shan State controlled by ethnic armed groups.

Beijing restricted imports after the ethnic Brotherhood Alliance seized large swathes of northern Shan during Operation 1027 in late 2023, threatening the regime’s grip on power. In mid-October it reopened the gate to Chinshwehaw, allowing through construction materials, electrical appliances, and telecoms products. There are also unverified reports that entry has been granted to explosives and chemicals used in Chinese-run gold and mineral mining operations.

Imports have also resumed through the 105-mile trade zone and the Kyinsankyawt crossing, both under Brotherhood Alliance control. Coupled with the groups’ infrastructure projects, the trade resumption points to changing patterns of cross-border economic activity beyond the Myanmar military’s control.

While the armed groups are seeking to consolidate their administration and secure revenue from trade, China wants to maintain border access, connectivity, and economic activity. Though lacking formal cross-border agreements, conditions are now ripe for China’s economic plans to proceed through cooperation with the armed groups. This development threatens Naypyitaw’s dominion over both border trade and multibillion-dollar infrastructure investments.

On Oct. 28, regime chief Min Aung Hlaing accused EAOs of using border trade revenue to bolster their military capabilities, undermining the peace process.

Implications for China’s Myanmar strategy

These developments suggest three broader implications for China’s engagement with Myanmar and the future of the CMEC.

First, China’s economic corridor plan may no longer depend entirely on agreements with Myanmar’s central government. The Chinshwehaw gate opening and planned Nongdao crossing upgrade suggest that components of the CMEC can advance under cooperation with ethnic armed organizations. While Beijing has neither abandoned Naypyitaw nor officially transferred responsibility for its projects to armed groups, practical opportunities for cooperation with local border authorities are now present.

Second, if ethnic armed organizations succeed in developing and managing border and trade infrastructure under China’s connectivity plans, Beijing’s engagement with Myanmar could diversify from its traditional focus on central government to EAOs and other actors who control strategic territory. While not necessarily accompanied by formal recognition, such a shift could mark a multi-layered approach to pursuing Beijing’s economic and security interests.

Third, such diversification could place Myanmar’s military regime under pressure on two fronts: the battlefield and China’s changing economic, security, and geopolitical calculations. The regime has repeatedly vowed to reclaim lost territories but has little to show for its efforts. If Beijing continues to facilitate border trade through EAO-controlled areas, revenues crucial to sustaining the regime’s military campaign against resistance forces will decline further.

Meanwhile, Naypyitaw’s bid to restore relations with the United States and Japan may also prompt China to rethink its regime-centric Myanmar policy.

Beijing also has a strong interest in preventing instability along its own border. Renewed fighting would disrupt trade routes and threaten Yunnan’s security and economy. China must balance engagement with groups controlling the border and maintaining relations with Naypyitaw.

Ultimately, the future of CMEC may depend as much on Myanmar’s shifting territorial realities as on agreements between Beijing and Naypyitaw. As long as the central government cannot exercise effective control over key border areas, Beijing will need to work with the authorities that govern them in practice.

Athena Awn Naw is an expert on ethnic conflict in Myanmar, focusing on China’s expanding influence across economic sectors.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Ramps Up Civilian Airstrikes as ASEAN Envoy Visits
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime continued bombing civilian targets even as it hosted ASEAN’s special envoy last week, killing more than a dozen people and wounding over 50 across four days.

Special Envoy Maria Theresa Lazaro visited the southern Shan State capital of Taungyi on an October 28-30 humanitarian mission, meeting the regime’s foreign minister during her trip.

Meanwhile, The Irrawaddy recorded nine regime airstrikes from October 29 to November 1, resulting in 16 deaths and 51 injuries. Over half of the attacks occurred in Rakhine State, which is almost entirely controlled by the ethnic Arakan Army (AA).

On Sunday, regime warplanes targeted Rakhine’s Kyaukphyu, a hub for China-backed projects and gas pipelines, along with AA-controlled townships of Kyauktaw, Pauktaw, and Mrauk-U.

In Mrauk-U, five people including a baby were killed and nine wounded when cluster bombs shattered a temporary maternity clinic.

The clinic was established after a December 10 bombing raid destroyed Mrauk-U District Hospital, killing at least 33 patients, caregivers and medical staff and injuring around 70.

Sunday’s airstrikes killed at total of 12 civilians and injured 32 others across Rakhine, according to an AA statement.

They came two days after the Arakan Civil Society Charitable Organizations (ACSO) and a coalition of 70 local and international Rakhine groups called on the UN Security Council, ASEAN, international governments, and global humanitarian agencies to enforce a no-fly zone over Rakhine State.

In Karenni State’s Loikaw, three children were killed and eight injured when two regime fighter jets and a Y-12 aircraft bombed their school in Wanngawt village as holiday meals were being served on Sunday.

Any hope of a break in the bombing campaign as the regime pushes for regional reintegration was shattered the day Lazaro arrived. As the special envoy touched down on Wednesday, blasts hit Tawkyaunglay village monastery in Sagaing’s Chaung-U Township, where around 60 worshippers were gathered for Patthana chanting. The attack wounded a 57-year-old monk. Bombs struck a former prisoner-of-war camp in Chin State’s Hakha on the same day, but no casualties were reported.

On Saturday, an airstrike on a temporary shelter at Thaezalauk village monastery in Sagaing’s Homalin Township left seven displaced people injured. The attack came shortly after resistance forces captured the local regime outpost. Elsewhere in Sagaing, a woman was killed and three residents injured when a pair of gyrocopters attacked Duhtauk village in Salingyi Township despite the absence of clashes on the ground.

Human rights activists criticized Lazaro’s visit as bid to create an image of a cooperative, humanitarian-minded regime to mask the reality of daily civilian atrocities and mass displacement.

According to data collected by the parallel National Unity Government, a total of 6,467 civilians have died in regime airstrikes since the February 2021 coup.

World.title: Regime, Thailand Discuss Russian LNG Supply Route via Dawei
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime and Thailand have discussed importing Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) through Myanmar and sharing supplies to help meet growing energy demand in both countries, according to regime media.

The proposal emerged during separate meetings in Bangkok on Saturday between junta Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin, Thai Energy Minister Akanat Promphan and Russian Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov.

According to the regime, discussions focused on a trilateral energy cooperation framework under which Russian LNG would be shipped to Myanmar and distributed to Thailand. Officials also examined the possibility of building an LNG terminal in Dawei and utilizing existing gas pipeline infrastructure linking Myanmar and Thailand to transport imported gas.

The latest discussions follow Akanat’s visit to Naypyitaw on October 19, when he met regime chief Min Aung Hlaing and held separate talks with Ko Ko Lwin on expanding bilateral cooperation in the energy and natural gas sectors.

During those meetings, officials reportedly discussed plans for a Myanmar-Thailand-Russia energy trade network centered on the Dawei area.

The proposal has gained momentum in recent months. In August, Ko Ko Lwin met his Thai counterpart in Bangkok alongside prominent Myanmar oil magnate Michael Moe Myint, whose companies cooperate with the regime in the oil and gas sector.

The inclusion of Russia’s economic development minister in the latest round of talks suggests the three sides are moving to advance the Dawei-based energy trade initiative.

Analysts note that the interests of all three parties largely align. Myanmar and Thailand face growing energy needs, while Russia is seeking new markets for its abundant natural gas exports amid Western sanctions.

During Min Aung Hlaing’s visit to Russia in August, Myanmar and Russia signed memorandums of understanding covering the power and oil and gas sectors. Russian President Vladimir Putin said energy would remain a key pillar of bilateral cooperation and highlighted significant potential for LNG exports to Myanmar, including possible re-exports to third countries.

The junta has already signed several agreements with Russia covering fuel imports, including LNG, and says it expects to conclude an energy cooperation pact with Thailand in the near future.

The effort is also linked to the junta’s attempt to revive the long-delayed Dawei Special Economic Zone and deep-sea port project, which has struggled to attract investment amid political instability and Western sanctions.

During his Russia visit, Min Aung Hlaing described the Dawei deep-sea port, special economic zone, and energy cooperation package including an LNG terminal, oil refinery, power plants and gas-based infrastructure projects as strategic pillars of Myanmar-Russia economic cooperation.

For Russia, closer ties with Myanmar could provide opportunities to expand investment and access new markets in Southeast Asia, which Moscow expects would offset economic restrictions imposed by Western countries.

Min Aung Hlaing has repeatedly portrayed Myanmar as a reliable partner for Russia in Southeast Asia, telling Putin that Myanmar stands ready to support deeper cooperation.

Thailand has long been involved in Myanmar’s energy sector through major offshore gas projects such as Yadana and Zawtika. Since the 2021 military coup, Thai companies have become some of the most significant foreign investors in Myanmar’s oil and gas industry after the withdrawal of several Western firms.

The junta also awarded the Min Ye Thu offshore project, the first new offshore project approved since the coup, to Thailand’s Gulf Petroleum Myanmar Co., Ltd.

Located off the coast of Tanintharyi in southern Myanmar, the Dawei Special Economic Zone is envisioned as a strategic hub incorporating a deep-sea port, industrial estate, power facilities and transport infrastructure, while giving Thailand direct access to the Indian Ocean.

In recent months, both Min Aung Hlaing and his deputy Nyo Saw visited Dawei to inspect “regional development tasks”. Myanmar military Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin also toured military commands in Tanintharyi Region in June, stressing the need to secure strategic projects including the Dawei deep-sea port and key transportation corridors.

However, analysts say ongoing armed conflict and instability in the region remain major obstacles to the realization of the Dawei project and broader energy cooperation plans.

World.title: China Reopens Trade Through Border Crossings Controlled by Armed Groups
World.content:
China has lifted restrictions on the flow of key goods into territories along the border that are controlled by ethnic armed organizations with ties to Beijing, allowing fuel, construction materials, medicines and other previously banned imports to enter Myanmar.

Residents and traders say China has recently relaxed some restrictions imposed when the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) and Kachin forces seized key border trade routes during anti-regime Operation 1027 in 2023–4.

At the military regime’s request at the time, Beijing blocked the flow of construction materials, machinery, electrical goods, fuel, medicines and explosives through those crossings.

“In Muse, previously restricted items can now be imported through Kyin San Kyawt border gate,” a Muse resident told The Irrawaddy. “Restrictions remain in place at the Sinphyushin and Nandaw gates that are still controlled by the regime.”

At the Namhkam border crossing controlled by the TNLA, trade has not yet fully resumed. TNLA spokesman Lway Yay Oo said only food and household goods are being allowed in to help improve living conditions for locals.

“The border gates have not fully reopened yet,” she told The Irrawaddy. “The relaxation benefits people living in border areas, but whether the crossings are fully reopened depends entirely on the Chinese government’s policy decisions.”

She added that a full reopening of border trade would help reduce shortages of fuel and medicine in the region.

The cash-strapped regime is furious that it can no longer tax imports and tries to intercept them elsewhere if they make their way further inland. In a cabinet meeting on Oct. 28, putschist president Min Aung Hlaing warned that smugglers are indirectly financing armed groups by paying them taxes, thereby strengthening their capacity and obstructing his own “peace” efforts.

In northern Shan itself, Chinese products are now plentiful and relatively cheap, but once they pass through Hsipaw, Kyaukme and Nawnghkio and onward to Pyin Oo Lwin, Mandalay and Yangon, it is a different story.

Transport operators say frequent inspections, unofficial payments and cargo checks at checkpoints have increased both delivery times and transportation costs, pushing up prices for consumers.

One transporter cited the example of a car tire that sells for around 380,000–400,000 kyats in the northern Shan capital of Lashio but can cost as much as 850,000–900,000 kyats in Mandalay.

“If the regime genuinely wants to reduce prices for consumers, it can establish a customs checkpoint in Lashio and allow legal imports with proper tax payments,” he said. “That would improve the flow of goods and bring prices down.”

Instead, Min Aung Hlaing has urged his ministers to intensify the crackdown on “smuggling” and ensure that cross‑border commerce is conducted only through regime-controlled channels.

World.title: ASEAN Envoy’s Farce: Humanitarian Aid as Smokescreen for Regime Atrocities
World.content:
Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Special Envoy and Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro has staged a farcical “humanitarian mission” in Taunggyi, a safe city in a military-controlled part of Shan State, where there has been no fighting or war-related destruction since the military coup in 2021.

Meanwhile, her hosts, the Myanmar military junta, continue to send paramotors, gyrocopters and fighter jets to bomb villages, schools, hospitals, markets, Buddhist monasteries and residential houses, killing and maiming women, schoolchildren, babies and displaced civilians.

What Lazaro has done is a grotesque spectacle, a cynical manipulation of humanitarian aid and a shameful betrayal of the people of Myanmar.

Let me be absolutely clear: Lazaro is not an innocent diplomat who has been deceived or manipulated by the junta. She knows perfectly well what is happening in Myanmar. She knows about the daily airstrikes, the massacres of civilians and the deliberate obstruction of humanitarian assistance to communities most desperately in need.

She knows what she is doing. She has willingly played her part in this cynical, carefully choreographed farce.

The purpose of this theatrical humanitarian performance is to manufacture a false image of a cooperative, humanitarian-minded military regime and provide ASEAN with another opportunity to rehabilitate Min Aung Hlaing and lift its ban on the criminal junta’s political representatives attending the bloc’s summits.

The junta decided where Lazaro could go, what she could see and whom she could meet. She was not allowed to meet Aung San Suu Kyi, despite repeated requests from the Philippines. She did not meet representatives of the National Unity Government, ethnic revolutionary organizations, local administrations or the civil society networks delivering humanitarian assistance in areas beyond junta control.

The military controlled the stage. Lazaro knowingly played her assigned role. She happily posed for photographs. And the junta collected the political dividends.

Her photographs from peaceful, junta-controlled Taunggyi are part of a carefully constructed smokescreen intended to conceal the reality of Myanmar: daily atrocities against civilians, relentless aerial bombardment, mass displacement and the systematic obstruction of humanitarian assistance precisely where it is needed most.

I do not object to food reaching people displaced by the junta’s deliberate burning of villages and bombing of towns and cities. Every bag of rice matters to those who receive it.

What is outrageous is that ASEAN’s special envoy has played along with this farce, allowing humanitarian aid to be used as a propaganda instrument to whitewash the very military responsible for creating Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe.

What did Lazaro achieve?

No meaningful breakthrough in humanitarian access to resistance-controlled areas, where atrocities continue, hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced, and millions of internally displaced people remain beyond the reach of international aid. No access to Aung San Suu Kyi. No genuine engagement with all relevant stakeholders. No commitment by the military to stop bombing civilians.

Instead, the junta proudly announced that its foreign minister had discussed with Lazaro the restoration of Myanmar’s “original role and rights” within ASEAN.

There it is. The real political dividend of this entire farce.

ASEAN’s own Five-Point Consensus requires an end to violence and engagement with all concerned parties. Yet Lazaro allowed the junta to dictate the terms of her mission, select her interlocutors and exploit humanitarian assistance for its campaign of international rehabilitation.

We should refuse to pretend that this was merely another unsuccessful diplomatic initiative undertaken with good intentions. Lazaro was not simply a spectator in this shameful performance. She was an informed and willing participant. She chose to cooperate in a spectacle that served the junta’s political interests.

She cannot hide behind diplomatic language about dialogue, humanitarian assistance and constructive engagement.

While Min Aung Hlaing’s forces continue their campaign of aerial terror against the people of Myanmar, ASEAN’s special envoy has knowingly helped project an image of his regime as a legitimate and cooperative partner deserving renewed international acceptance.

Instead of exposing and confronting the perpetrators of Myanmar’s humanitarian catastrophe, Lazaro has willingly participated in a performance that helps polish their bloodstained image.

The people of Myanmar do not need ASEAN’s humanitarian theater. They need humanitarian assistance that actually reaches those most in need. They need protection from the military’s relentless airstrikes. They need ASEAN to stop providing diplomatic cover and opportunities for international rehabilitation to those responsible for their suffering.

Igor Blazevic is a senior adviser at the Prague Civil Society Centre. Between 2011 and 2016 he worked in Myanmar as the head lecturer of the Educational Initiatives Program.

World.title: Kazakhstan Retains Central Asia’s Top University Rankings as Nazarbayev University Climbs 62 Places
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has retained its position as Central Asia’s leading higher education system in the QS World University Rankings: Asia 2027, with three universities placing among the region’s top 100. Nazarbayev University recorded the country’s most significant improvement, rising 62 places to 139th.

The rankings, released on Nov. 3 by international higher education analysts QS Quacquarelli Symonds, feature 1,722 universities from 26 higher education systems across Asia.

Farabi University remains Kazakhstan’s highest-ranked institution, placing 46th, although it dropped eight positions from last year. Gumilyov Eurasian National University ranked 62nd, while Satbayev University took 89th place, down 10 positions.

Kazakhstan has 51 universities in this year’s rankings, including seven new entrants, giving it the 10th-largest representation among Asian higher education systems.

Nazarbayev University was the country’s standout performer, climbing from 201st to 139th place in its second appearance in the rankings. It recorded particularly strong results in research collaboration and international faculty.

Sarsen Amanzholov East Kazakhstan University also made notable progress, rising 64 places to 618th. Meanwhile, SDU University experienced the sharpest decline among Kazakh institutions, falling 149 places to 691st.

Strengths in internationalisation, challenges in research

Kazakhstan’s universities performed above the Asian average in seven of the ranking’s 11 indicators. The country showed particular strength in student mobility, employer reputation and faculty-to-student ratios.

Its strongest result was in outbound exchange students, where Kazakhstan scored 58.8 against the regional average of 22.6. The country also exceeded the Asian average in employer reputation, with a score of 38.8 compared with 24.9, and faculty-to-student ratio, scoring 52 against 34.6.

Farabi University ranked 12th in Asia for both faculty-to-student ratio and outbound exchange students. Nazarbayev University placed 24th for international research network and 26th for international faculty.

The results reflect Kazakhstan’s continued efforts to strengthen international links in higher education, including the expansion of foreign university branches. More than 30 foreign university branches have opened in the country.

Research performance, however, remains a major challenge. Kazakhstan recorded an average score of 3.8 for citations per paper, significantly below the Asian average of 35.2. According to QS, 97% of Kazakh universities recorded weak results in this indicator. The country also saw widespread declines in research productivity, measured by papers per faculty member.

QS Senior Vice President Ben Sowter said Kazakhstan continued to lead Central Asia, but the latest results highlighted the need to turn increased research investment into stronger academic impact.

“Nazarbayev University’s rise into the top 200 shows what a research-intensive, internationally connected university can achieve. The challenge now is to translate rising R&D spending into research impact across the wider system,” he said.

The government has been increasing its focus on research development, with spending on research and development more than doubling since 2023.

Kazakhstan’s position in the regional rankings

The University of Hong Kong retained first place in Asia for the second consecutive year, followed by Peking University. Tsinghua University climbed from ninth to third, giving China two universities among the top three for the first time since 2023.

The National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University, which shared third place last year, fell to sixth and eighth, respectively.

China led the region in the number of universities in the top 20 and new entries, while Hong Kong SAR had the strongest improvement rate among higher education systems with at least five ranked institutions.

The QS World University Rankings: Asia assess universities using 11 indicators tailored to the region, including academic and employer reputation, research performance, teaching resources, internationalization and student mobility.

World.title: Kazakhstan Sets Aside $ 14.3 Billion for Infrastructure and Social Projects Through 2029
World.content:
ASTANA – The Kazakh government approved an action plan on Nov. 3 to implement the president’s state-of-the-nation address, allocating around 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) for key social and infrastructure projects through the end of 2029.

The plan includes 96 measures across 12 areas and was presented at a government meeting by Deputy Prime Minister and National Economy Minister Serik Zhumangarin.

The funding will support infrastructure development, housing construction, utilities modernization, and the provision of drinking water and natural gas to settlements. The government also plans to launch the Halyktyk Kurylys infrastructure development program, which will prioritize the use of domestically produced construction materials and equipment.

“Around 6.5 trillion tenge will be allocated from the National Fund for key social and infrastructure projects, with quality control over the work. The plan also provides for the modernization of housing and utilities infrastructure, continued housing construction, and the provision of drinking water and gas to populated areas,” Zhumangarin said.

New airports, railways and roads to strengthen connectivity

The plan calls for expanding the country’s transport infrastructure. New airports in Zaisan, Katon-Karagai and Kendirli are scheduled to open in May 2027. Construction of another airport in Astana is expected to begin in June 2027.

The Bakhty-Ayagoz railway line is scheduled for completion by the end of 2027.

Road construction and reconstruction projects will continue on national and regional routes, including the Aral-Caspian and Kokshetau-Petropavlovsk highways. The government also plans to complete the reconstruction of all road border crossings and transition freight transportation to electronic documents, supported by an intelligent transport system.

Government targets energy security and critical minerals

The government plans to build new power plants, modernize existing facilities, expand coal-fired power generation and develop electricity transmission lines. The country’s unified energy balance is to be updated through 2035.

By the end of 2027, Kazakhstan plans to establish a strategic state uranium reserve and sign an intergovernmental agreement on the Moyinkum nuclear power plant.

A national system for managing critical mineral reserves is expected to be established by the end of 2026. In 2027, the government plans to introduce mechanisms to accelerate industrial and technological development and expand the data available on its unified subsoil use platform.

Agriculture and water management

The plan also provides for long-term financing for livestock development and agricultural processing programs, as well as support for domestic tractor and combine harvester production.

“Next year, we plan to ensure equal access for all agricultural producers to the infrastructure of agricultural logistics centers. The National Water Resources Information System is expected to be completed in March 2027,” Zhumangarin said.

Wages, education and social support

The plan provides for an increase in the minimum monthly wage from 85,000 to 110,000 tenge (from US$188 to US$243). Salaries of primary health care specialists working at local clinics are also expected to rise through additional payments based on years of service and workload.

A pilot project testing new digital approaches to assessing family well-being is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2026. The government will also begin public awareness efforts to introduce a needs-based approach to social support.

In education, authorities plan to develop an early identification system for children with special educational needs by the end of 2027. The government also intends to reduce teachers’ administrative workload, including by cutting the number of reports required through digital platforms and information systems.

World.title: Two More Amur Tigers to Join Kazakhstan’s Wildlife Comeback in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is preparing the next stage of its tiger reintroduction program, with two cubs expected to be released into the wild in 2027, Kazinform reported on Nov.3.

The cubs are undergoing adaptation in special enclosures. Their release will depend on their health, behavior, and ability to survive independently. The program aims to release around 10 tigers into the wild by 2033.

Specialists are assessing how many tigers the Balkhash Region’s ecosystem can support. They are monitoring the first tigers released into the wild to determine how well the animals adapt to their new habitat, said Sergei Aramilev, director general of the Amur Tiger Center.

According to Aramilev, the release of two adult Amur tigers into the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve was designed as a scientific experiment. The findings will help determine whether the area can sustain a stable tiger population and identify which animals should be selected for future stages of the program.

The first adult female Amur tiger, named Umit, was released on July 31 in the reserve in southeastern Kazakhstan. Equipped with a satellite tracking collar, she has been moving independently through an area once inhabited by the now-extinct Caspian, or Turan, tiger.

The second tiger, a male named Amur, was subsequently released into the reserve as part of the reintroduction program.

“By assessing how the tigers adapt, we will understand how suitable the territory is and what size of population it can support. Most importantly, we will learn which tigers should be selected for the further development of the program,” Aramilev said.

Researchers will monitor how the predators adjust to natural conditions, establish territories and hunt. The findings will help experts refine plans to restore the tiger population.

Aramilev highlighted that the project could serve as an example for other countries considering efforts to restore populations of large predators that have disappeared from their territories.

“This project sends a signal to the world. No country has ever restored a historically extinct species of large mammal, especially a predator. The scientific experiment taking place here will show other countries that it is possible,” he said.

Umit has shown positive signs of adapting to the wild. Her first recorded prey was a wolf, followed several days later by a wild boar. Her hunting activity during the first 10 days indicated that she was adjusting well to her new environment.

The program’s first phase is expected to run until around 2033, with about 10 tigers planned for release. The overall initiative is designed to span approximately 35 years and could be extended if successful.

World.title: Build! Once Again – Build: Kazakhstan’s Construction Program to Boost Growth, Improve Living Standards
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is preparing for a nationwide construction drive that will direct nearly 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) toward infrastructure development through 2029, as President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev calls for a new phase of economic modernization built around tangible improvements in people’s lives.

The initiative, known as Khalyktyq Qurylys or the People’s Construction program, will cover roads, airports, railway stations, power plants, hospitals, schools, rehabilitation centers, sports facilities and other public infrastructure across the country. The government is expected to begin implementing the program next year, designated by Tokayev as the Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction.

“The entire meaning of the People’s Construction initiative can be expressed in simple words: ‘Build! Once again – build!’ We must leave present and future generations not merely programs and concepts, valuable as they may be, but tangible results, above all social infrastructure,” Tokayev said during a working visit to the Karagandy Region on Nov. 2.

Economic background

Kazakhstan’s planned construction drive comes amid sustained economic growth and expanding activity in several key sectors. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, the country’s gross domestic product grew by 6.5% in real terms in 2025. GDP per capita increased from $9,813 in 2019 to $15,006.4 in 2025, representing a 52.9% rise over the period.

Construction was among the fastest-growing sectors, expanding by 17.5% in 2025. These figures provide an economic backdrop for the government’s infrastructure plans.

Construction as an investment in quality of life

The government’s immediate priority is to identify the infrastructure most urgently needed in each region and prepare a coordinated list of projects before the end of 2026. At an Oct. 29 government meeting, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the ministries responsible for industry and construction, transport, energy, healthcare and education to work with regional administrations to assess demand for infrastructure and social facilities.

The review will cover local roads, housing and utility networks, educational institutions, cultural facilities and medical infrastructure.

“The People’s Construction program will become the largest infrastructure project in our history. The results of its implementation will depend on the clearly coordinated work of the government and regional administrations,” Bektenov said.

The emphasis on regional needs reflects the program’s stated objective of improving living conditions across the country, rather than concentrating investment in major urban centers.

Construction as a source of jobs and business opportunities

Beyond physical infrastructure, the nationwide construction drive is expected to create new economic opportunities, including employment, business development and cooperation between domestic and international companies.

“This is all part of one major effort to build Kazakhstan. At least, that is how I see it. And what does construction mean? Beyond modernization, of course? It is a process, jobs and opportunities that were not even visible before,” wrote financial analyst Andrei Chebotaryov, commenting on the address.

For regional businesses and potential investors, the program could also provide a basis for longer-term industrial cooperation.

“In my view, this opens up opportunities for regional partners to establish joint ventures in Kazakhstan, engage in technological cooperation and train specialists. Sustained demand allows businesses to plan production expansion,” said Aidar Kurmashev, head of the Asian Studies Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan.

Such cooperation could help strengthen domestic production capacity while bringing new technologies, expertise and investment into the country.

Modernizing industry and developing mineral resources

Alongside construction and transport, the address places renewed emphasis on Kazakhstan’s industrial base and its ability to develop the natural resources needed by emerging technologies. Tokayev has called for changes to the country’s approach to geological exploration. The Ministry of Industry and Construction has been instructed to integrate and structure the Unified Subsoil Use Platform, including through the application of artificial intelligence.

Digital tools could support the organization and analysis of geological information, helping to improve access to data and inform decisions on the exploration and management of mineral resources.

The government is also expected to work with the business community to develop specific measures for the further development of the mining and metallurgical sector by Dec. 15. One area under consideration is the use of offtake agreements, which can provide producers with guaranteed demand for their output. The broader objective is to connect resource extraction, processing and manufacturing more effectively, allowing regions to build on their existing industrial strengths.

Agriculture, water and digital management

The government’s development priorities extend beyond construction sites and industrial facilities to the resources required for sustainable economic growth. Agriculture is expected to play a greater role in meeting domestic demand and strengthening Kazakhstan’s export position. Achieving that goal will require investment in modern production, storage and processing facilities, supported by long-term preferential financing.

Digitalization is another element of the agricultural modernization agenda. The Ministry of Agriculture, working with the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence, has been instructed to establish the E-APK digital platform and complete the creation of a sectoral data lake in 2027.

In addition, the Ministry of Industry and Construction, the Ministry of Water Resources and regional administrations are expected to develop mechanisms encouraging large water consumers to switch to technical, circulating and reused water supplies where appropriate.

These measures connect infrastructure development with the efficient management of natural resources. New industrial and agricultural capacity will need reliable water supplies, while reducing losses and improving reuse will be important for balancing competing demands.

Turning national priorities into tangible results

Tokayev has said the program will extend across the country, covering cities and districts alike. New and renovated roads, airports, railway stations, power plants, hospitals, clinics, schools, rehabilitation centers, youth facilities and sports infrastructure are intended to serve present and future generations.

“The entire meaning of the People’s Construction initiative can be expressed in simple words: ‘Build! Once again – build!,’” he said.

With 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion), earmarked through 2029, the program is set to become one of Kazakhstan’s largest infrastructure investment drives. Over the coming years, the scale of this effort will become visible in the places where people live and work: in better roads, new public facilities, modernized utilities and expanded industrial capacity. For many communities, the changes will be measured not in figures or construction plans, but in what has actually been built and how it improves everyday life.

World.title: Japan, UNDP Commit $ 3 Million to Greener Mining in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Japan and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) provide Kazakhstan with $3 million to strengthen environmental oversight and promote sustainable development in its rare metal and rare earth mineral sector under a new initiative launched Oct. 30, reported the UNDP’s press service.

Funded by Japan, the project will be implemented by UNDP in partnership with Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Industry and Construction.

Kazakhstan has identified more than 120 rare-metal and rare-earth deposits nationwide. As global demand for critical minerals grows, ensuring that their extraction and processing meet environmental standards is becoming increasingly important.

The initiative will help Kazakhstan develop the analytical, regulatory and technological foundations for sustainable rare metal and rare earth mineral supply chains. It will focus on integrating environmental standards and digital monitoring at an early stage to identify and address environmental risks before large-scale industrial development begins.

“This joint initiative with UNDP and Japan will allow us to significantly strengthen our efforts by integrating advanced green technologies and international environmental standards into our production chains,” said Olzhas Alibekov, deputy chair of the Industry Committee at the Ministry of Industry and Construction.

According to Yasumasa Iijima, Japan’s ambassador to Kazakhstan, the initiative aligns with Japan’s priorities of Green and Resilience and Connectivity, announced at the December 2025 Central Asia-Japan Summit.

“Japan intends to provide comprehensive support for the project,” he said.

“The growing demand for critical minerals brings new economic opportunities, but it also calls for greater environmental responsibility. Strong environmental governance, pollution prevention and the protection of local communities must be central to the sector’s development,” said Katarzyna Wawiernia, UNDP Resident Representative in Kazakhstan.

“Through this partnership, UNDP aims to help Kazakhstan strengthen the standards, expertise and monitoring needed to manage environmental risks and ensure that development benefits people while safeguarding ecosystems,” she added.

Japan has long partnered with UNDP to advance sustainable development and resilience in Kazakhstan and across Central Asia.

UNDP and Japan are currently implementing four joint initiatives in Kazakhstan focused on flood risk management at dams, addressing the decline in the Caspian Sea’s water level, improving urban resilience to climate and disaster risks, and strengthening disaster preparedness in Central Asia.

The new project is the fifth initiative under the partnership and expands cooperation to environmental governance and sustainable natural resource management.

World.title: Kazakhstan Restores Oil Flows Through Key Export Pipeline
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has resumed oil transportation through the Atyrau-Samara pipeline after suspending operations following drone attacks on facilities in Russia, according to the Kazakh Ministry of Energy.

The pipeline returned to operation after specialists inspected the infrastructure and confirmed that the equipment was safe to use.

Oil transportation was suspended at 6:09 a.m. Astana time Monday, following drone attacks on facilities at the Samara production and dispatch center.

No casualties were reported, and the situation remains under the ministry’s control, according to the statement.

The Atyrau-Samara pipeline is Kazakhstan’s second-largest oil export route by transportation volume, after the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) system.

World.title: Global Tech Weekend 2027 to Launch in Tbilisi With Startup Pitches
World.content:
ASTANA – Global Tech Weekend (GTW) will hold the official launch event of its 2027 program on Dec. 5 at Mtatsminda Hall in Tbilisi. The event will feature an unconventional pitch session, with startup founders presenting their ideas to international investors aboard the Mtatsminda Ferris Wheel.

The ferris wheel session will be the evening’s main highlight. Each selected startup founder will have six minutes, or one full rotation of the ferris wheel, to pitch their business idea to investors. The pitches will also be livestreamed, allowing audiences beyond the venue to follow the presentations.

The winner will be announced later that evening during an awards ceremony.

According to the organizers, the format is designed to create opportunities for direct engagement between startup founders and investors while moving beyond traditional pitch sessions.

“The tech ecosystem has many promising startups whose growth depends, in part, on meeting the right investors, securing funding, and expanding internationally. The ‘Pitch in a Ferris Wheel’ experience is designed to facilitate these connections: six minutes, one rotation, and a direct conversation between a founder and an investor,” said Medea Janjghava, CEO of Global Tech Weekend.

Following the session, GTW will present its full calendar for 2027, along with its plans to expand its international network and establish new partnerships.

The event is expected to bring together representatives from more than 10 sectors, including technology, finance, international organizations, corporate leadership, creative industries and media.

In 2026, Global Tech Weekend expanded its activities across San Francisco, Tashkent and Tbilisi. Its Tbilisi festival, held June 19-21, brought together more than 10,000 attendees, 250 speakers, 300 investors and 150 partners from more than 12 sectors, according to the organizers.

The Global Tech Weekend 2027 Official Launch Event will be held in a closed format, with attendance available by prior registration only through Global Tech Weekend’s official Luma page.

More information is available on the Global Tech Weekend website.

World.title: Erdoğan Sends Warm Message to Tokayev While Flying Over Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan sent greetings to Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev while flying over Kazakhstan en route to South Korea, Aibek Smadiyarov, the Kazakh president’s press secretary, said on his Telegram channel on Nov. 2.

“On my way to the Republic of Korea for an official visit, I am flying over the territory of our historical ancestral homeland, friendly and brotherly Kazakhstan. The successful outcomes and warm memories of my visit to Kazakhstan in May this year, as well as your recent visit to Ankara to attend the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, remain fresh in our minds,” Erdoğan wrote.

“Taking this opportunity, I would like to extend my sincere greetings and best wishes for your good health and personal happiness, as well as continued prosperity and well-being for the brotherly people of Kazakhstan,” he added.

Tokayev thanked Erdoğan for the warm welcome extended to the Kazakh delegation during its official visit to Ankara and the OTS Summit.

“I express my heartfelt gratitude to Mr. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan for his attention and hospitality in Ankara. I am confident that the friendship and strategic partnership between our countries will continue to grow stronger,” Tokayev wrote on his X account.

World.title: Foreigners face higher costs and stricter requirements to obtain residency in Armenia
World.content:
Armenia’s new residency application rules

From 1 November, foreigners in Armenia have had to apply for residency permits entirely online. The government has also increased the state fees applicants must pay.

A temporary residence permit now costs 150,000 drams ($418), up from 105,000 drams ($293). A permanent residence permit now costs 250,000 drams ($698), compared with 135,000 drams ($377) previously. Applicants will not receive a refund if the authorities reject their application.

The Migration and Citizenship Service says the number of people seeking residence permits in Armenia has recently increased.

For example, Armenia granted residence permits to 10,561 foreigners in the first half of 2026, compared with 6,656 during the same period in 2025. That represents a 59% increase. Russian citizens make up the largest group among those who received temporary or permanent residence permits.

Analyst Artem Yerkanyan believes that Armenia is regulating the inflow of foreign nationals in line with its own interests.

He explains that making it harder to obtain residency clearly shows that the country is shifting its priorities from quantity to quality.

However, he sees no reason to believe that Armenia will stop attracting people relocating from abroad, particularly from Russia.

“For the overwhelming majority of Russian relocants, this reform will not be a life-changing ordeal. They will be able to adapt easily to the new conditions,” Yerkanyan said, pointing to the rules that apply within the Eurasian Economic Union.

Russia leads the EAEU, whose members include Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia. The union operates a customs framework that guarantees the free movement of labour, goods, services and capital.

Foreign nationals can obtain temporary residency if they have grounds to stay in Armenia for at least one year. These include studying, employment, family circumstances, business activities, Armenian ancestry or other grounds recognised by law.

Foreigners can qualify for permanent residency if they are married to an Armenian citizen, have a close relative who holds Armenian citizenship or have a close relative with special residency status. However, applicants must also have accommodation and sufficient means of subsistence, and must have lived in Armenia for at least three years. Applicants of Armenian ancestry or those who run a business in the country can also qualify for permanent residency.

Special residency status will no longer be granted: what is changing?

The changes, which took effect on 1 November, affect not only state fees but also the eligibility criteria for residency and the procedures for processing applications.

The Interior Ministry says temporary residence permits will now be valid for up to one year, while permanent residence permits will last five years.

The grounds for obtaining permanent residency include:

Armenian ethnicity;

making investments in Armenia;

providing exceptional services to the country;

having family ties or running a business in Armenia, subject to additional legal requirements.

From now on, Armenia will have only two types of residency status: temporary and permanent.

The authorities will no longer grant special residency status. However, those who already hold it will retain all their rights and obligations until their status expires.

Until 1 November 2026, Armenia also granted a special residency status valid for 10 years. The prime minister awarded it to foreign nationals of Armenian descent, as well as foreigners engaged in economic or cultural activities in Armenia. They received a special Armenian passport that allowed them to enter and live in Armenia without an entry visa. People with special residency status enjoyed the same rights and freedoms as Armenian citizens and had the same obligations. The only exception was that they could not vote. They were also exempt from compulsory military service in the Armenian Armed Forces.

Applicants must now submit residence permit applications through a single online platform. The authorities will make decisions within 30 days.

“EAEU regulations will remain in force” – deputy interior minister

Armenia’s Deputy Interior Minister Armen Ghazaryan said that citizens of Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) member states remain subject to special rules. These reflect the union’s principle of free movement of labour.

As a result, EAEU citizens do not need special permits to work in another member state.

“This provision remains in force. Throughout their employment in Armenia, citizens of EAEU member states – for example, Russia or Kyrgyzstan – are considered to be legally residing in the country.”

According to Ghazaryan, once EAEU citizens obtain a document confirming the legality of their stay in Armenia, they enjoy the same rights as other foreign nationals legally residing in the country.

The document confirming their legal stay costs 30,000 drams ($83).
