World.title: EDB outlines conditions for Central Asian electricity exports to China (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 3. Electricity exports from Central Asia to China could become a long-term strategic option for the region, but their implementation would require confirmed demand, clear commercial terms, and an assessment of technical feasibility.

This is stated in the report by the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB), "Energy Without Borders: Architecture of Energy Connectivity in Central Asia," provided exclusively to Trend.

According to the report, China has extensive experience in high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission technologies, renewable energy, grid construction and battery energy storage systems. This could give Central Asian countries potential access to capital, technology and new markets.

However, the eastward route should currently be viewed as a strategic project option rather than an established export corridor. The publicly available materials used in the report do not confirm a potential buyer, supply volumes, a route, a technical configuration, a commercial model, or the allocation of risks.

"The Chinese market is not homogeneous. The Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region is geographically close to Central Asia, but proximity does not automatically translate into demand for imported electricity. China is actively developing its own generation capacity, ultra-high-voltage grids, renewable energy and interregional transmission lines. The practical question, therefore, is whether there is a specific creditworthy buyer, a connection point, a pricing formula and a long-term contractual model," the report states.

From a technical perspective, electricity transmission eastward would likely require HVDC technology or another controllable grid interconnection scheme. Such solutions allow power flows to be managed and help reduce risks to grid stability without requiring the power systems to operate in strict synchronization.

However, the necessary infrastructure would require substantial capital investment and large, guaranteed electricity supply volumes, the report notes.

Another key consideration is how an export project would be integrated into Central Asia’s regional power system. According to the EDB, a model focused exclusively on exporting electricity from individual large power plants could have limited benefits for the region’s interconnected grid.

By contrast, integrating the eastward route into the broader regional energy system could increase the economic value of renewable energy, create additional external demand, build expertise in HVDC technologies and attract investment.

Realizing this potential would require a separate preliminary feasibility study, confirmation of buyer interest, an assessment of technical standards and an analysis of the potential impact of exports on the reliability of electricity supplies within Central Asia.

The EDB emphasizes that developing the region’s interconnected power system remains a necessary foundation for export projects. Coordinated efforts by Central Asian countries could strengthen the region’s negotiating position and reduce the dependence of potential electricity exports on a single external buyer.

World.title: Worried about high cortisol? You probably don't need to be
World.content:
Cortisol is a hormone many of us have probably heard of and there's no denying it gets a bad rap when it comes to our health.

It's become a buzzword on social media, where it's often blamed for high stress, fatigue and weight gain, among other things. But is there any truth to these claims?

We asked experts what cortisol does in our bodies and why they say it's being wrongly targeted as the cause of health issues.

Our experts Associate Professor Theresa Larkin , lecturer and cortisol researcher at the Graduate School of Medicine, University of Wollongong.

, lecturer and cortisol researcher at the Graduate School of Medicine, University of Wollongong. Professor Ann McCormack, endocrinology specialist at St Vincent's Hospital, Sydney.

What is cortisol?

Cortisol is a hormone made by our adrenal glands and is "essential for life", says Theresa Larkin, from the University of Wollongong.

"People only really relate it to the stress response, but when we say stress, we [also] mean the changes that happen throughout our body every day," she says.

" So, our circadian daily rhythms (waking up, going to sleep), eating and digesting that food, cortisol is there to help with those. "

Professor Ann McCormack says cortisol spikes are not something healthy people need to fear. (Supplied: UNSW Sydney)

She says one of its main roles is to make sure we have enough glucose (sugar), "so that we are mentally and physically alert".

Endocrinologist Ann McCormack says cortisol is a broad hormone with multiple and often complex functions.

"It's involved with making sure our blood pressure is doing the right things at the right time," she says.

"It's involved in the immune system regulation and also has a role in cognitive and emotional processing."

Can your cortisol levels be too high?

Our experts say it is normal and natural for cortisol levels to go up and down during the day.

"But then also we'll have spikes when we have to, for example, run across the road because there's the bus coming or we're preparing for a difficult conversation," says Dr Larkin.

TikTok is talking about cortisol There's been a surge of cortisol content on social media in recent months, but what does it actually say about health misinformation in an age of self-improvement?

Professor McCormack says this is when you may experience a sharp rise in adrenaline and cortisol as your body tries to counteract the perceived physical stress.

But she warns against buying into the "plethora" of social media videos on how to prevent cortisol spikes.

"Some warn against drinking coffee on an empty stomach or even doing certain exercises," she says.

" Cortisol spikes are not something healthy people need to fear. "

While chronic stress can be linked to health problems, Dr Larkin says "the problem is the stress" not the cortisol.

"It's being blamed for so many things, but chronic stress is the cause, which needs to be addressed."

Professor McCormack says there are some medical conditions, like Cushing's syndrome, where the growth of a tumour prompts the body to make high levels of cortisol.

"When it's really sustained elevations, then you can have osteoporosis, blood pressure problems, hypertension, diabetes, [and weight] gain."

But these conditions are rare.

For people who don't have Cushing's Syndrome or a similar condition (that is, most of us), Professor McCormack says the "data is not very strong" on the link between higher cortisol and health problems.

Can you check your cortisol levels?

Cortisol levels are not routinely measured because it requires "sophisticated testing", says Professor McCormack, such as urine, saliva and blood tests.

She warns that smart watches which can monitor your "stress" are also not a measurement of cortisol levels.

But she urges people who are concerned they might have high cortisol levels to consult their doctors.

" There are rare conditions where it needs to be dealt with or worked up properly. "

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Healthy cortisol responses start with lifestyle

Professor McCormack recommends focusing on maintaining an overall healthy lifestyle, rather than worrying about cortisol specifically.

"I think the focus needs to shift back to all the lifestyle things that we know are good for a variety of reasons," she says.

Is burning out a systemic problem? According to a survey, more than one in three Australian workers are experiencing burnout, and for those whose workplaces have "high levels of system friction" it is far more likely.

"Like having a better sleep will help your blood pressure, help your immune system.

"Humans are designed to basically get up at sunlight, be active, and then to be winding down and sleeping overnight. There are certainly things we could be doing better for our bodies to align with our natural rhythms, including cortisol."

Dr Larkin says while cortisol often gets a bad rap, she hopes discussion about it may lead to greater understanding of the science.

"Understand that what we need to address are the causes of stress; cortisol is just a hormone messenger in our body," she says.

"If that encourages people to think about their stressors and to really appreciate the influence of those small de-stressing moments, then I think that is important."

This is general information only. For detailed personal advice, you should see a qualified medical practitioner who knows your medical history.

World.title: Treasure hunt for rare orchid discovers thriving new cluster
World.content:
Tucked under the canopy of subtropical rainforest in northern New South Wales exists a very rare orchid, which only emerges above ground to flower for a week or two each year.

The critically endangered Bonville leafless orchid was thought to exist in only one location in Australia, on the NSW Mid North Coast, and is found nowhere else in the world.

Recently, teacher and botany enthusiast Nick Lambert went on a mission to try and find more of the orchids.

To the amazement of scientists, he discovered a second cluster near Boambee, about 5 kilometres away from the original site.

"I went to a rainforest near Boambee in the foothills of the mountains and managed to find another population of them, around 50 or so, and that was pretty awesome actually," he said.

Nick Lambert at the site where he discovered a cluster of the rare orchids. (Supplied: Nick Lambert)

Mr Lambert is friends with botanist Lachlan Copeland, after whom the orchid — officially named Danhatchia copelandii — was named following his discovery of the species on the property where he was living in 2018.

Last month, on October 22, Mr Lambert went with Dr Copeland to see the orchids while they were visible and flowering and it inspired him to go searching.

"The next day I was feeling adventurous, and thought, 'I am going to check out some spots and see if I can spot some more,'" Mr Lambert said.

Finding more of the "cryptic" orchid was not an easy task.

The Bonville leafless orchid only emerges above ground to flower, for one to two weeks a year. (Supplied: Nick Lambert)

It blends with the rainforest floor, has no leaves — and therefore no photosynthesis — and gets its nutrients solely from a fungus beneath the soil.

"It's a tiny little thing, about 10 centimetres tall, reddish and hairy and has these tiny little flowers that open up," Mr Lambert said.

" It's pretty special because you can't see it anywhere else in the world. "

Dr Copeland went to inspect the newly discovered orchids the next day, thrilled to confirm the finding.

Botanist Lachlan Copeland, after whom the orchid was named. (Supplied: Blake Copeland)

He said he had shown the original orchid site to about 30 botanists over the years, who had all "tried and failed" to find the species at other locations.

"And then Nick rocks up and finds a much bigger and better population in all respects, so he showed us all up, much to his credit," he said.

Dr Copeland said the finding added considerably to the existing known population.

He said in recent years he had seen only six to seven plants at the site at Bonville, and this spring had recorded 17 plants.

"Now we have [more than] 60 plants known altogether; that's infinitely better than what we had last year when I counted about six," he said.

"I've surveyed it quite thoroughly every spring, with the most plants seen being 43 and the least about four. It's only visible for a few weeks each year."

New hope for species

Dr Copeland said the new site would become part of the protected new Great Koala National Park, which was "great news" for the survival of the orchid species.

"So, by chance they are conserved, and by chance that area has escaped historical logging," he said.

The chief scientist at the Botanic Gardens of Sydney Brett Summerell said the finding was "very significant".

Dr Summerell says it was a "nice surprise" to have two blooms in a short period of time. (ABC News: Chantelle Al-Khouri)

"One of the issues we have to deal with, with threatened species, is often they have really small populations and really low genetic diversity," he said.

"Finding another population of a significant number of individuals really provides the potential for the genetic diversity.

"Also, if something happens in one location, we now have another back-up location."

Professor Summerell said the Bonville leafless orchid was one of only a relatively small number of leafless orchid species that relied on nutrients from an underground fungus, which lived on the plant's roots.

He said the growing conditions could not be simulated outside the wild.

"They are impossible to cultivate in propagation, we can't do that at the Botanic Gardens, so we are really dependent on making sure those populations in the ground are viable," he said.

"By protecting them we are protecting the whole biodiversity in that space … there's a whole connection with a range of different creatures … it's a whole web of life."

Professor Summerell said a specimen would be held at the National Herbarium of NSW at Mount Annan, in Sydney's south west.

"Lachlan Copeland … is an extraordinarily gifted botanist so we don’t have any doubt about the identity, but it will be officially identified through that process and incorporated into the herbarium collection," he said.

World.title: New museum's garden artwork recovered four lost First Nations words
World.content:
Amid the high-rises of Western Sydney's CBD is a pocket of greenery filled with native plants and a nod to a Burramattagal man who played a key role in documenting local flora.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the names of an Indigenous person who has died.

Daniel Moowattin's contributions were barely mentioned in official records, a history of silencing that the new Powerhouse Parramatta is trying to change.

Daniel Moowattin's contribution has been recognised in a series of bronze plaques. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

An artwork featuring bronze plaques imprinted with eucalyptus clippings celebrating Moowattin has been installed at the new museum, which officially opens this Saturday.

Artist Keg de Souza worked with Dharug elder Uncle Chris Tobin to retrace the work of Moowattin, who was integral to the work of British botanist George Caley in the early 1800s.

"The collector was always George Caley, but obviously Daniel Moowattin was actually the collector climbing up the trees and collecting those things," de Souza said.

Keg de Souza helped to rediscover the Moowattin's work. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

In his personal herbarium notes, Caley acknowledged he had received clippings from Moowattin, with a handwritten annotation that read "got by Dan".

However, these attributions were removed from official herbarium records.

de Souza worked with Uncle Chris to collect clippings from eucalyptus trees on Dharug country, including near the new Powerhouse at Parramatta Park.

"By following these people's journey, you start to get an understanding of that era," Uncle Chris said.

Uncle Chris Tobin worked with de Souza to collect the clippings (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Digging through archives

Curator Emerson Radisich searched nature archives for months to find herbarium records from Caley that had the annotations.

With one record from NSW, Mr Radisich searched every other state and territory before he found a second mention at the National Herbarium in Canberra.

"From that point, I just went around the world, and I started at Kew Gardens [in London] and I traced where those herbarium sheets were subsequently sent to or sold to," he said.

"Most of the major herbariums around the world had George Caley records, but they all had the original handwriting taken off them."

Emerson Radisich says Caley's annotations had been removed from records. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Mr Radisich said "if archival workers and botanists 200 years ago had cared", there could have been hundreds of records of Moowattin's contributions.

"There was a lot of silence that we experienced as we were doing this research," he said.

Eventually, Mr Radisich located about 100 herbarium sheets recorded by Caley at the Natural History Museum in the UK.

"We started to notice more handwritten notations that seemed to have Dharug language words on them," he said.

Eucalyptus clippings were collected from trees on Dharug country. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

Some of the words were still used today, Mr Radisich added, but there were a few words that did not come up in an online search, and were not familiar to any First Nations directors at the Powerhouse.

The research led to the recovery of four words related to eucalyptus species in the Dharug language.

The team worked with Bayala Aboriginal Corporation which confirmed Dhuramba as the Dharug language name for Eucalypt Paniculata.

The three other words will be confirmed by Bayala Aboriginal Corporation before being formally published.

Loading...

Cemented in history

de Souza used eucalyptus clippings collected with Uncle Chris to produce five bronze plaques that were embedded into the pavement of the Powerhouse rooftop.

She walked Uncle Chris around the garden while the finishing touches were underway ahead of the museum's official opening this Saturday.

Uncle Chris says the plaques have been done "respectfully". (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

It was the first time Uncle Chris saw the work cemented into the new cultural institution.

"It's proudly done, it is done respectfully so that people, hopefully, start to look at Aboriginal learnings and Aboriginal history with a lot more respect," he said.

"I think it helps raise our profile, and also people will start to appreciate that the Aboriginal story is part of Parramatta's story.

"It's foundational to Parramatta's story, it's one we're a part of; contemporary Parramatta too."

Five bronze plaques are embedded in the rooftop garden. (Supplied: Powerhouse Parramatta)

de Souza hopes the work invites people to learn more about local nature and Dharug language.

"This whole project for me is like a project of learning ... and I wanted people to have the opportunity to sort of learn and engage with it," she said.

World.title: Man United claims comeback win after fans launch tennis balls in protest
World.content:
Manchester United has staged a stunning comeback to recover from its worst start to a European home game by beating Roma 3-2 in the UEFA Champions League.

Elsewhere, Paris Saint-Germain set a new record as the fastest team to score four goals in European soccer's top competition by powering into a 4-0 lead after 17 minutes against Villarreal on its way to a 6-0 win.

In other major results, Barcelona beat Aston Villa 3-0 and Bayern Munich won 2-0 at Atletico Madrid.

But the biggest drama of the night came at Old Trafford, where United's troubled season looked set to plunge deeper into crisis after going 2-0 down after 17 minutes against Roma.

It was the fastest United had conceded twice in any European game at its iconic stadium.

But a rousing second-half performance saw Bruno Fernandes convert a retaken penalty and Matheus Cunha score twice before being sent off to seal a much-needed win for under-fire coach Michael Carrick.

The joyous scenes at the end were in stark contrast to earlier, when furious United fans attempted to disrupt the match by throwing tennis balls on to the field.

The pre-planned protest was the latest show of dissent from supporters who have long called for the club's American owners, the Glazer family, to sell their controlling stake.

A small number of balls were thrown in the 21st minute to mark 21 years since the Glazers staged a leveraged buyout of the storied club.

By then, Roma had already raced to a 2-0 lead through Matias Soule's 11th-minute strike and Donyell Malen's penalty.

It could have been worse by the break, with Roma having more chances to extend the lead.

But the game was turned on its head after half-time, with Fernandes's twice-taken penalty giving the home fans hope and then Cunha sealing the comeback with goals in the 83rd and 86th.

AP

World.title: Workers dumped from employer housing amid financial woes
World.content:
Former workers at an Indigenous youth services organisation that is experiencing financial issues in Western Australia's north say they were given less than a week's notice to leave their employer-provided accommodation.

The Wyndham Youth Aboriginal Corporation (WYAC) has provided education programs and a safe night space for people in the Kimberley town, 3,100 kilometres north of Perth.

The ABC reported last month that WYAC closed suddenly in mid-September, with its chief executive blaming federal agencies for reneging on promised funding.

This has led to its workforce being stood down and some being asked to leave their accommodation at short notice.

Wyndham Youth Aboriginal Corporation stopped youth services in mid-September, with no indication of whether they will resume. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

'Extremely unreasonable'

Ayesha Gomes worked for WYAC for more than a year as a provisional psychologist.

The Indian national's pathway to Australia was through sponsorship from WYAC, and she has now been left with uncertainty.

Ms Gomes was sent a text by WYAC chief executive Neville D'Silva on October 28 asking her to vacate the provided accommodation by November 1.

"Obviously that is extremely unreasonable," she said.

"Now my employment is terminated, I get only six months to find another sponsor to employ me, otherwise I will have to leave the country … it is concerning and scary."

Ms Gomes said she had unsuccessfully tried to contact WYAC board members.

Wyndham Youth Aboriginal Corporation has ceased providing services in the Kimberley town, leaving former workers and the community in limbo. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

She also contacted the Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations (ORIC) but was told she was not authorised to obtain information regarding the company's status.

"I would really appreciate it if WYAC were more transparent and responsive to the concerns raised by employees," Ms Gomes said.

" It's obviously our lives, right? It's not simple to lose a job and in my case, potentially losing accommodation altogether so suddenly. "

Financial issues

A second former WYAC employee, whom the ABC has chosen not to name, said the organisation stopped services after experiencing financial issues.

This led to workers being left in the dark about the future.

"We got stuck in the last few months; we didn't know what to do," they said.

" We weren't getting any help or support from anyone. It's very hard. "

The employee said they had also tried to contact ORIC for help and clarification.

"I first sent [ORIC] an email [and] I've got a reply saying they won't be able to do anything," they said.

'Termination is mandatory'

Mr D'Silva said federal bodies such as the National Indigenous Australians Agency had reneged on "contractually owed" funding commitments, leading to a "trading halt".

"WYAC is restructuring," he said in a statement.

Neville D'Silva gave workers three days' grace to move out of provided accommodation. (Supplied: Neville D'Silva)

In a statement to the ABC last month, the National Indigenous Australians Agency (NIAA) said it was unable to comment publicly on grant management discussions with individual organisations, but said it was "continuing to engage with WYAC".

In relation to employees losing their jobs and some losing their homes, Mr D'Silva said it was an "internal matter".

"There are no funds, so termination is mandatory," he said.

"We reassess and restructure in due course and subject to funders paying their contracted amounts."

Mr D'Silva, who stepped down from the CEO position for a period of time this year, could not confirm if or when programs would resume.

Youth services void

Shire of Wyndham East Kimberley president David Menzel said youth programs would be "sorely missed" in the town.

"My fear is it's going to take significant time to reinstate those services; I really feel for those young people that were quite reliant on the services," he said.

"If staff are dislocated out of housing, the easiest place to find housing won't be in our local area. So we potentially lose those staff too."

David Menzel says the town has been left with a void in youth services. (ABC Kimberley: Ted O'Connor)

A WA government spokesperson said they "acknowledged the concerns felt across the Wyndham community".

"The withdrawal of this support will be felt by many local young people and families who relied on these important services," they said.

The spokesperson said matters related to governance of Aboriginal corporations fell within ORIC's remit.

ORIC declined to comment on whether an investigation into WYAC or its finances was underway.

"Confirmation of whether ORIC is investigating a matter would not assist the community in understanding the current funding situation or when services may resume," they said in a statement to the ABC.

World.title: Diana Ross announces first Australian show in more than 20 years
World.content:
For the first time in more than two decades, music icon Diana Ross will return to Australia.

The 82-year-old singer will perform a one-off Sydney show on Mardi Gras weekend, as part of the Sydney Summertime concert series in Centennial Park.

It will be her first Australian appearance since 2006. British dance favourites Groove Armada will support, playing a DJ set.

Loading Instagram content

Few artists loom larger over the history of popular music than Ross.

Across six decades, she has helped define multiple eras of music while maintaining an enviable level of cultural relevance.

As a singer, film actor and fashion icon, her influence stretches across genres and generations.

As leader of The Supremes, Ross helped transform Motown into a global cultural force.

Songs such as Where Did Our Love Go, Baby Love and Stop! In The Name Of Love remain among the most recognisable recordings in popular music.

After leaving that group, Ross successfully reinvented herself as a solo artist, enjoying major success across soul, pop and disco.

Hits including I'm Coming Out, Upside Down, Touch Me In The Morning, Chain Reaction and Endless Love kept her all over pop charts and radio airwaves through the 1970s and 1980s.

Her impact can be heard everywhere: Beyoncé and Michael Jackson are just two of the superstars who have publicly proclaimed the influence Ross had on their careers.

The honours have followed accordingly.

Ross was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame as a member of The Supremes, received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award, and in 2016 was presented with the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then-US president Barack Obama.

There's a Tame Impala collab with soul legend Diana Ross incoming Kevin Parker has worked with the former Supremes singer on her first album of original material in over two decades.

Recent concerts have celebrated the full breadth of her catalogue, mixing beloved Supremes classics with solo hits and songs from her 2021 album Thank You.

Ross last visited Australia in 2006, performing shows in Sydney and Melbourne and appearing at the Melbourne Cup Chairman's Dinner.

She will perform as part of the Sydney Summertime series in Centennial Park on March 5.

General tickets go on sale on November 11.

World.title: Woman, 24, dies in NY marathon as father reveals she had rare condition
World.content:
A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over 3 kilometres from the finish line, and later died.

Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was approaching the finish line in last weekend's event when she collapsed, according to the New York Police Department. The city medical examiner's office said it was investigating the cause of Apa's death.

Her father told The New York Times that she had rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which muscles can break down during exertion, releasing substances that can poison the body. It was her first marathon, Steve Apa said.

Rachel Apa during the New York Marathon. (Supplied)

New York Road Runners, the nonprofit club that stages the race, said in a news release that a bystander administered CPR to Apa, and event medical staffers also performed CPR and used a defibrillator. Paramedics arrived and took her to a hospital but were unable to save her.

Apa, an industrial-technology product manager and former college field hockey player, had run to raise money for Parkinson's disease in honour of her grandfather.

"It's unfathomable," her father told The Times. He said his daughter had been in "perfect health".

Michaela Nicholas was watching the race, cheering on any runners whose names she could discern from their bibs, when Apa passed. Nicholas recalled on Tuesday, local time, that she called out a message of encouragement, then saw Apa collapse about 15 metres further along the route.

Nicholas, a hospital social worker, said she tried to comfort Apa while two other race spectators administered CPR.

"I just held Rachel's hand and talked to her and told her that she wasn't alone and that she's loved, and I prayed for her," Nicholas, a clinical social worker, said by phone.

The death occurred as the marathon marked 50 years in its five-borough format. Early editions of the race had been run only in Central Park. A record 61,000 runners reached the finish line.

Strintzos fifth in NY Marathon, Olympics in sight Australia's Haftu Strintzos takes a giant step towards the LA28 Olympics with a top-five finish at the New York Marathon.

"We are deeply saddened by Rachel's passing following running in Sunday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends and the entire running community," New York Road Runners said in its statement.

As word of Apa's death spread on Tuesday, money poured into her "Parkinson's Champions" fundraising page, quickly exceeding her $4,000 goal. The fundraiser was sponsored by the Parkinson's Foundation.

On the page, Apa said her grandfather, who had Parkinson's disease and died in 2022, "taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement".

Apa worked for TE Connectivity, which makes various electrical components and electronics. The company was grappling with the news on Tuesday and expressed condolences. So did Bucknell University, where Apa graduated in 2024 with a degree in markets, innovation and design, and where she scored a total of 17 goals for the school's field hockey team.

USA Field Hockey, the sport's governing body, said on social media that "Rachel's impact on the sport and those around her will not be forgotten".

World.title: Residents worried about naturally occurring asbestos on unsealed roads
World.content:
Len Elliott lives on an unsealed road in central west NSW, so dust is a fact of life.

"Our kids bring it into the house, it's on our clothes, circulates in our air conditioning," he said.

"We see the dust come in over our houses, over our yards where our kids play."

But irritation turned to genuine concern after asbestos was discovered in local road materials during a nearby highway upgrade in 2025.

"The risk was people inhaling asbestos fibres in the road dust," Mr Elliot said.

Asbestos is a naturally occurring mineral, but when disturbed its fibres can become airborne and cause lung cancers and fibrosis.

Len Elliot wants to rule out any risk of asbestos fibres in dust on several roads in Orange. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

Mr Elliott discovered he lived in a naturally occurring asbestos (NOA) corridor that had been mapped and made publicly available via the NSW government's Sharing and Enabling Environement Data (SEED) map.

"I entered asbestos [into the SEED map] and I saw the corridor that runs right through Orange."

Concerns raised with council

Mr Elliott approached law firm Slater and Gordon, which took on his concerns pro bono.

In September it wrote to Orange City Council to request testing on four roads with significant erosion and classified in government mapping as having medium-to-high NOA risk.

"Obviously, residents are concerned about a significant health risk associated with naturally occurring asbestos in the Orange area," Slater and Gordon senior associate Kirsty Ruddock said.

"We thought it was really important that we ensure that the council take preventative action here."

Asbestos was discovered in road materials used to build Orange's Northern Distributor Road in 2025. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

The council said there was no evidence to suggest the roads were affected, but that it would investigate the concern.

"[One of the roads mentioned] is some distance from the known NOA areas to the east of the City," an Orange City Council spokesperson said in a statement.

"However, given concerns raised by residents, Council will review the matter and have [sic] advised residents' legal representatives of that review."

Asbestos belt

About 1 per cent of the NSW land mass hosts seams of NOA, which is created when molten rock is infused with water at depth.

Naturally occurring asbestos was once mined for use in construction and engineering products due to its heat and water resistance, before being outlawed in 2003.

The NSW government has mapped the presence of naturally occurring asbestos in the state via its Sharing and Enabling Environmental Data (SEED) map. (Source: NSW Govt)

In the central west, a belt of host rock known as serpentinite snakes south from Wellington through Orange and Blayney before winding up at the small village of Rockley, south of Bathurst.

Occupational hygienist and asbestos assessor Juliet Duffy has lent her expertise to Orange City Council since NOA was mapped in the area more than 20 years ago.

"Even though you might [live in] a high-risk area it may be at depth, it may be sealed or it might be in a non-fibrous form," she said.

Ms Duffy said it was when NOA was disturbed, crushed or pulverised that microscopic, carcinogenic fibres would potentially be released.

"It's only when we disturb it that you risk inhalation of fibres," she said.

Ms Duffy said it was difficult to link NOA directly to poor health outcomes given "co-contributing factors" like smoking, historical land disturbance and the delayed onset of asbestos-related diseases.

"Through urbanisation and development, a lot of this material has been disturbed without people's knowledge," she said.

"It's very hard to relate it back to where you were and what triggered the onset of mesothelioma or lung cancer or asbestosis."

A seam of asbestos can be seen running through these rocks located in the NOA corridor near Orange, central west NSW. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

Ms Duffy said education was the key to managing risks associated with asbestos, especially for those living in an NOA corridor.

"Know what these products and what the raw material looks like," she said.

"So if you see something you can raise a concern and then seek to manage it safely."

Quarries shuttered

The legal letter to council also flagged concern over three quarries in Orange which had supplied road materials to the region before being sealed and shuttered roughly 15 years ago.

"Our clients are concerned the NOA may be present in the road base used to build [their] roads," the letter said.

Several quarries in Orange are located in medium to high risk asbestos areas and no longer operate. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

Mr Elliott said the implications of road material mined at these quarries containing NOA could be widespread.

"There is a total of 43.4 kilometres of unsealed road potentially all built and maintained by these same quarries and they need to be tested," he said.

" We're not asking that the roads be sealed, we're asking that they'd be tested to show that people are safe in their homes. "

Occupational hygienist Juliet Duffy says it is important people know what naturally occurring asbestos looks like. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett)

Orange City Council said in a statement that it had more than 22 years experience evaluating NOA in the region.

"If NOA were to be discovered it would be dealt with on a case by case basis," a spokesperson said.

"Advice on treatment options would be sought from a qualified occupational hygienist."

World.title: Canva to cut more than 1000 jobs in ‘hardest moment’ of its history
World.content:
Updated TechnologySoftware Canva to cut more than 1000 jobs in ‘hardest moment’ of its history David Swan Updated November 4, 2026 — 10:02am ,first published 7:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Canva will cut more than 1000 jobs in a major restructure in response to slowing growth at the graphic design giant. Co-founder and chief executive Melanie Perkins told staff on Wednesday the Sydney design software maker needed to “refound Canva” and return to small, empowered teams after its growth slowed this year for the first time in a decade. The shake-up will affect 1271 jobs, or 22 per cent of its workforce, with some staff members to lose their roles and others asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Canva co-founders Cliff Obrecht, Melanie Perkins and Cameron Adams. Bloomberg “This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history,” she wrote. “After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership, and focus on what matters most for our community.”



Canva will merge its product, growth and platform teams into a single product organisation and cut management layers. Sydney will become the primary home for more product teams, and hybrid staff will be expected in the office two to three days a week from January. Founded in 2013 by Perkins, her now-husband Cliff Obrecht and Cameron Adams, Canva makes online design software used by more than 265 million people a month to make everything from school posters and birthday invitations to work presentations and social media posts. ‘This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history.’ Canva CEO Melanie Perkins The company has workers in 37 countries, and Perkins said the timing of conversations with affected employees would vary to meet local requirements. Those leaving will keep access to the company’s Slack and Gmail until the end of the week. Perkins did not directly link the cuts to the rise of artificial intelligence, though she wrote that new technology was transforming what people create and what they expect from the products they use.



The shake-up comes as investor fears that AI will undercut software businesses have hammered design companies. Shares in rival Figma have plunged 44 per cent this year despite strong revenue growth. Related Article AI ‘Move faster’: Why our best AI founders are moving to America This is Canva’s first-ever company-wide redundancy round, but it has made smaller cuts before. In 2025, 10 of its 12 technical writers lost their jobs; earlier this year, it cut 32 jobs in its finance division. The restructure comes amid a torrid year for the local tech sector. Atlassian culled 1600 jobs in March, the same month that WiseTech Global announced it would slash 2000 jobs, nearly a third of its workforce. The very same day, the Commonwealth Bank confirmed 300 job cuts, with technology workers bearing the brunt of the cuts. With the global AI headwinds for software makers, Blackbird, Canva’s biggest venture capital backer, cut its valuation of the company by 17 per cent to $US34.9 billion ($50.1 billion) in August, down from its $US42 billion price tag in a share sale that Canva arranged last year. Another venture capital investor, Airtree, followed suit.



Canva itself slashed its own valuation of its business to $US31 billion as it downgraded its revenue forecast by a third to just 20 per cent this year. Sales grew 38 per cent in 2025 and 45 per cent the year before. It also delayed the rollout of its biggest AI-led software update because the cost of running AI for its more than 200 million free users was eating into its profits. “Historically, the cost to create a design cost us essentially nothing,” Obrecht said in August. “The cost of goods to serve a user has gone from cents per month to many, many more cents.” Canva had long been seen as a candidate for a sharemarket float, which would let staff and early investors cash in their stakes. Instead, it has run private share sales in each year from 2022 to 2025, and an IPO once expected for 2027 has reportedly been shelved. Canva has said it will list when it makes sense, and that with more than $US1.5 billion in the bank, it is in no rush. The wait is weighing on its backers, however. In August, Airtree asked its investors to extend the life of its first fund, raised in 2014, to July 2028 in the hope that Canva floats or offers another exit before then. Blackbird, which owns about 10 per cent of Canva, has said it still plans to hold on to its shares until a float. Most of Canva’s staff also hold shares in the company.



Related Article Software Inside Canva’s $100 billion gamble on an AI-first rebuild A Blackbird spokeswoman said the firm backed Canva’s move to downsize the business. “Decisions like this are never easy, but we back Canva’s decision to make the changes needed to set the company up for its next chapter,” the spokeswoman said. “We’ve backed Canva since the very beginning, and we remain optimistic about its future and long-term potential.” Departing staff will receive at least six months’ salary, 12 months of healthcare where Canva provides it, and they can keep their work MacBooks. They can also apply for $US10,000 grants to start their own ventures. Perkins will address staff at a company-wide meeting on November 10. World.title: US midterms results 2026 LIVE updates: ICE issues warning to ‘illegal’ voters as Americans flock to polls; Trump, Republicans remain under threat in House, Senate; New York county contest plagued by ballot scanning problem
World.content:
The Democrats appear to have flipped their first seat in the 2026 midterms – but it won’t count towards the 218 seats they need for a majority in the House of Representatives.

Unofficial partial results from the US Pacific territory of Guam showed the island’s former attorney -general Alicia Anne Garrido Limtiaco ahead of Republican incumbent James Moylan, according to Newsweek and The Wall Street Journal, citing the Guam Electoral Commission.

Newsweek said the initial figures suggested a divided result in Guam, rather than an across-the-board swing toward either party.

Guam – a few thousand kilometres north of Australia – has been a US territory since 1898.

It is represented in the House by a non-voting delegate, who takes part in committees and debates, but cannot vote on the passage of legislation. It does not have a senator.

World.title: Two Australians confirmed dead in horror Spain train crash
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeSpain Two Australians confirmed dead in horror Spain train crash Alexander Darling Updated November 4, 2026 — 9:53am ,first published 10:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Two Australians are among the 69 people killed in last week’s horror train crash in Spain, local authorities have confirmed. In a statement released on Tuesday, the Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Castilla-La Mancha – the body tasked with co-ordinating and overseeing the judicial investigation and legal response to the crash – confirmed it has formally identified all victims of the disaster. Loading The tragedy last week saw a high-speed train smash into the rear of another on the line running south from Madrid, killing 69 people and injuring almost 200. On Friday, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) said Australian diplomats were supporting the family of two Australians in connection with the collision.



The department expressed its “heartfelt condolences” for all affected by the train crash, but did not comment on the fate of the Australians involved in the tragedy. Most of those killed – 54 of the 69 victims – were Spanish nationals. Other foreigners among the fatalities who have been identified include four Americans, two Japanese and one each from Canada, France, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said on Wednesday (Australian time) that he was stepping down, six days after the accident. The announcement came at the end of an hours long appearance before lawmakers about the crash, with Puente saying that his position had become untenable after the crash – the second such deadly collision this year involving Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network.



“A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year,” he said. Earlier in the day, Puente announced safety measures the Spanish government would implement on the rail network, including improving conditions in control centres and pushing for a faster rollout of the standardised European Rail Traffic Management System for safety and signalling. Related Article Tragedy ‘Inexplicable’: How the catastrophic train crash in Spain unfolded Puente has blamed the disaster on human error, with a control centre in Madrid failing to tell the driver of a high-speed Renfe AVE service that another train, run by private operator Iryo, was stationary on the tracks ahead. But the minister’s comments provoked a furore, with rail unions accusing him of “scapegoating” the rail control workers and demanding his resignation, while the train operators offered different accounts of what drivers had been told.



The Renfe AVE train had 397 passengers, while the Iryo train was carrying 147. The crash in the province of Toledo came just nine months after another collision farther south on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 46 people. The collisions have shaken confidence in the Spanish rail network that has long been hailed for its speed and safety. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged an investigation and improvements to restore trust in the system that carried some 45 million travellers last year, including millions of tourists. DFAT was contacted for comment. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Updated SportSpain Soccer greats react to shock death of Spanish player during match Tommy Lund Updated November 4, 2026 — 9:48am ,first published 9:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died on Tuesday at the age of 30, a day after suffering a cardiac arrest following a collision during a match, the Spanish second-tier club said. The Segunda Division game against Andorra was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time after de Miguel collapsed after a clash with away goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had rushed out of his area to clear a long ball and struck the forward in the chest with his knee. Jesús de Miguel has died after a cardiac arrest. Instagram/@cdtoficial Spanish police have opened proceedings relating to a possible involuntary manslaughter charge following the death of de Miguel, a National Police source said. Judicial authorities in the Canary Islands said the investigation into de Miguel’s death was a routine procedure because any death deemed non-natural under Spanish law automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.



Santa Cruz de Tenerife chief prosecutor José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui told Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings were unlikely, noting that the collision occurred during play. “Racked with pain, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda,” the Tenerife club said. Jesús de Miguel duels for the ball against Andorra. AP “There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness.” Tenerife’s largest shareholder Rayco García said De Miguel’s body would be transported to Navahermosa, in the Toledo province, at the request of his family. He said De Miguel’s teammates and club officials would be present for a “final farewell.”



De Miguel lay motionless as players from both teams signalled for medical assistance. Owono was shown a straight red card. Medical staff treated de Miguel on the pitch for more than five minutes before he was taken to hospital by ambulance. Loading Owono deactivated his Instagram account on Tuesday morning. The Equatorial Guinea international has received abuse on his social media since the incident. Andorra said in a statement that they “share deeply” in Tenerife’s sadness.



“I’m sorry with all my heart. Rest in peace Jesus,” Andorra president Gerard Pique wrote on social media. The Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) postponed all matches scheduled for Tuesday, including fixtures in the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina. Players from FC Shakhtar Donetsk and Sporting Club de Portugal, match officials and fans stand for a minute’s silence in remembrance of Jesus de Miguel at London’s Stamford Bridge. Getty Images Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé said on social media: “So much sadness. There are no words.” Argentina great Lionel Messi said on Instagram: “There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends.”



Portugal star Cristiano Ronaldo called it a “tragedy.” “No words,” he said on Instagram. “Sending strength to the family. May he rest in peace.” English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media. UEFA announced that a period of silence would be observed before all European games this week. “We are heartbroken by the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda,” UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin said. “We have searched for words and found only silence.”



Clubs across Spain paid tributes to de Miguel, as did teams playing in the Champions League on Tuesday. Related Article Asian Cup Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos facing massive Popovic dilemma “Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times,” Barcelona said in a statement. The three Spanish teams hosting games – Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and Villarreal – chose not to play the customary Champions League anthem ahead of kick-off. “Real Madrid wishes to express its condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones,” the club said.



In those stadiums and others around Europe, like at Old Trafford where Manchester United was playing Roma, a moment of silence was held remembering De Miguel, while a picture of the forward was displayed on the big screens inside the grounds. Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta and midfielder Mikel Merino – both Spaniards – opened their news conferences on the eve of Wednesday’s match against Slavia Prague with a tribute to De Miguel. De Miguel was born in Madrid in 1996 and joined Tenerife from Castellon ahead of the 2025-26 campaign, scoring 11 goals last season. World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland councils Ousted Labor MP’s radical plan to cut Redlands councillors Courtney Kruk and Julius Dennis November 4, 2026 — 9:37am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Ousted Labor MP turned Redland City mayoral candidate Don Brown has sensationally pledged to cut the number of bayside councillors from 10 to six to save ratepayers millions of dollars. Brown, who served as the former state member for Capalaba for nearly 10 years, threw his hat into the local mayoral race last week after former Redlands mayor Jos Mitchell quit her post amid claims of bullying and harassment. In his pitch to voters, Brown promised to oppose the proposed Olympic whitewater centre at Birkdale and “end the infighting, fix the mess and get council back to basics”. He went further on Wednesday with a plan to cut the number of Redlands councillors, which he said would save ratepayers an estimated $2.4 million over a four-year term.



“In Brisbane, each councillor represents around 32,500 voters,” Brown said. Related Article Exclusive

Queensland councils Mayor resigns, citing ‘threats, accusations and harassment’ “In Ipswich, it’s approximately 19,500. Yet in Redlands, each councillor represents only around 12,000 voters. “Reducing the number of Redland City councillors from 10 to six would mean approximately 20,000 voters per councillor, bringing us into line with Ipswich. “As mayor, I will formally seek the support of the Queensland Local Government Minister and the Electoral Commission of Queensland to deliver this reform.”



Local Government Minister Ann Leahy has been contacted for comment. Jos Mitchell resigned as mayor, citing a culture of bullying and harassment. Dan Peled Brown is one of five candidates to put their hand up for the position following Mitchell’s sudden resignation. While he has seized on the bullying and harassment claims surrounding Mitchell’s exit, promising to end political infighting if elected, the former state MP has not been without his own controversy. In 2023, Brown paid his 2020 LNP opponent Bev Walters $50,000 to settle a defamation matter after he made remarks about her wanting to open borders during COVID-19 closures “because she owns a travel agency”.



Other candidates to express interest in the job include acting mayor Julie Talty, councillor Rowanne McKenzie (an ally of Talty), former One Nation and Trumpet of Patriots candidate Gary Williamson and local lawyer Jasmine Person. Related Article Queensland councils Ousted MP, acting mayor and former One Nation candidate among mayoral hopefuls More councillors are expected to enter the race, with insiders estimating up to five others could run. Should any win, a second byelection would be needed to fill their council seat. Leahy said her department would work with the commission to organise an election but would avoid sending voters to the poll during the Christmas period. “A key priority throughout this process is to ensure the residents of the Redlands community have a local government that works for them,” she said last week.



“I would encourage anyone considering standing for election as mayor to understand the commitment to the community that such a role entails.” Brown said the money saved from fewer councillors would be redirected into community sporting facilities, local infrastructure and services “families actually use”, such as free green waste disposal on weekends. “It’s time to clean up the mess, reduce the number of politicians and put ratepayers first,” he said. World.title: Person dead, car split in half during fiery crash in Melbourne’s south-east
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaTragedy Person dead, car split in half during fiery crash in Melbourne’s south-east James Costa November 4, 2026 — 9:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. One person has died, and two others were seriously injured when a car hit a pole and split in half in a fiery crash in Melbourne’s south-east overnight. The car, a gray BMW X5, crashed into a telegraph pole on Cheltenham Road near Bracknell Street in Keysborough about 12.40am on Wednesday, causing a “catastrophic” crash scene, detective acting sergeant Ash Pendrick said on Wednesday morning. The fatal crash in Keysborough caused the vehicle to split in two and burst into flames. Simon Schluter The car, which police believe was travelling at high speeds, collided with the pole, splitting in two and then bursting into flames, leaving debris strewn across the road. “The consequences are huge, particularly after such a horrifying weekend on our roads... to then be standing here three days later at another preventable collision, it’s devastating,” Pendrick said.



Video footage of the crash scene shows the two halves of the car a considerable distance apart and still smouldering, with powerlines down and only the splintered quarter of a telegraph pole remaining in the ground. A body, which has not yet been formally identified, was found inside the car after the fire was extinguished. Two people remain seriously injured after the horror crash. Simon Schulter A man aged in his 20s was found injured at the scene, while another man, who police say fled the scene, was found in the front yard of a nearby house with serious injuries. The two injured men are being treated at The Alfred hospital, Pendrick said.



The man who was found in a nearby front yard may have been attempting to flee, Pendrick said, however, “it hasn’t been confirmed yet, and he didn’t get a far distance away”. “Obviously, due to his injuries, he was located nearby,” he said. Police are investigating whether the rented BMW was stolen, as well as the seating positions of the occupants, Pendrick said. “[Detectives will] be here for a significant period of time, gathering all the evidence to... understand how the collision occurred, but also to confirm where all the occupants were seated and what the involvement was in the collision.” Traffic diversions remain in place around Chandler and Cheltenham roads, a busy arterial thoroughfare.





The driver, a 52-year-old man, stopped at the scene and provided immediate assistance. He will be interviewed by detectives. On Saturday night, a 26-year-old man was killed when his motorcycle lost control and crashed into a tree in the Mornington Peninsula suburb of Blairgowrie. The motorcycle’s passenger was airlifted to hospital with critical injuries. As of October 25, 2026, more than 219 people have lost their lives on the roads since the start of this year, according to Victoria Police. World.title: ‘I just kept believing’: Why Kurtley Beale never gave up on a return to the Wallabies
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘I just kept believing’: Why Kurtley Beale never gave up on a return to the Wallabies Iain Payten November 4, 2026 — 8:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

He never gave up on his dream of making it back to the Wallabies, but Kurtley Beale admits he was still pinching himself on a solo flight to join Australia’s spring tour squad in London at the weekend. Five years after he last played a Test match, Beale was last week a shock inclusion in the Wallabies’ squad as an 11th-hour replacement for Hunter Paisami. Kurtley Beale playing for the Western Force early this month in the Super Rugby AUS competition. Getty Images With the rest of the Wallabies departing from Sydney, the 37-year-old was told to fly to England from his home town of Perth where he plays for the Western Force. “I was still pinching myself on the flight over, to be fair, but really glad to be here,” Beale said on Tuesday at the Wallabies’ hotel in south-west London.



“[I feel] very honoured and it’s very humbling to be back in the Wallaby environment. It’s been a while now, but I’ve been working really hard. [I] just kept believing, to be able to get another opportunity, and obviously started that with the Force. “The body’s feeling good. Physically and mentally, good to go. I’ve always kind of built myself in that way to be able to be ready, and if an opportunity came, I’m able to take it.” There was ample opportunity for Beale to give up on making it back to the Wallabies. After joining the 2021 spring tour while based in Paris - and playing three Tests - Beale spent several years not playing, for long periods. After electing to leave Racing Metro to return to the Waratahs in 2023, Beale didn’t play professionally for over two years, due to injury in 2022 and being stood down for 2023 after being charged with sexual assault. Beale was found not guilty at trial, and returned to rugby with the Force in 2024.



But just weeks after being named in Joe Schmidt’s first Wallabies squad in 2024, Beale ruptured an Achilles tendon playing club rugby, which sidelined him for another nine months. Kurtley Beale playing against Wales on the 2021 spring tour. Getty Returning from an Achilles rupture is hard enough for a young athlete, let alone a player in their mid-30s. But despite admitting there were “tough days” on that comeback trail, Beale said he never felt his days of playing for the Wallabies were over. “With my experience, and being in and around the Force and Super Rugby the last couple of years, I always thought I was able to still add to the group, to the game, and I just kept believing,” he said. “I felt like there was some unfinished business, but I guess the focus was always on trying to make sure my body was right, my mind was in a good headspace. I had great support with my family, my wife, and two kids, so very blessed there.”



His call-up surprised many, but getting a call from Wallabies coach Les Kiss wasn’t a huge shock for Beale. He was selected for Australia A’s tour of the US last month and though he didn’t go due to visa issues, Beale was told to stay ready. Loading “[He is a] proven performer across the course of a 10, 15-year career, with a wealth of experience, a broad and consistent skill set, one which I think is tailored to the wide variety of positions he can play,” Wallabies assistant coach Jon Fisher said. “And the truth is we were monitoring him and his performances very closely across the course of Super Rugby AU competition, and he performed exceptionally well. So, clearly this is the level he belongs at, and he deserves to be in this squad.” Beale said he believed his role is to “create competition” and though he says the trio of No.10s in the squad - Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon and Declan Meredith - have ample experience at Test level, he will be on hand to pass on any wisdom gleaned from his 95 caps for Australia.



Another perspective Australian rugby Wallabies say pay war won’t distract as Rugby Australia go on the offensive with letter to players “I genuinely feel really excited for the opportunity,” Beale said. “For me to be able to compete and push the guys around me to a standard that’s high, and going to help us to be ready on the weekend, then I’ll be doing that. And I think if I do that, then if I do get an opportunity over here, then I feel like I’ll be ready.” Bizarrely, Beale was also announced last week as having agreed to stay at the Force on a modestly paid “train and trial” contract. Beale laughed when asked if the Wallabies call-up would earn him a contract upgrade, before saying he was just pleased to be playing next year, and having a shot at making a fourth World Cup. “It’s always been a motivation of mine,” he said. “I’m training and playing, and that’s all that matters to me.” Loading

World.title: Canva to cut more than 1000 jobs in ‘hardest moment’ of its history
World.content:
Updated TechnologySoftware Canva to cut more than 1000 jobs in ‘hardest moment’ of its history David Swan Updated November 4, 2026 — 10:02am ,first published 7:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Canva will cut more than 1000 jobs in a major restructure in response to slowing growth at the graphic design giant. Co-founder and chief executive Melanie Perkins told staff on Wednesday the Sydney design software maker needed to “refound Canva” and return to small, empowered teams after its growth slowed this year for the first time in a decade. The shake-up will affect 1271 jobs, or 22 per cent of its workforce, with some staff members to lose their roles and others asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Canva co-founders Cliff Obrecht, Melanie Perkins and Cameron Adams. Bloomberg “This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history,” she wrote. “After exploring a wide range of alternatives, I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough. To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership, and focus on what matters most for our community.”



Canva will merge its product, growth and platform teams into a single product organisation and cut management layers. Sydney will become the primary home for more product teams, and hybrid staff will be expected in the office two to three days a week from January. Founded in 2013 by Perkins, her now-husband Cliff Obrecht and Cameron Adams, Canva makes online design software used by more than 265 million people a month to make everything from school posters and birthday invitations to work presentations and social media posts. ‘This is without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history.’ Canva CEO Melanie Perkins The company has workers in 37 countries, and Perkins said the timing of conversations with affected employees would vary to meet local requirements. Those leaving will keep access to the company’s Slack and Gmail until the end of the week. Perkins did not directly link the cuts to the rise of artificial intelligence, though she wrote that new technology was transforming what people create and what they expect from the products they use.



The shake-up comes as investor fears that AI will undercut software businesses have hammered design companies. Shares in rival Figma have plunged 44 per cent this year despite strong revenue growth. Related Article AI ‘Move faster’: Why our best AI founders are moving to America This is Canva’s first-ever company-wide redundancy round, but it has made smaller cuts before. In 2025, 10 of its 12 technical writers lost their jobs; earlier this year, it cut 32 jobs in its finance division. The restructure comes amid a torrid year for the local tech sector. Atlassian culled 1600 jobs in March, the same month that WiseTech Global announced it would slash 2000 jobs, nearly a third of its workforce. The very same day, the Commonwealth Bank confirmed 300 job cuts, with technology workers bearing the brunt of the cuts. With the global AI headwinds for software makers, Blackbird, Canva’s biggest venture capital backer, cut its valuation of the company by 17 per cent to $US34.9 billion ($50.1 billion) in August, down from its $US42 billion price tag in a share sale that Canva arranged last year. Another venture capital investor, Airtree, followed suit.



Canva itself slashed its own valuation of its business to $US31 billion as it downgraded its revenue forecast by a third to just 20 per cent this year. Sales grew 38 per cent in 2025 and 45 per cent the year before. It also delayed the rollout of its biggest AI-led software update because the cost of running AI for its more than 200 million free users was eating into its profits. “Historically, the cost to create a design cost us essentially nothing,” Obrecht said in August. “The cost of goods to serve a user has gone from cents per month to many, many more cents.” Canva co-founders Cliff Obrecht and Melanie Perkins, with chief product officer Cameron Adams, in 2024. Bloomberg Canva had long been seen as a candidate for a sharemarket float, which would let staff and early investors cash in their stakes. Instead, it has run private share sales in each year from 2022 to 2025, and an IPO once expected for 2027 has reportedly been shelved. Canva has said it will list when it makes sense, and that with more than $US1.5 billion in the bank, it is in no rush. The wait is weighing on its backers, however. In August, Airtree asked its investors to extend the life of its first fund, raised in 2014, to July 2028 in the hope that Canva floats or offers another exit before then. Blackbird, which owns about 10 per cent of Canva, has said it still plans to hold on to its shares until a float. Most of Canva’s staff also hold shares in the company.



Related Article Software Inside Canva’s $100 billion gamble on an AI-first rebuild A Blackbird spokeswoman said the firm backed Canva’s move to downsize the business. “Decisions like this are never easy, but we back Canva’s decision to make the changes needed to set the company up for its next chapter,” the spokeswoman said. “We’ve backed Canva since the very beginning, and we remain optimistic about its future and long-term potential.” Departing staff will receive at least six months’ salary, 12 months of healthcare where Canva provides it, and they can keep their work MacBooks. They can also apply for $US10,000 grants to start their own ventures. Perkins will address staff at a company-wide meeting on November 10. The Democrats appear to have flipped their first seat in the 2026 midterms – but it won’t count towards the 218 seats they need for a majority in the House of Representatives.

Unofficial partial results from the US Pacific territory of Guam showed the island’s former attorney -general Alicia Anne Garrido Limtiaco ahead of Republican incumbent James Moylan, according to Newsweek and The Wall Street Journal, citing the Guam Electoral Commission.

Newsweek said the initial figures suggested a divided result in Guam, rather than an across-the-board swing toward either party.

Guam – a few thousand kilometres north of Australia – has been a US territory since 1898.

It is represented in the House by a non-voting delegate, who takes part in committees and debates, but cannot vote on the passage of legislation. It does not have a senator.

World.title: Two Australians confirmed dead in horror Spain train crash
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeSpain Two Australians confirmed dead in horror Spain train crash Alexander Darling Updated November 4, 2026 — 9:53am ,first published 10:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Two Australians are among the 69 people killed in last week’s horror train crash in Spain, local authorities have confirmed. In a statement released on Tuesday, the Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Castilla-La Mancha – the body tasked with co-ordinating and overseeing the judicial investigation and legal response to the crash – confirmed it has formally identified all victims of the disaster. Loading The tragedy last week saw a high-speed train smash into the rear of another on the line running south from Madrid, killing 69 people and injuring almost 200. On Friday, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) said Australian diplomats were supporting the family of two Australians in connection with the collision.



The department expressed its “heartfelt condolences” for all affected by the train crash, but did not comment on the fate of the Australians involved in the tragedy. Most of those killed – 54 of the 69 victims – were Spanish nationals. Other foreigners among the fatalities who have been identified include four Americans, two Japanese and one each from Canada, France, Argentina, Mexico, Portugal, Tunisia and the Czech Republic. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente said on Wednesday (Australian time) that he was stepping down, six days after the accident. The announcement came at the end of an hours long appearance before lawmakers about the crash, with Puente saying that his position had become untenable after the crash – the second such deadly collision this year involving Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network.



“A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year,” he said. Earlier in the day, Puente announced safety measures the Spanish government would implement on the rail network, including improving conditions in control centres and pushing for a faster rollout of the standardised European Rail Traffic Management System for safety and signalling. Related Article Tragedy ‘Inexplicable’: How the catastrophic train crash in Spain unfolded Puente has blamed the disaster on human error, with a control centre in Madrid failing to tell the driver of a high-speed Renfe AVE service that another train, run by private operator Iryo, was stationary on the tracks ahead. But the minister’s comments provoked a furore, with rail unions accusing him of “scapegoating” the rail control workers and demanding his resignation, while the train operators offered different accounts of what drivers had been told.



The Renfe AVE train had 397 passengers, while the Iryo train was carrying 147. The crash in the province of Toledo came just nine months after another collision farther south on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 46 people. The collisions have shaken confidence in the Spanish rail network that has long been hailed for its speed and safety. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged an investigation and improvements to restore trust in the system that carried some 45 million travellers last year, including millions of tourists. DFAT was contacted for comment. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.content:
Updated SportSpain Soccer greats react to shock death of Spanish player during match Tommy Lund Updated November 4, 2026 — 9:48am ,first published 9:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died on Tuesday at the age of 30, a day after suffering a cardiac arrest following a collision during a match, the Spanish second-tier club said. The Segunda Division game against Andorra was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time after de Miguel collapsed after a clash with away goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had rushed out of his area to clear a long ball and struck the forward in the chest with his knee. Jesús de Miguel has died after a cardiac arrest. Instagram/@cdtoficial Spanish police have opened proceedings relating to a possible involuntary manslaughter charge following the death of de Miguel, a National Police source said. Judicial authorities in the Canary Islands said the investigation into de Miguel’s death was a routine procedure because any death deemed non-natural under Spanish law automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.



Santa Cruz de Tenerife chief prosecutor José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui told Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings were unlikely, noting that the collision occurred during play. “Racked with pain, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe that this is true, from CD Tenerife we communicate the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda,” the Tenerife club said. Jesús de Miguel duels for the ball against Andorra. AP “There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this feeling overflowing with sadness.” Tenerife’s largest shareholder Rayco García said De Miguel’s body would be transported to Navahermosa, in the Toledo province, at the request of his family. He said De Miguel’s teammates and club officials would be present for a “final farewell.”



De Miguel lay motionless as players from both teams signalled for medical assistance. Owono was shown a straight red card. Medical staff treated de Miguel on the pitch for more than five minutes before he was taken to hospital by ambulance. Loading Owono deactivated his Instagram account on Tuesday morning. The Equatorial Guinea international has received abuse on his social media since the incident. Andorra said in a statement that they “share deeply” in Tenerife’s sadness.



“I’m sorry with all my heart. Rest in peace Jesus,” Andorra president Gerard Pique wrote on social media. The Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) postponed all matches scheduled for Tuesday, including fixtures in the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina. Players from FC Shakhtar Donetsk and Sporting Club de Portugal, match officials and fans stand for a minute’s silence in remembrance of Jesus de Miguel at London’s Stamford Bridge. Getty Images Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé said on social media: “So much sadness. There are no words.” Argentina great Lionel Messi said on Instagram: “There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends.”



Portugal star Cristiano Ronaldo called it a “tragedy.” “No words,” he said on Instagram. “Sending strength to the family. May he rest in peace.” English clubs Manchester United and Liverpool joined in offering their condolences on social media. UEFA announced that a period of silence would be observed before all European games this week. “We are heartbroken by the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda,” UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin said. “We have searched for words and found only silence.”



Clubs across Spain paid tributes to de Miguel, as did teams playing in the Champions League on Tuesday. Related Article Asian Cup Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos facing massive Popovic dilemma “Our thoughts and support are with his family, friends and loved ones during these difficult times,” Barcelona said in a statement. The three Spanish teams hosting games – Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and Villarreal – chose not to play the customary Champions League anthem ahead of kick-off. “Real Madrid wishes to express its condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones,” the club said.



In those stadiums and others around Europe, like at Old Trafford where Manchester United was playing Roma, a moment of silence was held remembering De Miguel, while a picture of the forward was displayed on the big screens inside the grounds. Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta and midfielder Mikel Merino – both Spaniards – opened their news conferences on the eve of Wednesday’s match against Slavia Prague with a tribute to De Miguel. De Miguel was born in Madrid in 1996 and joined Tenerife from Castellon ahead of the 2025-26 campaign, scoring 11 goals last season.
