World.title: Person dead, car split in half during fiery crash in Melbourne’s south-east
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaTragedy Person dead, car split in half during fiery crash in Melbourne’s south-east James Costa November 4, 2026 — 9:04am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. One person has died, and two others were seriously injured when a car hit a pole and split in half in a fiery crash in Melbourne’s south-east overnight. The car, a gray BMW X5, crashed into a telegraph pole on Cheltenham Road near Bracknell Street in Keysborough about 12.40am on Wednesday, causing a “catastrophic” crash scene, detective acting sergeant Ash Pendrick said on Wednesday morning. The fatal crash in Keysborough caused the vehicle to split in two and burst into flames. Simon Schluter The car, which police believe was travelling at high speeds, collided with the pole, splitting in two and then bursting into flames, leaving debris strewn across the road. “The consequences are huge, particularly after such a horrifying weekend on our roads... to then be standing here three days later at another preventable collision, it’s devastating,” Pendrick said.



Video footage of the crash scene shows the two halves of the car a considerable distance apart and still smouldering, with powerlines down and only the splintered quarter of a telegraph pole remaining in the ground. A body, which has not yet been formally identified, was found inside the car after the fire was extinguished. Two people remain seriously injured after the horror crash. Simon Schulter A man aged in his 20s was found injured at the scene, while another man, who police say fled the scene, was found in the front yard of a nearby house with serious injuries. The two injured men are being treated at The Alfred hospital, Pendrick said.



The man who was found in a nearby front yard may have been attempting to flee, Pendrick said, however, “it hasn’t been confirmed yet, and he didn’t get a far distance away”. “Obviously, due to his injuries, he was located nearby,” he said. Police are investigating whether the rented BMW was stolen, as well as the seating positions of the occupants, Pendrick said. “[Detectives will] be here for a significant period of time, gathering all the evidence to... understand how the collision occurred, but also to confirm where all the occupants were seated and what the involvement was in the collision.” Traffic diversions remain in place around Chandler and Cheltenham roads, a busy arterial thoroughfare.





The driver, a 52-year-old man, stopped at the scene and provided immediate assistance. He will be interviewed by detectives. On Saturday night, a 26-year-old man was killed when his motorcycle lost control and crashed into a tree in the Mornington Peninsula suburb of Blairgowrie. The motorcycle’s passenger was airlifted to hospital with critical injuries. As of October 25, 2026, more than 219 people have lost their lives on the roads since the start of this year, according to Victoria Police. Anyone who witnessed the crash or with dashcam vision is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: ‘I just kept believing’: Why Kurtley Beale never gave up on a return to the Wallabies
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘I just kept believing’: Why Kurtley Beale never gave up on a return to the Wallabies Iain Payten November 4, 2026 — 8:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

He never gave up on his dream of making it back to the Wallabies, but Kurtley Beale admits he was still pinching himself on a solo flight to join Australia’s spring tour squad in London at the weekend. Five years after he last played a Test match, Beale was last week a shock inclusion in the Wallabies’ squad as an 11th-hour replacement for Hunter Paisami. Kurtley Beale playing for the Western Force early this month in the Super Rugby AUS competition. Getty Images With the rest of the Wallabies departing from Sydney, the 37-year-old was told to fly to England from his home town of Perth where he plays for the Western Force. “I was still pinching myself on the flight over, to be fair, but really glad to be here,” Beale said on Tuesday at the Wallabies’ hotel in south-west London.



“[I feel] very honoured and it’s very humbling to be back in the Wallaby environment. It’s been a while now, but I’ve been working really hard. [I] just kept believing, to be able to get another opportunity, and obviously started that with the Force. “The body’s feeling good. Physically and mentally, good to go. I’ve always kind of built myself in that way to be able to be ready, and if an opportunity came, I’m able to take it.” There was ample opportunity for Beale to give up on making it back to the Wallabies. After joining the 2021 spring tour while based in Paris - and playing three Tests - Beale spent several years not playing, for long periods. After electing to leave Racing Metro to return to the Waratahs in 2023, Beale didn’t play professionally for over two years, due to injury in 2022 and being stood down for 2023 after being charged with sexual assault. Beale was found not guilty at trial, and returned to rugby with the Force in 2024.



But just weeks after being named in Joe Schmidt’s first Wallabies squad in 2024, Beale ruptured an Achilles tendon playing club rugby, which sidelined him for another nine months. Kurtley Beale playing against Wales on the 2021 spring tour. Getty Returning from an Achilles rupture is hard enough for a young athlete, let alone a player in their mid-30s. But despite admitting there were “tough days” on that comeback trail, Beale said he never felt his days of playing for the Wallabies were over. “With my experience, and being in and around the Force and Super Rugby the last couple of years, I always thought I was able to still add to the group, to the game, and I just kept believing,” he said. “I felt like there was some unfinished business, but I guess the focus was always on trying to make sure my body was right, my mind was in a good headspace. I had great support with my family, my wife, and two kids, so very blessed there.”



His call-up surprised many, but getting a call from Wallabies coach Les Kiss wasn’t a huge shock for Beale. He was selected for Australia A’s tour of the US last month and though he didn’t go due to visa issues, Beale was told to stay ready. Loading “[He is a] proven performer across the course of a 10, 15-year career, with a wealth of experience, a broad and consistent skill set, one which I think is tailored to the wide variety of positions he can play,” Wallabies assistant coach Jon Fisher said. “And the truth is we were monitoring him and his performances very closely across the course of Super Rugby AU competition, and he performed exceptionally well. So, clearly this is the level he belongs at, and he deserves to be in this squad.” Beale said he believed his role is to “create competition” and though he says the trio of No.10s in the squad - Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon and Declan Meredith - have ample experience at Test level, he will be on hand to pass on any wisdom gleaned from his 95 caps for Australia.



Another perspective Australian rugby Wallabies say pay war won’t distract as Rugby Australia go on the offensive with letter to players “I genuinely feel really excited for the opportunity,” Beale said. “For me to be able to compete and push the guys around me to a standard that’s high, and going to help us to be ready on the weekend, then I’ll be doing that. And I think if I do that, then if I do get an opportunity over here, then I feel like I’ll be ready.” Bizarrely, Beale was also announced last week as having agreed to stay at the Force on a modestly paid “train and trial” contract. Beale laughed when asked if the Wallabies call-up would earn him a contract upgrade, before saying he was just pleased to be playing next year, and having a shot at making a fourth World Cup. “It’s always been a motivation of mine,” he said. “I’m training and playing, and that’s all that matters to me.” Loading

World.title: Wellington Region's second Pacific-led medical centre opens in Hutt Valley
World.content:
A 27-year vision for a Pacific-led health centre in the Hutt Valley has become a reality.

The Epuni Medical Centre, owned by Pacific Health Service Hutt Valley (PHSHV), is only the second Pacific-owned and led general-practice in the Wellington Region.

It opened its doors on Monday, marking an important moment for Pacific primary healthcare in Aotearoa's capital.

The only other Pacific-led health centre is in Porirua.

The centre represents a long-term commitment to strengthening Pacific ownership and leadership within primary healthcare.

The PHSHV's aim is to provide high-quality care that is welcoming and accessible to everyone.

Ribbon cutting ceremony for the Epuni Medical Centre on 30 October, 2026. (L-R) Dr Tua Lealaiauloto Taueetia-Su'a and Reverend Au Liko. Pacific Health Service - Hutt Valley

Before its doors opened to the public a blessing ceremony led was held by Revered Au Liko, who is also the chairperson of the PHSHV's Board.

Rev Liko paid tribute to those who envisioned the centre.

"Today is the combination and fruition of a 27-year dream of Pacific health services which started by three Pasifika nurses and our CEO, Mr Nanai Muaau, and various boards over the years.

"I am currently the chairperson of the board, and I've been chairperson for the last 12 years, and this has always been a dream carried by successive boards," Liko said.

He said that Pacific communities want to have a stronger role in shaping and delivering their own healthcare.

"Access has been one of the huge barriers to our people getting quality healthcare, and for a lot of our unenrolled people, who either can't afford to be with a GP of who find it difficult to communicate GPs, we are trying to meet the gaps that a lot our people are falling through," he said.

Audio player for " New Pacific health clinic opens its doors in Wellington " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/pacific/2311138%2Fwellington-region-s-second-pacific-led-medical-centre-opens-in-hutt-valley

New Pacific health clinic opens its doors in Wellington Pacific Waves Download MP3 5m

Dr Tua Lealaiauloto Taueetia-Su'a was one of the nurses who wrote the proposal all those years ago.

She told RNZ Pacific why she felt it was important to have a Pacific-led health centre.

"In the time that I had been working at Hutt Hospital for a while. I noticed there was a need for our own people to service our own people, like Pacific people for Pacific people," she said.

One of the nurses who helped start the journey 27 years ago sadly passed away.

Members of the Hutt Valley's Pacific community joined funders at the blessing ceremony.

(L-R) CEO Tu Ora Compass, Justine Thorpe, Reverend Au Liko, Candice Apelu Mariner and Executive Director of Kupega o Moana, Joy Sipeli RNZ Pacific

Health NZ national chief of Pacific health Pauline Fuimaono-Sanders said the significance of the new centre's opening is the increased capacity of Pacific-led health services for the area and the wider Hutt Valley.

"Because for the central region, this will only be the second Pacific GP clinic that the central region has right now, so very significant for providing services for Pacific peoples," she said.

PHSHV general manager Candice Apelu Mariner admits the journey to building the new centre had its fair share of early challenges.

But she said over the past three decades relationships have been built and lessons learned.

"I think every part of the system has worked to enable this to happen, meaning our funders, like Te Whatu have seen the vision of investing in more Pacific providers to establish GP services because we are still dealing with our Pacific having negative outcomes.

"So, when I say partners, you need allies, you need people who also believe in your vision both Pacific and non-Pacific, so establishing this hasn't really been a challenge this time around."

She said what has certainly been a challenge is securing a workforce as the Pacific clinical workforce is small.

"We know that 2.8 percent of the total clinical workforce is Pacific, so there are very few and most of them are in Auckland.

"One of the challenges for any new services is its workforce. But to by-pass that, we worked really hard in the last four years to build the workforce, because we always knew that at a certain time we will set up a GP practice. But we needed to grow our own workforce so that's something that we really thought hard about and put a plan in place," Mariner said.

The medical centre will form part of PHSHV's wider two-site model in the Hutt Valley, extending the organisation's ability to provide more connected care across clinical and community settings.

Mariner said Pacific care takes a holistic approach, considering not just a patient's medical condition but also other factors in their life.

World.title: Majority of New Zealanders want govt, councils to share flood protection costs, poll finds
World.content:
A majority of New Zealanders want flood protection funded by central government as well as councils, a poll commissioned by Local Government NZ shows.

Released exclusively to RNZ, the Curia poll asks 1000 New Zealanders how things like stopbanks should be paid for.

58 percent said costs should be shared between central and local government

18 percent said funding should come from councils alone

14 percent said funding should come from central government alone

10 percent were unsure

Local Government NZ regional sector chairperson Deon Swiggs said the growing cost of flooding must be confronted in a cost-of-living election.

"It makes sense for regional councils to deliver and manage flood schemes, but many people would be surprised to learn there's no enduring central government funding for them.

"Ratepayers carry the baseline cost and government support arrives case by case, usually after a disaster."

Greater Wellington chairperson Daran Ponter said there was clear evidence investment before disasters would save money in the long run and help keep people safe.

World.title: New jobless figures: Unemployment rate rises to 5.7%
World.content:
Unemployment 5.7% from 5.6%

About 4000 jobs lost in quarter; labour force shrinks, participation falls

Underutilisation rate steady at 13.8%; Long term and youth unemployment rises

South Island unemployment generally lower than North Island

Annual wage growth remains at 2.1%; average weekly earnings rise annually 3.3%

Data worse than expected

Unemployment rose to its highest level in nearly 11 years as the economy shed jobs, and there are signs some people may have stopped looking for work.

Stats NZ said the unemployment rate was 5.7 percent in the three months ended September, up from 5.6 percent in the previous quarter.

A total of 174,000 people were unemployed, a rise of 3000 on the previous quarter and 14,000 higher than a year ago.

The data was above most forecasts.

Unemployment has held at decade highs as businesses have generally held on to staff, but been cautious about hiring because of weak demand and higher costs.

The numbers also showed a marked rise in the number of long term unemployed - those out of work for a year or more - making up about 21.5 percent of the total, and the highest since mid-1994.

Labour market spokesperson Abby Johnston said the level of employment had changed little from the previous quarter, but there had been changes to how people were employed.

"Casual and fixed term roles increased over the year, while there was a shift towards part-time employment over the quarter."

The number of casual employees increased by nearly 20 percent over the year, and those in fixed term jobs rose 19 percent.

Fewer participate in workforce

The labour force fell by 1000 over the quarter, but was up 34,000 on a year ago.

However, the number not in the labour force increased, as did the working age population, while the participation rate fell slightly.

The level of underutilisation, including the unemployed and under-employed, used as a measure of slack in the jobs market, stayed at a 12-year high of 13.8 percent.

The number employed fell by about 4000 in the quarter, but with 19,000 more people in work than a year ago.

The number of people between 15 and 24 years who were unemployed, not in education or training increased to 14.1 percent from 13.8 percent.

The regions with the highest unemployment were Northland at 8.3 percent, Auckland, Waikato, and Manawatu-Whanganui with rates above 6 percent. Most South Island regions were below 5 percent.

The broad measure of wages showed overall growth remaining near a five year low of 2.1 percent.

An alternate wages measure showed take home pay rose 3.3 percent compared to the 3.7 percent inflation rate.

There was a drop in the number of hours worked, which Stats NZ noted may be connected to an increase in those saying it was for holiday reasons.

The RBNZ has said subdued wage growth is needed to reduce inflation pressures.

World.title: NZ First plans new legal framework to ease accessibility barriers for disabled people
World.content:
Audio player for " Winston Peters discusses final week of election campaign " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2330604%2Fnz-first-plans-new-legal-framework-to-ease-accessibility-barriers-for-disabled-people

Winston Peters discusses final week of election campaign Morning Report Download MP3 9m

New Zealand First says it will establish legally recognised accessibility standards to ensure disabled and access needs people have an "equal opportunity to achieve their goals and aspirations".

The party will introduce legislation to ensure a "fully accessible New Zealand", noting the existing accessibility framework is "fragmented" across multiple laws, policies, and agencies, with many accessibility expectations remaining "voluntary or inconsistently applied".

New Zealand First's proposed Accessibility Standards Legislation would "establish a framework for creating legally recognised accessibility standards and a complaints mechanism to improve compliance and accountability", leader Winston Peters said.

In a policy announcement on Wednesday, ahead of visiting the Disability Expo 2026 being held in Manukau, the party noted the barriers that continue to affect many New Zealanders in their daily interactions with public services, transport, communications, banking, education, justice services, and essential utilities.

It also noted the issue extended beyond disabled people to include older New Zealanders, people recovering from injury, veterans, and others with access needs.

It referenced the 2023 Household Disability Survey that found 17 percent of people living in New Zealand households were disabled, representing approximately 851,000 people, including 98,000 children.

Peters said accessibility could be built in from the beginning when schools, hospitals, social housing developments, footpaths and so on were being designed from scratch.

"This is when standards do the most good and cost the least."

He said the absence of clear national standards meant accessibility was often addressed only after complaints arose, resulting in a reactive rather than preventative approach.

"Better accessibility supports workforce participation, productivity, customer access, independent living and stronger communities. Its benefits extend to older people, families, carers, businesses and the wider public."

Peters also noted the financial benefits in closing the disability employment gap , saying it would add more than half a billion dollars to GDP.

World.title: Average dairy prices rise 3 percent overnight
World.content:
The average dairy price rose 3 percent at the Global Dairy Trade auction overnight to US$4166 (NZ$7422) a tonne.

It was the second consecutive auction where prices rose and followed a 2.5 percent rise at the previous auction in mid-October.

In a note, New Zealand Exchange dairy analyst Rosalind Crickett said the prices has "well and truly exceeded expectations".

Crickett said global milk production remained "steady", but was starting to "slow across some major producing regions".

New Zealand's offerings starts to taper in November, with 5 percent less volume sold across global sellers.

Whole milk powder rose 5.9 percent to US$3971 (NZ$7075) a tonne - it's highest point since August 2025.

Skim milk powder also rose 3.1 percent to US$4109 (NZ$7321) a tonne - it's highest point since June 2022.

The auction also saw the gap widen between powders and fats again.

Butter prices dropped 4.7 percent to US$4503 (NZ$8014) a tonne

"The narrative behind continued milk fat declines remains the same, ample cream availability has caused a supply glut for both milk fat products," Crickett said.

World.title: Republicans make electoral gains across US Pacific territories
World.content:
Republican candidates have performed strongly in preliminary midterm election results in American territories, despite the expected anti-Trump swing on the mainland.

Republicans have won back the governorship of Guam, with Vicente Ada beating out Democrat Therese Terlaje 51 percent to 48 percent.

But they have lost their majority in the local Guam Legislature, with the Democrats winning 8 out of the 15, taking back the majority.

Congressional representative James Moylan has lost to a Democrat, Alicia Limtiaco.

Meanwhile, in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Republicans took back the Governor's Office and the local Senate, while independents improved their standing in the local House.

Former CNMI governor Ralph Torres is set to make a comeback, with the Republican beating out independent challenger Blas Attao 49 percent to 38 percent.

Republican Kimberly King-Hinds is also returned as the CNMI's delegate to the US Congress.

Results have yet to be posted for American Samoa, where Republican Aumua Amata is seeking re-election.

Both King-Hinds and Amata have been critical of the Trump Administration in recent years, in response to its dismantling fishing protections alongside tenders for deep-sea mining licenses in the waters of both territories.

The White House has also ended a visa-free travel programme for Chinese tourists to Guam and the CNMI, while house Republicans seek to end birthright citizenship in the territories altogether.

Delegates to Congress from the American Pacific territories have no voting rights in the House.

World.title: Spanish footballer dies after on-field collision
World.content:
Warning: the video in this article may cause distress for some readers

Spanish police have opened an investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter after a football player died following an on-field collision with the opposing team's goalkeeper in a second-division match.

Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel died after he suffered cardiac arrest following the on-field collision, his club said late on Tuesday night (AEDT). He was 30.

De Miguel was challenging for the ball near midfield on Monday when he was struck in the chest by FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono, who came running from the opposite direction in an apparent attempt to make a clearance. Owono was shown a straight red card for the incident, which happened in added time.

Spain's national police said on Tuesday, local time, that they had opened an investigation. Under Spanish law, deaths from non-natural causes, including accidents, are subject to judicial investigation.

Santa Cruz de Tenerife chief prosecutor José Luis Sánchez-Jáuregui told Spanish news agency EFE that criminal proceedings were unlikely, noting that the collision occurred during play.

De Miguel was taken to a hospital and the match, tied 2-2, was abandoned after the incident.

The club, based in Spain's Canary Islands, said it was "heartbroken."

Fans laid flowers in memory of Jesus de Miguel at the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium upon hearing the news of his death. (Europa Press Canarias via Getty Images)

Tenerife's largest shareholder Rayco García told reporters that De Miguel's body would be transported to Navahermosa, in the Toledo province, at the request of his family. He said De Miguel's teammates and club officials would be present for a "final farewell."

On Saturday, fans will gather at the team's stadium to honour the player, García said.

"We will all join forces and get through this together," García said.

Club president Felipe Miñambres said players and their families would likely need help to cope with De Miguel's death.

Teams playing in the Champions League on Wednesday morning observed a minute's silence in memory of de Miguel. (John Walton/PA Images via Getty Images)

"We will need professional help and the help of all of our fans," he said. "They will be feeling the same way that we are feeling today."

The club has asked to postpone its league game at Granada this weekend.

The heavy collision happened when Owono rushed out of his area all the way to midfield to challenge for a long ball that De Miguel was trying to reach.

De Miguel initially curled on his knees, clutching his torso for a few seconds, before he fell over onto his back, with his arms falling to his sides.

Owono was walking off the field after being shown the red card but turned around and joined the other players rushing to check on De Miguel.

Heartbroken fans shed tears while paying tribute to de Miguel. (Andres Gutierrez/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Another player with the same last name of Owono, Michel Owono, who plays for sixth-division Spanish club Can Vidalet, denounced a wave of racist insults against him by people thinking he was the Andorra goalkeeper.

De Miguel, a Madrid native, began his senior career with Leganés B in 2015 and later played for several lower-division clubs in Spain. He joined Tenerife last year.

No local media reported that De Miguel had a pre-existing health condition. The precise medical cause of death was not immediately disclosed.

Spanish media said De Miguel is survived by his wife and their daughter.

"There are no words of comfort," the club statement read. "There is absolutely nothing that can alleviate this profound sense of sorrow. We stand with his devastated family, his loved ones, and the entire Tenerife community."

Gerard Pique (pictured), owner of FC Andorra, paid tribute to de Miguel alongside several other football icons. (Walter Cunha/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Tributes poured out for De Miguel after news of his death broke. Lionel Messi, Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappé and Gerard Piqué, the owner of Andorra, all extended their condolences, while Real Madrid, Manchester United and Liverpool also paid tribute.

The Spanish football federation postponed all Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina matches scheduled on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. UEFA said it would observe a moment of silence at all its matches this week.

Life-threatening injuries from collisions in football are extremely rare.

Last year in Spain, a 19-year-old goalkeeper died from head injuries suffered during a collision in a fifth-division match. Colindres goalkeeper Raúl Ramírez had two cardio-respiratory arrests, one on the field and then in the ambulance while being transported to a hospital. He was declared brain dead two days later.

In 2001, Ukrainian goalkeeper Serhiy Perkhun died from head injuries sustained in a collision during a match while playing for CSKA Moscow.

Malaga goalkeeper José Antonio Gallardo died in January 1987, more than three weeks after a collision with Celta Vigo forward Baltazar in a second-division game.

World.title: Djokovic breaks Paris Masters record and sets up clash with Aussie
World.content:
Novak Djokovic is looming ominously as a threat to Alex de Minaur's hopes of reaching the ATP Finals with his opening victory at the Paris Masters — but a fellow Sydneysider will be out to do 'Demon' a big favour.

Djokovic, a seven-time champion in the ATP 1000 event, had to negotiate a scare late in the second set before ousting the in-form Monegasque Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5-7), 7-5, 6-1 in the first round on Tuesday (Wednesday AEDT).

Serving at a set down and 4-4, the 24-time grand slam champ had to save three break points to prevent Vacherot, fresh from winning the Swiss Indoors in Basle, from serving for the match at the Plenitude Arena before he rallied to grab a hard-fought win.

At 39, Djokovic set yet another record as the oldest winner in the tournament's history, and couldn't resist a little shot at those who've dared suggest he's over the hill by declaring: "For an old guy, not so bad, huh?!

"People think I am too old and slow, but somehow I find a way to win these kinds of matches that go the distance. I am still there, and I am still holding on and trying to find my best tennis when it matters."

The win strengthened his 10th position, just one behind Alex de Minaur, in the live Race to Turn standings as the pair both jostle to be among the eight qualifiers for the ATP Finals.

Should Djokovic and de Minaur meet in the third round, the loser may well see his Finals hopes end, but before then, the Australian must beat Argentine Tomas Martin Etcheverry while Djokovic will have to defeat de Minaur's Davis Cup teammate Rinky Hijikata in round two.

Hijikata is having a great week after three victories — two in qualifying and one first-round win — without dropping a set, and he could take extra confidence after Djokovic needed a medical timeout in the second set against Vacherot to have his right shoulder treated.

Djokovic will face Australia's Rinky Hijikata (pictured) next. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

An early off-day could spell curtains for either Djokovic or de Minaur, who began the week in eighth spot before young Spanish star Rafael Jodar edged ahead in the live standings with his first-round win.

World no.31 Etcheverry will be a potentially awkward hurdle for world No.9 de Minaur but the Australian may well have preferred to play him than old foe Andrey Rublev, who lost 6-4, 6-7 (4-7), 7-6 (7-3) to the Argentine on Tuesday.

The fight is really on now to get to Turin with Taylor Fritz, just behind Djokovic in the race, having also won on Tuesday against Frenchman Benjamin Bonzi 3-6, 6-3, 6-4.

In other first-round matches on Tuesday, French teenager Moïse Kouame, the young home sensation at the French Open earlier in the year, bowing out 6-3, 6-1 to Nuno Borges, while 2022 champion Holger Rune, on the comeback trail after his Achilles injury, lost 7-5, 6-4 to No.12 seed Tommy Paul.

World.title: The 'hard, gruelling sport' that has helped to shape Suns AFLW players
World.content:
Ava Usher was quick to make an impact in her first season of AFLW.

Before her one-match suspension for a high bump in round 11, she was the outright favourite for the Rising Star.

Part of what made the 19-year-old integrate so easily into the AFLW was her multi-sport background, having competed in little athletics, swimming, basketball, boxing, footy and surf life saving (SLS).

The latter is a particularly common sport for Gold Coasters growing up, including many Suns players.

"I think most people [who have done it] would say that it's a very hard, gruelling sport," Usher told ABC Sport.

"I started at four years old and [began] competing when I was about 10 or 11. It teaches you a lot of discipline, and it definitely has carried over to footy."

In her first season at the Suns, Ava Usher has become one of the club's most important players. (Getty: Matt Roberts)

Gold Coast currently have nine players with SLS backgrounds, including five in the women's program (Usher, Havana Harris, Nyalli Milne, Lucy Single and Bronte Parker), and four in the men's (Jed Walter, Will Graham, Ethan Read and Jai Murray).

SLS competitions feature water-based events such as individual and team swims, board and ski paddling, and beach-based events, including high-speed sprints, relay races, and the intense "Beach Flags" elimination competition where athletes lie face-down in the sand and sprint for a baton upon a signal.

They also teach practical lifesaving skills, such as resuscitation, spinal management, rescue tube tows, and multi-person medical response.

Ava Usher did Surf Life Saving, little athletics, swimming, basketball, boxing and footy growing up. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

"There's a lot of setbacks in surf lifesaving, it's a very unpredictable sport," Usher said.

"You might be ranked the best, but you never know how you're going to race on the day and what the conditions are going to be.

"It just prepares you for that kind of unknown … You never know what you're going to do on the day and, you never know, your life could flash before your eyes."

Single, one of Gold Coast's co-captains, competed in SLS throughout school, specialising in beach running.

She says that experience made running on a football field seem easy by comparison.

Lucy Single competed in beach sports before becoming an AFLW player. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

"I was a 'beachy', as they call it, and we actually trained on a lot of different surfaces. So obviously majority on the beach, but then we also trained on a track and on a grass track … and a lot of gym work too."

While they are full-time footballers now, when not at the club, they will probably be at the beach. They say this helps with both physical and mental recovery.

"You always know after a game, the majority of us will be in some sort of body of water along the ocean," Single said.

"I don't know the science behind it, but there's something about being in a big body of water. It kind of feels like a reset of the soul.

Havana Harris and Ava Usher became friends through Surf Life Saving and then were both drafted to the Gold Coast Suns. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

"And just being out in nature and being in such a gorgeous place. You can't help but feel good."

With the Suns drafting a high percentage of local talent from their academy, many players know each other before joining the club.

Of the 33 players on the Suns's women's list, 16 are Gold Coasters.

Usher, for example, used to compete with her good friend Harris in SLS before joining the academy at 13.

Havana Harris grew up competing in Surf Life Saving, netball, tennis, gymnastics, little athletics, oztag and footy. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

Single used to watch the pair run around with her own younger sisters before joining the Suns.

In round one alone, Gold Coast had eight graduates debut: Sunny Lappin, Georgia Davies, Mikayla Nurse, Dekota Baron, Usher, Alannah Welsh, Parker and Heidi Talbot.

The new injection of homegrown academy talent has helped Gold Coast go from wooden spooners last year to a fifth-placed finish.

"Something in the Gold Coast waters, eh?" Single said.

Havana Harris was drafted to the Suns in 2024, Ava Usher a year later. (Getty: Matt Roberts/AFL Photos)

World.title: Ciaron Maher makes Cup history — but is it good for racing?
World.content:
Peak sporting performances are always amazing to watch.

Whether it's individual or team sport, or horse racing which is a bit of both.

There have been plenty of big performances at the Melbourne Cup over the years — many of them attached to the name of Bart Cummings — but even the Cups King would have been impressed by what transpired at Flemington yesterday.

Not even Cummings managed what Ciaron Maher did, training the first three horses home in the Melbourne Cup.

In fact no-one has ever done it before. Not just that, but four out of the top five. And five out of the top six — and even six out of the top 10.

It's a stupendous performance. It's unprecedented.

But as we draw breath after a dramatic spectacle and a huge crowd for the race that stops the nation, the question does arise — is this level of domination good for racing?

Before the Cup there was plenty of talk about the fact that Maher and Irish trainer Joseph O'Brien had more than half the field between them — a combined 12 runners out of a starting field of 23, after the scratching of Asterix.

But after the first few hundred metres, once Royal Supremacy had crossed over from barrier 20 (originally 21) to lead going out of the straight, it was not O'Brien who had a hold on the Cup.

Ciaron Maher had both an irresistible force and an immovable object at the front of the race.

Jockey Ben Allen proceeded to do his best impression of riding Pride of Jenni in a 2,000m race, trying to drive rivals into the ground and growing the lead to six lengths, with the field strung out. The others decided early not to go hard in response.

Three of Maher's other chances, Juja Kibo, Zahrann and Point of Law were between 10th and 13th at halfway, but crucially not breaking their hearts to go after their stablemate who was out by nine lengths by that stage.

By the time they hit Chiquita Lodge at the 1,200m the lead was a crazy 15 lengths, like a cyclist trying to gain a lap in a race in the velodrome.

It didn't stop, with the peak lead hitting 20 lengths 1,000m out.

With 700m to go Juja Kibo was starting to make a move, but Point of Law and Zahrann were still well back.

Melbourne Cup quick hits The 2026 Melbourne Cup was over before it even began for one runner, while another couldn't emulate his namesake's story, as celebrities stole the show on and off the course. Here's the quick hits from the 2026 Melbourne Cup.

As the bell rang at Flemington to mark the turn and the crowd roared in the Flemington stands, Ben Allen was eyeing a Melbourne Cup robbery.

He pushed his mount forwards with the lead still 12 lengths at the 400m.

As things opened up in the long Flemington straight, there was room for Juja Kibo and Zahrann to come into contention down the middle to outside as Royal Supremacy began to paddle.

The chasers began to swallow him up, but as the two Maher horses looked to go past the leader, suddenly there was a clear run near the fence, and Ethan Brown aimed Point of Law at it and charged through.

There had been queries about Point of Law's endurance based on an exciting but narrow win in the Geelong Cup — all were answered.

The horse formerly known as King Charles's equine young gun motored through and put paid to the race in the space of five or six strides.

He went on to win by 3.75 lengths, an eternity in the Melbourne Cup.

Zahrann and Juja Kibo filled the places, with only the Joseph O'Brien challenger Sons And Lovers stopping an even more-unbelievable top-five sweep for the Cranbourne-based trainer.

What went right (or wrong) at Flemington?

The winner is a return to the days of the late 2010s, when Northern Hemisphere three-year-olds with low weights and few races under their belts beat the handicapper to win the Cup.

Ethan Brown's brilliant ride led Point of Law home ahead of four more Ciaron Maher horses in the top six of the Melbourne Cup. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Royal Supremacy's front-running effort was something Irish trainer (and Joseph's dad) Aidan O'Brien would have loved to have in his own Cup campaigns.

The difference was that this leader led all the way past the clock tower to inside the 150m mark.

It was a fair tactic, and it nearly worked. The fact that nearly all of Maher's other horses (Mr Monaco finished 17th) were also finishing fast at the right time is a brilliant training performance plus a sign of solid to great rides by the respective jockeys.

It might also be a sign of the embarrassment of riches at Maher's disposal, although there should be criticism for the rest of the field not trying to go a little faster in stages. The winning time in the end was 3:21.88, more than five seconds outside Kingston Rule's race record.

How Saintly won the Cup Thirty years ago this week, the brilliant galloper Saintly won the Melbourne Cup to give Bart Cummings his 10th victory in the race that stops the nation.

It's up to everyone else to lift their game, but when you have a frontrunner who can nearly steal the race but also a string of high class horses all charging home at the end of 3,200m. That's more than a challenge.

We have to acknowledge and doff our collective caps to the professionalism of Maher's training operation. Well done to everyone on Team Maher who contributed.

The optics of one trainer dismissing the rest of the challengers is not great, even though our first instinct is to look on in awe.

There have been times before when trainers or owners dominated the race for periods of time.

Bart Cummings won an unbeatable 12 Melbourne Cups, including five quinellas where he sent home the first two.

Owner Lloyd Williams won a record seven Cups over 40 years — and he had as many as six horses racing in his colours in a single race (on two occasions).

Maybe this is just another of those situations. Maybe this could have happened at various points in recent Cup history.

Maybe this is just how the Melbourne Cup is now. But the fact that no-one outside the Maher horses could get within five lengths of the winner after the way the race was run leaves questions.

The Melbourne Cup has had times where it's faced criticism, including regarding the internationalisation of the race.

But while locals decried the flood of overseas horses taking spots once filled by Australian horses and trainers, this level of single domination is arguably more concerning.

If this is a one-off, then this will stand out as one of those amazing moments in Cup history. And it will regardless.

But if it happens again (and maybe again), then perhaps consideration may need to be given to putting number limits on horses from individual trainers or owners.

The Cup always moves on, but progress is not always for the best.

World.title: Quick hits: A-listers, mistakes and the king's Melbourne Cup connection
World.content:
The 2026 Melbourne Cup race day has provided on-course action and off-track celebrities.

With a generous A-lister shouting fans dinner, a heartfelt message from MND sufferer Nathan Charles and the royal connection to race winner Point of Law, there was a little bit of everything at Flemington.

Here's the quick hits from the race that stops a nation.

1. Waller fined $50,000 for 'honest mistake'

Chris Waller was fined heavily for an error. (AAP: James Ross)

Some mistakes are more costly than others on Melbourne Cup Day, and it's fair to say that Chris Waller paid dearly for an error made by a member of his team on race day morning.

The New Zealand horse Asterix was found to have had Penetrene administered to both forelegs in its stable just hours before the race.

"Unfortunately, there was a topical treatment applied to the horse this morning which is allowed during the week but not on race day," Racing Victoria chief steward Rob Montgomery told Nine.

"It just is an honest mistake but unfortunately has big consequences."

Penetrene is used to relieve muscle soreness and inflammation and is permitted for use, but not on race days.

Waller was fined $50,000 for the error, but said there was no blame for the incident.

"It's a very basic liniment most stables use and I guess the pressure of race day, the person that looks after the horse, put it on his legs right in front of the security guard," Waller said.

"Nothing was hidden … as soon as it happened we knew there was a problem.

"It's not [the stablehand's] fault, I've got to wear the responsibility, it's my team."

2. The Generous Mr Foxx

Jamie Foxx has been particularly generous in Melbourne of late. (Getty Images: Sam Tabone)

The Melbourne Cup is known for attracting everyone and anyone who wants to be seen in high society and this year is no exception.

Hollywood A-lister Jamie Foxx has been in Melbourne shooting his latest film, Deadlocked.

Between takes though, he has been mixing it with the Melbourne public, including at the evocatively named Maison Bâtard where, according to The Age, he paid for several people's dinner by surprise.

He was at Flemington and told the Daily Mail Australia that he was taking his girlfriend, Alyce Huckstepp, and her family to the races as a surprise.

What a generous guy.

3. Nathan Charles flipping the script

On a more serious note, former Wallaby Nathan Charles was also at Flemington today.

The 37-year-old has recently been diagnosed with motor neurone disease and, despite the shock of such a devastating diagnosis, is intent on raising the profile of the disease and living his life to the full at the same time.

"In life, everyone has adversity. I've always been a believer in you should be judged not by how you fall over, but instead how you stand back up. And it's a really unfortunate circumstance," he told Nine.

"But it is my journey and I've just got to keep on moving forward.

"I sort of took the week to get my emotions together.

"And then I just thought, you know what, I gotta flip the script.

"Instead of doing things for the last time I want to start doing things for the first time.

"And I want to provide inspiration and hope to young Australians that they can achieve in the face of adversity."

4. Robbie Williams still entertains us

Robbie Williams wowed onlookers with his pre-race performance. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Racegoers were given a real musical treat ahead of the race, with 52-year-old British legend Robbie Williams performing both pre and post-race at Flemington.

Ahead of his latest Australian tour, which starts at Adelaide Oval on Saturday, Williams performed singalong favourites Feel, Rock DJ, Angels and then Let Me Entertain You.

The crowd at Flemington were up on their feet.

And they'll have another opportunity to enjoy the British legend later on too, when he performs another set at the course.

5. From King Charles to Coaster

Point Of Law claimed the Melbourne Cup, having previously been owned by King Charles III. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour/Racing Photos)

Cup winner Point of Law has had quite the colourful past.

The four-year-old, who was sired by unbeaten British legend Frankel, formerly belonged to King Charles III, who sold the colt earlier this year.

King Charles's mother, the late Queen Elizabeth II, was a noted horse racing fan, with her gleeful celebration of Estimate's victory in the 2013 Ascot Gold Cup a particular highlight.

She even finished sixth in the 1997 Melbourne Cup with Frankie Dettori on Arabian Story.

One can only guess how she'd have felt about her son selling a horse that would go on to win the race later that same year…

A consortium of Australians bought Point of Law, among them legendary West Coast and Carlton superstar, Chris Judd.

6. The Cinderella Horse

The Melbourne Cup offers something for everyone each year.

Sure, there are plenty of punters who study the form guide intently, listen to all the shows, read all the previous and make an educated selection based on all those factors and more.

And then there's the rest of us, who pick the horse with the name they like best or whose colours remind you of your favourite flag.

For tangential sports fans, there may have been one name that stuck out: James J Braddock.

James J Braddock, boxing's Cinderella Man. (Getty Images: Keystone France/Gamma-Rapho)

Film buffs may well recognise this name better than sporties, because James J Braddock was the subject of the 2005 biographical film, Cinderella Man, starring Russell Crowe.

Braddock was an American boxer in the 1930s who, due to persistent hand injuries, jacked in his ring career to work in the docks during the Great Depression.

He came back to the ring though and, after a couple of impressive victories, managed to land a fight against the heavyweight champion of the world, Max Baer, at Madison Square Garden in 1935.

So monumental was the upset and the way he had come back from near retirement, that the press christened him the Cinderella Man.

Braddock's next fight was against Joe Louis, who knocked him out in the eighth round of their bout in Chigaco in 1937.

As for his equine namesake, he finished a credible seventh in the Cup.

World.title: Saudi Arabia Asian Cup postponed due to conflict in Middle East
World.content:
The Socceroos will have to wait another year for the chance to win a second Asian Cup, with the 2027 tournament postponed by nearly a year.

Scheduled to be played in Saudi Arabia in January and February of 2027, the tournament will now be played from December 23, 2027 to January 21, 2028.

The new dates are pending approval from FIFA.

The decision has been forced by conflict in the Middle East, with Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis claiming responsibility for a series of attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.

A strike on Riyadh's international airport last month killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300.

"The Organising Committee for AFC Asian Cup approved to reschedule the flagship national team tournament in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," an AFC statement read.

The Saudi government has invested heavily in sport through its Public Investment Fund in recent years and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting the World Cup in 2034.

Disruptions in travel and security concerns have affected other sporting events in Saudi Arabia, with golf's Asian Tour postponing the Saudi International indefinitely, while cycling's Urban World Championships were also cancelled.

The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has been moved from October to December and FIFA postponed the FIFAe Finals 2026 video game competition in Jeddah until an unspecified future date.
