World.title: This Samoan superman is the World Cup's greatest comeback story
World.content:
As he prepares to lead his nation into a World Cup semifinal against Australia, sometimes Ronald Volkman still can't believe this is happening.

He'd have settled for one NRL game this year with Parramatta and after what he's been through, that really would have been enough.

But instead the best season of his budding career will continue when he lines up for Samoa against the Kangaroos with a World Cup final berth up for grabs, standing on the shoulders of giants with the whole rugby league world watching.

It still feels more like a fantasy than a reality for the 24-year-old, even as he's living it.

"I didn't see myself playing NRL and I didn't see myself playing for my country, in a World Cup, on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"I grew up watching this, I'm still pinching myself that I got to get on these fields.

Ronald Volkman will start in the halves for Samoa against Australia this weekend. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"The players in this team, you look left, you look right, you see guns. It gives you so much confidence in what you can do and that you can take it to the next level."

It has been a long journey. It was only a few years back that Volkman thought his football career was over.

Bad shoulder and hip injuries in 2023 scuppered a move from the Warriors to St George Illawarra the following season, sending Volkman to rock bottom in a full year out of the sport.

The physical pain was such that Volkman could barely move and without the game he loved he lost his way.

He stopped training and put on weight. He didn't know himself and when he was out and about, he'd pull his hood up so nobody would know him.

Mates would reached out to support him, but Volkman often ignored them, trapped in a downward spiral with a heart set on suffering, haunted by football dreams he could barely remember.

At his lowest depths, he leant on the things that mattered most to him.

Ronald Volkman's career and life fell apart after he left the Warriors. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"A big one for me was my faith. I fell down to that faith, my God, my loved ones, my family and my partner family," Volkman said.

"They were there for me during those tough times and it'd be slack for me not to take the opportunity I've had this year and showcase my talent, not for myself but for my loved ones.

"They've been through it as much as I have."

There's a lot of loved ones to repay.

Volkman is one of eight siblings and Samoan on both sides of the family. Growing up they'd go back to the islands every second year.

His father, Tas, wept tears of joy when his son debuted for the Warriors in 2022 and did so again when Volkman made his rugby league return in a pre-season trial for Parramatta last year.

Volkman did the same during the Samoan anthem on Sunday night but Emeline, Tas's mother, doesn't give as much away.

She still lives in Samoa, in a village called Vaitele Tai in the western outskirts of Apia, where she watched her grandson come on against Tonga and score a key try.

Loading Instagram content

Volkman played the final 27 minutes after Chanel Harris-Tavita strained his hamstring while kicking for goal, sparking a Samoan revival that just fell short despite the Toa outscoring Tonga four tries to three.

"I got rattled in the ribs early and struggled to breathe for about five minutes, but it's so good to be out there with my usos (brothers)," Volkman said.

"The first thing I thought was about Chanel. You never want to see a teammate go down like that and to me the way to honour him, to show respect, was to get on and do a job.

"He did a pretty good job for the majority of the game and it made my job easy."

Ronald Volkman has rebuilt his NRL career with Parramatta this year. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Volkman's play — the sharp feet, quick hands, a nose for the tryline and a big shot on Tongan backrower Siua Wong — would have been familiar to any Parramatta fans in the record-breaking crowd.

He made his NRL return for the Eels last year and just getting back at all and having his shoulder hold up was a blessing, even if they lost the two games by a combined total of 88-24.

This season, with the highly-rated Jonah Pezet arriving for one year, Volkman didn't expect to play any first grade.

But instead he relieved the injured Pezet in Round 6 and never looked back, playing every game for the rest of the season and signing a new two-year deal with the Eels in September.

He finished the year a blue and gold fan favourite, with Volkamania running wild among the Parramatta faithful.

In 2027 he'll act as a back-up to Mitchell Moses and Jarome Luai, but the latter has already had an impact on Volkman through Samoa camp.

"He's given me confidence to do what I do," Volkman said.

"The way he trains and prepares himself during the week is relentless.

"He's such a competitor but that's all I can say, because if he hears this he'll think I love him."

Tonga and Samoa can be Origin for the new century The scale and spectacle of Tonga's Rugby League World Cup win over Samoa was not just an instant classic, it proved a demand for this clash that rugby league must find a way to supply.

But before Volkman and Luai are club teammates they will be brothers in arms against Australia, starting in the halves together as the masters of Samoa's chaos.

A win over the Kangaroos would be a glittering prize at any time but with a World Cup final berth on the line the stakes are even higher it shapes as the biggest night of Volkman's career.

It would be Samoa's second and Volkman remembers watching the first four years ago and dreaming of being a part of it. Now, against all odds, that dream is real and the best could still be yet to come.

"I'd just started my first pre-season with the Warriors and it was mind-blowing, to see Samoa on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"We have the chance to do it again next week, so let's do it. I can't wait."

Tech.title: Sonos adds new Presets and prepares for the 27voice AI beta
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Sonos is rolling out a big app update that includes new Presets and early access to its AI voice assistant. You can create a preset to play music at a specific volume in a certain room, which will appear directly on the homescreen so you can quickly start playback.

If you’re in the US, you can also 

As teased by Sonos previously, you’ll be able to use the assistant to do things like start music, move playback to another room, group and ungroup speakers, and set timers. But Sonos says it can also complete more complicated requests using natural language, such as “Play the album with a sardine tin on the cover,” or “Who was the singer at the superbowl? Play their latest album on Hallway.”

These updates are part of efforts to recover from a disastrous app redesign in 2024, which Sonos CEO Tom Conrad has promised to reverse. The company launched a revamped Sonos 27 app operating system update in September with the ability to connect AI agents to the app. Sonos plans to allow users to create up to 10 custom agents as well.

Related How Sonos rebooted itself

Other features coming to the Sonos app in this update include the ability to swipe on the “Now Playing” screen or mini player to skip tracks, and a way to rearrange your favorites. The Sonos app can also work with the iOS-only System Health feature, which can help you spot problems in your setup.

Tech.title: Valve is making changes to deal with a ‘significant increase’ in Steam game submissions
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In a new post today, Valve acknowledged that it’s seen “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months” and says it’s “running a little behind” by taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews instead of the typical 3-5 days.

Indie developers have recently expressed frustrations over lengthy approval times for Steam games, even causing some games to miss planned launch dates. Valve says that “much” of the delay is having to re-review games, so it’s making some changes to the release checklist for developers to hopefully “cut down on re-reviews for basic functional issues.”

Related Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up

The changes include requiring developers to run games through Steam for at least five minutes. “Believe it or not, sometimes we review builds that have not ever been played through Steam,” Valve says. “This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam.”

Other requirements include making sure that achievements are ready and confirming any required common redistributables, like DirectX or Visual C++, that Steam may need to install.

Valve also says more improvements are in the works for the build review process.

Tech.title: Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

The largest crypto theft to date was pulled off by combining some well-known hacking techniques over the course of a few months, according to Binance. A postmortem from the company says the process that started with one developer downloading a tampered installer in June apparently spread by a malicious Google ad, exposing details about the engineers and how they work. Then, in September, another engineer was targeted by someone pretending to be interested in hiring them, who set up a series of calls and multiple rounds of interviews, sharing social media pages to build trust, and eventually prompting them to download a fake interview assignment that was actually malware.

Binance claims that its security teams did detect the first installation of malware in June, and replaced the worker’s device, but that its security tools didn’t detect the second attack that deleted the pyenv executable and replaced it with a malicious version that gave them backdoor access:

The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.

By October 20th, the story goes, the attackers, who the FBI has identified as a North Korean unit dubbed “TraderTraitor,” used Binance’s own internal AI tool to gain control over wallets for the first engineer compromised in June, as well as another third employee, before logging into the third employee’s computer on October 29th and launching their attack.

The post-mortem also goes into why Binance wasn’t able to stop the transactions that occurred nearly two hours after the first unauthorized transfers, saying that “Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations.” Binance says that it’s prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, and CEO Richard Teng writes that no user is bearing the loss, with about $2.85 billion in stolen assets frozen or intercepted: “At this moment, 98% of impacted tokens had been replenished; we’re completing the remaining 2%. Withdrawals have broadly resumed.”

What’s less clear is why this particular attack worked — the danger of job interviews that ask people to download and execute code on machines with access to employer material has been warned about for years, and there’s little detail on the “internal AI tool” that was used by the attackers and why it was able to help them in the first place.

Tech.title: Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
Tech.content:
It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions.

What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.

The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.

The onboarding process is quite clear.

Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)

Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.

Previous Next



1 / 3

I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had an organic, lengthy spoken conversation yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a feel for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims. I’ll keep testing and will add an update once I’ve finally received my first Siri Recap.

What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Again, I’m still waiting on my first Siri Recap, but what Apple’s said publicly so far is that these are meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.

In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

Tech.title: Those Jeff Bezos hair transplant photos are very fake
Tech.content:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and actor Jason Statham have a distinctive feature in common: They’re both famously bald, and that definitely hasn’t changed in the last few days. However, there are some images of the two men circulating around X, Threads, and Bluesky in which they both have substantially more hair than their usual shaved look, which in Bezos’ case appears to be very freshly transplanted. It’s all just photo editing fakery, AI or otherwise.

It’s unclear how viral these posts are, but they’re prevalent enough that a few members of the Verge team have encountered them in their social media feeds. Some people who shared them claimed (or were seemingly fooled into believing) that Bezos and Statham had undergone hair transplant surgery. Generative AI tools have made this kind of photo manipulation or outright creation more accessible and convincing, and because AI labeling solutions on social media broadly suck at flagging this fakery, it’s easy to be misled unless you’re wary of everything you see online. In a world where social media shitposters can turn engagement into a revenue stream, they’re not going to stop churning out attention-grabbing fabricated nonsense anytime soon.

We don’t know if AI tools were used to make the follicled Bezos and Statham edits — none of the images I tested flagged for Content Credentials or SynthID markers. We also can’t fully establish when they were first posted or who made them, but they are definitely fake, and it only took me a couple of minutes to confirm it.

In both cases, I ran the photos through Google’s reverse image search tool. For the Bezos debunk, I found photographs of him in a similar background environment and wearing the exact same outfit (with, yes, no hair) that included a watermarked image credit at the bottom left. Searching for the credit then led me to the original photographs in their unaltered state, which were taken in 2023. Finding the original tressless images of Statham was even easier — the reverse image search immediately surfaced watermarked versions of the originals, which were snapped by a paparazzo in 2011.

Both of the original photos were actually taken on the same day, at around the same time, but anything for clicks, right? Image: Eliot / Spread / MEGA

There’s other evidence too if you know what to look for. The main flag is that it’s probably impossible for Bezos and Statham to be realistic candidates for hair replacement surgery anyway; it requires you to have enough “donor” hair to sacrifice from the back and sides of your head to then replant closer to your desired hairline. You can technically take it from other places (or even other people), but doing so is incredibly rare due to undesirable results and rejection concerns. Transplant patients also typically experience some pretty dramatic facial swelling for the first week or so, which Bezos shows no signs of. Wigs, toupees, and other hair systems can also be used as nonpermanent hair restoration solutions, but as someone who used to make and install them professionally, it would be an astounding whoopsie for someone as rich and connected as Bezos to go this route and still end up looking like a Chia Pet.

This isn’t the first time photo-manipulated fakery has fooled people across social media, and with ongoing generative AI advancements, it probably won’t be the last. Previous incidents gave us the viral swagged-out pope, and recent trends have seen paparazzi photographs of celebrities like Callum Turner, Harry Styles, and Noah Schnapp being manipulated to remove their shirts. These kinds of edits are typically designed to rack up likes, reposts, and other engagement — they play into our fascination with celebrities’ lives with fabricated situations that are just outlandish enough to be believable, grab our attention, and be shared around as the latest hot gossip by those who are fooled, or who simply don’t care to verify the facts.

If you’re ever unsure if there’s fakery afoot with images of famous faces, just remember that most of the convincing edits (AI or otherwise) are based on real photos that you can hunt down to verify the original source.

Tech.title: The Pixel Buds Pro 2 have returned to their lowest price to date
Tech.content:
Android owners looking for an earbud upgrade are in luck. The Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are back down to $169 at Amazon , Best Buy , and the Google Store , matching the lowest price we’ve seen. Google’s site claims the deal will last until 11:59PM PT on November 8th, and other retailers will likely follow suit. Some colors are already sold out, however, so it’s worth checking multiple retailers if you don’t see your preferred option.

The Pro 2 are great for Android owners and work particularly well with Pixel phones, which receive some extra tricks, including tighter Gemini integration. We praised the wireless earbuds for their improved design, which cut both weight and size while improving the comfort and fit. They have more powerful noise cancellation and a better transparency mode, though they still don’t quite match up to some of the best in the industry, like the latest Bose Ultra Earbuds. The default tuning leans towards clarity and crisp detail, rather than boosted bass, with both presets and a five-band EQ to adjust them to your liking.

Tech.title: iPhone 18 rumors suggest a bigger battery, higher price next year
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After Apple raised iPhone prices earlier this year, a new rumor claims it plans to launch the base iPhone 18 with a higher price, too. A Weibo post from leaker Digital Chat Station, spotted by 9to5Mac, says the base iPhone 18 is getting a couple of upgrades with the price hike, including a larger battery and a new 2-nanometer A20 chip. However, it reportedly won’t have the smaller Dynamic Island featured on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

The base iPhone 18 wasn’t included in Apple’s fall iPhone launch event, but Digital Chat Station claims it will arrive early next year, in line with previous reports. It’s rumored to launch alongside a second-gen iPhone Air and the iPhone 18e, which Digital Chat Station also mentions.

The leaker doesn’t specify how much the iPhone 18’s price might increase compared to its predecessor. All of Apple’s old models, including the iPhone 17, got a $100 price hike in September. Google and Samsung have also raised phone prices by the same amount over the past year, driven by shortages of RAM and other components. Earlier this week, Apple reported record-breaking iPhone sales despite the higher prices.

Tech.title: Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple will now let Siri AI perform actions across third-party apps. As part of the iOS 27.3 update rolling out on Tuesday, Apple announced developers can now integrate Siri AI’s new features in “all apps,” allowing the voice assistant to draw on a user’s personal context, process natural language prompts, and use on-screen awareness to complete requests.

The update, which is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview, also adds a new “app skills” feature that third-party developers can create to combine several tasks into a single action. In Apple’s developer documentation, the company says users won’t have to mention an app’s name in their request while it’s in the foreground, during a Live Activity, or in a conversation with Siri AI about the app.

“For example, a person might request a ride with a ride share app, follow updates to the app’s Live Activity while they wait for their ride to arrive, then request to move the pickup location to a different address by saying ‘Hey Siri, change my ride pickup to a new address,’” Apple says. As noted by 9to5Mac, Apple previously made a smaller set of features available to third-party developers.

Apple is bringing Siri AI’s expanded capabilities to its own apps as well, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather apps. “Users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year,” according to Apple. The company notes that users can ask Siri AI what it can do in each app.

Tech.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
Tech.content:
Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday.

The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout.

For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said.

Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years, according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment told Bloomberg last week.

In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early-to-mid 2030s.

Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets.

In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April.

In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines.

Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.

Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two.

Tech.title: Ted Schlein’s Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom
Tech.content:
Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused venture capital firm co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein (pictured above, second from the right), is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds, TechCrunch has learned through regulatory filings.

The San Francisco-based VC firm filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission this week to raise $360 million for its third flagship fund, matching the size of its previous fund raised in 2024, and another $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. Neither fund had recorded any sales at the time of filing.

The fundraising plans come as the growing use of artificial intelligence has raised concerns about more sophisticated cyberattacks. The rise of AI agents has also created new opportunities for cybersecurity startups and the venture capital firms backing them.

Founded in late 2021, Ballistic Ventures’ founding team includes Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah and Roger Thornton, who co-founded security companies Fortify Software and AlienVault. The firm has backed companies including Talon Cyber Security, acquired by Palo Alto Networks, and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike, alongside startups such as Armadin, GetReal, Nudge Security and Oligo Security.

Ballistic’s ties to storied venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins, where Schlein spent more than two decades, help set it apart from rivals, a cybersecurity investor at another VC firm told TechCrunch. Its investment strategy, however, is similar to those of other cybersecurity-focused investors, including Forgepoint Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures, the person said.

In 2022, Ballistic announced its $300 million debut fund and raised another $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. It also raised about $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund A, per PitchBook data. The new Fund B is targeting a similar amount.

U.S. cybersecurity startups raised $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest since 2022, a recent report by JPMorgan Chase said, citing PitchBook data. AI-enabled companies accounted for about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May this year, compared with 36% in 2019, the report said.

Separately, Microsoft, in its annual Digital Defense Report released last month, warned that hackers are increasingly using AI for activities ranging from phishing and social engineering to malware development. The technology is allowing attackers to operate faster and at greater scale, even as many of their underlying techniques remain unchanged.

Ballistic Ventures declined to comment on its fundraising plans.

Tech.title: Hiding inside Palantir’s skyrocketing quarter is a foreboding signal
Tech.content:
Palantir delivered such a huge third-quarter earnings report on Monday that its press release even bragged that the numbers were “crushing consensus expectations.”

Yet, retail investors were lukewarm on the company on Tuesday, with the stock trading slightly down. That’s because Palantir’s enterprise sales, its big growth area, showed signs of slowing.

First, the good news for the company’s investors. Revenue grew 96% year over year to $2.31 billion, the first time it has ever surpassed the $2 billion mark. Palantir’s revenue, which also grew 20% from the previous quarter, beat analysts’ expectations of $2.18 billion. Palantir also reported adjusted earnings per share of $0.44 versus analysts’ expectations of $0.41. The company even upped its revenue guidance for the full year. Normally, that alone would send a stock soaring.

The clincher was that Palantir’s U.S. commercial revenue surpassed U.S. government revenue for the first time ever. The company reported $984 million in commercial contracts (up 148% from the year-ago quarter), versus $953 million in U.S. government revenue.

The reason for all this love from enterprises? They are signing up for the company’s AI software that can run frontier models and custom-train open-weight models securely, without sharing any of their data and business processes with outside AI labs. Plus, Palantir has always offered what is today known as “forward-deployed” software engineering, which helps customers customize its wares.

However, Palantir also revealed a less-than-rosy signal: Even as enterprises are moving faster than ever., they are often signing short-term trials.

“What Ryan and I are seeing on the front line and commercial is this much quicker interaction, much quicker to deployment, shorter duration of the contract but then an ability to expand that contract dramatically,” CEO Alex Karp (pictured above) told Wall Street analysts on the quarterly conference call.

Palantir is experiencing one of the unique phenomena of AI in the enterprise right now. Corporations are willing to quickly try AI software without their typical bureaucracy, but they are also more willing to cancel contracts.

Karp used one off-color metaphor after another to describe how unconcerned he was about holding onto his enterprise business.

“We’ve gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team, kind of thing,” he said describing the influx of prospective corporate customers were flowing in. “Conversely, you know, once you go Palantir, you don’t go back, and that’s just that’s how it is, and you see it in our numbers.”

The numbers don’t yet confirm Palantir’s long-term success. While the company closed a hefty $1.46 billion of total contract value from U.S. enterprises in the quarter, that’s actually a decline from its record-setting $2.13 billion of enterprise TCV in the previous quarter. That suggests decelerating sales, at least last quarter.

The next earnings will show if Palantir has solidified its role as a rising U.S. enterprise AI provider. Historically, many enterprises sign their biggest tech purchases in the final quarter of the year. Certainly Karp and team are confident. They increased guidance for U.S. commercial revenue to be “in excess of $3.559 billion, representing a growth rate of at least 143%.”

Tech.title: Orbital Matter 3D printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space
Tech.content:
A satellite built by the German startup Orbital Matter 3D printed a half-meter long beam out of a custom plastic material, in what executives called a first for a free-flying spacecraft in orbit, and a step toward constructing large structures in space.

The company’s small satellite, Replicator 2, was launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission this summer, with four of the company’s 3D printers onboard. Each printer can create a rigid, cylindrical beam by extruding coils of resin that are cured by an ultraviolet light, which the company analogizes to cement and water.

Loading the player…

This technology matters because future spacecraft will need to be larger in order to generate more electrical power and radiate a more heat into the vacuum of space, particularly if they’re going to serve as orbital data centers. But they’ll still need to fit into the tight confines of the fairing on top of the rocket that carries them into orbit. If spacecraft are able to construct their own structures in orbit, the power and heat-dissipation challenges may get a lot easier to solve.

“Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands,” said Jakub Stojek, CEO and co-founder of Orbital Matter. The company is partnering with the European Space Agency and Thales Alenia, a leading European satellite builder, with which it collaborated on Replicator 2.

Today’s large structures in space are origami projects — large solar arrays or telescope mirrors are folded up and then deployed on orbit. That’s a tricky engineering project, and so the idea of making and assembling those structures in space is appealing. NASA has funded some efforts at the idea, notably a mission with the company Redwire that 3D printed structural beams in a vacuum chamber in 2023 but never got off the ground.

Two of Orbital Matter’s printers are designed to deploy a flexible solar array, but an anomaly led one of the printers to fail. Still, the boom that was created successfully deployed the solar array, and is an important proof of concept. Previous 3D-printing efforts in microgravity were limited to the pressurized environment onboard the International Space Station.

“That’s why we put so many printers on this single satellite. We preferred to learn in orbit and adapt the software as needed rather than waste years testing every possibility on the ground,” Orbital Matters CTO Robert Ihnatisin told TechCrunch.

The boom’s length is limited by the amount of resin carried onboard the satellite, and the company’s engineers believe that 100 meter booms are feasible. For comparison, SpaceX’s Starlink V2 satellites — among the most powerful mass-produced satellites in orbit — uses solar arrays that are 20 meters long.

Orbital Matter was co-founded in 2022 by Ihnatsin, who previously worked at 3D-printing company FormLabs, and Stojek, and raised a $3 million seed round.

Now, Orbital Matter is working on another demonstration mission, scheduled for launch in 2028, that will test a larger version of its printer on a bigger satellite that the company hopes will deploy a solar array that can generate 5 kw of power. That will be a “stepping stone” toward larger deployments of 100+ KW per wing by 2030.

The company is also collaborating with satellite builders that are considering incorporating its PADS (printer-assisted deployment system) into their spacecraft to extend solar panels, antennas, or other components.

Tech.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist
Tech.content:
Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop.

Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months.

This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network.

The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program.

In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware.

That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto.

Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft.

The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems.

These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters.

By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.”

But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention.

While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise.

A Binance spokesperson referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack.

The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident.

The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history.

Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph.

Tech.title: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges
Tech.content:
In Brief

Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.

The startup announced its Series E and F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)

The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted.

Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations. But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials.

Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon.

Tech.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount
Tech.content:
Just days after warning investors about declining search traffic and a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast, Reddit is looking for more ways to make money from its existing users. On Tuesday, the company announced that it’s beginning to test ad placements in its search results pages, allowing advertisers to reach users as they search for products, recommendations, and other information on its platform.

“Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query,” Reddit shared in its announcement about the new ad placements. “This is an initial test with a select group of eligible advertisers. During this test, we will evaluate and understand how users respond to these ads so we can refine the experience for users and advertisers over time.”

The company offered examples of what sort of ads might appear, suggesting that a search for “espresso station” might display ads for espresso machines, coffee, or mugs, while a search for “home office setup” could surface ads for things like monitors, desks, and office chairs.

Image Credits:Reddit

The ad test comes at a time when Reddit is reckoning with how AI has been changing the web’s landscape, and subsequently its reach.

Despite beating Wall Street’s estimates for revenue and earnings per share, the company’s stock dropped after it reported its third-quarter results last week, with fourth-quarter guidance that predicted sales of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, below expectations of $1.05 billion. This was tied to Reddit’s declining search traffic referrals resulting from Google’s move to an AI-powered search experience. AI search now sends less traffic to publishers’ websites, as features like AI Mode provide answers directly on Google’s Search Result pages, reducing clicks to other websites.

Reddit also said that its global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in the quarter, and were down 2% year-over-year. The company noted that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low double-digit percentage by the fourth quarter.

This leaves the company needing to earn more revenue from its existing users, which is where these new ads come in. The ads could prove to be more valuable to Reddit after it makes its planned shift to a logged-in experience, which was also announced during earnings. The company said it will make the transition gradually, initially in markets outside the U.S.

The decision to limit its content to logged-in users serves multiple purposes — it protects Reddit’s site from unauthorized AI scraping, and it increases its value to advertisers. Logged-in users are worth more to advertisers because they provide additional signals about their interests and behavior, allowing for better-targeted, more profitable ads.

Tech.title: Ten years later, ‘Pokémon Go to the polls’ still haunts the internet
Tech.content:
In the lead-up to a presidential election that would irrefutably transform American culture, Hillary Clinton took the stage at a rally in Virginia as she campaigned to become the first female president.

“We’re going to have a lot of jobs — jobs from building infrastructure to coding. Creating new apps,” she said. “I don’t know who created Pokémon GO, but I’m trying to figure out how we get them to have Pokémon Go to the polls.”

Ten years later, it is once again Election Day in the United States. Now, most app developers aren’t even writing their own code anymore, thanks to AI, and Pokémon GO has been sold to a company wholly owned by Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. The only thing about that political moment that hasn’t changed is that “Pokémon Go to the polls” memes still crop up on every Election Day.

“It was very bold and confident, and also just sounded so terribly out of touch and corny,” Cesar Ruiz de Castilla, an elected ward committee member in Philadelphia, told TechCrunch. “I don’t know if the mainstream media cared that much about it, but everyone was making a meme about it and talking about it online.”

Since then, digital culture has become increasingly inextricable from the fate of American politics. Donald Trump tweeted his way through his first term, then later started his own social media platform; presidential campaigns hire meme managers; the White House invites podcasters and content creators to press briefings; Elon Musk even spun up his own advisory group under Trump that named itself after the cutesy doge meme and then slashed international aid programs.

A Google Trends analysis of the search term “pokemon go to the polls” Image Credits:A Google Trends analysis of the search term "pokemon go to the polls" /

“The 2016 election was such a monumental moment in internet history, and we were all there for it — our politics have become more, not just divided, but segmented online,” Organizer Memes, a political influencer who teaches Gen Z activists how to reach their peers online via memes, told TechCrunch. “It’s a relic of an optimistic, bygone political era.”

Now, people who weren’t even old enough to vote in 2016 reflect on the year as a cultural turning point, even calling it “the last good year.” It’s a sentiment that isn’t so much political as it is rooted in nostalgia for an era of internet culture before AI slop, when we used social media to connect with friends, rather than doomscrolling through an algorithmic feed of people we don’t even follow.

At the start of the new year, this yearning for the old internet became a viral sentiment as millions of people shared throwback photos from 2016 on Instagram.

Spotify reported that user-generated playlists featuring 2016 in their titles spiked 790% in the first three weeks of the year, and the company changed its Instagram bio at the time to say it’s “romanticizing 2016 again.”

Never mind that, at the time, the internet perceived 2016 as a cursed year, even before the election — months earlier, one Slate columnist wondered how 2016 compared to 1348, the year the Black Death took hold in Europe.

“[Pokémon Go to the polls] is in that era of the singular internet, when Facebook and Twitter and Tumblr were all kind of bouncing content back-and-forth and not just this complete anarchic mess of 25 platforms that we now have and don’t use,” Organizer Memes said.

Organizer Memes also notes that some cultural touchstones that felt more significant then — like the obsession with Harambe the gorilla — haven’t had as much staying power as “Pokémon Go to the polls.”

Perhaps this is because we’re bound to remember “Pokémon Go to the polls” every few years on Election Day, and because it appeals to both sides of the aisle. On the right, it’s a way to make fun of Democrats, and on the left, it’s a shared groan of embarrassment.

“It’s like if all the kids in a class are making a joke, and then the teacher gets in on the joke, and it stops being funny,” Mack Finkel, who canvassed at the polls on Tuesday on behalf of a healthcare workers’ union, told TechCrunch. “I think there’s a key essence of millennial cringe happening here, and it’s the same reason that all my friends are rewatching [HBO’s] ‘Girls.’”

Clinton’s decade-old, corny comment can be seen as a precursor to the “Kamala is brat” meme. While the former vice president’s record as a prosecutor initially made her unpopular among some left-leaning young voters, they rallied around her once she became the only alternative to Trump. Gen Z rallied around Harris by creating flashy, absurdist “fan cam”-style edits of the candidate’s best quips in the aesthetic of Charli XCX’s album “Brat,” which soundtracked the summer of 2024.

“Previously the views I saw about Harris were making fun of her being a cop, like her history as attorney general in California with truancy laws,” Jess Rauchberg, an assistant professor of communications at the University of Leeds, told TechCrunch at the time. “Now we see that same style of memeification, but it’s an endorsement.”

It’s hard to say why “Pokémon Go to the polls” jokes still make us laugh — whether we’re mocking Clinton or expressing solidarity with others who keep showing up to vote, even as each passing year leaves us feeling more cynical.

“Pokémon Go to the polls” is a way of urging others to make the time to vote and take Election Day seriously, while still acknowledging disappointment with aging lawmakers who don’t know what it’s like to come of age in the social media era. It’s shrouded in enough irony to project a sense of jaded detachment, yet remains a desperate, earnest plea to our friends: Please, just go vote.

Tech.title: $1,200 Off the iPhone Duo? Here’s How Carrier Deals Actually Work
Tech.content:
Don’t expect Apple to offer a sale on the iPhone Duo. The company almost never discounts its products, especially new ones that are selling like hotcakes (it’s backordered). With the Duo starting at $2,000, it’s very expensive for most people to buy Apple’s first foldable, and the best way to get a deal may be through a carrier.

Of course, there are some stipulations, but if you qualify, you could “save” significantly on an iPhone Duo—as much as $1,200, knocking the price to $800 (keep reading, there’s a catch). Here are some of the potential deals we found.

Shipping times are stretching into January, so it may be a while before you can get your hands on an iPhone Duo, even with one of these offers.

Save $1,200 on an iPhone Duo at T-Mobile

If you 

Here’s how the actual deal works.

You don’t get $1,200 upfront. Instead, T-Mobile spreads that amount across 36 monthly credits on your bill. For the 256-GB base model, for example, you’ll pay $22.22 a month for the phone on top of the monthly plan; those payments total about $800 over three years, plus the Experience Beyond 2.0 plan is $100 a month, excluding taxes and fees. The deal doesn’t apply when you pay in full or choose a cheaper plan. If you hate expensive contracts, this isn’t for you.

T-Mobile offers several other incentives for the iPhone Duo, including $1,200 off with trade-in or $1,000 off for seniors, military personnel, students, and first responders. To see what you might qualify for, click on the “see promotions” link on the T-Mobile iPhone Duo purchase page.

If you’re not clamoring for the iPhone Duo, T-Mobile’s incentives also apply to the new iPhone 18 Pro and other models.

Verizon and AT&T Also Have Similar Incentives on iPhone Duo

AT&T and Verizon are also offering incentives on the iPhone Duo. AT&T has a similar trade-in plan to T-Mobile’s: You’ll pay $22.23 a month for the phone for 36 months, which is equivalent to $1,200 off after you’ve fulfilled your contract. AT&T also has a “contract-breaking” deal that will get you an $800 reward card when you switch to AT&T, but you’d still have to pay the full price of the iPhone Duo.

The same goes for Verizon. You can get $1,200 off a 36-month Unlimited Ultimate plan, with or without a trade-in, as a new or existing customer. As an extra incentive, Verizon is including your choice of an Apple Watch Series 12 or iPad.

Whichever company’s deal you pursue, you’re entering into what is essentially a contract. The phone will also be locked to the carrier until you’ve made your final payment. You’ll also pay more after fees and taxes are added, although there’s no monthly interest. When you factor everything—the cost of a particular plan and the discounted phone—it could be what you're currently paying for a premium plan, or possibly much more.

We usually don’t recommend cell phone contracts; it’s best to get a phone unlocked, even if it means paying full price. However, if you plan to stay with a carrier long-term and want to lower the cost of the iPhone Duo, it’s still worth considering. But do the math before committing.

Tech.title: The Internet’s Conspiracy Theorists Are Desperate for Voter Fraud
Tech.content:
Voting had only been underway in the US for a few hours and polls still hadn’t even opened in some parts of the country, but Republican strategist and pro-Trump influencer Joey Mannarino had apparently seen enough.

“MASSIVE AMOUNTS OF VOTER FRAUD BEING REPORTED ALL OVER THE COUNTRY!” Mannarino asserted on X at 9:02 am EST, offering no evidence to support his declaration. “The Democrats are stealing our country right out from under us!”

As in any other election year, as polling places opened, people began showing up to vote, and voting machines started whirring into action, some jurisdictions ran into problems.

Severe flooding along Florida’s Space Coast meant about 20 polling places had to be moved. Bad storms over the weekend likely caused brief power outages in Arizona’s Maricopa County, forcing the temporary closure of several polling places. Pennsylvania’s Luzerne County was missing a scanner box. And in Westchester County, New York, voting in the hotly contested House race between incumbent Republican representative Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley hit a roadblock early on Tuesday morning when machines stopped accepting paper ballots.

Voting machine malfunctions—much like bad weather and power outages—are fairly common during elections. While typically attributable to some mundane problem like ageing components, these malfunctions are often the source of rumors or conspiracy theories.

And like other election years in recent memory, there’s a network of MAGA influencers, Republican lawmakers, pro-Trump trolls and administration officials with enormous online audiences who are waiting for anything—literally anything—that they can claim is evidence of voter fraud. The Trump administration has also been laying the groundwork, priming their electorate to believe that the American voting system is rigged against them.

Within minutes of reports that ballot scanners in Westchester weren’t working, some of the biggest proponents of election conspiracy theories seized on the county-wide glitch to claim that Democrats were sabotaging equipment to prevent Lawler from winning.

The Westchester County board of elections initially blamed the fault on “the thickness of the paper ballots” in a statement issued two hours after polls opened. But 20 minutes later, county officials updated the statement, removing the reference to the thickness of the paper and instead blaming a general “issue involving paper ballots.”

In a separate statement published online, Westchester county executive Ken Jenkins said that once the issues with the ballot machines are resolved, he’ll “convene a bipartisan team to conduct a thorough review of the decisions and failures that led to this debacle, determine where accountability lies and ensure that this never happens again. “I want to be absolutely clear,” Jenkins wrote. “This situation is unacceptable.” Later in the day, New York State officials put out an additional statement, saying that the problem was that most machines in the county had outdated programming, which meant they could not recognize and process Election Day ballots.

Tech.title: Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist
Tech.content:
For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.

Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.

Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.

“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”

Tech.title: Here’s Why You Shouldn’t Use AI to Vote
Tech.content:
As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.

Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.

But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.

Even supposedly nonpartisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.

Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections, and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.

Tech.title: Roli Has Fallen Apart—and Left Customers Holding the Bag
Tech.content:
Roli has not publicly communicated about its future strategy with customers. The company did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment; Lamb did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Roli’s primary financial backers, investment firms TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, also did not respond.

A Change of Seasons

Roli has faced financial struggles before.

The company started in 2009 but really took off after musician Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony’s Innovation Fund in 2018. Musicians like Dream Theater keyboardist Jordan Rudess supported and touted Roli’s gadgets. Ryan Gosling’s character played a Seaboard Grand in the 2016 movie La La Land. In the late 2010s, the tech and the company were hailed as a hit.

That tune changed in 2020. The British government’s Future Fund—a taxpayer-funded relief package issued to help businesses during the pandemic—partially bailed out Roli from a Covid-19-induced financial crisis. Even then, Roli went into administration for the first time in 2021. It survived by relaunching as Luminary Roli and focusing on music-learning devices like the light-up Lumi keyboard and the Airwave, a digital theremin that doubled as an AI piano teacher.

Through all of that, customers have had issues with how the company communicates. Users who ordered the Lumi keyboard found orders unexpectedly delayed, with no indication from the company on what was happening.

Got a Tip? Are you a current or former Roli employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at boone.10.

“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise, tells WIRED. “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.”

Pull Me Under

Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims. Every person we spoke with who worked with Lamb compared him to a Steve Jobs-esque character. One person described the experience of being at Roli as being in a movie, where Lamb saw himself as the main character and everyone else as extras or set pieces.

“I love the company, love the culture, love the people—I didn’t love working for him,” the employee said. “Everyone has their story with him. You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.”

Tech.title: Apple iPad Mini (2026) Review: A Dream Device, but Who Is It For?
Tech.content:
The star attraction of the new iPad Mini is its 8.5-inch display. That’s a slightly larger screen than the previous generation, yet the overall dimensions are barely bigger. But the change from IPS to OLED is what matters. It uses an OLED Super Retina XDR display, which is not the tandem OLED seen on the iPad Pro (and OLED MacBook Pro). It doesn’t have the 120-Hz refresh rate, nor is it quite as bright. It can reach 600 nits in SDR and 1,200 nits in HDR, which is 400 nits less than the iPad Pro. It’s more or less similar to the Mini-LED M6 MacBook Pro in terms of brightness, though, which is still impressive for OLED.

The iPad Mini OLED’s brightness is sufficient for most uses, even in bright lighting conditions. But you can take it to the next level by opting for a nano-texture display, which is totally worth the extra $100 it costs. (It’s the model I tested.) It’s not an antireflective coating or a matte layer; it’s actually etched into the glass. The result is a surface that almost entirely diffuses outside light without reducing the screen’s perceived brightness. Reading outside with the iPad Mini is particularly enjoyable, as the nano-texture display not only resists reflections but even gives it a paperlike crispness. This option is also available on the MacBook Pro and iPad Pro, and there’s really nothing else like it.

The iPad Mini one-ups its siblings in sharpness. Its smaller size gives it 19 percent higher pixel density than every other iPad. And yes, it really does look incredibly clear and sharp.

There’s more to it than the display. Part of the magic is how lightweight it is—barely over half a pound, and it doesn’t feel much heavier than my phone in my hand. One-handed use feels completely natural. That’s always been true of the iPad Mini, but this latest version emphasizes that even more.

Lastly, the color options have been pared down from four to just two. The lighter goldish Starlight is still available, but now there’s the introduction of the blackish, navy-blue Midnight. This is a finish carried over from the MacBook Air. The more playful Blue and Purple color options are both gone, as is Space Gray. More options are always better, but for a device that costs $700, I can see why these more professional colors make sense.

Meant for the Road

Apple has also completely redesigned the iPad Mini’s four-speaker sound system, and a couple of interesting changes are happening. As part of its process of making the device IP67 water-resistant, Apple removed the speaker grille from the sides to create a completely sealed enclosure. Instead, the tweeters sit behind two small slits on the edges of the display glass. And then bass drivers are built directly into the display. Apple calls it an Acoustic Display.

The stereo image sounds fullest when you hold the device in portrait, as long as you keep your fingers away from the display. The vibration caused by the location of the speakers isn’t terribly noticeable unless you have the volume on full blast. Overall, the audio sounds decent for a device this size, but it won’t compare well to larger devices like an iPad Air or MacBook Air. But for watching videos or the occasional movie, it suffices.

Tech.title: The Endlessly Meme-able Steve Kornacki Is Not a Meme Person
Tech.content:
Standing in front of a gigantic map isn’t a traditional path to fame. But in 2020, during the presidential face-off between Donald Trump and Joe Biden, Steve Kornacki became America’s sweetheart for his enthusiastic delivery of state-by-state election results. The NBC data analyst gracefully guided teeth-grinding, fist-clenching viewers through Biden’s eventual victory, and the rest is history: That same year, Kornacki was named one of People’s sexiest men alive; the internet became obsessed with his khaki pants; and he earned the nicknames “chartthrob” and “map daddy.”

Kornacki further established himself as the king of election season with the “Kornacki Cam” during 2026 midterm primary election nights, when his nonstop behind-the-scenes livestreams amassed 42 million views. Now that midterm election day is upon us, Kornacki is acutely aware of how many viewers have come to rely on him. “I get very anxious about being prepared for election night,” he says, “and then thinking of all the things that I might not be prepared for, and then just taking the phone out and trying to get prepared.”

For someone who spends a lot of time logged on, Kornacki doesn’t exactly have the habits of someone who is chronically online. He seems to know nothing at all about memes, FaceTime really isn’t his thing, and he isn’t quite sure what a subreddit is. Ask him about who’s most likely to win today’s races, though, and he’ll have no shortage of knowledge to share.

Phone model: iPhone 17 Pro

Basically, I break one phone per year, so I recently upgraded to it. They always say the camera's better. It never is any different to me, and the battery's always great for 10 days.

Computer model: a Dell

It's been in its office probably as long as I've been at NBC. It has a thing on it that says Windows 7 Pro, which I think is old. This thing is on its last leg because I've just been too lazy to replace it. I never really got into Macs. I think I had one once, and I just remember not really liking it. I know it's supposed to be user-friendly, but it actually drove me a little crazy.

Average daily screen time: 3 hours, 35 minutes

That is depressing. That's more than 12.5 percent of my life. And then you take out the eight hours of sleep, it's an even bigger piece of the pie. I thought about taking dramatic steps to change it and, like most of my thoughts about dramatic steps to change my life, I never actually do it.

Tech.title: Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo Bring More AI to the Travel Booking Experience
Tech.content:
Between Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s, it’s the time of year when your luggage stays packed. With millions of Americans planning to travel sometime between now and the end of the year, it’s time to start thinking about how to make the most of your trip.

Right on time, Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo just rolled out more than 30 new travel features. Expedia Group, which owns all three brands, said the goal is to make trip planning and execution easier with practical AI.

“Travel is a series of decisions, and travelers want the joy of discovery and planning to last through every stage of the journey,” Shilpa Ranganathan, chief product officer at Expedia Group, said. “That’s why we’re building AI-powered experiences across our brands that help travelers make informed decisions, give them flexibility and value, and personalize every step of their trip. And when travelers need a person, our human agents step in with the full context to make things right.”

More from CNET

Here’s what’s new from each travel brand.

Expedia

Property Expert/Expedia

Expedia says it’s introducing a more personal homepage, flexible travel packages, more straightforward bookings for families, interactive maps of your travel destination for easier planning and expanded airport perks like Clear Plus discounts and free lounge access for flight delays.

Two new AI-powered products are also rolling out to make trip planning smoother once a trip is already booked. Expedia’s new Activity Planner is an AI-powered conversational shopping assistant that can find and book activities, restaurants and events based on your itinerary. You can also receive tailored recommendations based on your preferences.

Another is a Property Expert, which lets you ask questions about a business and get AI-generated insights on the property, reviews, reservations and other details.

Hotels.com

The platform is improving its AI Compare experience to help you compare multiple hotels in one place. The comparisons are personalized to your interests and preferences for location, amenities, price and policy details.

The Hotels.com homepage will also adapt to the type of trip you booked, such as a vacation or work trip, and include suggested links tailored to your booking, like options to extend your stay and access to receipts for easier work-trip expenses.

Vrbo

The Airbnb rival is launching several new features and services, including a tool to make group bookings easier to manage, an option to reserve now, pay later, and enhanced customer support.

With Vrbo’s natural language search, you can describe in plain language what kind of rental property you’re looking for. Rather than spending hours researching options one by one, you can simply say you’re looking for a beachfront home in South Florida with a kitchen and outdoor gathering space that’s dog-friendly. The enhanced search feature allows you to narrow down your options without relying on traditional filters.

Vrbo’s Arrival Experience is getting an upgrade to make your rental details more accessible. Key property information, such as check-in and checkout times, door codes, directions and house rules, will now be aggregated in one place, so you can stay on top of your booking without searching through multiple emails or messages.
